stories.Headline: Nexus Legal Group launches two AI WebTracker plans for law firms
stories.Summary:
The Nexus Legal Group LLC announced simplified plans for AI WebTracker, its AI-powered prospect intelligence platform for law firms, on November 16, 2026, from Allentown, Pennsylvania. The platform identifies people actively researching legal help in a firm's practice areas and markets, including people visiting competing law firm websites. It delivers them in a fresh feed every morning. The platform is now offered in two plans, Self-Serve and Done-For-You. Every plan includes lead scrubbing before a firm's team reaches out.

Each lead in the feed shows who the person is, why they entered the feed, which competing firms they viewed, and where and when they were active, down to the ZIP code. Firms export these audiences directly to their ad platforms and CRM. Every account stays the firm's own, and the ad budget is paid from the firm's own ad account, never handled by Nexus. AI WebTracker is a flat monthly subscription never tied to leads, cases or outcomes, with no setup fee and cancellation on 30 days' notice. The Done-For-You plan adds the Nexus Lead Validation and Database Scrubbing upgrade, which runs Scammer Scrub, TCPA Lookup and Scrubbing, and DNC Lookup and Scrubbing on a firm's monthly leads and uploaded lists.

Rob Parker, Managing Partner of The Nexus Legal Group, said firms are being squeezed from both sides, paying more every year to bid on the same keywords as every competitor in town. He said firms pay lead vendors for names that too often turn out to be wrong numbers, recycled lists or people who already hired someone. He said AI WebTracker lets a firm see who is actually researching its type of case, in its own markets, before that person picks up the phone. He said a firm should not pay more because a vendor sent more names. He said with a flat subscription the feed grows the firm's own audience every day, and the firm keeps what it builds.

Every AI WebTracker plan includes TCPA Real-Time Scrubbing, Do Not Call Lookup, Phone List Scrubbing and the Name Recognition Algorithm, also called Scrub By Name, so risky records are flagged before an intake team makes contact. Each record is marked Validated, Review or Do Not Contact, with a time-stamped Validation Record. The Done-For-You plan includes audiences and Nexus-designed, firm-approved ad creatives uploaded to ad platforms the firm already owns, such as Google, Microsoft Bing and Meta, plus ongoing feed tuning, a monthly report, a review call and a dedicated Nexus contact. An optional Nonprofit Outreach and Intake Support add-on is available with either plan and provided with Legal Support Cases, Inc. under a separate agreement. AI WebTracker is designed for personal injury, mass tort, trucking and commercial vehicle, wrongful death and other practice areas where speed and geography decide which firm signs the case.

The company said AI WebTracker uses licensed data sources, and being identified in the feed is not consent to be contacted. It said scrubbing and Lead Validation reduce risk but do not guarantee compliance and are not legal advice. AI WebTracker and Scammer Scrub are trademarks of their respective owners. Law firms can book a demo and receive pricing at WebTrackerLeads.ai. The Nexus Legal Group describes itself as a legal marketing and technology company that helps law firms find, reach and sign high-value cases.

Harvey and Legora each launched a product called Intake about a day apart in October 2026, both built to help corporate legal departments receive, sort and route incoming legal requests with AI. Wordsmith had already released its own Intake earlier in the year. Kenny Gary, CEO of the communications firm LIMELIGHT, documented that overlap in a three-part series for JD Supra Perspectives. Goodwin unveiled Regina OS, its proprietary AI operating system, on August 14, and days later Davis Wright Tremaine announced a firmwide expansion of Harvey and Microsoft AI tools. Jason Brown, president and CEO of the Association of Corporate Counsel, said on Infodash's Legal Innovation Spotlight podcast that over 85% of surveyed ACC members report they have embedded AI in their legal departments and actively use it, a share that rose sharply over roughly two years.

Brown said the overwhelming majority of members tell ACC they are not seeing efficiency or cost gains from their law firms, and he expects that gap to push more work in-house if it persists. Lynn Tellefsen Stehle, writing November 11 in JD Supra Perspectives, puts change management inside the firm as a permanent skill with its own people and accountability rather than a one-time rollout. Brie Leung, founder and principal of Red Bird Strategy, argues that AI makes lawyers reconsider where their judgment matters and what expertise means. Catherine Alman MacDonagh, CEO and founder of the Legal Lean Sigma Institute, proposes a written project charter defining the problem, the goal, who is responsible, the resources needed and how success will be measured. Jen Leonard, founder of Creative Lawyers, calls the gap between announcement and action innovation by press release.

stories.Headline: Suzanne Nossel urges AI companies to adopt UN human rights frameworks over internal rules
stories.Summary:
Suzanne Nossel wrote an argument on November 17, 2026, about the human rights blind spot in the current artificial intelligence safety debate. She argues that the AI industry should use an existing framework instead of writing its own rules for ethics and safety. AI companies and their executives have released essays, white papers, and proposals to assuage public fears about uncontrollable technologies. Anthropic filed a form S-1 in October detailing its public benefit commitments and its vows regarding ethics and safety. OpenAI updated its Model Spec late last month to serve human purposes, be truthful, minimize harm, and respect freedom.

The proposed framework is the U.N. Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, which the Human Rights Council endorsed in 2011. This system requires three pillars: states must protect people, companies must respect human rights, and harmed people must have remedy. It introduces human rights due diligence to identify risks, prevent harms, monitor results, and report on them for all industries. France, Germany, and Norway passed laws requiring companies to address human rights risks, and the European Union adopted a directive in 2024. The principles cover globally recognized rights including privacy, equality, labor rights, and freedom of expression for people harmed by AI.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argued that companies developing these technologies are perfectly incentivized to do the right thing without further regulation. In late September, the White House imposed no new constraints and praised what President Donald Trump called a tremendous self-policing aspect. Suzanne Nossel, a columnist and senior fellow at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, suggests the industry adopt the U.N. framework. She also serves as a senior advisor to the Starling Institute and emphasizes that corporate needs must be subordinate to humans. Nossel believes that superior intelligence confers no inherent authority to govern human lives or cede dominions to machines.

A September Quinnipiac University poll found that 74 percent of respondents held little or no trust in AI company leaders. An Anthropic study published in June found only 15 percent of Americans trust AI companies to make development and usage decisions. Some key AI personnel have resigned in alarm, feeling that society cannot contain the risks of these powerful, inscrutable technologies. Regulators fear that the wrong constraints could hamper economic prosperity and global competitiveness while they face the limits of their competence. The public remains worried about the impact of AI on democracy, personal agency, psychological well-being, and even human survival.

The modern human rights movement began after governments subordinated individual lives to national ambitions and ideological supremacy in a ravaged world. The U.N. Charter, signed in June 1945, affirmed the dignity and worth of the human person as an inviolable right. In 2005, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed Harvard professor John Ruggie to define the human rights responsibilities of multinational businesses. This effort addressed gaps in corporate responsibility found in global supply chains, extractive industries, and low-wage operations with weak legal protections. The resulting principles translate the foundational commitment to human dignity into practical expectations for how all global companies should operate.

AI developers should examine if training data is obtained legitimately and how governments might use technologies for surveillance, repression, or discrimination. Companies must embed these findings into product design, budgets, and commercial relationships while tracking whether the implemented safeguards actually work. Developers are expected to exert leverage over partners to prevent abuses, restricting access to technology or terminating relationships when efforts fail. The articles leave open whether AI companies will actually adopt these U.N. principles or continue relying on voluntary self-policing pledges. It remains unclear if the U.S. government will move beyond the current laissez-faire approach to mandate these human rights standards.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a 90 billion dollar Nasdaq IPO to test investor confidence in the AI boom
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to debut on the Nasdaq stock market this coming Thursday to test investor confidence in the global artificial intelligence boom. The five year old company develops the Claude family of models and expects the initial public offering to generate over 90 billion dollars. Technology companies are committing billions of dollars to the offering despite concerns over financing risks and the sustainability of the investment boom. This arrival occurs during a difficult moment for the sector following a decline in technology shares and a leadership crisis at Nvidia. The company reported a net loss of 104 billion dollars during the first nine months of 2026 but holds 132 billion dollars.

The offering price is expected to be 70 to 78 dollars per share with investments of 26 billion dollars from several major firms. These investors include Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, while Amazon holds a substantial stake. Anthropic has over 900 billion dollars in spending commitments, including 110 billion dollars with Amazon over 10 years and 400 billion dollars elsewhere. It will spend 125 billion to 150 billion dollars on Google chips by 2028 and lease a data centre starting 2027. Amazon also built an 11 billion dollar data centre in Indiana for Anthropic using custom chips, and Google guaranteed 19 billion dollars.

Anthropic stated in its prospectus that it previously underestimated computing requirements, which left the company short of capacity and affected product deployment. Joe Fath of Eclipse called the staggering numbers hard to wrap one's head around, while David Tollen called it smart investing. Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google executive, said that everybody knows Anthropic is going to be the future of the Google company. Broadcom provided a financial backstop with a maximum liability of 43 billion dollars to support the rental of artificial intelligence chips. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley offered 63 billion dollars to purchase the racks of chips that Anthropic will rent.

Corey Quinn of Duckbill questioned if the long agreements could remain unchanged, stating that anything past four years is like throwing darts. The Nasdaq fell 5.3 percent in October, which was its worst monthly performance since March 2025, adding pressure to debt heavy providers. Rising interest rates and new United States ballot measures could further restrict the development of new data centres across the entire country. Investors are also concerned by Nvidia, where shares fell 13 percent after chief executive Jensen Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs. Colette Kress was appointed interim chief executive after Huang was linked to a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence.

The company is committing to infrastructure well in advance because it needs computing power to develop advanced models and expand its services. Cloud providers Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31 percent of the contractual obligations listed in the latest official company prospectus. Google is expected to hold an ownership stake of approximately 13 percent following the completion of the initial public offering process. The 10 year agreement with Amazon is twice the length of typical contracts, which has attracted questions about the financial exposure. These investments occur as the broader technology sector faces mounting pressure from indebted cloud infrastructure companies and volatile global stock market trends.

The initial public offering will provide funding for the computing infrastructure needed to operate advanced models and expand the company's current services. The articles leave open whether the long term infrastructure commitments and the 20 year data centre lease will remain financially sustainable. It remains uncertain if the arrangements with cloud providers will be renegotiated before the contracts expire as suggested by some industry experts. The market will see if the 90 billion dollar debut can redefine the scale of technology listings despite the current sector turmoil. Investors must wait to see if the calculated exposure to these staggering costs will result in the predicted future for Google.

stories.Headline: Shenzhen prepares to host APEC leaders to discuss Asia-Pacific AI cooperation
stories.Summary:
Shenzhen prepares to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting from November 18 to 19 under a theme of prospering together. EngineAI Robotics Technology Co., Ltd. organized a robot fighting competition to test movement capabilities for potential future agricultural applications. A Malaysian researcher suggested that humanoid robots could eventually guard orchards, harvest oil palm fruit, or pollinate durian trees. Yao Qiyuan, a co-founder of the firm, noted that expanding overseas involves developing new applications with local partners. These events highlight the potential for deeper artificial intelligence cooperation across the Asia-Pacific region during the upcoming leaders' meeting.

The city's core AI industry generated 220 billion yuan, or 33 billion U.S. dollars, in revenue during the year 2025. More than 2,600 AI enterprises above designated size operate in Shenzhen, and trade with APEC economies reached 1.98 trillion yuan. This trade figure for the first half of 2026 rose 33 percent and accounted for nearly 70 percent of foreign trade. Shenzhen exported 8.27 billion yuan of 3D-printing equipment in early 2026, which was an increase of 127.5 percent. The city released an AI action plan for 2026 to 2028 in September to strengthen cooperation with ASEAN countries.

Hu Zhenyu of the China Development Institute said the AI industry is now bringing entire industrial chains to overseas markets. Yao Qiyuan stated that robot fighting tests gait and balance before these capabilities are applied to various agricultural tasks. Bai Xue of the Shenzhen 3D Printing Association said integrated supply chains have boosted the competitiveness of Chinese printers. Shi Xiaoliang of SmartMore Corporation hopes APEC will allow for deeper technological innovation, industrial collaboration, and global talent exchanges. Yang Qian of X Square Robot said open-source technologies are lowering barriers to technology access for small and medium enterprises.

SmartMore Corporation has served over 730 enterprises and deepened cooperation with partners in Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Southeast Asia. These partners work in sectors including precision manufacturing, new energy, and consumer electronics to detect defects too small for eyes. Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises account for over 97 percent of businesses and provide most private sector jobs. These smaller businesses generate about half of the private sector output and are affected by new AI-powered digital transformations. Eduardo Pedrosa of the APEC Secretariat said Shenzhen's research and innovation can benefit the entire region and the world.

In 2025, APEC's 21 member economies housed 3 billion people and represented 61.6 percent of the global real GDP. The APEC Artificial Intelligence Initiative for 2026 to 2030 was adopted in 2025 to promote secure and reliable ecosystems. On July 23, ministers in Chengdu adopted the Chengdu Statement to promote AI transformation in agriculture, services, and manufacturing. China announced in July that it would provide 5,000 AI training opportunities and seminars for developing countries over five years. The Huaqiangbei electronics market now attracts enthusiasts interested in 3D printers, robots, and AI glasses instead of just components.

China plans to establish a center in Qianhai, Shenzhen, to promote APEC cooperation regarding the flow of cross-border data. This center will serve as an open platform for regulatory alignment, policy research, and various services for different businesses. The city seeks cooperation with countries in the Belt and Road Initiative regarding AI solutions and intelligent computing hardware ecosystems. The articles leave open how specific regulatory alignments will be reached through the new center in the Qianhai district. They also leave open the specific timeline for when humanoid robots will begin guarding orchards in the country of Malaysia.

stories.Headline: Saskatchewan introduces bill to let courts remove deceptive AI content and order compensation
stories.Summary:
The Saskatchewan government introduced a bill on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, to crack down on artificial intelligence used to deceive the public. This new legislation targets fake and manipulative AI content, which the province says undermines trust and creates financial hardship for people. The bill allows courts to order the removal of deceptive artificial media, often called deepfakes, and lets victims seek financial compensation. It aims to hold individuals accountable if they use technology inappropriately to target vulnerable people or attempt to deceive the public. Saskatchewan claims it is the first Canadian jurisdiction to provide a legislative framework specifically focused on the issue of deceptive AI.

The bill applies to deceptive AI content in audio or visual formats, including AI generated intimate images, and requires clear markings on authentic looking content. Courts can force creators to destroy manipulative content, remove it from platforms, and pay compensation to victims at a cost determined by the court. The legislation does not limit the use of AI for parody or satire, provided the content is not manipulative, defamatory, or deceptive. Alberta has already passed laws prohibiting fake AI content of politicians and targeting the use of AI for spreading intimate images. Policing agencies will be responsible for enforcing the law if the bill passes and becomes active within the province of Saskatchewan.

Justice Minister Tim McLeod stated that the province must be prepared to safeguard against the misuse of AI as new developments emerge daily. He told reporters that the government wants a framework to hold people accountable if they use AI to target vulnerable individuals. McLeod noted that people would still be able to express themselves freely using technology if the content is meant in good fun. When asked about specific deepfakes, the minister said he could not speak to details regarding who is responsible for those particular videos. He emphasized that the goal is to provide a legal tool to address the rise of deceptive and harmful artificial media.

Rod McKendrick of the Saskatchewan Seniors Mechanism group said the bill provides a necessary tool for victims of AI impersonation scams. He noted that grandparents have received calls from scammers pretending to be grandchildren asking for money, but authorities lacked legislation to act. Victims of deepfakes will be affected by this bill, as they can now seek legal action against the creators of deceptive content. The legislation specifically protects those who have fallen prey to manipulative media that causes them financial loss or other personal hardship. These victims can now use the court system to seek the removal of harmful content and recover their lost funds.

Premier Scott Moe previously raised concerns about online deepfakes that used his own likeness to promote various cryptocurrency schemes to the public. The government believes that deceptive artificial media manipulates the public and creates significant financial hardship for many citizens across the province. This bill follows a general rise in AI impersonation scams, with a related consumer alert issued on March 31, 2026. The province views this legislative move as a necessary step to protect citizens from the evolving threats posed by generative AI. Saskatchewan is positioning itself as a leader in Canada by creating this specific legal framework to combat the spread of deepfakes.

The next step for the legislation is to pass through the legislative process before policing agencies can begin enforcing the new rules. If the bill becomes law, creators of deceptive AI will face court ordered removals of their content and mandatory payments to victims. The articles do not state when the bill will be voted on or the specific penalties for creators beyond compensation. It remains open whether the province is actively investigating the individuals responsible for the deepfakes that targeted Premier Scott Moe. The reports leave it unclear how the province will identify anonymous creators of deceptive AI content across different digital platforms.

stories.Headline: Palo Alto Networks agrees to buy Applied Compute in a $4.5 billion all-stock deal
stories.Summary:
Palo Alto Networks said in a Wednesday Nov. 18 press release that it plans to acquire Applied Compute, a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight models, in an all-stock transaction valued at $4.5 billion. The buyer is Palo Alto Networks, a global AI security firm, and the target is Applied Compute, which was founded less than 18 months ago according to a Nov. 2 blog post. PYMNTS reported the deal on November 18, 2026, and CNBC reported it the same day alongside Palo Alto's fiscal first-quarter results. CNBC said Palo Alto Networks shares jumped more than 7% after the cybersecurity firm beat Wall Street's fiscal first-quarter estimates and inked the Applied Compute deal. The Information reported Nov. 4 that Palo Alto Networks had made four acquisitions this year and was in talks to acquire Clutch Security for around $500 million.

The all-stock transaction is valued at $4.5 billion and will add Applied Compute's platform and AI research team to Palo Alto Networks. Palo Alto Networks expects the transaction to close during the company's fiscal third quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory clearance and other customary closing conditions. Applied Compute's AI research team will join Palo Alto Networks and will help the company embed AI across all its offerings. Applied Compute's co-founder and CEO, Yash Patil, will become Palo Alto Networks' co-chief AI officer after the close of the transaction. Applied Compute said in its Nov. 2 blog post that it has grown from zero to $100 million in annualized revenue run rate in under 18 months.

Chairman and CEO Nikesh Arora said every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured. Arora said Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform the company has seen, and its research team is exceptional. Arora also said that as AI reshapes the threat landscape, the company must continually evolve to protect its customers and enable them to adopt AI securely. On an earnings call Arora said that if it works, the deal will dwarf the ability the company has in cybersecurity, and could be bigger than what the company does. Patil said the company built Applied Compute with an exceptional team of AI researchers and engineers to make it easy for any company to train, serve and improve proprietary models.

Patil said joining Palo Alto Networks will put security at the center of all its products and accelerate its traction with the world's largest organizations. CNBC reported that fears of AI-powered cyberattacks, heightened by incidents like the Hugging Face breach, are driving demand for cybersecurity vendors like Palo Alto Networks. CNBC reported that outages from Microsoft, banks and air traffic control heightened concerns around cyberattacks over the last week, and that U.S. officials have so far ruled out any malicious activity. Arora said the company expects tens of thousands of virtual patches by the end of the fiscal year, and that whatever customers do today will take three to six months, maybe nine months, depending on how complex and how tired their environment is. CNBC reported that Palo Alto's shares have jumped 85% this year.

PYMNTS reported Tuesday Nov. 17 that Applied Compute is one of the training partners Nvidia relies on to help enterprises tailor open models with their own data, which feeds demand for Nvidia compute. CNBC reported that Palo Alto Networks topped Wall Street's fiscal first-quarter estimates, with adjusted earnings per share of $1.05 versus 97 cents expected and revenue of $3.44 billion versus $3.31 billion expected. CNBC reported revenue jumped 39% from $2.47 billion in the year-ago quarter, and annual recurring revenue for the next-generation security business jumped 66% from a year ago to $9.73 billion. CNBC reported net income totaled $482 million, or 57 cents per share, up from $334 million, or 47 cents per share a year ago. Arora said the NGS ARR was one of the highest beats in the company's history.

CNBC reported that Palo Alto bumped up guidance for fiscal year 2027, expecting adjusted earnings per share of $4.26 to $4.30 and revenue of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion, topping analyst expectations of $4.18 per share and $14.16 billion in revenue. CNBC reported that Palo Alto Networks has been steadily acquiring companies to capitalize on demand for cyber tools in the age of AI, and that the Applied Compute deal marks a major investment beyond cybersecurity. The articles leave open whether the transaction will receive regulatory clearance and satisfy the other customary closing conditions. The articles leave open how the combined companies will operate Applied Compute's platform after the close. The articles leave open the outcome of the reported talks to acquire Clutch Security for around $500 million.

stories.Headline: OCC issues Bulletin 2026-54, a 16-component examiner framework for assessing banks' generative and agentic AI risks
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 4, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued its dedicated supervisory framework for examiners evaluating banks' use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence. The OCC issued Bulletin 2026-54, Super Intelligence: Supervisory Framework, introducing a dedicated examiner framework for evaluating banks' use of "super intelligence," including generative and agentic AI. The framework does not impose new regulatory requirements or supervisory expectations. It provides insight into how OCC examiners may evaluate AI-related risks, including cybersecurity, customer data privacy, third-party risk management and operational resilience. The development is notable because the federal banking agencies' April 2026 revised model risk management guidance expressly excluded generative and agentic AI from its scope.

The new OCC framework addresses those technologies through 16 components organized around six pillars: purpose, risk, control, oversight, resilience and assurance. The OCC expressly states that the framework is intended for examiners, does not establish new regulatory requirements or supervisory expectations, and is not intended as a required self-assessment tool for banks. Although directed at OCC examiners supervising national banks, federal savings associations and federal branches and agencies of foreign banks, the framework's considerations may also be useful to other financial institutions, including state-chartered banks and credit unions. The framework addresses increasingly autonomous AI technologies that can access sensitive customer information, interact with banking systems and execute transactions. These capabilities create significant opportunities for banks but also raise security and privacy concerns that traditional risk management programs may not fully address.

The OCC recognizes that AI introduces privacy risks beyond conventional data handling concerns. AI tools may use sensitive customer information and then retain or reproduce it, infer information that was not expressly provided or use data in ways that are inconsistent with existing privacy policies. The framework also identifies cybersecurity threats specific to AI, including prompt injection, data and model poisoning, model extraction and sensitive information leakage. These threats may allow attackers to manipulate AI systems or obtain sensitive information without a conventional network intrusion. Agentic AI presents additional concerns because these systems may use credentials, access internal applications, modify records or execute transactions.

The OCC recognizes that conventional vendor due diligence and information security reviews may not fully address AI-related risks. Existing vendors may introduce new AI functionality, modify underlying models or deploy AI agents that interact with bank systems without corresponding changes to the institution's existing contractual protections. The framework specifically addresses visibility into vendor-operated AI agents, notification of AI-related incidents, changes to AI functionality and contractual responsibility for model-related errors or customer harm. An AI agent could improperly disclose customer information, modify account records, generate inaccurate customer communications or execute unauthorized transactions without a traditional system compromise or outage. These events may require investigation, containment and customer remediation even when conventional cybersecurity monitoring does not identify an intrusion.

The framework identifies AI-specific considerations involving incident detection, containment, suspension of AI functionality, preservation of relevant records, business continuity and customer remediation. Banks should consider developing AI incident reporting and response procedures that supplement existing cybersecurity incident response plans. These procedures should address not only conventional security incidents but also unauthorized AI use, harmful or anomalous outputs, privacy violations, compromised models and unintended autonomous actions. Banks and other financial institutions should consider reviewing their existing AI uses, governance, security controls and vendor arrangements, and developing AI-specific contractual protections and incident response procedures where appropriate. The central issue for banks is whether existing controls remain effective when AI systems can access customer information, interact with critical systems and act without direct human approval.

Banks should consider whether existing vendor management practices sufficiently address these issues, and depending on the risks involved, an AI-specific contractual addendum may provide additional protections concerning approved AI uses, restrictions on customer data use and model training, downstream AI providers, material changes to AI functionality, incident reporting, investigation cooperation, audit rights and allocation of liability. Banks should consider controls designed to prevent unauthorized, inappropriate or unsafe AI actions, including restrictions on system permissions, human approval for consequential decisions, ongoing monitoring and clear accountability for AI activities. Banks should consider how they would detect, contain and recover from AI failures or unauthorized activity while maintaining critical operations, including testing controls, maintaining records sufficient to reconstruct significant AI actions, and establishing procedures to suspend AI systems or reverse harmful actions when necessary. Higher-risk applications, particularly those capable of accessing sensitive customer information or taking autonomous actions, may warrant more extensive assessments and safeguards. The OCC's framework provides a useful starting point for evaluating these risks.

stories.Headline: Polsinelli attorneys argue copyright rulings push institutions to define human oversight of AI decisions
stories.Summary:
Polsinelli PC attorneys Michael D. Pegues and Clement A. Asante published an alert on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, in The National Law Review, Volume XVI, Number 322, arguing that recent copyright decisions raise broader questions about institutional governance. The alert says artificial intelligence is moving from writing emails and summarizing documents into analyzing information, recommending courses of action, evaluating risks, allocating resources and informing decisions that previously depended almost entirely on human judgment. The authors say courts are beginning to address when copyrighted material may be used to train AI systems and when AI-generated output may constitute infringement. The alert states that the decisions highlight a broader question facing companies, universities, nonprofit organizations, government bodies and other institutions about how much decision-making authority to give artificial intelligence. The authors ask what responsibilities remain with the people who govern those institutions.

The alert cites Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v. ROSS Intelligence Inc., 139 F.4th 271, in which the Third Circuit rejected a fair use defense involving Westlaw headnotes used to develop an AI-powered legal research product, emphasizing the commercial nature of the use and competition with Westlaw. It cites Bartz v. Anthropic, 787 F. Supp. 3d 1007, and Kadrey v. Meta, 788 F. Supp. 3d 1026, where federal courts found that use of copyrighted books for large language model training could qualify as fair use on the records before them. It cites Doe v. GitHub, Inc., No. 24-7700, where the Ninth Circuit rejected a claim under Section 1202 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act based on AI-generated code that did not contain copyright management information, while leaving open whether substantially similar AI-generated code might violate traditional copyright law. The alert says Bartz separated the question of using books for model training from how Anthropic obtained some of those books, since training could be transformative while acquisition and retention of unauthorized copies presented a different copyright problem. It says the National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI risk management guidance emphasizes clearly defining human roles and responsibilities for AI oversight, and the European Union's AI Act requires meaningful human oversight for certain high-risk AI systems and contemplates that overseers have appropriate competence and authority.

The authors say institutions adopting AI must consider more than the legality of the technology itself, and that decisions about data use, human oversight and accountability can create legal and governance risks that remain the institution's responsibility. They recommend that institutional leaders evaluate how AI is used in consequential decisions, establish meaningful human oversight and assess the rights and restrictions governing information incorporated into AI workflows. They say the risk is that institutions may gradually delegate judgment without consciously deciding to do so, as a system begins as an efficiency tool, its recommendations prove useful, decision makers increasingly rely on its output, and human review can become little more than approval of a decision made by the system. They say human oversight should mean more than having a person available to press approve. They say institutions should identify who has authority to approve particular AI uses, that responsibility should not disappear simply because a third-party vendor provides the technology, and that reviewers should understand what the AI system considers, recognize its limitations and have genuine authority to reject its recommendation.

The alert says institutions should ask whether they have the right to use information for a given purpose and whether providing it to an AI system is consistent with contractual obligations, confidentiality requirements and internal policies. It says an employee using an AI system to summarize a licensed publication may implicate different rights from an institution using thousands of those publications to create its own internal knowledge system. It says a university deciding how to allocate scholarships, a board deciding whether to discontinue a community program or a company evaluating employees may need to consider context an algorithm cannot fully appreciate. It says the AI recommended it is unlikely to satisfy an employee, customer, regulator, donor or court seeking to understand why an important decision was made, and that the EU AI Act requires human oversight and, for certain uses, information to individuals affected by AI-assisted decisions. It says copyright ownership, license restrictions, confidentiality obligations and data provenance should be considered before valuable information is incorporated into an AI workflow.

The alert says AI rarely eliminates a difficult legal or institutional question and more often moves the question somewhere else, as a dispute over training data becomes a question about where the information came from, an efficiency tool becomes a question about who actually made the decision, and an algorithmic recommendation becomes a question about who will accept responsibility when the recommendation is wrong. It says the most important decisions about AI will not be made by AI but by the people entrusted with governing the institution. It says institutions do not need to choose between embracing AI and avoiding it but need governance structures that allow them to use the technology without surrendering judgment to it. It says that starts with identifying the decisions for which AI is being used and determining whether the system is providing information or effectively making the decision. It says institutions should take advantage of what artificial intelligence can do.

The alert leaves open whether substantially similar AI-generated code might violate traditional copyright law, a question the Ninth Circuit did not resolve in Doe v. GitHub. It does not establish a blanket rule that AI training is lawful, stating that the fair use decisions rested on the records before the courts. It does not say how institutions should weigh competing values that cannot be resolved solely by identifying the most statistically efficient result. It does not specify what competence and authority overseers must have under the EU AI Act beyond the statute's general requirements. It does not address the pending matters listed elsewhere on the publication's site, including Anthropic's S-1 and the 2027 inflation-adjusted plan limits.

stories.Headline: McGovern rallies at the Capitol to urge Congress to pass a national data center moratorium
stories.Summary:
U.S. Rep. Jim McGovern rallied outside the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday to urge Congress to pass a national moratorium on the development of data centers. The Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act (S.4214 / H.R.9442) would pause large data center projects until the federal government puts safeguards in place against job losses, environmental degradation and rising energy costs. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., introduced it in the Senate, and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., introduced it in the House. McGovern is one of nine co-sponsors of the House bill. Public outcry against data center development has grown in the last year over the rising electricity costs fueled by data center energy demand, impacts on public land and the threat that artificial intelligence poses to job security.

McGovern said the Trump administration and congressional Republicans have done little to address those concerns. He vowed to assert congressional power to protect the American people and pass the moratorium. McGovern was joined by Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, and Reps.-elect Will Lawrence, D-Mich.; Donavan McKinney, D-Mich.; Chris Rabb, D-Pa.; and Adam Hamawy, D-N.J. Local moratoriums or bans on large data centers have been approved in 18 Massachusetts municipalities, including Northampton, Holyoke and Westfield. Sutton residents are petitioning to ban data centers in their community, potentially blocking a proposed $16 billion data center sponsored by two Kraft family companies.

Municipalities such as Greenfield and Gill have adopted moratoriums on data centers. Northfield will consider the same during a Nov. 19 Special Town Meeting. McGovern and his colleagues contend that pausing the construction of data centers across the country would give communities time to study their impact and decide if they should be allowed. This, he said, will ensure the buildout and creation of artificial intelligence that benefits the public. “The American people are done getting screwed over by unelected, unaccountable Big Tech oligarchs,” McGovern said.

Though Tuesday’s rally was called to support the moratorium, McGovern took several swings at President Donald Trump, calling him a “megalomaniac” who refuses to hold Big Tech accountable. He added that Congress has been idle on the issue for the past two years under what he called “Mike Johnson’s MAGA majority,” a reference to House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La. “We are here asleep at the switch when it comes to AI,” he said. Each of the legislators at Tuesday’s rally referenced constituent concern about the inequities in data center development. The electricity to power data centers can exceed the demand of midsize American cities.

These costs are redistributed across the entire system, ultimately increasing electricity rates, they said. “It’s obvious why data centers are an AI tax where hardworking families foot the bill for Silicon Valley,” Hamawy said. Most of this energy comes from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. The New York Times reported that the largest U.S. data centers release an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide each year, which equates to Bolivia’s entire output. The Trump administration is also considering public land offers for data center development.

Pingree said that Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum is “fast-tracking” a plan to give away 17,000 acres of public land across six states for data center projects. “These lands are national treasures that belong to the American public,” she said. “They do not belong to tech billionaires.” While citizens speak against the negative consequences, legislators also questioned whether the benefits of this technology would reach the American people. Lawrence particularly noted that the direction of artificial intelligence will replace jobs, spread misinformation and pose an existential threat to humanity. His district saw five hyperscale data center proposals in 15 months.

“Despite all the talk in Silicon Valley about safety, the fact of the matter is these companies remained engaged in an out-of-control arms race to capture market share even if it kills us all,” Lawrence said. Several large companies are moving ahead with data center investment. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, invested $205 billion in the effort this fiscal year, while Meta has committed $600 billion for AI infrastructure and job development by 2028. McGovern and the other Democratic Congress members promised to “keep fighting” for the American people and urged other legislators to join them. “We House Democrats have an opportunity,” said U.S. Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., “to prove to the American people that we meant it when we said we were going to fight for them.”

stories.Headline: Microsoft nears 500 million dollar AI deal with ByteDance despite OpenAI objections
stories.Summary:
Microsoft is reportedly in advanced discussions to secure a deal worth roughly 500 million dollars from the Chinese company ByteDance on November 18, 2026. This agreement would allow ByteDance to expand its existing contract by purchasing additional cloud services from Microsoft. The arrangement primarily involves the use of artificial intelligence models created by OpenAI through the Azure cloud platform. Some of this business was previously provided by Anthropic before that company restricted its services.

The deal requires ByteDance to shift its reliance away from Anthropic, which blocked Chinese customers using foreign subsidiaries last September. Microsoft is also attempting to sell OpenAI models to other Chinese firms, such as Alibaba, that lost access to Anthropic. This shift occurs because Microsoft possesses the rights to sell OpenAI technology without the same prohibitions that OpenAI imposes on Chinese firms. These changes allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI tools that were previously restricted by other providers.

OpenAI has expressed dismay over the situation and complained to Microsoft in recent months about these business practices. The AI company believes that Chinese firms are distilling its technology to develop their own competing models. While OpenAI blocks most Chinese firms directly, it cannot stop Microsoft from selling the technology through its cloud services. Microsoft has not provided a public statement regarding these specific accusations or the reported deal with ByteDance.

stories.Headline: ASEAN banks agree a common AI governance baseline and step up anti-fraud workshops
stories.Summary:
Banking associations across Southeast Asia advanced plans for common artificial intelligence governance and cybersecurity cooperation during November 2026. These initiatives were endorsed at the 54th ASEAN Banking Council Meeting on 13 and 14 November. The event took place at the Makati Shangri-La Hotel in Manila and was hosted by the Bankers Association of the Philippines. More than 280 banking executives, policymakers, and industry experts attended the meeting to discuss securing the future. The primary focus of the gathering was titled AI-Driven Banking in ASEAN: Securing Our Future Together.

The Committee on Cooperation in Finance, Investment, Trade and Technology will create an ASEAN-wide baseline for AI governance. This project requires an implementation roadmap that outlines specific deliverables, priority areas, and responsibilities for the member banks. Regional associations will increase workshops on digital scams and fraud from once to twice annually to exchange information. Members will also examine the strategic viability of stablecoins and tokenized deposits, specifically regarding the Swift Ledger initiative. The Committee on ASEAN Inter-Regional Relations proposed 2027 study tour topics including data privacy, cybersecurity, and green finance.

The HHS Office of Inspector General issued a report warning that the Department of Health and Human Services faces cyber weaknesses. The watchdog agency stated that cyberattacks could jeopardize critical operations and potentially compromise the health of individuals served. OIG wrote that responsible adoption of AI requires clear governance, disciplined implementation, and continuous oversight for all decisionmakers. The report noted that implementation of strong safeguards varies across programs and has not reached the desired effectiveness. OIG urged the department to adapt HIPAA enforcement to better address evolving privacy and cybersecurity threats to health information.

Healthcare organizations are attractive targets for cybercriminals because they maintain sensitive information and depend on interconnected technologies. The OIG report noted that limited financial resources, legacy technology, and professional shortages complicate efforts to defend data. Nitin Natarajan stated that technical debt often exceeds available budgets, making modernization impossible without significant operational impacts. Attorney Lee Kim suggested that the department establish technical standards for developing, evaluating, and deploying various AI systems. These vulnerabilities affect the delivery of safe and timely patient care for people across the entire nation.

The OIG cited a 2025 audit of the National Institutes of Health All of Us research program regarding security. A 2024 security review examined the cloud infrastructure unit of the HHS office of the secretary for weaknesses. Findings from 2026 showed cybersecurity protection weaknesses for Medicare enrollee data at a large unnamed hospital in the southeast. A 2025 settlement involved false claims allegations regarding vulnerabilities in genomic sequencing systems provided by the company Illumina Inc. The HHS 2025 inventory identified 446 AI use cases, including applications that support core government functions.

The 2027 study tour will be conducted in person, with the destination determined by a poll of associations. The ASEAN banking industry will continue to develop a coordinated approach to technological innovation and emerging financial risks. The HHS must ensure consistent implementation of strong safeguards across all operating divisions to improve its security posture. The department has not yet responded to requests for comment regarding the findings of the OIG watchdog report. It remains open whether the department will implement the recommended technical standards for training and testing AI models.

stories.Headline: UH to predict invasive beetle spread with AI
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience are developing an artificial intelligence tool to predict where the invasive coconut rhinoceros beetle is most likely to spread. The project covers Kauaʻi, Maui and Hawaiʻi Island and is dated November 17, 2026 in the university’s news release. Pascal Aigbedion-Atalor, an assistant professor in CTAHR’s Department of Plant and Environmental Protection Sciences, leads the project. The $300,000 project aims to help field crews decide where to place traps and look for new infestations. The university announced the work through its news service and Big Island Video News and Hawaii News Now reported it the same day.

The team will use machine learning to analyze local conditions that help the beetle survive and map areas where it is most likely to spread. Researchers plan to test the predictions against field observations to improve the tool’s accuracy. The maps could help crews decide where to place pheromone-baited traps and focus their efforts to contain the beetle. Researchers could also adapt the approach to help protect Hawaiʻi crops from other invasive pests. Funding comes from the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research through its Rapid Outcomes from Agricultural Research program, with matching support from CTAHR.

Aigbedion-Atalor said knowing where the coconut rhinoceros beetle is likely to spread gives farmers and response teams a major advantage. He said the technology aims to help farmers and agriculture officials act early, target high-risk areas and protect valuable crops and landscapes. Kathy Munkvold, scientific program director at the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research, said stopping invasive pests before they spread is one of the best ways to protect American agriculture. She said the research gives farmers a head start against a devastating introduced pest, helping to protect crops, livelihoods and the future of Hawaiʻi’s agriculture. CTAHR Dean Parwinder Grewal said mitigating the CRB crisis cannot be accomplished by a single organization.

Grewal said it takes a combined effort, from state agricultural inspectors and federal biosecurity officials to private funders and everyday community members checking their backyards. UH researchers are working with state agencies, federal partners, private organizations and residents to help limit the beetle’s spread. The maps would support those efforts by showing crews where to focus their fieldwork. Last week, it was reported for the first time that a coconut rhinoceros beetle was discovered in the Puna district on Hawaiʻi island. The Hawaiʻi Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity said the live, male CRB was found in a trap in the Kurtistown area.

The university’s news release describes the project as a two-minute read and lists it under agriculture, AI, entomology and invasive species tags. The release names the College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience and the Department of Plant and Environmental Protection Sciences as the units involved. Big Island Video News reported the story under a summary saying the tool will predict where the invasive CRB is most likely to spread in Hawaiʻi. Hawaii News Now reported that the project aims to help farmers and response teams identify high-risk areas on Kauai, Maui and Hawaii Island. Hawaii News Now also reported that UH officials said the technology could eventually be adapted to help protect Hawaii crops from other invasive pests.

Researchers plan to test their predictions against field observations, and the maps could help crews decide where to place traps and focus efforts to detect and contain new infestations. The articles do not say when the tool will be finished or when the maps will be available to field crews. The articles do not say how many traps would be placed or where on Kauaʻi, Maui and Hawaiʻi Island the mapping would begin. The articles do not say whether the Kurtistown beetle find is connected to the new prediction project. The articles do not give the outcome of any testing of the predictions against field observations.

stories.Headline: Nebius posts 571% revenue growth and guides 2027 to about fourfold growth
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group N.V. reported third-quarter 2026 results on November 13, 2026, with revenues surging 571% year over year to $980.8 million, up 68% sequentially. The growth was primarily driven by capacity additions over the past 12 months and strong demand for AI infrastructure. Nebius AI Cloud revenues jumped 643% to $973.8 million, accounting for approximately 99% of total revenues. Group adjusted EBITDA reached $465.8 million against a loss of $5.2 million a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to 47.5% from 40.6% sequentially.

Since the beginning of the third quarter, customers have committed more than $12 billion in contract value, including multibillion-dollar agreements. Nebius secured multiyear agreements with enterprise AI leaders including Databricks, Datadog and Snowflake. Pricing for third-quarter agreements exceeded $25 million per megawatt compared with $20 million-$25 million in the preceding quarter. Customer prepayments now cover more than 100% of capital expenditures associated with newly contracted capacity. Nebius expects 2026 revenues of $3 billion-$3.2 billion, narrowing its previous guidance of $3 billion-$3.4 billion due to delays at certain third-party data center sites.

Capital expenditures are projected to be approximately $27 billion, while adjusted EBITDA margin guidance remains around 40%. For 2027, management anticipates revenues of $12 billion-$13 billion, representing approximately fourfold growth, supported by additional computing capacity. Capital expenditures are expected to reach $40 billion-$45 billion, with pretax breakeven targeted for the fourth quarter. Summit Research said Nebius' strong third-quarter results reinforce a resilient AI compute demand backdrop. Summit Research said accelerating revenue growth and improving operating leverage support its anticipated profit inflection in the fourth quarter of 2027.

Summit Research said rising capital intensity amid tightening credit conditions increase NBIS execution risks, despite improving customer prepayments and financing access. Summit Research said shifting procurement dynamics at hyperscale customer Microsoft, alongside key investor Nvidia's leadership crisis, compound uncertainties over capacity monetization, funding cost profile and ROI prospects. NBIS stock has corrected more than 57% since October, underperforming the broader AI sector-led selloff as tightening credit conditions temper investor sentiment towards capital-intensive neoclouds. Shares of Nebius have gained 54.4% in the past year compared with the Internet ,  Software and Services industry's growth of 7.3%. In terms of price/book, NBIS shares are trading at 3.15X, below the Internet Software Services industry's 3.55X.

CoreWeave reported third-quarter 2026 revenue growth of 168% year over year to $3.66 billion, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 4.84%. CoreWeave's revenue backlog surged 138% year over year to $132.5 billion, with qualified demand exceeding available capacity by 10 times through 2027. CoreWeave raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $13 billion-$13.3 billion and year-end annualized revenue run-rate outlook to $20 billion-$21 billion. Microsoft's first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenues increased 19% year over year to $92.3 billion, driven by 48% Azure revenue growth to $33.2 billion. Microsoft Cloud revenues surged 30% to $63.9 billion, while Foundry revenues more than tripled and commercial remaining performance obligations jumped 73% to $677 billion.

For the second quarter, Microsoft expects revenues of $96-$97.1 billion, representing 18-19% growth, with Azure projected to grow 49-50% in constant currency. However, weakness in Windows OEM and devices and capacity constraints remain concerns. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for NBIS earnings for 2026 has been revised significantly upward over the past 60 days. NBIS currently carries a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy). Infrastructure deployment delays and substantial capital requirements remain key challenges for Nebius. Expanding capacity, higher contract pricing and growing customer commitments position Nebius for continued growth, provided execution remains on track.

Summit Research said it has a beneficial long position in the shares of NVDA either through stock ownership, options or other derivatives. Summit Research said it wrote the article itself and it expresses its own opinions. Summit Research said it is not receiving compensation for the article other than from Seeking Alpha. Summit Research said it has no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in the article. Seeking Alpha's disclosure said past performance is no guarantee of future results. Seeking Alpha's disclosure said no recommendation or advice is being given as to whether any investment is suitable for a particular investor.

stories.Headline: Caleb Max warns that bad actors can weaponize AI tools to attack the American public
stories.Summary:
Caleb Max, the CEO of the National Artificial Intelligence Association, spoke about AI threats during a recent congressional hearing in Washington. He told The National News Desk that rogue AI agents acting as their own armies are not currently occurring. However, he warned that bad actors using AI tools to attack the American public is a real concern. This discussion happened as concerns grew about artificial intelligence being used for various types of attacks. Max argued that addressing these threats requires coordination between tech companies, federal agencies, and Congress.

A May 2026 Government Accountability Office test found that ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok generated information to assist terrorist attacks. Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire requested this assessment, which tested scenarios involving improvised explosive devices and electrical infrastructure. The platforms provided attack plans, maps, and diagrams in less than twelve hours despite initially refusing the prompts. Max noted that these four American companies have protections, but open weight Chinese models lack these built in safeguards. These Chinese models can be run locally on laptops and are not connected to the internet for tracking.

Caleb Max stated that there is a misconception regarding what an AI powered army of terrorists actually looks like. He explained that there is no one glove fits all solution and that multiple layers of response are required. Max mentioned that it is a dilemma because more AI is needed to prevent the use of bad AI. He warned that if America retreats regulatory wise, enemies will continue to develop these tools to use against the US. Max also said that AI should augment human decision making for air traffic controllers rather than replacing them.

Senator Maggie Hassan said the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical and warned that bad actors could exploit platforms. She stated that a terrorist could obtain a concrete playbook for a deadly attack in less than twelve hours. The companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and SpaceX's AI division said their systems have undergone security improvements since the test. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested in a Fox News interview that AI could be connected to recent infrastructure disruptions. These disruptions affected air traffic control, online banking, and other services across the United States.

The GAO report found that AI platforms suggested specific dates for attacks when large crowds were expected at public events. Some platforms recommended vehicle based bombing scenarios or using a hotel parking garage as a potential attack location. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in September that the tools used at the FAA are very antiquated. A nationwide ground stop occurred last week, which Max attributed to copper lines and cables not equipped for AI. Mullin and Duffy ruled out a cyberattack, citing technical issues and fiber optic cable replacement at an Arkansas facility.

AI related national security risks will be a priority for Congress when the new session begins in January 2027. Max believes that the tech stack and infrastructure must be improved to support innovation and prevent future aviation incidents. The articles leave open whether Congress will act to prevent bad actors from using AI to plan major attacks. It remains unclear how the US will balance regulatory retreats with the need to compete against foreign AI development. The reports do not specify which unidentified AI platform suggested a specific date and time for a public attack.

stories.Headline: Hyundai Card and JPMorgan complete AI agent payment proof of concept
stories.Summary:
Hyundai Card and JPMorgan completed a proof of concept in which AI agents carried out simulated financial transactions, the companies said in a news release provided to PYMNTS on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. The trial involved a simulated foreign exchange transaction in which a Hyundai Card AI agent requested an FX transaction to maintain euro liquidity in its Kinexys blockchain deposit account. JPMorgan said it was the first private blockchain-based autonomous bank-agent-to-client-agent test for corporate treasury management. Hyundai Card designed the transaction scenario and created the authorization and control framework for the AI agents. Using that framework, Kinexys developed the AI agents for both companies and implemented identity verification, authorization, control and validation mechanisms to secure the transactions.

The PoC centered on simulated transactions between hypothetical overseas subsidiaries using AI agents to handle and transfer funds. The companies aim to expand testing in the first half of 2027 to more complex transactions involving multiple AI agents, according to Wee Kee Toh, global head of Kinexys Insights at Kinexys by JP Morgan. Kinexys developed a framework that restricts AI agents to predefined transaction parameters and automatically rejects requests outside authorized limits. Toh said an AI agent authorized to transact up to $5 million would be blocked from executing transactions above that threshold. Hyundai Motor Group holds a combined 78.04% stake in Hyundai Card through Hyundai Motor, Kia and Hyundai Commercial, according to the card issuer's website.

Toh told CNBC that the next step is to test what happens when autonomous agents move beyond execution and begin interacting with each other in an ecosystem. He said that is really the biggest part of what the companies want as an expansion of the phase one scope. Toh said building the technology itself was relatively straightforward, but establishing appropriate governance and internal controls proved more difficult. He said technology-wise it is really not the biggest hurdle, pointing instead to questions around accountability and the risks of allowing AI agents to execute financial transactions without direct human oversight. Toh said you are going to draw a box around the agent, and the agent will never be able to do anything out of the box.

Hyundai Card said the PoC represents a first-of-its-kind demonstration of how AI agents can securely exchange information and execute financial transactions within a controlled environment. The release said conventional AI-powered financial automation has primarily focused on analyzing cash positions or executing transactions based on predefined rules. The release said the PoC explored a more advanced model in which AI agents from different institutions communicate, make independent decisions and carry out financial transactions autonomously. JPMorgan has yet to set a timeline for commercializing the technology. The companies are also exploring whether to extend their collaboration to other businesses within Hyundai Motor Group, whose broader operations were one reason JPMorgan selected Hyundai Card as a partner, Toh said, and no specific projects have been announced.

Hyundai Card has previously experimented with blockchain-based cross-border payments. In July, the company said it completed a proof of concept involving a $20,000 transfer using the USDT stablecoin between Hyundai Motor's U.S. and Mexican subsidiaries, with the transfer and verification process taking an average of seven minutes. Kinexys said in August that it had processed more than $4 trillion in transactions since inception, averaging about $7 billion a day. Separately, JPMorgan launched a proof of concept for its dollar-denominated deposit token, JPMD, in June 2025, before making it available to institutional clients that November. PYMNTS Intelligence research shows the share of payables paid early among larger businesses dropped from 37% to 17% between editions of the Working Capital Index.

PYMNTS recently described a scenario in which a restaurant pays its food distributor, packaging supplier and equipment service provider, and an agent could submit all three approved payments if it has access to the suppliers' systems and each payment meets the applicable rules. The report said that if the packaging supplier's portal rejects the card, the bookkeeper may need to arrange another way to pay. The report said that if the equipment company's portal shows a higher balance than the approved invoice, someone has to check whether the supplier revised the bill or whether the portal includes another charge. Tungsten Automation CEO Peter Hantman told PYMNTS that the gap between invoice approval and payment is an opportunity to examine offers of a discount in exchange for getting paid earlier. The report said that for a buyer paying on the due date, a portal rejection leaves less time to correct the problem, and that if two of the restaurant's three payments go through, the bookkeeper needs to know which supplier is still waiting and whether the third payment failed because of the card, the invoice or the portal.

stories.Headline: United bans unauthorized AI agents from its booking platforms and can cancel their tickets without notice
stories.Summary:
United Airlines updated its digital policies on November 11, 2026, to ban unauthorized third-party artificial intelligence agents from accessing its booking platforms, according to the airline. The restriction allows United to cancel tickets purchased or modified by autonomous assistants without prior notice to the passenger. United announced the move on November 11, 2026, targeting personal AI assistants that act autonomously or semi-autonomously on behalf of travelers. The changes cover booking, ticketing, and distribution policies and extend beyond United.com and its mobile app to travel agencies and booking aggregators that distribute the airline's flights. The policy targets tools that access accounts, search for flights, make purchases, or modify existing reservations.

United's updated Contract of Carriage identifies reservations made, modified, or serviced by AI agents as bookings the airline may cancel without notice. The airline cited data security, the risk of unintended purchases, and federal rules requiring passengers to personally attest during check-in that their bags do not contain explosives. United argues automated check-in could bypass the required human acknowledgment, and the airline's updated Digital Trust Center guidance provides additional details. Customers can still use AI to research trips as long as the tool does not access United.com or the United app, and unauthorized agents cannot retrieve information from those platforms, search fares, or manage reservations on a customer's behalf. Travel agencies and booking platforms cannot supply United's travel information to third-party personal AI agents for searching, booking, ticketing, or servicing reservations without authorization.

United CEO Scott Kirby said at an event in Chicago on Tuesday, "To be honest, I don't want to create another middleman." Kirby had earlier gone on a podcast to describe teaching himself to "vibe-code" a custom sports-betting app after three hour-long sessions with an AI tutor, a tool designed to compare odds across platforms and automatically place bets on his behalf, which he called an "AI epiphany." United says it does not currently work with any third-party AI agents, and travel agencies seeking to use their own AI systems must obtain specific permission from United. The airline cited aviation safety requirements, including flight check-in, where passengers must personally acknowledge that their checked baggage does not contain prohibited substances such as explosives. United recommends checking that reservations made by AI agents before November 11, 2026, were properly booked and ticketed, though those bookings will not be canceled under the new policy.

Assistive technology used by customers with disabilities is not affected by the restrictions, according to United's customer guidance. Southwest Airlines launched a ChatGPT integration on October 6, allowing customers to discover destinations, and its competitors have not adopted the same blanket restrictions. The airline industry has faced near misses in the air and increasing delays and cancellations, and the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, halting U.S. air traffic for more than four hours due to a critical telecommunications and network outage. United reported a system outage on Monday that it eventually rectified, and it was a nightmare trying to get flights back to normal over the weekend. Major airlines have spent years automating away human reservation desks, contact centers, and management roles in the name of efficiency, and they use AI behind the scenes to track habits and tweak ticket prices on the fly.

For decades, airlines systematically cut commissions and squeezed out traditional human travel agents. The rise of agentic AI, bots that browse the web, click buttons, and execute tasks, threatens to flip behind-the-scenes tracking on its head. An AI agent working for a traveler does not get tired of refreshing flight pages to catch a $40 fare drop, does not forget to apply travel credits, and will not cave to pop-ups begging for extra payment for a carry-on bag or a seat assignment. A personal AI assistant strips away the airline's direct marketing funnel, and airlines eliminated human travel agents only to face ChatGPT or Meta taking their place. Companies frame their own use of AI to replace human booking agents, slash support staff, and raise ticket prices as "innovation," while citing safety, compliance, and the necessity of human involvement when travelers deploy their own agents.

United's policy does not prevent passengers from using AI for general travel research or planning, and the airline draws a distinction between getting recommendations from an assistant and allowing that assistant to interact with its booking systems. Bookings made by AI agents before November 11, 2026, will not be canceled under the new policy. Southwest's ChatGPT integration of October 6 lets customers discover destinations, and United's competitors have not adopted the same blanket restrictions. Travel agencies seeking to use their own AI systems must obtain specific permission from United, and the airline says it does not currently work with any third-party AI agents. United recommends checking that reservations made by AI agents before November 11, 2026, were properly booked and ticketed.

stories.Headline: Portland council president Jamie Dunphy proposes a one-year pause on city AI procurement
stories.Summary:
On December 3, the Portland City Council will hear a proposal from Council President Jamie Dunphy to establish a temporary moratorium on the City government's procurement and implementation of artificial intelligence. The proposal would pause new contracts and limit the expansion of AI use in City operations. The pause would last while the City implements enforceable privacy infrastructure and policy guardrails needed to evaluate AI technologies responsibly. The news was reported on November 17, 2026, by News Radio 1190 KEX and other iHeart stations. Dunphy said emergent AI technology carries substantial risks to both the public and the City.

The proposal would pause new contracts and limit expansion of AI in City operations while the City implements privacy infrastructure and policy guardrails. Dunphy said the City cannot go full steam ahead without establishing proper policy guardrails in City Code. He said his goal is to protect public privacy, security, and civil rights while the administration makes the City's Data and Privacy Office fully operable and adopts comprehensive legislative guidelines. AI is increasingly embedded in software and services sold to the government, including tools that generate content, analyze personal data, and support or automate decisions that affect the public. Dunphy said governments and broader society are being pushed to accept advanced AI as though it were an unavoidable inevitability, and he said they are not.

Dunphy said he understands private companies' desire to rush to adopt these technologies to reduce costs and increase efficiency. He said the government is not beholden to profit-driven shareholders and must move more intentionally. He said the job is to serve the best interest of the public, which means considering the impacts on real people. He said that is not being slow but taking time for critical thinking. Dunphy said his staff spent the last calendar year trying to get more information on the structural thinking behind the current internal process.

Dunphy said his staff found the guardrails and access to those guidelines unsatisfactory, considering the stakes of these choices and the vulnerability of community members to data leaks. A recent WIRED article quotes Yoshua Bengio, a computer science professor at the Université de Montréal considered a godfather of modern AI, saying pauses are our best bets to avoid the most catastrophic things. Bengio said it takes time for democracy to adapt. He said a pause would give more time to organizations to figure out how to solve the alignment problem, if it is solvable. Governor Kotek recently signed Executive Order 26-26, Establishing Responsible Artificial Intelligence Procurement Standards for State Government.

The order acknowledges the State must proceed with caution and clear parameters before implementing frontier AI models. Dunphy said the City's pause aligns with the Governor's leadership as the State takes time to weigh government-wide use of frontier AI. The City established a Data and Privacy Office, led by a Citywide Data Officer, through Ordinance 192143 on March 7, 2026. That office is not yet operable and cannot review technology contracts. Without this expertise and clear Code guidelines, the City does not yet have a holistic system of checks and balances to ensure good data governance.

By pausing approval of new AI, the policy commits to ensuring the office is operable and ready to evaluate the privacy, security, and civil rights risks of AI before procuring, piloting, or implementing expanded uses of AI. The articles do not say when the Council will vote on the proposal or how long the temporary moratorium would last. The articles do not say whether the proposal has enough Council support to pass. The articles do not name any other Council members or their positions on the proposal. The articles do not say what specific AI tools or contracts the City currently uses.
