stories.Headline: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress tightens review of circular AI financing after record quarterly revenue
stories.Summary:
Nvidia posted record third quarter revenue of 115.8 billion dollars during the period from August to October 2026. This financial result followed the dismissal of former chief executive Jensen Huang from the company. Colette Kress took over as interim CEO and also serves as the chief financial officer. The company reported that its revenue grew 103 percent compared to the same period a year earlier. These results marked the sixteenth consecutive quarter that the company beat earnings expectations on a per share basis.

The company reported earnings per share of 2.70 dollars and guided fourth quarter revenue to reach 130 billion dollars. Future commitments rose to 518 billion dollars from 366 billion dollars, while supply commitments grew to 390 billion dollars. Free cash flow more than doubled to 43.7 billion dollars in the third quarter from 21.3 billion in the second. Nvidia raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecast to 75 percent from a previous estimate of 70 percent. The firm will now tighten its review of circular financing for neoclouds to brake large scale GPU supply guarantees.

Interim CEO Colette Kress declared that the company would apply stricter standards to the massive payment guarantees extended under Huang. She stated that the company would tighten its review of circular financing for neoclouds to manage infrastructure expansion. The company noted in a regulatory filing that revenue topped the 109.1 billion dollar market consensus from the London Stock Exchange Group. These financial figures confirm that the latest artificial intelligence chips developed under the previous chief executive surged in sales. The interim leader signaled a change in the AI infrastructure ecosystem by limiting these specific payment structures.

Analysts said that circular financing could shrink, which might squeeze the ecosystem of cloud providers dedicated to AI workloads. Investors are concerned about excessive AI investment, with a Bank of America survey showing technology stock allocations plunging to 12 percent. This allocation figure dropped from 37 percent in October, and 52 percent of respondents expect hyperscalers to cut capital spending. Domestic AI infrastructure related stocks may see their short term momentum weaken due to the contraction of the neocloud ecosystem. The shift in investment is moving from chip manufacturing toward data storage infrastructure like hard disk drives.

The company previously operated under Jensen Huang, who called himself a piece of shit before he quit the firm. The current market environment shows a trend of funds shifting toward high capacity storage because it is cheaper than NAND. This shift led Stanley Druckenmiller to cut TSMC by 94.5 percent and sell all stakes in AMD, Arm, and SanDisk. He expanded holdings in Seagate by 180.2 percent and added Western Digital to his portfolio at the third quarter end. These moves reflect a broader expectation of surging demand for storage as AI data centers continue to expand.

Nvidia will now implement a strict review of circular financing to manage the supply and payment guarantees for neoclouds. The company will monitor if the neocloud ecosystem contracts and how this affects the broader AI infrastructure landscape. Market observers are watching to see if the momentum for domestic AI infrastructure stocks will weaken in the coming months. The articles leave open whether the new stricter standards will significantly slow the overall expansion of AI cloud services. It remains unclear how the transition to an interim CEO will affect long term strategic decisions at Nvidia.

stories.Headline: Giga Energy signs $1 billion lease for 60MW Texas AI data center
stories.Summary:
Giga Energy, an AI data center developer based in the United States, announced on November 17, 2026 a $1 billion lease agreement with an undisclosed U.S.-based AI cloud provider for a 60MW GigaBase AI data center in Hunt County, Texas. The company broke ground on the project, called Project Clay, in July and will develop, own and operate the campus for the customer. The roughly 30-acre campus is scheduled to be ready for service in spring 2027 and will provide AI computing capacity for hyperscale and AI cloud customers. The project is designed to meet priorities that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has called for, including protecting local resources, investing in dedicated infrastructure and ensuring communities benefit from growth.

The development is expected to create about 300 construction jobs during the build phase and 24 permanent full-time positions with estimated annual salaries ranging from $116,000 to $180,000. It is also expected to generate millions in new recurring annual tax revenue for local schools, infrastructure, emergency services and other public needs. The project includes an investment in new electrical infrastructure that taps underutilized capacity on dedicated power infrastructure in the county, and it is designed so it does not draw on distribution capacity serving existing homes and businesses. Instead of open-loop evaporative cooling, Project Clay uses a fully closed-loop system that operates independently of local water supplies, with the only local water used for sinks and employee bathrooms, on par with the usage of two homes annually.

Giga says the project will finish in under eight months, less than half the time of traditional builds, using a factory-first construction model in which much of the facility is manufactured off-site before final assembly in the community. Brent Whitehead, president and co-founder at Giga Energy, said the company believes AI infrastructure should leave a community stronger than it found it, through high-paying jobs, an expanded local tax base and long-term investments that benefit residents for decades. He said Hunt County is gaining an economic engine that will support schools, public services and future growth for generations. Whitehead also said the project is exactly the kind of AI infrastructure Texas needs, and that communities should not have to choose between economic growth and protecting local resources.

Giga Energy describes itself as a U.S.-based developer, operator and manufacturer of AI data centers, with factories in Long Beach and Houston, and says it has delivered gigawatts of sites and critical infrastructure across the country. The project aligns with Texas' growing emphasis on water-efficient data center development in drought-prone regions, according to the announcement. Giga Energy leaders say that as demand for AI infrastructure continues to accelerate across the United States, the next generation of data centers must do more than power technology and must also earn the trust of the communities where they are built. With this project, Giga officially unveils its GigaBase system, which the company says is engineered to address lengthy construction timelines, heavy water consumption and pressure on local utilities.

stories.Headline: Max Roser finds every high-quality US survey shows more negative than positive views on AI
stories.Summary:
Just Capital released the third edition of its monthly National AI Monitor on November 18, 2026, asking Americans how they experience AI as workers, consumers, community members, investors and environmental stewards. The survey was conducted online within the United States by The Harris Poll on behalf of Just Capital from October 19 to 21, 2026 among 1,008 U.S. adults ages 18 and older. Just Capital reported that Americans' experiences with AI have trended positive or remained steady across every measure since the organization began this research in August 2026. The results show clear divides across demographics and stakeholder categories in how Americans experience AI, and the differences become more pronounced when respondents are asked about the years ahead. Full-time workers, college graduates and adults ages 35 to 44 maintain a positive outlook, while retirees, people not employed, those with some college but no degree, and Americans 65 and over turn net negative.

Scores are calculated as the percentage of positive responses minus the percentage of negative responses, producing a range from -100 to +100. The overall score was +35 in August, +37 in September and +42 in October, while the forward-looking score for the next few years was +15, +12 and +14 across the same months. Work scored +48, +44 and +47, customer experience +21, +25 and +26, community engagement +7, +12 and +15, investments +21, +24 and +31, and environmental stewardship -17, -12 and -9. Changes month to month are not statistically significant, but changes between August and October are statistically significant for community engagement, investments and environmental stewardship. The sample data is accurate to within plus or minus 3.6 percentage points using a 95% confidence level, a credible interval that will be wider among subsets of the surveyed population.

Just Capital CEO Martin Whittaker said Americans feel more positively about AI when they see tangible opportunities for themselves in the AI-powered economy. He said the latest results indicate that experience is most pronounced among working, educated Americans who are more likely to say AI has beneficial effects in their work, investments and communities. He also said there are early signs that people can feel good about AI in their own lives while worrying about what it means for society at large, and that AI can bridge existing divides or compound them. Whittaker said whether America successfully embraces AI economically, socially and politically rests on how good the country is at closing the gap between what ordinary working Americans expect the technology to deliver and what they actually experience. He said decision makers in tech, business and government will ignore this at their peril.

Drivers of positive experience include the ability to focus on more fulfilling work, cited by a 58-year-old man in Florida with an associate's degree who is self-employed part-time, lower income and a very positive respondent on AI at work. Speed, convenience and personalization were cited by a 37-year-old woman in Texas who completed graduate school, is employed full-time, upper income and a very positive respondent on AI as a customer, though she worries about data privacy, inaccurate information and less human interaction. A 33-year-old man in California who completed graduate school, is employed full-time, middle income and a very positive respondent on AI in the community cited optimization of local traffic management to cut city gridlock. Drivers of negative experience include environmental impacts such as data centers, water use, electricity use and grid strain, cited by a 73-year-old woman in Texas who completed some college but no degree, is retired, lower income and a very negative respondent on AI and the environment. A 32-year-old woman in Ohio, a college graduate who is self-employed part-time, lower income and a very negative respondent on AI overall, said she lost her job to AI while it makes her technology increasingly unusable.

Our World in Data's Max Roser wrote that he searched for a range of recent high-quality surveys and put them together in a chart, including only surveys based on probability samples. Quinnipiac called randomly generated landline and cell phone numbers, while the other four surveyed members of online panels recruited at random, mostly by mail to randomly selected addresses: Pew's American Trends Panel, the Gallup Panel, the panel used by the Annenberg Public Policy Center and Ipsos's KnowledgePanel. All five surveys weight their results to match the US adult population and publish the full wording of their questions and their results, and Roser excluded polls based on opt-in online panels, citing an opt-in poll that found 20% of Americans under 30 agreed the Holocaust is a myth when Pew's probability-based panel found 3%. In Pew's survey, 37% took a middle answer when one was offered, and in both Pew's and Gallup's surveys only 9% chose a positive view. In Pew's survey 52% say they are more concerned than excited and 9% more excited than concerned, a ratio of more than five to one, compared with about two to one when Pew first asked this in 2021.

In the Ipsos survey, 17% said AI is an extremely bad thing for society and just 2% said extremely good, while 50% said AI is a good thing for them personally and 49% a bad thing, with 15% saying extremely bad for them personally against 3% extremely good. In a Quinnipiac poll in September 2026, 35% said they are somewhat concerned and 38% very concerned that future AI systems could potentially threaten human survival, with 14% not so concerned, 11% not concerned at all and 1% don't know or no answer, and 73% believe there is a risk AI could threaten the survival of humanity. In Pew's survey, 56% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans are more concerned than excited about AI, and in both parties only around one in ten are more excited than concerned. In Quinnipiac's March 2026 poll, 55% expected AI to do more harm than good in their day-to-day life against 34% who expected more good, and 86% supported independent safety standards for AI companies. Pew's survey of 3,488 US adults on the American Trends Panel was conducted June 22 to 28, 2026, with November 2021 data from the same panel collected November 1 to 7, 2021, and the Gallup and Bentley University survey of 3,270 US adults on the Gallup Panel was conducted May 4 to 11, 2026.

Quinnipiac's telephone survey of 1,397 US adults was conducted March 19 to 23, 2026, the Annenberg survey of 1,320 US adults was conducted June 16 to July 19, 2026, and the Ipsos survey of 2,545 US adults on the KnowledgePanel was conducted October 9 to 13, 2026. Quinnipiac's September poll was a telephone survey of 1,202 US adults conducted September 24 to 27, 2026 using random digit dialing, with live interviewers calling landlines and cell phones. Roser wrote that the survey's wording does matter and that what surprised him is how consistent the overall result is, with every survey finding more Americans have a negative view of AI than a positive one. He wrote that few Americans are enthusiastic about AI and that when people have strong feelings they are mostly negative, and that concern about AI is not confined to one party. He wrote that many find the prospects of AI exciting but that for more Americans the concerns are larger, and that if the industry wants to earn the public's trust it will have to take these widespread concerns much more seriously than it has so far.

stories.Headline: UN chief Guterres warns autonomous weapons cross a moral red line as Geneva talks open
stories.Summary:
United Nations negotiations regarding rules for lethal autonomous weapons are currently taking place in Geneva. These talks focus on killer robots and occur during a week of meetings in November 2026. The conference on Certain Conventional Weapons meets only once every five years to discuss these issues. Supporters believe this meeting is the last best chance to agree on rules before it is too late. Experts warn that weapons capable of choosing targets autonomously could exist within just a few months.

The proposed rules would govern autonomous weapons in places like Ukraine and Gaza where AI assisted tools are used. At least 50 countries, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France, and Germany, want a strict timetable for binding rules. The United States, Russia, and Israel oppose binding rules, with Washington proposing a five year timetable for non binding guidelines. These rules would address the Geneva Conventions and the protection of wounded soldiers or those surrendering. The 1995 ban on blinding lasers serves as a previous example of achieving consensus on specific weapons.

United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres stated that allowing autonomous weapons to kill would cross a moral red line. Georgia Haines of the Red Cross said these weapons cannot understand contextual signals like a human can. She warned that the risk of misidentifying a target is incredibly high based on current technology. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently warned against quoting laws to men with swords in a keynote speech. OpenAI leaders Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, and Ilya Sutskever suggested an international authority similar to the IAEA.

Humanitarian organizations and the Pope argue that the decision to kill must remain in human hands. Human rights groups warn that cheap AI technology could be used by terrorist groups or repressive regimes. They fear drones could be programmed to kill people based on language, posters, or wearing a red sweater. AI researcher Yoshua Bengio told the UN Security Council that frontier AI should be licensed like medicine or aviation. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker compared the threat of artificial intelligence to the danger of nuclear weapons.

AI assisted weapons have already been used in Gaza and Ukraine, where civilians report being hunted by drones. The United States previously avoided the Ottawa Convention on landmines but eventually reduced its own stockpiles. Nuclear nonproliferation is often cited as a model, though it relied on coercion by the US and allies. Some states like India, Israel, North Korea, and Pakistan acquired nuclear weapons despite existing nonproliferation regimes. China has tripled its number of nuclear weapons during the current decade, showing the limits of management.

Diplomats may compromise with an open ended negotiating period for rules that states adopt as binding or non binding. Some campaigners believe this approach is merely kicking a dangerous can down the road to avoid immediate action. The US could lead by disclosing risks, limitations, and findings before deploying powerful and risky AI systems. Future requirements might include reporting serious safety failures or publishing conditions for pausing the development of AI. The articles leave open whether the international community can reach a consensus or if nations will act alone.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO as the stock falls nearly 30% in a month
stories.Summary:
Nvidia stock fell nearly 30 percent in one month by November 17, 2026, as investors worried about the company's future leadership. This decline happened after Jensen Huang resigned from his roles as president and chief executive officer of the chipmaker. David Jagielski suggests that investors consider three other artificial intelligence stocks that may be safer buys than Nvidia right now. These alternative options include Alphabet, Amazon, and Broadcom, which the analyst believes are more attractive for investors today. The Motley Fool also notes that the artificial intelligence market is only finishing its first research and development phase.

Alphabet has a market cap of 3.4 trillion dollars and a forward price to earnings multiple of under 20. Amazon has a market cap of 2.8 trillion dollars and a forward price to earnings multiple of 24. Broadcom trades at a forward price to earnings multiple of 18 and fell 30 percent from its 495 dollar high. Berkshire Hathaway ended September with 377.4 billion dollars in cash and Treasury bills to use for future investments. ASML trades at a forward price to earnings multiple of 23 and has a market cap of 576.26 billion dollars.

David Jagielski says Alphabet is an underrated stock that the market does not value fairly given its diverse business opportunities. He believes Amazon is a cheap looking stock because it has far more room to rise higher than its current valuation. Jagielski describes Broadcom as a growth beast and a safer investment with less downside risk after its recent stock decline. Adam Spatacco predicts that Berkshire Hathaway could use its cash to buy ASML because it possesses a monopoly like market position. Spatacco notes that ASML provides indispensable equipment that other companies need to compete in the semiconductor industry.

Amazon shoppers are affected by the new Amazon Haul service, which helps the company appeal to more price conscious customers. Customers like Intel, Samsung, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing rely on ASML to manufacture the most cutting edge semiconductor chips. The Motley Fool Stock Advisor team identified ten best stocks for investors, but they did not include Alphabet on that list. This team claims that investing 1,000 dollars in Netflix on December 17, 2004, would have grown to 327,620 dollars. An investment of 1,000 dollars in Nvidia on April 15, 2005, would have become 959,410 dollars by November 2026.

Amazon reported 12 percent revenue growth for the September quarter, while Amazon Web Services grew at a rate of 39 percent. Broadcom saw revenue rise 86 percent year over year to 29.6 billion dollars for the quarter ending August 2. ASML generated 11.7 billion euros in revenue and 5 billion euros in net income during its third quarter. ASML is the only commercial manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, which are essential for producing advanced semiconductors. Berkshire Hathaway expanded its investment in Alphabet after opening a position in the third quarter of last year.

Broadcom expects its growth rate to rise to 93 percent for the last quarter of its current fiscal year. ASML management guided for full year revenue between 44 billion and 45 billion euros with a 56 percent margin. Some ASML customers are already expressing interest in equipment deliveries that are scheduled for the years 2029 and 2030. The Anthropic initial public offering takes place on November 19, where investors will learn three key details about the company. The articles leave open whether Berkshire Hathaway will actually use its cash to purchase shares of the company ASML.

stories.Headline: South Korean stocks fall for a fourth day as AI concerns deepen
stories.Summary:
South Korean stocks sank for the fourth consecutive session on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, as lingering concerns over artificial intelligence dampened investor sentiment. The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index lost 132.02 points, or 2.59 percent, to close at 4,968.48. The index fell below the 5,000-point mark to its lowest level in nine months. The Korean won weakened against the U.S. dollar. Trade volume was light at 183.09 million shares worth 14.19 trillion won, or $10.61 billion.

Decliners far outnumbered advancers 709 to 182. Foreigners sold a net 1.44 trillion won, while institutions and individuals bought a net 543.56 billion won and 421.79 billion won, respectively. Top market cap Samsung Electronics decreased 3.3 percent to 190,300 won, and chip giant SK hynix shed 1.96 percent to 1.1 million won. SK Square, the parent of SK hynix, retreated 1.31 percent to 679,000 won. Power equipment manufacturer Samsung Electro-Mechanics sank 3.95 percent to 754,000 won.

The Korean won was trading at 1,338.2 won against the U.S. dollar as of 3:30 p.m., down 1.7 won from the previous session's close. Bond prices, which move inversely to yields, closed higher. The yield on three-year Treasurys shed 1.8 basis points to 3.725, and the return on the benchmark five-year government bonds fell 0.5 basis point to 3.825. Kang Jin-hyuk, an analyst at Shinhan Securities, said the market came under pressure from continued fallout surrounding Nvidia. He also cited U.S. restrictions on remote access to Nvidia's AI chips and concerns over the sustainability of AI demand, which dampened investors' risk appetite.

On Wall Street, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped about 2.5 percent Monday, while AI chip giant Nvidia shares slid 4.1 percent. The Nvidia decline came amid continued uncertainty following the departure of its CEO, Jensen Huang, last week. Nvidia is scheduled to report its earnings Tuesday, with investors closely watching its outlook for AI chip demand and infrastructure spending. Investors are also keeping an eye on AI giant Anthropic's planned Nasdaq debut Thursday. The AI sector is also facing increased regulatory scrutiny after the U.S. government issued new rules Monday restricting remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers.

An electronic board showing the Korea Composite Stock Price Index stood at a dealing room of the Hana Bank headquarters in Seoul on Tuesday. An employee stood before an electronic display board in Hana Bank's headquarters in central Seoul on Nov. 17. Financial data was shown on a screen in the dealing room of Hana Bank in Seoul after the market closed on Nov. 17, 2026. The Korea Herald published its report on Nov. 17, 2026, at 15:51:26. The Korea JoongAng Daily published its report on November 17, 2026, at 5:00 p.m.

Nvidia is scheduled to report its earnings Tuesday, and Anthropic's planned Nasdaq debut is set for Thursday. Investors are closely watching Nvidia's outlook for AI chip demand and infrastructure spending. The U.S. government issued new rules Monday restricting remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers. stories.Headline: ZeroEyes deploys AI gun detection at Cornerstone Christian Academy in Las Vegas
stories.Summary:
ZeroEyes announced on November 17, 2026, that it deployed AI gun detection software at Cornerstone Christian Academy. This proactive technology was installed to protect the school community from gun related violence. The deployment occurred at a private school located in Las Vegas, Nevada. This system helps the academy identify weapons to keep them off the campus. The software provides situational awareness to enhance the safety of students and staff.

The school serves about 500 students from 18 months through 8th grade on 4.6 acres. ZeroEyes layers onto 100 existing 4K cameras to identify guns and knives in real time. The system sends images to the ZeroEyes Operations Center, a 24/7 U.S. based facility. Verified threats are reported in seconds to school leadership and local law enforcement officers. The academy also uses Centegix, secure entrances, emergency response systems, and instant alert lanyards.

Vice principal Sean Stafford said keeping students safe is the top priority over the last four years. He described the ZeroEyes addition as an exciting next step to add another layer of protection. CEO Mike Lahiff stated that ZeroEyes is proud to partner with schools investing in safety strategies. Security directors Marco and Michael Saunders, retired law enforcement, said safety is their top priority since 2022. JT Wilkins explained that the system takes snapshots of firearms or edged weapons for verification.

Parent Dr. Tessa Rivera said that feeling safe affords children the opportunity for learning and peace of mind. She noted that kids today are jarringly familiar with soft and hard lockdown drills in their vocabulary. Preschool director Kate Anyanwu believes the technology could be preventative by making potential intruders think twice. Anyanwu mentioned that the system is like a barking dog that might deter someone from breaking in. The system once notified staff about a water gun fight, which the center verified as harmless.

ZeroEyes was founded in 2018 by elite technologists and Navy SEALs to mitigate gun related incidents. The company is headquartered in the Greater Philadelphia area and uses a proprietary dataset of millions of images. Its technology is the first AI gun detection platform to achieve full SAFETY Act Designation from the government. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security recognized the patented system as an effective solution for anti terrorism. The platform is used in thousands of locations across India, Mexico, the Caribbean, Latin America, and the US.

The company continues to advance its platform to deliver high reliability as security needs evolve over time. ZeroEyes also provides active shooter preparedness training, system integration support, and various security assessments for its customers. The articles do not state if the school plans to add more AI tools in the future. It is not mentioned if other Nevada schools will adopt this specific weapons detection software soon. The text leaves open whether the system will be expanded to other private campuses in the region.

stories.Headline: Moody's chief economist Mark Zandi warns AI boom raises inflation and borrowing costs while diverting investment
stories.Summary:
Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi warned in a post on X on Sunday that the artificial intelligence boom is driving up inflation and borrowing costs while pulling investment away from the rest of the U.S. economy. He wrote that AI has been a boon to economic growth and job creation, but that its rapid expansion is bringing significant side effects. According to Zandi, AI is adding to inflation by driving up electricity and consumer electronics prices. He also said AI investment is pushing up interest rates by soaking up capital to finance the AI build-out.

Zandi said the massive flow of money into AI infrastructure is coming at the expense of other investment. Since ChatGPT debuted four years ago, he said, AI has gone from a rounding error to accounting for nearly two-thirds of the growth in investment. At the same time, growth in everything else has slowed by more than half since mid-2024, he added. He concluded that the bet on AI had better pay off in higher productivity, because the rest of the economy is not investing enough to deliver it.

Other economists and institutions have raised related concerns in recent months. Last month, economist Peter Schiff warned that rising borrowing costs could weaken AI investment and expose broader economic vulnerabilities, while potentially benefiting gold and gold-mining stocks during an impending recession. Former Federal Reserve adviser Danielle DiMartino Booth also suggested a recession may already be underway. In September, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said AI infrastructure spending could reach $1 trillion in 2027, adding about 1% to GDP growth annually while potentially contributing to inflation, and cautioned that it was too early to identify winners and losers in the AI boom.

In July, the International Monetary Fund warned that weaker-than-expected AI productivity gains could trigger a pullback in technology investment and a sharp correction in highly valued tech stocks. The IMF also raised its 2026 global inflation forecast to 4.7%. The Benzinga article carries a disclaimer stating that its content was partially produced with the help of AI tools and was reviewed and published by Benzinga editors. It also notes that Benzinga does not provide investment advice.

stories.Headline: Code Effects releases Version 7 with secure AI agents and rule auditing for .NET
stories.Summary:
Code Effects Software, LLC released Code Effects Version 7 on November 18, 2026, according to an announcement dated Atlanta, Nov. 18, 2026. The release was reported by GlobeNewswire and published by The Manila Times on November 19, 2026. The company described itself as a provider of embeddable .NET business rules engine technology. Version 7 introduces AI-assisted rule authoring, secure AI agent integration, centralized rule repositories, version management, testing, production evaluation auditing, and AI-powered reporting. The platform lets organizations incorporate artificial intelligence into business rule management while preserving deterministic execution, granular permissions, and human oversight of production operations.

Version 7 includes an embeddable Model Context Protocol server that lets external AI clients and autonomous agents interact with business rules, source objects, versions, tests, and evaluation history. It supports user-delegated agents, which operate on behalf of authenticated users and inherit their permissions and access restrictions, and independent agents and services, which operate under separate identities with individually configured permissions. Both models are subject to additional, non-bypassable security restrictions enforced internally by Code Effects, even if the host application mistakenly grants permissions authorizing the operations. AI agents and independent services cannot approve rules, delete rules or source objects, publish rules to production (Go Live), or take production rules offline. AI-generated changes also require human approval before production deployment.

Users can create, modify, and investigate business rules through natural-language interactions, and an AI assistant can translate business requirements into structured rules using the fields, methods, and operators exposed by the host application. Generated rules remain readable and editable in the Code Effects visual Rule Editor and are validated against the application's source definitions. The platform follows a Bring Your Own AI approach, allowing organizations to integrate any commercial or privately hosted language models without depending on a proprietary AI provider. Through the MCP server, authorized users and agents can request rule explanations, compare versions, investigate failed tests, analyze evaluation history, and generate reports using natural language. The new Code Effects Rule Repository provides embeddable web-based interfaces for managing rules, source objects, versions, tests, approvals, and user activity.

Version 7 introduces centralized rule storage, rule and source versioning, draft management, approval workflows, and permission-controlled access. Built-in testing allows users to define input values, specify expected outcomes, execute tests against individual rule versions, and inspect detailed results, and saved tests support regression testing when business logic changes. The new Code Effects Audit component records production rule evaluations, including executed rule versions, relevant inputs, results, and execution details, and authorized users can investigate why a particular decision occurred, review historical evaluations, analyze rule behavior, and replay recorded evaluations for testing and troubleshooting. AI assistants can use this information to answer questions about rule performance, execution history, and decision outcomes, subject to the requesting identity's permissions. Audit is designed to operate asynchronously without unnecessarily delaying normal rule execution.

Version 7 also enhances the core rules engine and editor with additional operators, collection functions, string and date operations, improved nullable-value handling, inline rule execution, rule composition, and enhanced validation. The engine continues to execute approved business logic deterministically within the host application's .NET environment, without requiring an LLM for ordinary rule execution. Code Effects Version 7 remains an embeddable, self-hosted platform, and customers maintain control over their infrastructure, authentication, permissions, business rules, and evaluation data. The repository initially supports Microsoft SQL Server and PostgreSQL, with Oracle and MySQL support planned for subsequent releases. Core assemblies target .NET Standard 2.0, while the MCP server requires .NET 8 or later.

Code Effects was founded in 2009 and develops embeddable business rules engine and rule management technology. Code Effects Version 7 is available through the company's distribution and licensing channels, and product development contact Sergey Minin can be reached at [email protected]. Code Effects also plans to release the entire Version 7 platform for Java in Q1 2027, including the rules engine, visual editor, repository, audit, MCP server, and AI integration capabilities. The articles leave open the pricing of Version 7 and the timing of Oracle and MySQL support. The articles also leave open how the Java release will be delivered and licensed.

stories.Headline: Warsh leads San Francisco Fed panels on how AI could reshape productivity and jobs
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh opened a conference at the San Francisco Fed on Monday at 9 a.m. Pacific with 15 minutes of remarks, then led panels for most of the morning. The panels featured Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, Stanford economist Nick Bloom, and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, according to the published agenda. The topic was how artificial intelligence, which the Fed calls superintelligence, will change productivity and jobs. Warsh was sworn in as Federal Reserve Chair on May 22 under pressure from President Donald Trump to lower interest rates.

The conference took place as the $31 trillion Treasury market sent Warsh a signal. The Fed lifted the upper bound of its target range to 4.00% in September, from 3.75%. Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, above the 2% to 3% range considered healthy trend growth. In the week ending November 13, the 10-year Treasury yield rose from 4.86% to 5.15%, and the 30-year reached 5.47%. Data centers could use up to 12% of U.S. electricity demand by 2028, according to Energy Department projections.

Core Personal Consumption Expenditures prices, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose 0.3% in September. Warsh said at Jackson Hole in August that "We've come to a hinge point in history" and called AI "potentially a new factor of production." He asked whether AI would "cause a significant, sustained rise in productivity across the economy" and who ends up with the gains. At his October 28 press conference, he said "Productivity growth is strong and capital investment robust" while noting inflation has run above target "for close to six years." He asked whether AI would bring a rapid productivity miracle or gradual gains, and whether it would make price stability easier or harder.

Warsh said capital spending sits "at a historically high share of GDP," led by high-tech investment. The independent market monitor for PJM Interconnection, which runs the largest U.S. power grid, concluded that "data center load growth is the primary reason" for its tight supply and high prices. Inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings were $11.26 in October, a preliminary figure, down from $11.38 a year earlier. The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index fell to 48.1 in September, a level associated with recessions.

Unemployment sits at 4.1%, so AI has not caused mass layoffs, and it has yet to show up in paychecks. Warsh has said the task force's findings will inform future policy judgments, not dictate immediate decisions. Bond investors are betting against an AI productivity miracle, with the 10-year Treasury yield jumping and the 30-year hitting 5%. If AI lifts productivity fast enough, the Fed could hold or cut rates, easing mortgage costs and supporting stocks well beyond NVIDIA.

If spending keeps outpacing efficiency gains, the Fed is dealing with a classic overheating economy, and long-term yields above 5% could stick. Data centers compete with everyone else for power, chips, and electricians, which pushes prices up well before any productivity return. The efficiency gains come later, but the construction bills are due now. Monday is unlikely to bring a rate signal, so two things are worth tracking instead.

The first is whether Warsh presents strong productivity as a reason for patience on rates. The second is the next reading of core Personal Consumption Expenditures prices. Cooler readings alongside 3% growth would be the first real evidence of an AI productivity boom. The articles leave open whether AI will deliver a rapid productivity miracle or gradual gains, and whether it will make price stability easier or harder to achieve.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave raises full-year revenue forecast as quarterly revenue jumps 168%
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported third-quarter results on Nov. 10, and its stock jumped about 14% in premarket trading the next morning, while Nvidia, Nebius, Iren, Oracle and many other AI-related stocks rose with it. The report came after a rough few weeks for AI stocks, when the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on Nov. 5 alone, leaving it about 12% below the record it set in October. CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren had each fallen at least 40% from the Nasdaq's Oct. 6 peak, and Nvidia lost more than $400 billion of market value in one two-day slide. That slide came before the scandal and departure of CEO Jensen Huang came to light. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told analysts the company is largely sold out through 2027, with roughly 10 times as much qualified demand as available capacity through the end of next year.

CoreWeave's revenue rose 168% year over year in the third quarter, handily surpassing analyst expectations, and management raised its full-year revenue forecast to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion, up from $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion in August. CoreWeave's revenue backlog, the value of signed customer contracts it hasn't yet recognized as revenue, rose 138% from a year earlier to about $132.5 billion. OpenAI, Perplexity and Jane Street all expanded their relationships with CoreWeave during the quarter, and the company expects to collect about $9 billion of customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months. Management said CoreWeave doesn't plan to issue additional unsecured debt at the parent company level through 2027 and expects cash flow from existing contracts to cover its debt repayments. CoreWeave's debt more than doubled this year to about $47 billion at the end of September.

Intrator told analysts the company is largely sold out through 2027, with roughly 10 times as much qualified demand as available capacity through the end of next year. Management raised its full-year revenue forecast to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion, up from $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion in August. Management said CoreWeave doesn't plan to issue additional unsecured debt at the parent company level through 2027 and expects cash flow from existing contracts to cover its debt repayments. Management expects net interest expense to be $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion in the fourth quarter. CoreWeave's net interest expense was $846 million in the third quarter, more than twice its adjusted operating income, and the company still lost $709 million under generally accepted accounting principles.

Analysts at Bernstein called it about the best quarter we could have asked for, but they also warned that CoreWeave will be among the first and hardest hit when the shortage of AI computing capacity eases. Amazon still expects about $220 billion of capital expenditures in 2026, and Alphabet expects its spending to increase significantly in 2027. Several candidates who won in last week's midterm elections campaigned for tighter regulation of data centers, including moratoriums on new construction in Texas. On Nov. 10, SoftBank took a $3.7 billion write-down on payments for equipment to power its U.S. data centers. Borrowing costs have climbed, with the 10-year Treasury yield topping 5.3% in October.

CoreWeave rents out Nvidia-powered computing capacity to AI developers, and it has borrowed heavily to build its data centers. Its debt more than doubled this year to about $47 billion at the end of September, which made its report one of the most closely watched tests of the AI build-out this earnings season. Most of the recent fear has centered on the cost of building AI infrastructure, especially for companies that need to borrow money to fund the build-out. CoreWeave sits at the center of those concerns. The report lines up with what the biggest AI spenders said a few weeks ago.

Nvidia is set to report earnings after the close on Tuesday, and investors will be watching the close, not just for the company's growth metrics, but for management's commentary in its first report since founder and CEO Jensen Huang stepped down. Nvidia reports after the close on Nov. 17. CoreWeave's report answered the most pressing question hanging over AI stocks, whether customers are still willing to pay for AI computing capacity, and for now the answer looks like a strong yes. The bigger risk for the sector seems to be the cost of financing the build-out, not demand. One strong quarter doesn't end the debate about an AI bubble, and there are still concerns worth keeping an eye on.

stories.Headline: Oakland City Council unanimously extends its AI data center moratorium for 10 months
stories.Summary:
The Oakland City Council voted unanimously this week to extend the city's moratorium on AI data centers for 10 months, passing the extension at Tuesday's council meeting. The extension keeps the existing 45-day moratorium in place until Oct. 5, 2027. The original 45-day moratorium passed on Oct. 6 and was set to expire on Nov. 20. Councilmember Carroll Fife is leading the City Council's efforts to pass the moratorium. The city must produce a policy that protects residents from the public health and safety dangers posed by the proliferation of data centers.

Fife said two of the giants in the tech industry have leased space in West Oakland, and another has shown interest in a downtown location. Mayor Barbara Lee backed the original 45-day moratorium in her recent State of the City address. Lee said residents need to weigh in on any industry that is trying to come to Oakland. Other California cities that already have passed data center moratoriums include San Francisco, Hayward, Oakley, Richmond, Monterey Park, Gilroy, South El Monte, Montebello, and Calexico. Thirty-five public speakers signed up to talk about the moratorium extension, and almost all of them supported it.

Fife said the city is seeing basically an uprising across the country over how data centers operate in regard to land use, impacts to the environment, excessive water use and pollution, air pollution, noise pollution, and a host of things negatively impacting communities. Fife said she felt it was imperative that she take immediate action to protect Oakland residents from what has been seen in other parts of the country. Fife said the move is not a rejection of technology or of economic growth but guardrails against an industry that has steamrolled individuals throughout the entire globe. Fife said it is important that staff have the ability to do the appropriate study and the appropriate outreach to the community, so the community has a voice in anything that will impact their lives. Bill Gilchrist, director of the city's Planning and Building Department, said the city is committed to looking at areas that might be most severely impacted by land use and residential proximity and to engaging community members who historically have not been able to participate.

Laney College professor Peter Brown said people should not cast their vote based on the illusion of the old economy, where corporate investment in Oakland meant thousands of lasting, good-paying jobs and property, business, and income taxes flowing into city coffers. Brown said those days are long gone in this new economy, where every investment is just another asset to be exploited and used as collateral for more investment, and every corporate move is to extract from communities. Nyah Tisdell, an East Oakland community organizer with Communities for a Better Environment, said community members say no to data centers that would go straight to East Oakland, which already has so much industry and so much pollution. A speaker for Care for Community Action said her organization has surveyed more than 400 residents and found that 73% favor a permanent ban on all data centers being built in Oakland. Rev. Leslie Bowling-Dyer said data centers are part of the necessary infrastructure for the rise of an economically and politically untouchable class, and that technological innovation is not equivalent to social progress.

Protesters rallied against data centers outside Oakland city hall in September, according to a photo courtesy of Saumya Roy/Al Jazeera. Some of the speakers urged the council to consider a permanent ban on data center development in the city. Gilchrist said the idea for the city is to do no harm. Fife said she represents a district that many of these potential entities are interested in. The article was written by Ken Epstein.

The moratorium extension gives the city time to produce a policy protecting residents from the public health and safety dangers posed by the proliferation of data centers. The city is to look at areas that might be most severely impacted by land use and residential proximity during the moratorium. The article does not state what policy the city will produce or when beyond the Oct. 5, 2027 date. The article does not state whether the council will consider the permanent ban that speakers urged. The article does not state what action the city will take on the leased West Oakland space or the downtown interest.

stories.Headline: Chinese entities use output from US AI models to train domestic rivals amid chip curbs
stories.Summary:
Chinese entities are using output from leading American AI models to train domestic rivals, according to a review of over 300 documents. This practice, known as distillation, has moved from academic experiments into mainstream industrial use to offset tightening US chip curbs. The process involves a powerful teacher model generating answers that developers then use to train a smaller student system. Chinese researchers use these models to produce computer code, find solutions to difficult problems, and answer various questions. This trend continues as China aims to broaden its AI strategy and reduce its reliance on American technology.

Washington announced on November 16 that it would further restrict China's access to chips from companies like Nvidia. In November 2024, Shanghai Jiao Tong University researchers used 5,000 answers from OpenAI's o1 model to train Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B model. Alibaba researchers used OpenAI's GPT-4 and GPT-4o in April 2025 to generate training material in languages other than Chinese. In February 2026, Meituan and Shanghai Jiao Tong University used GPT-4o to train a model to organize AI agents. Beijing is encouraging distillation to make AI cheaper and easier to deploy across the manufacturing sector in China.

US Commerce Department officials raised concerns in Chengdu in July that some distillation activities could amount to intellectual property theft. A US official stated that industrial-scale distillation is the main reason Chinese AI models have narrowed the gap with rivals. Chinese officials defended the practice as a standard development technique and said they were open to acting against theft. The US Commerce Department and China's Cyberspace Administration did not respond to requests for comment on these matters. Chinese officials made no concrete commitments to the US regarding the regulation of these specific AI training activities.

OpenAI and Anthropic have terms that restrict using their model output to develop competing systems without receiving prior permission. US authorities publicly accused Chinese companies in September of conducting aggressive, targeted distillation of American AI models on an industrial scale. Two people familiar with Chinese operations disputed US claims, citing advances in algorithms, data, and model design as factors. Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Alibaba, and Meituan did not respond to requests for comment regarding their specific research papers. Researchers cautioned that excessive reliance on distillation could stifle original innovation and leave developers dependent on more advanced providers.

Eight Chinese government agencies published a national AI+Manufacturing policy package in January supporting model training, fine-tuning, and distillation. The cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen have also encouraged techniques that reduce the computing requirements for artificial intelligence. Distillation is not illegal and is prevalent in other parts of the world, though it cannot reproduce full capabilities. The process helps developers preserve selected skills in smaller systems that cost less to operate than the original models. These policies reflect Beijing's ambition to deploy smaller and cheaper AI systems across the world's second-largest economy.

President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Chinese AI developers have recently asked Beijing's industry regulator for guidance on the boundaries of organized collection of output. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology did not respond to requests for comment regarding this request for guidance. The articles leave open whether the US and China will reach an agreement on intellectual property during the summit. It remains unclear if Chinese regulators will implement concrete restrictions on the industrial use of American AI output.

stories.Headline: Alibaba Cloud expands global data center network to meet AI demand
stories.Summary:
Alibaba Cloud plans to expand its global data center network over the next year to meet growing AI computing power demand. This expansion was outlined by Yuan Zhiming during the company's Hong Kong summit held on Tuesday, November 18, 2026. Meanwhile, Amazon withdrew plans for four data center buildings on its Ashburn campus following an agreement reached on October 20. Loudoun County supervisors will vote on November 17 to pause new legislative data center applications for up to twelve months. These separate corporate moves reflect the intense global competition and local regulatory challenges surrounding the rapid growth of AI infrastructure.

The Alibaba expansion prioritizes Hong Kong because its three leased data centers there can no longer meet the current market demand. Amazon's withdrawn Ashburn project involved over 800,000 square feet on a 122-acre campus purchased for around 427.3 million dollars. Under Project Potomac Promise, Amazon will convey 25 acres to the county and seek to rezone the rest for housing. Loudoun County hosts about 233 data center buildings, which generated 1.2 billion dollars in tax revenue for fiscal 2026. This revenue accounted for 39 percent of the budget, with fiscal 2027 projections estimating 1.3 billion dollars or 40 percent.

Yuan Zhiming, the vice president of international business, stated that financial firms are adopting AI into their core business workflows. Amazon's Josh Weissman said the company took pointed community concerns seriously and chose a shared vision over costly litigation. Board Chair Phyllis Randall noted that the Ashburn campus was the wrong location due to resident opposition and needed infrastructure. AWS CEO Matt Garman cautioned that over 100 data center moratoriums are currently being considered across the United States. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy stated that capacity constraints continue to yield unserved demand despite adding 3.9 gigawatts of power.

Residents and Loudoun County supervisors opposed the Ashburn development, leading Amazon to abandon the Bridgefield Tech Center site plan. Governor Abigail Spanberger believes the decision to approve or block data center projects should rest with the community, not the state. State Senator Russet Perry has drafted a three-year statewide moratorium on data center approvals to address these growing local concerns. Dominion Energy requires new data centers to post 1.5 million dollars per megawatt in collateral to protect residential customers. Oracle is also affected, having issued a force majeure notice regarding its 2.45 gigawatt Project Jupiter in New Mexico.

Loudoun County previously used a 2000 zoning ruling that allowed data centers to be built by right as office buildings. Since March 2025, new data centers have required a special exception approved by a board vote rather than administrative processes. Amazon purchased the Ashburn campus in March 2026 and filed its site plan for the tech center in July. AWS reported 46 billion dollars in third quarter sales and a backlog totaling 578 billion dollars in the same period. Amazon's leases not yet commenced rose to 164.9 billion dollars in the third quarter, up from 137.2 billion dollars.

Amazon plans to spend meaningfully more in 2027 than the roughly 220 billion dollars it has planned for 2026. AWS and Nvidia plan to deploy over 2 million more GPUs on AWS during 2027 and 2028 to increase capacity. The county's final vote on November 17 will determine if new rezoning requests are delayed for up to one year. It remains open whether the 17 grandfathered applications totaling 11 million square feet will proceed without any further legislative delays. The articles leave open the final outcome of the air-permit decision regarding Oracle's Project Jupiter in Doña Ana County.

stories.Headline: Fed governor Michael Barr warns AI poses risks to trading, cybersecurity and consumer protection
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr on Monday laid out a range of perils that AI could bring to trading, cybersecurity and consumer and investor protection. He built on a central bank report issued the previous Friday that showed a surge in concern about the risks the new technology poses to financial stability. Barr spoke in prepared remarks for delivery in Milan, Italy. His remarks came hours before Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was to open a conference at the San Francisco Fed. AI developers, business leaders and academics were expected at that conference to discuss the implications of the new technology for productivity, jobs and the economy more broadly.

Some 87% of contacts surveyed for the Fed's latest Financial Stability Report, issued on Friday, cited AI as a salient risk to the financial system. They pointed to worries about cyberattacks, complex AI-related financing, and the possibility of an AI earnings slowdown spurring broad stock market declines. Barr expanded on some of those concerns and added several more. He cited the potential that increased reliance on AI models in trading could lead to herd-like behavior that could disrupt markets. He cited the possibility that self-learning algorithms could manipulate and destabilize markets.

Barr said banks may be unable to confirm whether an AI agent attempting to take actions in retail customer accounts is actually authorized by the customer to do so. He said even legitimate AI agents acting at lightning speed on behalf of retail banking customers could accelerate bank runs and overwhelm traditional safeguards. He pointed to cyber risks from AI-enabled cyberattackers or even rogue AI agents exploiting vulnerabilities in the financial system. He said AI developers struggle with ensuring their models are well controlled, numerically and legally precise, explainable, and replicable. He said the risk needs to be reduced that AI reinforces biases in consumer lending.

Barr said there is also a need to guard against risks that could result from the use of AI in financial markets, including collusion, market manipulation, or trading strategies that result in significant market volatility or even systemic risk. He did not comment in his prepared remarks on the outlook for monetary policy or the economy. A new Federal Reserve review of the best available evidence suggests the emerging AI revolution is still in its early days when it comes to seeing a return on AI investment. The Fed economists find that the data show AI adoption is high and growing. AI-adopting firms tend to apply it in only a couple of business areas at a time, such as IT and HR, or marketing and strategy, rather than across the entire organization.

Research and development, a business area where AI might provide a particularly significant boost to more fundamental innovation and productivity gains, has relatively low uptake, according to the Fed economists. Business areas like IT, marketing, finance, and strategy seem to be the most common AI applications, with less use in HR and actual production. More dramatic changes, such as using AI as part of a firm's core production process, engaging in wholesale reorganization, or fully automating some tasks, might be necessary to sustain any productivity boost over the long term. The establishment of new AI-centered businesses could also be an important channel for longer-run productivity improvements. Demand for new AI products has resulted in AI adoption growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all.

A report from METR, an AI research nonprofit, finds that Anthropic's internal use of AI has helped the company roughly double the pace at which its models improve on tasks that can be clearly measured. AI pundit and podcaster Dwarkesh Patel said he has come to the view that the world is only a couple years away and possibly only a couple months away from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research. Anthropic's S-1 public offering document offers a bunch of underwhelming case studies of how customers are using its models. As the company puts it, it believes enterprises are still in early phases of deployment, and it believes most knowledge workers have yet to fully experience what frontier AI can help them accomplish. The Fed paper concludes that AI is not yet playing much of a role, if any, in the recent upturn in US productivity growth.

The Fed paper's conclusion leaves open when AI will play a role in US productivity growth. Barr's remarks leave open what the Fed will do about the risks he listed. The articles do not say what the Milan remarks or the San Francisco Fed conference will lead to. The articles do not say how the Fed's review or the Financial Stability Report will change policy. The articles do not say what Anthropic's public offering will result in.

stories.Headline: FBI warns hackers use Artex AI tool to breach global networks in under three hours
stories.Summary:
The FBI warned that hackers are using an autonomous AI tool called Artex to launch cyberattacks globally and across the United States. These malicious actors have used the software to breach networks in under three hours, moving from initial targeting to privileged access. The agency issued a flash cybersecurity advisory on November 13, 2026, to alert businesses and government organizations about these threats. Cybercriminals and state-aligned groups have utilized this tool to target several different industries in recent months. The campaigns included a widespread hack of customers of the American IT company ConnectWise and South Korea's financial industry.

The tool requires connections to frontier large language models from OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as open-source or non-U.S. models. Artex is an open-source penetration testing framework that has been used for attacks since its public debut in July. It targets sectors including defense, tech, government, financial services, law firms, healthcare, and phone and internet companies. In South Korea, the tool stole personal data from at least 68,000 people due to a lack of multi-factor authentication. Hackers also accessed Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 ConnectWise customers using this specific AI-powered framework.

The FBI stated that AI makes sophisticated attacks faster, easier to automate, and potentially more difficult for organizations to detect. They noted that Artex intrusions are often noisy, generating large amounts of traffic that may trigger a company's defensive alerts. The agency warned on X that the tool allows attackers with limited technical expertise to carry out complex operations. Federal investigators explained that the framework can rapidly scan networks for weaknesses and exploit simple bugs like stolen passwords. They emphasized that the speed of these tools makes it much harder for human defenders to keep up.

Microsoft identified a China-aligned threat actor known as Storm-0940 as the group behind the Artex campaigns targeting hundreds of organizations. Barracuda, a cybersecurity company, reported a breach where criminals used an exposed third-party credential to access customer data stores. Arve Kjoelen, the chief information security officer at Barracuda, said defenders often arrive after the attacker has already finished. A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to requests for comment regarding the claims made by the FBI. These attacks affect various downstream tenants and organizations that rely on traditional security spotting to identify malicious activity.

Artex was originally developed for legitimate cybersecurity testing before being weaponized by hackers starting at least in August 2026. The tool scans for security flaws and spreads across networks to find mailboxes, databases, and other sensitive information. Recently, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online that were placed on the internet without any passwords. This included the specific Artex system used to target South Korea, which was likely a result of misconfiguration. These developments occurred alongside separate supply-chain attacks involving Optimizely that exposed malicious code on 178 different organizations' websites.

The developer of Artex made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks, but the FBI says open-source versions still circulate. The agency warns that the previous version remains widely accessible for use in cyberattacks against businesses and government organizations. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated that recent banking outages were not cyberattacks, but were caused by ageing computer infrastructure. Barracuda changed all customer credentials because its logs were not detailed enough to rule out unauthorized access to data. The articles leave open exactly how many customers were affected by the breach at the cybersecurity company Barracuda.

stories.Headline: Baidu CEO Robin Li urges companies to monetize AI and overhaul organizational structures to avoid a bubble
stories.Summary:
Baidu CEO Robin Li spoke about the urgent need for artificial intelligence adoption during the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on November 17, 2026. He explained that the actual spread of AI applications is moving more slowly than people expected despite the intense competition in the technology sector. Li argued that companies must prioritize the monetization of these tools to prevent the risk of a market bubble. He believes that the industry cannot sustain its current growth without finding clear ways to generate revenue.

The process of reaping the benefits of AI requires a complete overhaul of traditional organizational structures within a company. Robin Li stated that he has made radical attempts to break down the boundaries of traditional jobs at Baidu to better integrate these new technologies. This shift involves reorganizing how teams operate to ensure that AI is not just a tool but a core part of the business model. Such changes are necessary to keep pace with the rapid evolution of the global tech map.

As the leader of Baidu, Robin Li is responsible for guiding his company through this transition while advising other executives on the necessity of structural change. He suggested that the current way of organizing work is an obstacle to the full potential of artificial intelligence. By removing rigid job descriptions, he believes companies can become more agile and responsive to technological breakthroughs. He emphasized that those who fail to reorganize their internal systems will likely struggle to compete in the future.

stories.Headline: Apple launches an AI health study with OpenEvidence to enroll up to 200,000 US iPhone users
stories.Summary:
Apple launched a new research app on November 15, 2026, to study how people use AI for health. The company is partnering with OpenEvidence, a clinical artificial intelligence platform, to conduct this virtual research project. This study examines how users interact with conversational AI when they are seeking various types of medical information. Apple wants to understand if people trust the responses and find the information useful in everyday healthcare situations. The initiative focuses on how clinically grounded answers can help people comprehend and evaluate health AI in life.

The study requires participants in the U.S. who are over 21 and use an iPhone 15 Pro or later. These users must run iOS 26 or later with Apple Intelligence enabled to download the dedicated study application. Apple aims to enroll up to 200,000 participants for a period of more than 12 months for this research. The app uses clinical data from Nature, the Journal of the American Medical Association, and The New England Journal of Medicine. Participants can optionally share HealthKit data, including sleep, activity, laboratory results, and resting heart rate, for more personalized suggestions.

Sumbul Desai, Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness, said that responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. She stated that a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with health AI. Desai believes insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation regarding technology and trusted health tools. The company says the app is not intended to diagnose or treat medical conditions or replace qualified healthcare professionals. Apple also noted that the app can help participants prepare for doctor visits and guide them to specific providers.

The Verge reported that participants can rate AI answers based on their relevance, detail, and accuracy to provide researcher feedback. Users are affected by the study's goal to make complex medical information more understandable through the use of simpler language. The research addresses concerns that consumer AI chatbots can sometimes provide medical information that is either incomplete or very unclear. Participants will also be asked to provide their feedback and experiences through a series of recurring monthly research surveys. The system includes safety measures to identify concerning health questions and encourage users to contact a professional healthcare provider.

Apple specified that data will be anonymized before it is sent to a secure third-party cloud provider for the study. The company stated that the collected information will not be used to train any kind of artificial intelligence models. OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours to maintain the privacy of the study participants. This research reflects a growing interest in connecting consumer health technology with traditional services to support patient and clinician communication. OpenAI previously noted that its users were asking over 300 million health-related queries every week earlier this year.

The app is available for download starting today for eligible users who reside within the United States of America. Researchers will examine whether personal health context makes AI information more relevant and easier for the average person to understand. The study will evaluate if AI tools help patients organize questions about medications, symptoms, and test results for doctors. It remains unclear if Apple intends to release AI-powered answering features to Siri or the standard Apple Health app. The articles leave open whether the company will expand the availability of this research study to international users.

stories.Headline: FIOR completes NCSC-assessed cyber resilience evaluation of its AI Gateway version 26.2
stories.Summary:
FIOR, a UK-based AI security company, completed an independent cyber resilience assessment of its AI Gateway, a product that identifies AI agents, controls their permissions and blocks unauthorized actions before they execute. NCC Group evaluated 72 security claims under the UK National Cyber Security Centre's Principles Based Assurance methodology, according to FIOR. The published report identifies no unmet claims and one area of doubt concerning accessibility. The assessment, announced Nov. 16, covers AI Gateway version 26.2. FIOR's CEO and CTO both said it is the first AI identity and enforcement platform to publicly complete an NCSC CRTF assessment.

The report, dated Nov. 9, records no unmet claims and no assumptions, and the single doubt concerns accessibility, with assessors not satisfied that FIOR had shown people with disabilities can securely install, use and maintain the product. Assessors recommend completing accessibility testing against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. The findings apply only to version 26.2, and later releases require reassessment. Version 26.2, released Nov. 12, adds expanded discovery, model and tool catalogs, threat intelligence and identity integrations. The assessment report documents outbound HTTPS connections to a FIOR-hosted control plane and does not specify what data those connections transmit.

Founder and CEO David Williams said the company had already made its first commercial deployments and sought the assessment to give government and enterprise customers an objective basis for evaluating the product, a process he said took under six months. Williams said many companies have told FIOR they cannot exploit the benefits of AI until they are confident that the controls governing those agents are based on an identity that is secure. NCSC CEO Richard Horne said the rise in incidents is not because AI has invented new attacks, but because weaknesses organizations have tolerated for years can now be found and exploited at scale. At a Nov. 11 World Bank webinar, ITU-T Study Group 17 Chair Arnaud Taddei said agents already act with no verifiable identity and no proof of authority. World Bank senior digital specialist Marie Eichholtzer said confirming that a specific action falls within an agent's authority remains to be built.

Eichholtzer assessed that authenticating the person who approves an action through a national ID system rates strong, establishing on whose behalf the agent acts rates partial, and proving that someone may represent a company rates weak and often rests on administrative records alone. She pointed to Abu Dhabi's TAMM AutoGov, which proactively renews disability cards for individuals and trade licenses for businesses before they expire, and Ukraine's Diia.AI, which lets citizens request income certificates through a chat interface and delivers them to their government portal accounts. Singapore has tested a computer-use agent that guided applicants through a mock social assistance application in a sandbox. Eichholtzer said every grant should record the principal, the grantor, the actor, the permitted acts and their limits, whether the action is individual or joint, its validity and status, and whether it can be delegated further. Finland's Suomi.fi e-Authorizations service lets online services check in real time whether someone may act for another person or organization.

The assessment comes two weeks after the NCSC warned that UK critical national infrastructure should prepare for a ransomware attack using AI-powered malware by 2028. In its State of the Cyber Nation report, released Nov. 3, the agency said hostile actors' use of AI is highly likely to increase the scale and efficiency of ransomware, social engineering and vulnerability exploitation within two years. In August, the NCSC issued interim guidance on agentic AI after several incidents in which AI systems carried out unsanctioned or unintended actions. Joint guidance the NCSC issued in May with cybersecurity agencies from the U.S., Australia, Canada and New Zealand called for continuous runtime authentication with a central policy decision point for every agent action. In July, SG17 launched the Focus Group on Trust and Identity for Humans and Agentic AI, backed by 54 governments and 48 companies.

The FG-TIDA's first in-person meeting takes place at UNESCO in Paris on November 30 and December 1, with registration closing November 20, and participation is free and needs only an ITU account, not membership. The group is building a model to prove that a citizen or business has legally authorized an agent to act for it, something FIOR's identity and policy controls do not establish on their own. The government's Digital Standards Strategy 2026, 2030 aims to strengthen UK influence in global standards bodies while identity, biometric and AI frameworks are still being set, with the NCSC shaping security standards and the shift to post-quantum cryptography a stated priority. The articles leave open what data the outbound HTTPS connections to the FIOR-hosted control plane transmit. The articles also leave open how FIOR's claim that no information leaves the enterprise will be clarified.
Orgs: united kingdom national cyber security centre
