stories.Headline: Autodesk commits $350 million to prepare workers for AI jobs
stories.Summary:
The New York Fed found in September that 61% of service firms in the New York region now report using AI, up from 25% in 2024, while only 4% reported laying off anyone because of AI. Microsoft, Barclays and Kroger have joined a lengthening list of companies citing AI as they cut jobs. In March, Governor Hochul launched FutureWorks, a blue-ribbon commission charged with figuring out what AI means for the state's workforce. Cornell Tech's Urban Tech Hub and Appleseed, an economic development consulting firm, worked together to develop the AI Job Exposure Calculator. The interactive website allows anyone to map how different AI futures could play out across New York State's workforce.

The calculator computes current employment in each of 845 occupations across New York State's 10 labor markets using IMPLAN, a commercial software tool widely used for regional economic impact analysis. It isolates the share of jobs exposed to AI by drawing on Yale Budget Lab's synthesis of six different methods for measuring the technical feasibility of AI automating work in each occupation. The model samples adoption values from 35% to 75% and uses a displacement range of 15% to 50%. The most likely middle-of-the-road scenario, with adoption at 57%, displacement at 30% and protection at 52%, results in about 628,000 jobs threatened statewide, roughly 6.3% of the labor force. The 2008-9 recession took roughly 335,000 jobs over an 18-month period, and the COVID-19 pandemic resulted in nearly 2 million job losses in a few weeks in March-April 2020.

The city comptroller's office has modeled outcomes ranging from no job losses to an "AI Shockwave" that would cut more than 110,000 private-sector jobs in a single year. The state's new AI Jobs Institute aims to prepare 40,000 workers and students for AI-related jobs. The state has raised the level up to which wages and salaries are subject to UI taxes and increased the maximum weekly benefit to $869. The legal minimum wage is $17 an hour in New York City this year, and since 2017 some of New York's largest banks, including Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, Citi and M&T, have set and raised hourly floors, typically $20 to $25 by 2025. Costco and Amazon have done the same in retail.

Parminder Singh, Country Head for Design & Manufacturing and Media & Entertainment (India & SAARC) at Autodesk, said AI is a capability enhancer for Design and Make industries and will reshape jobs far more than replace them. Singh said every major technological shift, from CAD to cloud computing, has automated routine tasks while creating new opportunities for innovation and productivity. Autodesk said AI-related jobs across the Design and Make industries increased 147% in two years, while demand for AI skills grew 75% faster than for non-AI roles. Autodesk's AI foundation models, developed in collaboration with MIT and Cornell University, are designed to reason across 3D geometry, materials, fabrication methods and performance constraints. Autodesk Design and Make Studio launched at Anna University in Tiruchi.

Autodesk announced a $350 million commitment over three years in June 2026 to prepare talent for AI-powered jobs. By 2028, the initiative aims to provide free software access to 60 million students and educators, train nearly one million people in AI workflows and enable more than 200,000 to earn certifications. The authors used Claude Code to design a Monte Carlo simulation that spins three global dials representing AI adoption, AI displacement and AI protection and re-runs the formula 20,000 times in a row. The authors describe their model as an educated guess, akin to a weather forecast in the pre-satellite, pre-radar era. The authors write that AI will land on an economy already being reshaped by an aging population, a weakening ability to attract immigrant workers and international students, disrupted trade and travel with Canada, and costs driven up by tariffs and the war with Iran.

The authors write that the model tells you the size of the exposure, not the date it arrives. The authors say the Department and the Division of the Budget should continue to monitor closely the financial health of the State's UI program. The authors say New York State should press private-sector employers to sign on to industry-wide standards and should look for ways to extend the equity stakes that AI-company employees enjoy to contract workers in building maintenance, security and food service. Autodesk said India's large engineering and creative talent pool could benefit significantly from the transition, provided educational institutions and industry work together to bridge the gap between academic learning and workplace requirements. The articles leave open where AI adoption will top out and how much AI use results in layoffs rather than better productivity.

stories.Headline: Generative AI sparks productivity gains and plagiarism fears across the gaming industry
stories.Summary:
Generative AI is causing productivity gains and plagiarism fears within the gaming industry. Some practitioners view the technology as a revolution, while others fear it destroys the developer ecosystem. The 2026 Game Industry Report by GDC shows 40 percent of workers use generative AI. However, 55 percent of those respondents believe AI brings negative impacts to the industry. These conflicting views create a tense environment for current game developers.

Tencent's Ma Huateng discussed organizational restructuring during the November 11 LinkTime event at the company headquarters. He proposed that core businesses embrace AI and explore AI Native businesses. This statement led to rumors that 8,000 people or 50 percent of staff would be laid off. On November 12, Public Relations Director Zhang Jun clarified that 50 percent referred to resource allocation. Tencent Culture later released notes on November 16 urging colleagues to turn anxiety into excitement.

Tencent employees fear being replaced by AI or having their hard work easily copied. Penpen, producer of Jade Scratch Card at Insomnia Games, said AI knockoffs shorten the market window. He noted that Game Jam platforms are now treated as idea banks by ill-intentioned companies. Penpen believes independent developers lack practical measures to protect original works from these AI tools. He stated that many developers around him have already given up on creation.

Independent developers are most affected, as seen with Needle in a Haystack Simulator. After its video went viral on X, 14 knockoffs appeared on Roblox within 48 hours. Steam saw 9 copies, and over 40 appeared on WeChat Mini Programs. ReVamp and The Drunken Goddess's Drunken Deception both restricted their public demos to avoid plagiarism. Large companies also report that AI tools help players unpack unreleased projects and expose assets.

The industry has a history of copying, such as Hole.io referencing Donut County. 2048 also replicated the design of Threes! in one week instead of one year. AI simply makes these existing phenomena of content scraping and homogenization happen faster. Steam Next Fest saw over 8,000 signups, doubling the number from the June event. Daily new pages on itch.io reached 6,000, though downloads and purchases did not grow.

Steam refuses to be a gatekeeper and hopes to filter works by optimizing algorithms. Itch.io requires developers to mark assets and has removed terabytes of low-quality AI games. Anthropic modified Claude Code prompts to target game cloning, but these are easy to bypass. Insomnia Games is pursuing legal action, though DMCA processes are costly for overseas developers. The articles leave open whether complex, stylized games can remain safe from AI replication.

stories.Headline: WEBUY GLOBAL LTD launches WeTrip app on ChatGPT to help travelers plan tours in China
stories.Summary:
WEBUY GLOBAL LTD. launched the WeTrip app on ChatGPT on November 18, 2026, to help travelers explore tours in China. This new digital distribution channel connects conversational travel discovery with booking services led by consultants to reach more prospective customers. The app allows users to move from asking an initial travel question to reviewing a relevant itinerary and requesting quotations. Travelers can describe their interests and the length of their trip to find multi-day tours and refine their preferences.

Final bookings and payments are handled separately through WeTrip after consultants confirm the pricing and availability for the tailored proposal. The app operates on ChatGPT and serves the China inbound business of WEBUY GLOBAL LTD., which is listed as Nasdaq: WBUY. The company provides travel services for international markets and customers in Singapore and Indonesia through its website at www.webuy.global. Separately, AVATAR Industries Limited, formerly ASL Industries Limited and listed as NSE: AVATAR, launched a new website at www.avatarindia.com on November 17, 2026. This company created a wholly-owned subsidiary called AVATAR AI MINDLAB PRIVATE LIMITED to serve as a growth engine for advanced AI initiatives.

AVATAR Industries targets the Indian AI market, which is projected to grow from 10.9 billion dollars in 2025 to 43.5 billion dollars by 2030. Xue Bin, the Chief Executive Officer of WEBUY GLOBAL LTD., stated that AI is changing how travelers discover destinations and journeys. He said the WeTrip app creates a direct path from a first question to a request for a personalized travel proposal. Bin noted that the company focus is turning this access into qualified inquiries, completed bookings, and lasting customer relationships. Richa Rathod, Managing Director of AVATAR Industries Limited, said the true commercial value of AI lies in effective enterprise implementation.

Rathod believes her company can bridge the execution gap to make AI adoption commercially viable for various businesses. International travelers researching China are affected by the WeTrip app, which helps them clarify requirements before they speak with consultants. The commercial contribution of this channel depends on platform availability, customer adoption, and the conversion of inquiries into completed bookings. In India, micro, small, and medium enterprises are a massive untapped market because they contribute 31.1 percent to the national GDP. Many of these businesses face high barriers to entry because they lack the technical expertise needed for AI integration.

AVATAR Industries aims to help these enterprises identify operational bottlenecks and integrate AI applications into their existing workflows. WEBUY GLOBAL LTD. is a technology-enabled travel services company that provides curated leisure experiences and cross-border tour services in Southeast Asia. The company is developing an integrated travel platform that incorporates service excellence, AI, and strong regional supplier relationships and operating capabilities. AVATAR Industries is transitioning into the AI ecosystem by focusing on practical AI adoption and enterprise technology solutions for businesses.

The Indian AI market is expected to have a compound annual growth rate of approximately 32 percent through the year 2030. AVATAR Industries is leveraging a strong financial foundation from the 2026 fiscal year to drive sustainable and technology-led growth. WEBUY GLOBAL LTD. will use the app to complement its broader use of AI tools in sales follow-up and customer service.

AVATAR Industries plans to capture market share by expanding AI product offerings and securing strategic technology partnerships for its clients. The company will use AVATAR AI MINDLAB PRIVATE LIMITED to develop proprietary business solutions that provide high margins for the firm. The articles leave open how many travelers will actually adopt the WeTrip app and convert their inquiries into bookings. They also do not specify which proprietary AI solutions AVATAR AI MINDLAB PRIVATE LIMITED will develop for the Indian enterprise market.

stories.Headline: Samsung Fire joins government project to insure 380 billion dollars in AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Samsung Fire and Marine Insurance joined a government project to insure artificial intelligence data centers on November 18, 2026. The insurer is participating in a public-private push to manage risks for these expensive facilities. This move aims to create a system for handling losses from cyberattacks, blackouts, and fires. Samsung Fire is the only insurance company attending the relevant meetings for this specific project. The company joined the AIDC Alliance to help distribute the financial risks of these centers.

The project involves 550 trillion won, or 380 billion dollars, for the first phase of investment. The government plans to build 18.4 gigawatts of capacity by 2035 in South Korea. The AIDC Alliance, launched in July, includes roughly 400 companies and institutions from various sectors. Samsung Fire hosted the Global AIDC Forum 2026 on November 18 at the Samsung Finance Campus. This event in Seocho-gu, Seoul, drew 160 participants from government, academia, and the financial industry.

Choi Young-hwa, head of the Corporate Safety Research Institute at Samsung Fire, proposed a new approach. He called this method Insurability by Design to weigh risk management from the initial design stage. Choi stated that risks must be quantified across design, construction, commissioning, operation, and expansion phases. He argued that coverage should be calculated from actual loss scenarios like probable maximum loss. This approach aims to improve accident prevention, resilience, and the overall insurability of the facilities.

Financial industry officials noted that the need for risk management grew during the AIDC build-out. The AIDC Alliance now includes safety management and risk distribution because the scale of investment grew. Allianz Commercial found that water damage caused 21 percent of claims in 221 data center cases. Intentional acts and cybercrime accounted for 19 percent, while fire and equipment failure followed behind. These findings show that large facilities face significant threats from leaks, flooding, and digital attacks.

S&P Global estimates that large data center campuses during construction have insured values of 10 to 30 billion dollars. This is three times the typical 5 to 10 billion dollar limits for bridges and tunnels. Swiss Re projects that global premiums for these centers will total 91 billion dollars from 2026 to 2030. In China, four government bodies promoted technology insurance in February to pursue multi-layered risk distribution systems. A Chinese joint underwriting body provided 6.5 trillion yuan in coverage to 33 companies by 2025.

The industry must now determine how to objectively calculate the economic value of lost data. Current insurance standards make it difficult to assess the scale of loss for digital information. Experts are discussing how to factor insurance into the design and construction stages of these centers. The articles leave open whether sufficient insurance limits can be reached using layering or joint underwriting. It remains unclear how a new approach to risk assessment will be implemented for data losses.

stories.Headline: OpenAI says its models cut AMD flagship GPU power, performance and area by up to 14% and speed chip design
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said on November 18, 2026 that its models are quickly improving the chips that power AI, and in August it shared how OpenAI engineers used frontier models to accelerate development of its first custom inference chip, Jalapeño. OpenAI started using GPT-4o to help design Jalapeño in early 2025, and even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements. The company evaluated successive model generations on two open-source processor designs, PicoRV32 and OpenTitan’s Ibex, to measure ability at end to end chip design tasks. OpenAI is working with Synopsys to integrate frontier intelligence with the electronic design automation tools engineers already use to design and verify chips. OpenAI partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and saw up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP.

In the vector unit, which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. In the matrix unit, an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits, and one multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. Across the broader Jalapeño design effort, the team estimates model-proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit, and these optimizations were silicon proven during Jalapeño’s silicon bring-up. On AMD, the model identified further improvements by rewriting SystemVerilog RTL, representing roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months.

OpenAI said AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing and added others to its production design files for use in future versions. OpenAI said it observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect, and the model used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block’s behavior and to evaluate trade-offs in power, performance, and area. AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by OpenAI’s model. OpenAI said it expects further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline. OpenAI is partnering with Synopsys to train GPT-Synopsys, a new model, to use Synopsys EDA tools the way expert chip designers do.

PicoRV32 is a compact core designed for reprogrammable chips called FPGAs, and OpenTitan uses Ibex as the embedded processor in its security chip, each a complete processor core for embedded, microcontroller class workloads. OpenAI gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput, the number of instructions the core can execute per second. Designs scored zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core’s area, and for designs that passed OpenAI measured instructions per clock cycle on workloads hidden from the models, took the geometric mean across those workloads, and multiplied it by the maximum clock frequency estimated with Yosys. For each core OpenAI assigned the best throughput observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0, and the charts show the average score across runs, including those that scored zero. With a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT-6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores, and GPT-6.1 Sol also outscored GPT-5.6 Sol on both.

On the existing PicoRV32 core, GPT-6.2 Astra has the highest mean score at the larger comparable budgets, and around 112,000 tokens its score is about twice GPT-6 Astra’s. On the existing Ibex core, GPT-6.2 Astra’s mean score continues to climb across the higher budgets it reaches, while GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol are closer together. For the second task OpenAI gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system, and the model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core OpenAI kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task, and at about 112,000 tokens per run all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design, which held for both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT-6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32, and the full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets.

Starting from a PicoRV32 specification, GPT-6.2 Astra passes a mean score of 0.7 near 112,000 tokens and scores higher at the next two observed budgets. On Ibex, GPT-6.2 Astra averages about 0.75 near 112,000 tokens when designing from a specification, and its curve stays above the others at larger shared budgets. OpenAI said starting from written requirements gives the models room to omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions, and those features may do little to improve throughput on the test workloads, which could explain part of the score advantage. OpenAI said requiring those features, setting a tighter limit on circuit area, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test more representative of production chip design. OpenAI said it has demonstrated that its models can explore new processor architectures in RISC-V evals and contributed net new improvements on top of sophisticated production designs such as Jalapeño and AMD’s next generation flagship GPU and CPU.

stories.Headline: US banks halt loans for Asian AI data centers following new Commerce Department rules
stories.Summary:
U.S. banks halted loans for Asian AI data centers in November 2026. This action followed new rules from the U.S. Commerce Department. The administration moved to tighten rules after allegations that Nvidia chips were rerouted to China. Lenders withdrew from deals to avoid risks of violating these new government regulations. The suspension showed that Asia's financial industry was unprepared for this abrupt action.

The rules require licenses for chip shipments to Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand. They also restrict remote access to AI chips from Southeast Asia and other countries. Aolani Cloud, a Singapore partner of Nvidia, was denied a 480 million dollar loan. This loan would have funded graphics processing units for a data center in Malaysia. The hardware was intended for use by the Chinese technology company ByteDance.

The Commerce Department said it investigated Megaspeed's chip procurement since 2024. They coordinated with Singapore authorities to block Chinese companies from reaching technology remotely. Aolani Cloud stated it worked with regulators to ensure compliance without project disruption. The company spent considerable time with financing partners to anticipate regulatory risks. These efforts to secure the loan for the Malaysia project were unsuccessful.

Aolani Cloud and other data center operators are affected by these licensing requirements. Michelle Condie of the Center for Advanced Defense Studies said circumvention became easier. She noted that this allowed China to get around export controls regardless of legality. Lenders are now assessing billions of dollars in AI borrowings that are in progress. Some banks are also reviewing deals that were already closed.

The rules follow a scandal involving Alice Huang, the leader of Singapore company Megaspeed. Huang allegedly moved 7.5 billion dollars of Nvidia chips through Chinese companies since 2023. Last year, JPMorgan, Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, Mitsubishi UFJ, and Sumitomo Mitsui lent to Bridge Data Centres. Bridge Data Centres, backed by Bain Capital, sought 2.8 billion dollars for Thailand and Malaysia. Megaspeed was the counterparty for those loans, while ByteDance was the main tenant.

Bridge Data Centres replaced Megaspeed with Los Angeles based Zenlayer this year. A new loan from existing lenders was finalized in May. Malaysia is checking if Speedmatrix, a 2024 Megaspeed unit, re-exported chips to third countries. The articles leave open whether the banks that lent early last year did anything wrong. It remains unclear how many other AI related borrowings will collapse entirely.

stories.Headline: Cato Networks launches AgentSense to block harmful AI agent actions in real time
stories.Summary:
Cato Networks launched AgentSense this week to block harmful AI agent actions in real time. The company announced this patented breakthrough from Cato AI Labs on November 17, 2026. This new security capability is built into the cloud-based secure access service edge platform. It stops AI agents from carrying out harmful actions prompted by untrusted content. The tool protects the integrity of decisions, actions, and outputs as agents operate autonomously.

The tool targets indirect prompt injection found in emails, documents, webpages, or tool responses. Administrators enable it via a toggle in the Cato SASE platform in Tel Aviv-Yafo, Israel. It includes three rules covering high-risk operations, external sensitive information exposure, and critical resource changes. AgentSense is included at no additional charge for customers with Cato AI Usage licenses. It reduced attack success from 19 percent to 0.05 percent on the Agent Dojo benchmark.

CEO and co-founder Shlomo Kramer said security must intervene before autonomous agent actions cause harm. He believes enterprises need confidence to put agents in charge of critical business processes. Itay Ravia, head of Cato AI Labs, noted that AgentSense helps preserve trust against attackers. He mentioned prompt injection vulnerabilities like DuneSlide, EchoLeak, and CurXecute as reasons for this tool. The company says Untrusted Influence Detection distinguishes trusted instructions from untrusted content within sessions.

Nithin Reddy of Dayforce said scaling AI safely requires detecting actions that risk customers or data. Grace Trinidad from IDC stated that security must connect agent permissions to their business purpose. Gartner reports that 71 percent of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within twelve months. However, only 21 percent of these organizations currently have agentic AI governance capabilities in place. These gaps leave enterprises vulnerable to data exposure, system compromise, and business process manipulation.

Agents cannot reliably distinguish between trusted instructions and untrusted data they pick up while working. This architectural weakness allows attackers to hide malicious instructions in various digital materials. Gartner forecasts that ungoverned AI agent abuse will drive 25 percent of enterprise breaches by 2028. Cato describes a lethal trifecta where prompt injection becomes a significant business risk. One example involved Claude Code attempting to modify a sensitive local file after reading a webpage.

Cato opened a public challenge where the first three eligible winners receive 10,000 dollars each. The company will use findings from this adversarial testing to evaluate and improve the guardrail. Future plans include Drift Detection to check if actions still serve the user's original task. Cato also plans to implement controls for which specific resources and data an agent can reach. The articles leave open how these future capabilities will be integrated into the existing platform.

stories.Headline: Hacker ioma8 uses large language models to accelerate reverse engineering processes
stories.Summary:
In November 2026, a hacker used AI to speed up reverse engineering, and the SANS Institute launched its annual Holiday Hack Challenge. The hacker utilized large language models to analyze binaries, while SANS opened a free cybersecurity game for a global community of players. This game, called The Pyramid on the Ice, began on November 18, 2026, and allows anyone to build vital security skills. The hacker reported achieving successes in six months that would have previously taken years to complete using only manual methods. Both the individual hacker and the SANS event highlight the growing role of artificial intelligence in modern cybersecurity and reverse engineering.

The hacker used DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, Ghidra with an MCP bridge, and radare2 or kuna, while also employing Codex with Luna or Terra. He used Python with UV tooling for prototyping and Rust for implementing hacks, and he applied skills from Matt Pottock and ioma8. The SANS challenge, based in Bethesda, Maryland, runs from November 18, 2026, until January 5, 2027, and features six different mini-games. It includes Grand Challenges developed with Microsoft and focuses on AI/ML security, cloud infrastructure, web apps, networking, systems, and binary reverse engineering. Players can join cohorts or use Discord, and a new award for Best AI Orchestration recognizes those who leverage AI tools.

The hacker, known as ioma8, stated that LLMs provide a turbo boost to his curiosity and that he loves getting results quickly. He explained that his long experience helps him steer agents and that he no longer misses the process of manually analyzing assembly. Ed Skoudis, President of the SANS Technology Institute, said the challenge is the place to practice real techniques inside a fun story. Skoudis noted that utilizing AI is how a growing number of practitioners already work in the field of cybersecurity today. He added that the Microsoft partnership ensures players work on problems drawn from platforms they defend every day in their professional lives.

The SANS event affects a global community, drawing between 15,000 and 19,000 annual players, including students, career changers, and skilled cybersecurity practitioners. These players can compete for prizes such as a SANS Summit pass, a SANS OnDemand course, and a CyberStudio course. The 2026 SANS research report found that 60 percent of organizations see a skills gap as a bigger problem than staffing. Additionally, 60 percent of those organizations name a lack of time due to workload as their greatest barrier to training. The free nature of the Holiday Hack Challenge aims to help those who cannot afford expensive training between budget cycles.

The hacker has a two decade history of hacking hardware and software and understands both assembly and hardware for his personal hobby. He successfully hacked an Alphasmart NEO, an EmWave biofeedback device, Sony Alpha mirrorless cameras, and various musical synthesizers like the Arturia MiniFreak. His other achievements include creating custom firmware for the Xteink X4 ebook reader and fixing an old HP printer driver for MacOs. He also cracked license-locked abandonware, developed a lightweight Evernote client, and built a custom Photoshop editor a year before ArtCraft. The SANS Institute was established in 1989 as a research organization and now provides training and certification to government and commercial institutions.

The SANS Holiday Hack Challenge will conclude with a live webcast ceremony and the announcement of winners on January 20, 2027. The hacker continues to use a hypothesis-driven debugging loop, recording results in CSV tables to stop AI agents from going in circles. He encourages everyone to try their own hacks to free their minds and explore the boundaries between reverse engineering and development. The articles do not state if the hacker will release more public skills or if SANS will expand its Microsoft partnership. It remains open whether other security organizations will adopt similar AI-driven training models to close the reported global cybersecurity skills gap.

stories.Headline: UOB deploys A*Star Meralion AI model to aid relationship managers across five ASEAN markets
stories.Summary:
UOB announced on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, that it is deploying a new artificial intelligence solution for customer interactions. The bank is using a model developed by the Agency for Science, Technology and Research to support its staff. This multilingual tool helps relationship managers better understand and engage with clients through a specialized AI system. The deployment aims to improve how the bank provides advice and handles conversations across several different Asian markets. This initiative marks the first time a bank has explored this specific call intelligence solution for regional engagement.

The Meralion model supports processing in English, Malay, Thai, Vietnamese, Mandarin, Cantonese, Hokkien, Bahasa Indonesia, Tamil, Burmese, and Singlish. It will be used in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam under the bank's strategic Project Aura programme. The solution, called the Compliance Intelligence Engine and Evidence-Grounded Post-Call Compliance Review System, interprets various accents and styles. It provides prompts on risk disclosures and product details to complement the professional judgment of the bank's relationship managers. The system also automates post-call reviews to ensure fair dealing standards are met and to reduce manual translation.

UOB Chief Financial Officer Leong Yung Chee stated that banking is built on trust and every customer conversation matters. He said the bank wants to apply AI with purpose to help staff navigate cultural and language nuances. Professor Lim Keng Hui of A*Star said that multilingual AI research creates more impact when tested against real-world needs. He noted that the collaboration explores how the model works in demanding environments where accuracy and explainability are critical. Both leaders believe the partnership brings together research and banking expertise to develop safe and assured financial technology.

The tool affects relationship managers who remain accountable for the advice they provide while using AI as a complement. It also impacts over eight million UOB customers across ASEAN who may switch languages during a single banking exchange. The system helps these clients by enabling more seamless and personalized banking experiences through better understanding of local expressions. By automating parts of the review process, the bank can provide more targeted coaching for its relationship managers. This approach aims to reinforce fair dealing and deliver more consistent outcomes for customers across the diverse region.

UOB is a leading Asian bank incorporated in 1935 with about 430 branches and offices in 19 global markets. A*Star is the lead public sector research and development agency in Singapore with entities in Biopolis and Fusionopolis. The Meralion model has achieved the lowest average word-error rate among open-source models across several different languages. This project builds on a broader collaboration between A*Star and the Future of Finance Institute from the Monetary Authority. The bank currently holds high credit ratings from Moody's Investors Service, S&P Global Ratings, and Fitch Ratings.

UOB and the A*Star Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing signed a memorandum of understanding to explore further applications. The parties are investigating other emerging technologies that could strengthen innovation, resilience, and decision-making within the financial services sector. The bank will continue to assess if the Meralion capabilities can be applied safely across its regional franchise. Success will be measured by whether the solution can scale across markets and if it strengthens overall governance. The articles leave open the specific results of the pilot and the exact timeline for full regional scaling.

stories.Headline: Pittsylvania schools weigh AI policy as LA County approves AI governance rules
stories.Summary:
The Pittsylvania County School Board in the late fall of 2026 looked at developing an artificial intelligence policy to manage AI in schools, the Chatham Star-Tribune reported on Nov. 18, 2026. Pittsylvania County Schools joined other school divisions in Virginia and across the nation in contending with the rise of artificial intelligence and its impacts within the education realm. Division administrators acknowledged that AI is not going anywhere and that school divisions must craft policy and regulation around its usage. Administrators said they seek to be strategic, careful and responsible as the technology changes many aspects of life and education. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors approved a policy Tuesday governing the safe, ethical and transparent use of artificial intelligence technologies across county government, MyNewsLA.com reported on Nov. 17, 2026.

The Los Angeles County policy establishes standards, responsibilities and governance requirements for AI systems developed by the county, procured from outside vendors or accessed through third-party platforms. The policy requires county departments to follow principles involving human-centered design, security and safety, privacy, transparency, equity, accountability, effectiveness and workforce empowerment. Under the policy, AI systems must protect personally identifiable information, protected health information, criminal justice information and other sensitive data from unauthorized access, disclosure and manipulation. The policy requires the county to disclose the purpose and use of its AI systems to the public and identify work products generated by AI. It prohibits fully automated high-impact decisions without meaningful human review, covert tracking or social scoring of people, and the cognitive or behavioral manipulation of people or vulnerable groups.

Steve Mayhew, PCS superintendent, said the goal is to develop a human-centered policy that is ethical and equitable, protects users and the school division, and provides adequate training for individuals most in need of it. Mayhew said the goal is for students to develop important life skills and succeed academically without using AI to do the work, while balancing digital literacy and education. Mayhew said people use AI for a lot of things and that he thinks it is a tool but not something supposed to be used instead of creativity. Emily Reynolds, chief information technology officer with Pittsylvania County Schools, said the issue is something IT directors in school divisions everywhere are talking about. Reynolds said students do not have access to AI and teachers only have access right now to MagicSchool, which is geared toward instructional purposes.

Reynolds said that within MagicSchool teachers can create AI-resistant assignments for students and that the push is to teach teachers how to build assignments more resistant to a student putting a prompt into a chat bot and getting output of an assignment. Reynolds said programs exist where teachers could upload content to see whether it has AI-generated components, but even that gets murky because it is effectively AI telling users whether something was AI generated. Kevin Mills, Westover district representative, was concerned with AI's reputation for spitting out erroneous information or producing information that aligned with user bias, telling individuals what they want to hear rather than strict facts. Mills said use of this technology could mislead students trying to use it as a study aid. Mark Shields, school board chair and Chatham-Blairs district representative, said his biggest concern with AI in schools were growing reports of students using AI programs such as ChatGPT to write essays.

Kelly Merricks, Dan River district representative, pointed out that if teachers give students assignments to complete on the spot during class, it gives educators the chance to recognize students' authentic work. Merricks said that familiarity makes it easier to spot a student's use of artificial intelligence to complete essays or other assignments. Mayhew suggested forming a taskforce to focus on AI and its regulation in the schools, comprised of teachers, principals, division administrators, parents and potentially a school board member. In the broader education realm, proposals have been made to begin introducing digital citizenship to students beginning in Kindergarten, effectively starting to teach five-year-olds about AI, computer technology and responsible use. The premise of this digital citizenship push would level up the digital literacy and AI education through the grade levels.

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, in part of her administration's recently announced Moving Virginia Forward agenda, aims to target finding a better balance that limits student screen time in school and encourages use of more traditional educational methods where possible. This agenda is set to get in motion in 2027, per the governor's office. The memo reads that the agenda would require school divisions to minimize unnecessary student screen time, prioritize teacher-led and high-quality instruction, and regularly assess and develop plans to reduce excessive or low-value use of instructional technology. Adopting an AI policy was the first official step into the fray, and regulation and implementation will follow that baseline as the situation develops. PCS has kept tight reins on unrolling AI in the division so far, administrators said, and that has been much to their benefit as other school divisions in the Commonwealth are trying to rein the technology in.

The Los Angeles County policy says AI should be used to enhance jobs and provide training and retraining opportunities for workers, rather than replace county employees or contractors. It assigns oversight responsibilities to the county's chief information officer, chief information security officer, chief privacy officer and department-level information technology managers. The policy allows no exceptions, according to the county. County Counsel reviewed the proposal, and the Audit Committee approved it Sept. 16. According to the board letter, there will be no fiscal impact to the county on the proposed AI Policy.

A board letter from the county's chief executive officer said AI technologies are increasingly used across county departments to enhance service delivery, improve operational efficiency and support data driven decision making. The letter said that as these technologies advance, it is critical for the county to maintain clear governance structures, safeguard sensitive information and ensure that AI is deployed responsibly and ethically. The letter states that the AI Policy establishes consistent requirements to ensure that any AI technologies developed, procured or used by county departments comply with applicable laws, protect county information assets, maintain public trust and mitigate the risk of bias or misuse. County employees are barred from uploading nonpublic or regulated county information to unapproved AI platforms, using such platforms to make official decisions or relying on AI-generated work as an authoritative source without independent human verification. The articles leave open how the Pittsylvania taskforce would be formed and what its regulation and implementation would contain.

stories.Headline: Satya Nadella warns AI speeds up bug fixes and risks more frequent tech outages
stories.Summary:
Satya Nadella, the chief executive of Microsoft, warned on Wednesday at the DealBook Summit in New York that global infrastructure instability might come. He spoke less than a week after a global Outlook outage that knocked millions of people and governments off email for one day. This event occurred around November 18, 2026, and was part of a wider series of disruptions affecting various American technology industries. Other outages hit the banking and aviation sectors, including a rare nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday. These disruptions affected core Microsoft 365 services, including Copilot, Exchange Online, and Teams, across 74 different countries during the previous week.

The Microsoft outage resulted from a software update made over the summer that was tested on older equipment and hit a latent bug. This problem became apparent when two other issues pushed more traffic onto servers, leaving more than 80 percent of servers unresponsive. The FAA grounded flights for over four hours after instability in legacy equipment disrupted radar information and communications for aircraft across America. Banking customers at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, and Capital One reported outages on Monday that eased by Tuesday. Other affected entities included Cox Internet, Amtrak, American Airlines, and United Airlines, all of which rely on the open internet for their operations.

Satya Nadella said that AI tools find cybersecurity bugs at a breakneck pace, forcing companies to deploy fixes instantaneously to stop active exploitation. He explained that this speed leaves less time for testing patches, which could lead to more buggy updates being pushed into operation. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that superintelligence might be responsible for the outages by overwhelming older systems with rapid changes. Mullin told Fox News that AI self-fixing code is like a change order on a house where one change causes ripple effects. He stated with 98 percent certainty that a cyberattack was not responsible and noted no footprints of such an attack.

Former national security adviser Michael Flynn suggested on social media that the outages were suspicious and looked like a massive, coordinated cyberattack. He argued that adversaries are using these events to examine vulnerabilities and the level of crosstalk between governmental and nongovernmental institutions. President Donald Trump weighed in on Tuesday, stating that such things happen when you are big, powerful, and have all the money. The outages affected millions of global users, including businesses and governments, as well as travelers and customers of the largest U.S. banks. Officials from the Transportation Department and the FAA reiterated on November 14 that the aviation issues were not connected to AI.

Microsoft's outage was described by Nadella as a perfect storm of events that triggered a latent bug within the company's existing global infrastructure. Nadella compared the current situation to the late 1990s when the world feared a global meltdown from the Y2K computer code quirk. He noted that while Y2K was one bug on one day, AI systems continue to improve and create persistent, nation-state level threats. Mullin previously emphasized that there was no connection between the FAA ground stop and the issues that were affecting Microsoft's various services. The DHS also issued 84 billion dollars in fines to illegal immigrants on July 23, 2026, as part of separate agency actions.

Nadella remains unsure when or if the situation will improve as the race between hackers and defenders continues to evolve and balance. He warned that physical infrastructure, such as heating, cooling, and transportation systems, is harder to update despite being connected to the internet. The articles leave open whether the race between defenders and AI-driven attackers will ever reach a stable point of global security. Authorities have not yet identified a common cause for the simultaneous disruptions across the banking, aviation, and technology sectors in the United States. It remains unclear if the fragility of online systems will lead to more frequent and prolonged outages for global infrastructure in future.

stories.Headline: Four Baltimore students sue Omnilert and police after an AI gun alert led to their handcuffing
stories.Summary:
Four Baltimore area students filed a lawsuit after an AI system allegedly mistook a bag of Doritos for a firearm. This incident occurred in 2025 outside Kenwood High School and triggered a police response. Armed officers ordered the four teenagers to the ground, handcuffed them, and searched them. Police later determined there was no weapon and no threat present. The students are now seeking damages for the violation of their constitutional rights.

The incident happened on 20 October 2025 after football practice when a coach passed out chips. Taki Allen, then a junior, held bags near picnic tables when six police cruisers arrived. Omnilert developed the AI gun detection system that flagged the chips with 90 percent confidence. The lawsuit names Omnilert, Baltimore county police, the board of education, the principal, and individual officers. The Maryland office of the inspector general for education found 99 percent of alerts were false.

Damon Hewitt represents the students as the executive director of the Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights Under Law. He stated that students were failed by prone technology and adults meant to keep them safe. He noted that the teens were met with guns and traumatized instead of receiving protection. An Omnilert spokesperson said the company was reviewing the lawsuit and felt sorry for the fear experienced. A Baltimore county spokesperson stated the district cannot comment on pending litigation.

Taki Allen says he no longer feels safe waiting for rides and now pays for transport. Freida Winfield, mother of student Keith, said no child should face danger while waiting for a ride. The students reported feeling pain from tight handcuffs and lasting emotional distress after the event. One officer allegedly joked to the plaintiffs to be careful with their chips bags on school property. Another officer allegedly complained about stupid AI cameras and the Omnilert system as he left.

The AI system scans security footage for firearms and markets itself as having fewer false positives. The lawsuit claims the alert continued even after staff and police reviewed the image as a mistake. Texts from the school principal allegedly used laughing emojis to make light of the incident. The complaint states that the principal did not apologize to the students for the police action. The case attracts national attention regarding the intersection of artificial intelligence, public safety, and constitutional law.

The court must decide if an AI alert alone supports a stop and search under the Fourth Amendment. It remains open whether police can legally detain bystanders who happen to be standing nearby. The case will examine if officers were justified in drawing weapons based on computer generated alerts. Liability may rest with the software company, school officials, the acting officers, or a combination of all. The outcome could impact how schools, businesses, and government agencies use AI for public safety operations.

stories.Headline: Anthropic weighs raising its IPO size and price as demand reaches about $500 billion
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is considering upsizing its initial public offering, according to people familiar with the details, as the artificial intelligence lab weighs setting the price well above $80. The company closed its order books and locked in total demand on Tuesday, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing. Anthropic is expected to set its final IPO price after market close Wednesday. The stock is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT on Thursday. Anthropic will make final decisions Wednesday afternoon, the people said.

The AI lab said last week that it would offer 825 million shares in the IPO at a price range of between $70 and $78 per share, which would net up to $64.35 billion at the high end of that range. Institutional demand for the offering is around $400 billion, while retail demand is approaching $100 billion, according to the people. The orders are indications of interest and are not binding, and all of the details are subject to change. Demand for the offering is higher than it was for Elon Musk's SpaceX, even though the rocket maker had a bigger market offering. SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq in June in by far the biggest IPO on record, ultimately raising $85.7 billion.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in the company's roadshow video that if done right, "we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia." Amodei said the company has to make sure that all the risks and all the ways things can go wrong with this technology are very carefully addressed as it brings the benefits and has a viable business at the same time. Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus that their aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles. The co-founders wrote that everyone who owns the stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort. A representative for Anthropic declined to comment.

Amazon and Google both own stakes in Anthropic valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, agreed to collectively invest $26 billion in the IPO. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD. Anthropic's listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds. Anthropic's IPO has reportedly drawn six times too many orders for its available stock shares.

Amodei co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses. Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027. Anthropic has faced two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year over its positions on safety, regulation and national security.

For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said, it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said. Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO.

stories.Headline: Democrats sweep midterms and AI data center stocks fall as investors brace for tighter oversight
stories.Summary:
The Verge's roundup on the AI data center buildout opens with a link to a Bloomberg piece, which is the first announcement its headline points to. The Verge, in a post by Jay Peters dated November 4, 2026, pointed to Bloomberg's report that the AI data center boom is set for upheaval after the Democratic rout in the US election. The roundup itself gives only that headline and notes that AI data center projects keep appearing across the US, often meeting opposition from locals worried about their impact. The substance behind the Bloomberg headline comes from coverage of the same election by Investing.com, which reported that Democrats swept the midterms on Tuesday and captured majorities in both the Senate and the House.

According to Investing.com, the result triggered a selloff in AI data center stocks, as investors braced for tighter regulatory oversight, possible rollbacks of tech tax incentives and heightened antitrust scrutiny. Democrats flipped traditionally Republican-leaning states including Texas and Kansas. Texas and Georgia, which together account for roughly a third of all AI data center spending and projects, both saw Democratic wins at the governor level. In premarket trading, CoreWeave fell as much as 3.2%, Applied Digital fell 3% and Nebius dropped 1.3%, while Oracle, which recently priced a combined $20 billion stock and debt offering, was down about 1.2% after gaining 5.85% on Tuesday.

Analysts at Evercore ISI, led by Amit Daryanani, said a more restrictive environment for data center development could create incrementally more negative sentiment for AI infrastructure names. They added that the initial reaction would likely be to sell AI stocks, and that the real question is how far the political shift alters fundamentals and whether other factors such as inflation and yields offset it over time. Several Democratic governor-elects have already voiced support for more AI regulation. Any Democratic legislation would still need President Trump's signature to become law, a check analysts say limits near-term legislative risk, though it does not fully remove the threat of executive branch regulatory action or the chilling effect that uncertainty can have on capital spending.

The political change adds a federal layer to pressures that were already building. Data Center Watch found that in the second quarter of 2026, at least 45 data center projects worth $68 billion were disrupted by local opposition. The broader AI trade was also weakening before the vote: the Goldman Sachs Broad AI basket fell 15% in October and had dropped more than 24% from its peak heading into Wednesday's session. The Verge's roundup also lists local fights, including a scuttled $1.6 billion project in a small Wisconsin city and a delayed data center in San Diego. Neither article lays out specific next steps, so what the new Congress does on data center rules remains to be seen.

stories.Headline: Ashish Mishra urges governance for AI agents that act without human oversight
stories.Summary:
Ashish Mishra, Lead Solutions Architect for Agentic AI Services at NTT DATA, published an article on 16 November 2026 about governing AI that acts rather than only answers. He described a voice bot his colleague had asked to suggest an itinerary for a trip to France, which instead supplied one for India. Mishra called it an obvious hallucination that could be verified easily. He wrote that the consequences can be far more serious when an autonomous AI agent makes the wrong decision and runs with it. He said organizations are moving away from “vanilla” AI, which simply answers questions, toward AI that can make decisions, act and carry out entire business processes.

Mishra wrote that existing governance will remain relevant, covering the quality and accuracy of AI, data protection, privacy, security and bias. He said agentic AI does not change any of that and simply gives organizations more to govern. Traditional AI produces an output and a person decides what to do with it, while agentic AI can use other tools and systems, communicate with people or initiate the next step in a process without any human intervention. He said this means questioning the output as well as the activity throughout the workflow. He wrote that every agent should have a clear business purpose and a named owner, its own identity and access only to the information and tools required for its job.

Mishra said the excitement around new technology is understandable but that letting it get ahead of the controls is a mistake he sees far too often. He wrote that by the time you discover a problem, the agent may already have acted on it. He said organizations without effective AI governance can face compliance failures and operational problems, and that when AI acts without guardrails those consequences are amplified. He said an action that is difficult or impossible to reverse needs a different level of control than a simple day-to-day task. He wrote that if something goes wrong, you should be able to see what information the agent was working with, which tools it used and what approvals it received.

Mishra wrote that AI risk is no longer confined to the information an agent produces and now extends to the running of the business. He said AI agents can take information from emails, documents and websites and interact with different tools, systems and even other agents. He said testing an agent before it starts working is essential but you cannot stop there, because the information it receives and the environment it operates in will continue to change. He said you need to know what an agent can retain, how long it keeps that information and whether anything sensitive could be exposed. He compared an agent carrying out one small, contained task to hiring a freelancer for a specific piece of work.

Mishra cited NTT DATA’s 2026 Global AI Report: A Playbook for AI Leaders, which found that 55.9% of AI leaders use a centralized governance model, compared with 37.6% of other organizations and 33.3% of AI laggards. He wrote that NTT DATA has learned many of these lessons by being its own client zero, experimenting with AI internally and encountering security and compliance issues before taking that experience to clients. He said one of the most important lessons is to start with the end in mind, being clear about what an agent should achieve, how its value will be measured and what it is prepared to let the agent do. He wrote that trying to add the right controls once an agent is already operating across your business is far more difficult. He said applying governance to AI agents does not limit their freedom but puts the right rules in place for them to operate as intended.

Mishra wrote that before you build, you should be clear on the agent’s purpose, who owns it, the data it will use and how much freedom it should have. He said that before an agent goes live you should check its permissions, testing and approvals and make sure you can reverse or stop an action if something goes wrong. He said that once it is working you should monitor how well it performs, the decisions and actions it takes, how much it costs to run and whether it delivers the results you expect. He wrote that if you cannot see every agent operating in your business, trace what happened or step in quickly, you should start with visibility. He directed readers to learn more about NTT DATA’s Agentic AI Studio and how it can help build, govern and manage AI agents across their lifecycle.

stories.Headline: Lucidity launches AI Action Engine to automate cloud cost fixes across its savings modules
stories.Summary:
Lucidity launched its AI Action Engine for cloud cost reduction, and the system is now available across the company's savings modules, according to IT Brief Australia on 18 November 2026. The launch adds an automation layer to Lucidity's existing cloud savings products, which the company says are used by more than 100 enterprises across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. Lucidity launched the AI Action Engine at Microsoft Ignite, according to a GlobeNewswire release published by The Manila Times on 18 November 2026. The engine uses AI agents to move cloud savings from recommendation to the bill and sits behind every Lucidity savings module. The new engine is intended to move cloud cost reduction from identification to implementation, the company says.

The product works in three stages: it first analyses how cloud resources are used rather than relying only on billing data, then adds operational context to each potential saving, and finally applies approved changes while monitoring and logging the result. According to Lucidity, each opportunity includes information on whether a resource is in production, which sizing rules apply and whether a fix has already been made. Users can require approvals, set change windows and apply policies by account, environment or team, and Lucidity says disk changes can be made without downtime. Every change is reversible and logged, the system does not read application data, and the company is SOC 2 Type II certified. Lucidity says AI agents find about 2x more savings than generic FinOps tools, and customers can see up to 40% lower cloud costs.

Nitin Bhadauria, co-founder of Lucidity, said enterprises do not need another tool to report on cloud waste but need it gone, and that the AI Action Engine finds waste across the cloud and fixes it autonomously with hyper-customizable guardrails. Karunakar Bojjireddy, Head of SaaS Operations at Commvault, said disk operations used to take up the SRE team's time and that with Lucidity that involvement is removed from disk operations. Bojjireddy also said Lucidity has helped Commvault's storage utilization go from about 60% to nearly 90%. Lucidity argues that many FinOps products can identify underused resources, but engineering teams often lack the time to check whether recommended changes are suitable for production systems or whether the issue has already been addressed. The GlobeNewswire release states that FinOps tools surface savings but delivery waits on engineers, so most recommendations sit in the backlog.

Commvault, one of the main reference customers cited in the launch, uses Lucidity across an Azure estate covering more than 3PB, 3,500 virtual machines and 11,000 disks, according to the company. Lucidity says Commvault has reduced cloud storage costs by about 40% and recorded more than USD $2 million in Azure savings to date, with no downtime on backup servers. Lucidity says it has identified more than USD $500 million in savings, and it named World Market, Klöckner and Kemper among the companies using its products to improve storage utilisation and reduce spending. The company is positioning the product at enterprises that want to automate at least part of their cloud cost management work while keeping controls around production changes, and customers can choose which actions require approval and which can be automated. Ignite attendees can meet the Lucidity team at booth #5338 in San Francisco from November 17 to 19.

Founded in 2021, Lucidity began with cloud storage management and has since expanded across multiple cloud platforms, and it now works across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud for 100+ enterprises. The company says it has raised USD $32 million from investors including Alpha Wave Global, WestBridge Capital and Beenext. The Manila Times article was published by GlobeNewswire on November 18, 2026, and dates the launch announcement to San Francisco on Nov. 17, 2026. The IT Brief Australia article was written by Finance Editor Karen Joy Bacudo and published on Wednesday, 18th November 2026. The GlobeNewswire release lists Akhil Kintali, Product Marketing Lead at Lucidity, as its media contact.

The articles say customers can require approvals, set change windows and apply policies per account, environment or team, and that AI agents make changes with the customer's approval or on their own for actions the customer chooses. The articles state that every change is monitored, verified, logged and reversible, and that live disk changes run with zero downtime. The articles say Lucidity is SOC 2 Type II certified and never reads application data, and that only changes safe for the workload are surfaced. The articles leave open which specific actions customers can automate without approval and how the approval process is configured in practice. The articles do not say when the engine became generally available beyond its launch at Microsoft Ignite.

stories.Headline: Wolters Kluwer finds 36% of accounting firms have a written AI policy
stories.Summary:
Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting released the third edition of its Future Ready Accountant report on November 18, 2026, based on responses from more than 2,600 accounting professionals worldwide. The report found that firms are growing, confident, and widely adopting AI, but few have redesigned how information, workflows, and professional expertise work together. Jason Marx, CEO of Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting, said adopting AI is only the first step and the real advantage comes from connecting it to how the whole firm works. The report states that this transformation is what will turn today's growth into lasting value. The report also found that just 1% of firms see AI as a threat to their business model.

Among firms that expected AI to improve client advisory, 70% say AI has delivered better-than-expected results in client advisory services, followed by research and learning and real-time financial insights at 68%, and fraud detection and risk management at 67%. Only 11% of firms globally report that at least 75% of their technology solutions are integrated. Investment plans show 55% plan to implement AI-enabled tools, 52% plan to improve technology integration, and 51% plan to increase workflow automation. Thirty-six percent of firms have a written, firm-wide AI policy, while 44% provide general AI guidance without a formal policy. Among firms with AI policies or guidance, 57% require professional review of all AI-generated technical outputs.

Ninety-five percent of firms with formal AI governance are optimistic about the profession's future, compared with 77% of firms with no governance. Forty percent of owners and directors report a written AI policy, compared with 30% of staff. Globally, 96% of firms now offer advisory and consulting services, up from 93% in 2025, with 62% considering advisory a key service. Among firms where advisory isn't yet a core service, 40% say clients still see them primarily as "tax people," and the same share say compliance workload leaves too little time for advisory work. Marx said there is no single model for becoming future-ready and firms across markets begin from different regulatory, technology, and talent realities.

Marx said what should remain consistent is the standard of trusted information, professional review and accountability, and relevance to the client. He added that future readiness is a leadership choice requiring firms to decide where expertise creates the greatest value and how new capacity will improve client outcomes. Fifty-eight percent of firms are highly interested in partnerships or joint ventures, and 53% in private equity or third-party investment. Among firms that received PE investment or completed M&A, 90% say their technology infrastructure helped attract the deal. Eighty-five percent of firms report increased revenue, and 81% report improved profitability.

Bain's article by Matthew Crupi, Sanjin Bicanic, and John Hazan describes a mining company's capital projects team that spent a Monday afternoon setting up review of its most critical investment projects. By Tuesday morning, agents had reconciled tens of thousands of documents against cost and schedule data, and the first pass was on the table. Bain defines a signal as a fast and trustworthy read on whether work was done correctly, and says competitive advantage accrues to companies that build signals no one else has. Bain's March 2026 cross-industry survey found 91% of respondents said AI helps them be more productive, and 53% reported higher-quality work. Only 27% said AI helps them do new types of work.

Bain reports that Anthropic says human review became the new limit as agent-written code moved through its own organization. Climate Corporation built soil and climate measurement data across US farmland, Monsanto acquired it for about $930 million in 2013, and Bayer inherited it when it bought Monsanto in 2018. Bayer traces its current AI capability to that deal, and its CIO argues the data, not the model, is the part competitors cannot copy. Bain says agentic AI concentrates judgment into four human responsibilities: intent, constraints, validation, and stewardship. Bain says most failures it has seen were not AI model failures but trace back to one of these four responsibilities going unassigned.

stories.Headline: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier pursues multistate litigation against AI companies
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced several legal priorities during a Tuesday radio interview in Tallahassee on November 18, 2026. He stated that his office will not defend the 2018 state ban on bump stocks and certain trigger enhancements. Uthmeier urged state lawmakers to revisit the 2018 firearm restrictions, including the three day waiting period for purchases. He also wants the legislature to reconsider the law that raised the minimum age to purchase a firearm to 21. The Attorney General believes the current bump stock statute is overly broad and unconstitutional under recent Supreme Court rulings.

The 2018 statute includes devices like forced reset triggers that do not convert firearms into fully automatic weapons, according to Uthmeier. He is coordinating with House Speaker Sam Garrison, a Republican from Fleming Island, on proactive state policies regarding artificial intelligence. This effort includes multistate litigation against AI companies and a specific lawsuit filed against the company known as OpenAI. Uthmeier is also investigating the Democratic Socialists of America regarding potential unlawful financial support from Beijing, China, and Havana, Cuba. He issued subpoenas to see if the organization received items of value tied to delegation trips to those countries.

Uthmeier said that nonprofits violating Florida law by receiving foreign monetary support or fundraising will have to pay for it. He believes that pushing common sense policies helped Republicans survive one of the toughest election nights in their history. The Attorney General noted that Florida has record crime lows and that his office will not stop there. He stated that other states are looking to Florida to lead multi state legal challenges on regulatory and constitutional issues. Uthmeier also highlighted that his office increased fentanyl prosecutions by more than 500 percent over the last eighteen months.

Fentanyl deaths statewide dropped by 60 percent and fentanyl encounters declined by 80 percent, according to the Attorney General. He cited a case where a couple faces mandatory minimum sentences of 25 years for pressing fentanyl into pills. Senate President Jim Boyd, an insurance executive from Bradenton, said it is imperative that the state tackle affordability issues. Boyd wants to offer more choices and lower rates for property insurance while maintaining the integrity of the reformed industry. House Speaker Sam Garrison said his priorities are a strong economy, safe streets, and providing children with quality schools.

The articles mention that Florida voters recently approved Amendment 3, which will dramatically reduce property taxes for homeowners in the state. This amendment will reduce revenues for local governments, which may lead to service cuts or the raising of other fees. Governor Ron DeSantis wants a special session before the end of the year to help implement this new constitutional amendment. DeSantis also wants to limit the ability of local governments to do tax shifts through a Taxpayer Bill of Rights. Boyd and Garrison noted that the state must preserve natural beauty as the population increases to remain a beacon.

Governor Ron DeSantis wants the special session now, but leadership indicated it may not happen until Byron Donalds is governor. Boyd believes there is enough time during the regular session to address the concerns regarding the implementation of Amendment 3. Speaker Garrison created a committee to explore the risks of AI, which he compared to the disruption of the Industrial Revolution. He expressed concern that AI technology could improve so quickly that humans lose the ability to understand or control it. The articles leave open whether the legislature will commit to the Taxpayer Bill of Rights requested by Governor Ron DeSantis.

stories.Summary:
President Donald J. Trump announced over 17 billion dollars in commercial deals and strategic investments on November 18, 2026. These agreements followed a two-day visit to the Philippines for a State Visit and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit. The president worked with regional leaders to support tens of thousands of American jobs and bolster security in the Indo-Pacific. These efforts aim to protect the United States from illicit activity and ensure a free and open region.

The deals include a 12 billion dollar sale of up to 20 Boeing 787 aircraft with GE Aerospace engines to Philippine Airlines. The United States and the Philippines will pursue a Foreign Military Financing loan package exceeding 2 billion dollars, plus another 400 million dollars for South China Sea deterrence. Other agreements involve a 200 million dollar satellite connectivity project by Astranis and a 40 million dollar fuel depot by Subic Grain. In Thailand, a trade deal will eliminate tariffs on 99 percent of goods, while a 123 million dollar HIMARS sale is planned. Additional investments include a 2 billion dollar coal project in Indonesia, a 1 billion dollar materials deal between Sila and Panasonic, and a 100 million dollar coal agreement with Malaysia.

President Trump and President Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr. committed to eliminating the U.S. trade deficit through increased Philippine imports of American energy and agriculture. The president stated that his America First Arms Transfer Strategy ensures that increased spending by allies benefits the U.S. defense industry. He noted that leveraging strategic infrastructure secures critical supply chains and opens new markets for American businesses. The administration also focused on Super Intelligence technology, partnering with Malaysia and Brunei to establish American technology as the global standard.

The United States and the Philippines are exploring a first-of-its-kind intergovernmental agreement on civil-nuclear technology to generate gigawatts of energy. The Philippines will also modernize Basco Airport to improve commercial supply chains and disaster response in its northernmost islands. In Malaysia, a U.S. consortium will develop a sovereign cloud for the government through the U.S.-ASEAN SI SPARK program.
