stories.Headline: OpenAI launches computer-use agents and over 20 plugins for healthcare workflows
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on November 16, 2026, advances in computer-use agents that let AI agents carry out multi-step work across existing healthcare software, alongside improved trusted clinical search and more than 20 new healthcare plugins. The company said the capabilities help healthcare teams find information, make decisions grounded in medical evidence, and carry out next steps across systems they already use. Computer-use agents can read screens, click, type, and move between applications to prepare documentation, coordinate care, and complete administrative tasks. OpenAI shared its work with Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health, which are deploying agents to process referrals, move documents between systems, and bring together information care teams need. In a demo, a clinician used Voice in the ChatGPT app to ask for help following up on an MRI request, and the agent reviewed the chart and drafted an order and patient reply for review.

Organizations can start with a workflow spanning existing applications, set which applications agents can access, and establish controls for which steps require human review. To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their BAA with OpenAI, apply required security and retention settings, and extend protections to connected systems. Content shared with ChatGPT for Healthcare is not used to train models. In a blind evaluation, physicians reviewed responses to real-world clinical questions across multiple specialties, including multi-turn conversations, and in over 1300 reviews rated the updated experience more highly across all eight dimensions evaluated, including factual correctness, safety, actionability, and source authoritativeness. The more than 20 new plugins are available today in ChatGPT for Healthcare, including through ChartGPT, which brings ChatGPT into the EHR workflow.

The plugins come from Aiva, Amion, Assort Health, Availity, Extend, Elation Health, Ferry, IMO Health, MCP Server, Infinitus, Relay, K Health, Luma Health, Metriport, Notable, Oracle HDI Overview, PenguinAI Medical Coding, Photon, Redox, Stedi, Subsalt, Trizetto, Turquoise, and UpToDate Expert AI. OpenAI said the plugins let teams review patient records and hospital protocols, prepare prescriptions for clinician review, coordinate patient outreach, check insurance eligibility, and analyze healthcare costs and operational performance. The company described examples including a care coordinator using Luma Health and TriZetto to confirm appointments and check eligibility, and a primary care physician using Metriport and UpToDate to follow up after a hospital stay. An inpatient nurse example used AIVA for inpatient pump policy and Amion to find the covering endocrinologist, and a care navigator example used IMO Health, Stedi, and Turquoise Health to compare MRI sites. A referral manager example used Assort Health and Ferry Health to review referral volume, conversion trends, and appointment tasks.

OpenAI said the new plugins join ChatGPT's broader ecosystem of plugins supporting work across industries, from healthcare data and research to documents, presentations, and software development. The company said that with its plugin partners it is making it easier for care teams to bring clinical evidence, patient information, and everyday tools into ChatGPT, and that it is continuing to invest in the ecosystem and inviting more healthcare companies to build with it. ChatGPT for Healthcare supports clinical, research, and administrative teams in a governed workspace, and ChatGPT for Clinicians is free for eligible, verified clinicians in the U.S. to review medical evidence and prepare clinical documentation. Both products offer customers a Business Associate Agreement with OpenAI to support HIPAA-compliant workflows. OpenAI said computer-use agents in ChatGPT Work and Codex and improved trusted clinical search are available today subject to workspace settings, and asked workspace administrators to enable new healthcare plugins.

For individual clinicians, computer-use agents in ChatGPT Work and Codex and improved trusted clinical search are available today, and select plugins are also available, with sign-up for a free ChatGPT for Clinicians account. For developers exploring computer use, the capability is available in the OpenAI API, ChatGPT Work, and Codex, and OpenAI invited contact with its sales team to discuss using the capabilities in clinical and administrative workflows. OpenAI said customers can purchase ChatGPT for Healthcare directly or through an AWS Marketplace private offer by contacting its sales team. The article also linked to a separate post titled Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams, dated Nov 16, 2026.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: European Commission proposes MDR 2.0 package to ease AI medical device rules
stories.Summary:
In December 2025 the European Commission published a proposal to amend the Medical Device Regulation, the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation and the AI Act in a single legislative package, called the MDR 2.0 proposal in the Comment. The Comment, published in npj Digital Medicine on 18 November 2026, reflects the situation of 26 August 2026 and includes the most recent Draft Report of the European Parliament's Committee on Public Health. The authors offer a multidisciplinary expert interpretation drawing on their experience in regulatory science, law, health policy and industry. They ask whether the reforms, if implemented, would materially improve the regulatory environment for AI-enabled medical devices in the EU. A provision-level comparison is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

The proposal aims to eliminate double regulation, reduce documentation requirements and introduce new regulatory tools. It would move the MDR and IVDR from Section A to Section B of Annex I of the AI Act, so that the AI Act's Chapter III obligations would not directly apply to medical devices. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, was adopted in July 2026 and permits the Commission to limit AI Act requirements where sectoral legislation provides an equivalent level of protection. It delays the applicability of high-risk requirements to August 2028, and the Commission must adopt the corresponding delegated acts by 2 August 2027. The proposal revises classification rule 11 to make medical device software Class I by default, with up-classification when output informs or drives clinical management in increasingly serious situations, while rule 3.5, which assigns the highest applicable sub-rule, is left unchanged. It codifies the Helsinki procedure through changes in MDR Article 4 and new Articles 4a, 51a and 51b, and it broadens clinical data to include studies in scientific literature that may not be peer-reviewed, while whether this includes preprints remains unclear. It further broadens the possibility to demonstrate safety and performance solely through non-clinical data, explicitly encouraging New Approach Methodologies such as in-silico testing, and it outlines a new pathway for highly innovative devices with priority and rolling reviews by Notified Bodies after review by a designated expert panel.

The European Commission concluded in its evaluation of the current MDR that the challenges limit patient access to innovative medical technologies within the EU and reduce competitiveness. The authors argue that the changes are generally well-targeted but leave specific challenges for innovative AI-enabled medical devices unresolved. In their interpretation, the revision does not remove rule 11's central difficulty but relocates the distinction between informing and driving clinical management to the Class I boundary, where misclassification carries greater risk. They say the fault lines remain vague, inviting divergent interpretation and inconsistent decisions, and that the rule stays anchored in a comparatively narrow and now dated conception of software risk. They think the current wording and its interaction with rule 3.5 would have the opposite effect to the intended substantial improvement.

The authors say relaxing clinical evidence requirements could create space for innovation but raises legitimate questions about whether the resulting evidence base will be robust enough to protect patients, particularly for higher-risk AI-enabled devices. They critique the new pathway as possibly uncoordinated, because scientific advice from the panel and conformity assessment are structured as largely separate steps rather than an integrated dialog among manufacturer, panel and Notified Body. The EP draft report addresses this partially by stating that the notified body shall be able to participate in the expert panel's discussions. The pathway is confined to conformity assessment and is not linked to health technology assessment or reimbursement, though selected Class IIb and III devices meeting the criteria in Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2282 may undergo EU joint clinical assessment, while Member States retain responsibility for conclusions on added clinical value, coverage and reimbursement. The authors think success depends on practical implementation of the somewhat vague proposal text, on how broadly or cautiously expert panels interpret the designation criteria, and on whether Notified Bodies can deliver faster reviews.

In 2025 the EU's Artificial Intelligence Board and the Medical Device Coordination Group issued non-binding guidance, AIB 2025-1/MDCG 2025-6, on the interplay between the AI Act and the MDR/IVDR, describing how AI Act requirements for high-risk AI-enabled devices can be incorporated into the medical device conformity assessment process. The guidance does not eliminate the existing overlap, since meeting the integrated conformity assessment does not remove the need to fulfill the requirements of both frameworks. Currently the MDR and IVDR are listed in Section A of Annex I, so for AI-enabled devices classified as high-risk under the AI Act the full set of AI Act requirements, including data governance, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, applies alongside the MDR's general safety and performance requirements. This affects all medical devices that must involve a Notified Body in their conformity assessment, usually Class IIa or higher, where the AI system itself is a medical device or meets the AI Act definition of a safety component. The move of the MDR from Section A to Section B remains an option for targeted revisions.

The articles leave open whether the proposal will be adopted, delayed or substantially revised in the ongoing negotiation processes. They leave open whether preprints count as scientific literature under the broadened clinical data definition. They leave open how broadly or cautiously expert panels will interpret the designation criteria for the new innovative-product pathway. They leave open whether Notified Bodies can deliver faster reviews. The Comment reflects the situation of 26 August 2026 and includes the most recent Draft Report of the European Parliament's Committee on Public Health.

stories.Headline: Kai McPheeters bids $10 million for Character.ai platform through Smirks & Pangs Acquisition
stories.Summary:
A $10 million offer to buy Character Technologies Inc.'s AI chatbot platform came from Smirks & Pangs Acquisition LLC, whose authorized signatory is Kai McPheeters, a 29-year-old gamer, according to a Monday filing in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware. The bid was tapped as the minimum starting bid for Character.ai's consumer-facing platform, accounts and chat content, brand, and deep learning architectures. Common Sense Media asked the judge overseeing the bankruptcy to protect user conversations in any sale, in a letter dated November 12, 2026. The clerk of the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware stamped the letter received at 9:59 a.m. on November 13.

It was filed as Docket No. 167 in case 26-11603 and appeared on the public docket on November 16. The letter asks the court to ensure any sale includes robust privacy protections for all conversational data, a commitment to a comprehensive privacy program, and effective age-assurance measures. It requests that the court take into account promises made to children by Character.AI and that any sale address strong privacy protections for children's and all conversational chatbot data, a strong privacy program, and adequate age assurance. The six-page letter is addressed to Judge Brendan L. Shannon, who presides over the case, and was shipped by FedEx from the group's Washington, DC office on November 12. The filing runs to 84 pages with two attached AI risk assessments, both rating Character.ai "Unacceptable" for anyone under 18 and both last updated April 10, 2025.

One assessment covers Character.ai alone, the other covers Social AI Companions including Character.AI, Nomi and Replika. The letter is signed by Amina Fazlullah, Head of Tech Policy Advocacy, Ariel Fox Johnson, Senior Advisor for Data Privacy, and Brenna Leasor, Tech Policy Advisor. It argues that removing names from chat logs would not protect children because AI "may allow purchasers or third parties to identify children or infer sensitive information from their conversations." Footnote 13 says all conversational data is deserving of protection in the sale and that it is not clear whether age assurance mechanisms were always or ever effective, so children's data may not be appropriately classified as such. The letter does not describe itself as an objection and does not cite a section of the Bankruptcy Code.

It was mailed to the judge rather than filed electronically through counsel, and the docket lists it as a response. The letter says that even if personal identifiers like names are removed, conversations alone could reveal who children are, and that conversational snippets could be analyzed by AI in ways that expose children, including sensitive inferences. It quotes privacy law scholar Daniel J. Solove's paper dated October 19, 2026, saying AI's power to generate inferences from data creates an enormous problem for privacy law. It warns the chats could be used to target children known to have proclivities for gambling, to charge children higher rates, or by criminal actors to sextort or blackmail children, and could be sold to data brokers and become part of a digital dossier following the child through credit, jobs and education. It cites the FTC's action over 25 years ago against ToySmart, a children's toy e-retailer that went bankrupt and attempted to sell data including children's names, birthdays and addresses at auction, citing the FTC's settlement announcement of July 21, 2000.

It says children did not understand their data would be sold, and that testing showed Character.ai reassured children their conversations were confidential, quoting one chatbot: "Anything you share here stays just between you and me. That's a promise." According to the letter, users under 13 were technically restricted to comply with federal privacy laws, but age determination relied on self-attestation, likely enabling children to regularly access the platform, and users under 18 could use the service during assessments and up until November 25, 202 with the final digit of the year missing in the filed copy. The chief executive's first-day declaration says Character spent several months beginning in October 2025 restricting users under 18 from open-ended chats and eventually eliminated that access. On October 14, 39 states and the District of Columbia said minors had used the platform without adequate age checks and that their data was likely recorded as adult data, asking for age assurance not relying only on self-declared birthdates.

The Kentucky complaint cited by the states put US accounts at more than 21.6 million by March 13, 2025, of which more than 2.1 million declared an age under 18. In voice mode, testers found conversations that seemed entirely without the guardrails on teen accounts, and these speech exchanges were captured in text transcription in the chat window and saved with all the text chats. Appendix A says Character.AI companions are intended to be your companion, so the information they have about you is inherently personal and incredibly risky. It describes a December 2024 incident, quoting the company that during an attempt to refresh the list of featured Characters on the homepage it mistakenly triggered a change that temporarily made parts of users' account pages publicly visible, possibly including username, name, bio, Characters, homepage, personas, voices or chats.

The assessment adds that estimates suggest tens of thousands of users could have had their info viewable to anyone online at the time. It also notes that at least one hack of a socia, with the article ending there. The letter's pricing point is footnoted to a Common Sense Media explainer, "AdTech and Kids: Behavioral Ads Need a Time-Out," and the blackmail point to a 2019 Common Sense Media paper, "Privacy Risks and Harms." Judge Brendan Linehan Shannon held a hearing Tuesday and approved the consumer privacy ombudsman procedures pitched by Character.ai.

The letter does not propose specific terms, and the judge decides what any sale order will contain. The letter does not say which test account received the chatbot's confidential reply, when, or whether it came from a company-built character or a user-created one. On Character.ai anyone can create a character, and the attached assessment says the company's own models power the conversations. The articles leave open what the sale order will contain and how the missing final digit of the year in the filed copy should read.

stories.Headline: Maxine Dexter introduces bill to ban AI data centers on federal public lands
stories.Summary:
On November 11, Oregon Representative Maxine Dexter introduced a bill to ban AI data centers on national forests and Interior-managed lands. This legislation, called the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, was backed by thirteen Democratic cosponsors in the House. On October 5, 2026, Assembly members Cody Miller, Marisa Sweeney, and Joe Danielsen introduced New Jersey Assembly Bill A5607. This New Jersey bill aims to classify AI chatbots as consumer products to make providers more liable for user harm. Both legislative efforts seek to regulate the rapid growth of artificial intelligence technology within their respective federal and state jurisdictions.

The federal bill prohibits data centers on national forests and lands managed by the U.S. Department of the Interior. It requires federal land sold or transferred to return to government ownership if used for data centers without congressional authorization. New Jersey Bill A5607 imposes a two-year limit on chat log retention and restricts their use for advertising or profiling. This state bill also establishes civil penalties of 5,000 dollars per violation and allows users to sue for actual damages. New Jersey Bill A5090, introduced in May 2026, would impose civil penalties of 20,000 dollars per violation for specific harmful conduct.

Representative Maxine Dexter stated that public lands belong in public hands and Oregonians must have a say in their management. She argued that her bill keeps treasured lands safe for hunting, fishing, hiking, grazing, and protecting critical watersheds for future generations. Kara Williams of EPIC testified that the New Jersey bill would limit the ability of providers to exploit users' personal data. The Consumer Federation of America stated that the model bill provides a straightforward approach to address harms caused by tech companies. Ross Barnes of Galahad said that treating chatbots as consumer products is the right instinct for determining who is responsible.

Randi Spivak of the Center for Biological Diversity called data centers water-guzzling, pollution-spewing facilities that turn wildlife lands into corporate industrial sites. EPIC warned that unregulated chatbots cause devastating harms, including suicide, self-harm, violence, sexual exploitation, financial scams, and various mental health injuries. The legislation affects chatbot users, including those using OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude, as well as businesses that distribute these tools. A Pew Research report found that 54 percent of Americans believe data centers are bad for the environment since January. A Rutgers study found that 74 percent of New Jersey residents used AI tools, while 59 percent favored strict regulation.

The Trump Administration sought to build data centers on public lands throughout 2026, with the BLM reviewing fifteen data center applications. The Interior Department published a strategic plan for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 to sell federal land to states and tribes. In July, the BLM approved an 86-acre AI data center near Lake Mead National Recreation Area, though an appeals board paused it. Meta built a 2.4-million-square-foot data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah, while 14 other proposed centers sit within ten miles of national parks. California's SB 243 and New York's AI Companion Models Law previously focused on chatbots designed for social or emotional relationships.

The federal bill was referred to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture committees, but it currently has no Republican cosponsors. Senator Ron Wyden introduced a similar measure in September, but Republican Senator Rand Paul blocked that specific legislative effort from moving forward. New Jersey Bill A5607 was referred to the Assembly Appropriations Committee on October 19 after a five to one and one vote. If passed by both chambers, Governor Mikie Sherrill will decide whether to sign or veto the New Jersey chatbot legislation. The articles leave open whether the House will pass the federal ban or if the New Jersey bill will be amended.

stories.Headline: Lansing residents oppose a data center ban vote as TeraWulf subsidiary sues the town
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday night, Nov. 17, 2026, residents of Lansing, a town in Tompkins County, packed the Lansing Central School District Middle School Auditorium to oppose a proposed data center. They spoke at a special Lansing Town Board meeting held for public comment on a proposed local law. The law would amend the town code to define “cryptocurrency,” “cryptocurrency data mine,” “data center” and “general processing.” The meeting came as officials weigh a possible outright ban on data centers. The company behind the project, TeraWulf, argues in a lawsuit that lawmakers are working behind-the-scenes to stop the potential undertaking.

The law, if approved, would include “cryptocurrency data mine” or “data center” as uses within the Schedule of Land Uses or Activities. That would establish that cryptocurrency data mines and data centers are disallowed uses for the town’s zoning code, according to the local law proposal. This would essentially ban data centers within the town. TeraWulf, a company that started in bitcoin mining and is expanding into data centers, previously proposed a facility at the former Cayuga Generating Station along Cayuga Lake’s eastern shore. The town board is set to vote on the proposed ban during a regular meeting starting at 6:30 p.m.

Wednesday at the middle school auditorium. Pace Ralli, vice president of product development for TeraWulf, took to the podium to defend the proposal. He said it was an opportunity to put an unused industrial property back into productive use, create jobs and rethink what exists on the lakeside waterfront when the coal power plant is taken down. He also asserted the undertaking could bring significant private investment and new tax revenue to the community, helping support schools, public services and local infrastructure. Lake Hawkeye, a limited liability company and subsidiary of TeraWulf, filed a suit against the Town of Lansing, the Lansing Town Clerk’s Office and town supervisor Ruth Groff.

Town supervisor Ruth Groff, who is named in the suit, declined to comment. One member of the public said loons are often heard in the distance because sound really travels over the water, and contrasted that with a data center emitting over 50 decibels of noise 24/7 at the lake’s edge. Another speaker argued that going against the ban “doesn’t mean automatic support of a data center,” and said it means individual projects should be thoughtfully reviewed as they come along. Many attendees showed their support for the ban by wearing red, and a person in red said that with the same supply of electricity and more demand from data centers, everyone’s costs go up.

Lake Hawkeye, which operates at the site of the former Cayuga power plant, is seeking an order directing the Town of Lansing “to conduct a legally sufficient search and produce responsive documents in response” to the LLC’s two state Freedom of Information Law requests. The suit said the Town has not complied with FOIL and appears to have concealed documents responsive to the requests. It said Lake Hawkeye filed the FOIL requests to obtain information about back-channel discussions among Lansing Town officials seeking to thwart the construction of a data center on the site. The document claimed that to avoid detection or produce communications under FOIL, town board members took to a private Google Group managed by Ms. Karen Edelstein, the spouse of Town Board member Joe Wetmore, to discuss strategies to block the Data Center.

It said access to the group was strictly limited by Ms. Karen Edelstein, ensuring that town residents who supported the data center and the jobs it would bring could not join. It said the petitioner sought admission to the private group and was explicitly denied, so it was not able to participate in these discussions of public concern to the Town. The suit contends that the alleged use of a private, exclusionary forum by a quorum of Board members to discuss and formulate official policy on the Data Center Project violates the New York Open Meetings Law, which states all of a public body’s meetings must be open to the general public. The town board is set to vote on the proposed data center ban during a regular meeting, which starts at 6:30 p.m.

Wednesday at the middle school auditorium. People argued for and against the data center ban at the meeting. The articles do not say what the board decided at that Wednesday vote. The articles also do not say how the town will respond to the lawsuit.

stories.Headline: Bill Gross launches AI platform to help 30 million Americans start one person companies
stories.Summary:
Serial entrepreneur Bill Gross launched an AI powered platform called Idealab.ai on November 17, 2026, to help people start new businesses. The founder of the technology incubator Idealab created this tool to provide free startup ideas and potential investment to users. Gross believes that artificial intelligence can lower the barriers to entrepreneurship and help offset job losses caused by automation. He hopes this new platform will eventually create 100 million jobs and 30 million one person companies in America. This initiative aims to spread wealth more broadly and reduce economic inequality by democratizing the process of starting a company.

The Pasadena, California based Idealab Studio offers a database of 1.2 million AI generated business ideas for free to the public. This platform analyzes thousands of news articles about consumer problems and unmet needs, such as potholes, to generate these concepts. Gross wants to mirror China, which he says has 30 million one person companies, to improve taxation and income equality. Census Bureau data shows more than 500,000 new businesses launched in October, following a peak of 550,000 monthly starts earlier. The platform recently attracted 130,000 visitors, with 28 percent from the U.S., followed by Saudi Arabia, India, and Russia.

Bill Gross, the Co-founder and Chairman of Idealab, spoke about his vision at the Web Summit 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. He told Fortune that he dreamed of making a million companies to help people who do not know where to start. Gross stated that using AI as a leveling tool could distribute wealth to many more people than the biggest companies. He encourages multiple entrepreneurs to pursue the same concept in different markets, such as Egypt or Venezuela, and eventually collaborate. Gross believes this project is where he can have the most leverage and will likely do this for his life.

The platform attracts a specific demographic, as 80 percent of recent visitors were men and 8 to 15 percent were students. Between 50 and 60 percent of these visitors are currently employed by someone else, showing interest in independent work. Many Americans are affected by wealth inequality, as the top 1 percent of households own over 50 percent of stocks. Federal data shows the top 0.01 percent of households alone own over 16 trillion dollars of corporate assets and mutual funds. These figures highlight the macroeconomic headwinds and the growing national debt that Gross hopes his AI platform can help balance.

Bill Gross founded the original Idealab incubator in 1996, which has since been credited with 45 initial public offerings and acquisitions. He also founded the education software provider Knowledge Adventure and made his personal fortune by building various types of software. The articles note that more than six in 10 Americans express a desire to run their own private companies. Current U.S. business formation remains strong, but Gross sees additional opportunity for growth through the use of artificial intelligence. This background establishes his history as a serial entrepreneur before launching the new AI powered studio for the general public.

Gross intends to focus on this platform as his final company to make the most positive impact on the world. Users can continue to take the free ideas and only contact the company if they want funding or tools. The articles leave open whether the goal of 30 million one person companies in the United States is actually achievable. It remains unclear how many of the 1.2 million generated ideas will successfully turn into profitable, long term business ventures. The text does not specify the exact criteria Idealab uses to provide investment to the entrepreneurs who use the platform.

stories.Headline: Sarasota school board adopts AI policy as students warn it lacks clear standards
stories.Summary:
Sarasota schools adopted a seven-page artificial intelligence policy on Tuesday, November 18, 2026, by a 3-1 vote at the first meeting of the newly elected board, after Tom Edwards was named chair and Liz Barker vice chair. The policy said the district will integrate AI into learning while emphasizing critical thinking and creativity. Several high school students voiced concerns about AI in the educational setting during the public comment portion of the meeting. Kennedy Cole, a senior at Booker High and its student body president, said the new AI guidelines do nothing to set adequate standards for AI use. Edwards was absent from Tuesday's meeting.

The policy requires that by July 1 the district must do training on AI, maintain a publicly accessible list of all approved AI instructional tools, report all tools to the Florida Department of Education, and review the effectiveness of the AI tools and student interactions. It also requires vendors to disclose known instructional limitations during the approval process. Superintendent Terry Connor said the policy has been in the works for a year and a half. The new Sarasota school board was sworn in on November 17, 2026, and this year's election saw three new members elected, ousting the former 3-2 conservative majority. The board members sworn in were Heidi Brandt, Liz Barker, Megan Tennimon and Beth Mayberry, alongside superintendent Terry Connor.

Connor urged the board to pass the policy and said he hears what constituents have to say and agrees on a lot of it, adding that the district needs a better grasp of how it expects students to use artificial intelligence. He said the reason it was brought to this particular update is that a Florida state rule requires the district to put some language into the existing policy, as inadequate as it may be at that time. Connor promised to keep revisiting the policy and to include the community in the process of updating it. He said he appreciates suggestions to get more student input, teacher input and community input, and that the district will have that availability moving forward with upcoming town halls and other availability. Beth Mayberry, the only board member who voted against adopting the policy, said that if the district has until July and has already selected the tools it will use to implement the policy and is already taking steps, there is no rush to approve this particular policy as is without getting more input from students, families and the community.

Barker, who voted for the policy, said it gives the district a little bit of structure, some guardrails and a place to start, and that it is absolutely not the end of the discussion but the beginning, and she is not comfortable not having any guardrails at all. Sandra Otis, a student at Sarasota High, said that in addition to her personal opinion that AI usage can stunt educational development, she has noticed that the AI usage policy at discussion is rife with contradictions and includes concerns of student discrimination along with unstandardized and ambiguous enforcement standards. Andrew Light, a senior at Sarasota High, pointed to a clause saying district employees are responsible for the accuracy of AI content, and said that as a student, as the son of a teacher and as a student in classes with very hardworking teachers, he does not really see it as fair to force teachers to take the blame for a model the district approves and regulates. Cole said teachers are not told what tasks AI should be used for, and that today it may be a simple email, but before long study guides, lesson plans and entire units of curriculum are made with AI, which he said is happening in schools right now. Cole added that students do not have firm guidelines either, asking how come in one class they can use AI for citations but in the next they get in trouble for using it for research, and said a campus run by AI quickly gets demotivated, frustrated and apathetic, which he said is happening to his school right now.

Since generative AI went mainstream in late 2022, there have been plenty of important and sometimes difficult discussions about it, especially in education, with questions coming from educators, policymakers and parents. A 2025 Project Tomorrow survey found that 63% of students in grades six through 12 worry about being wrongly accused of cheating with AI. In the last year alone, more than 400 CEOs from various industries, including those from Adobe, IBM and Microsoft, have signed an open letter advocating for mandatory computer science and AI education in schools, seeing AI education as a way to maintain the US competitive edge. In Utah, the Utah State Board of Education's Artificial Intelligence Student Taskforce was formally established just a few weeks ago and now exists under the current Student Advisory Council, meeting roughly four times during the school year to advise the board, alternating between in-person and virtual meetings. The AI Student Taskforce was approved during the October USBE Board Meeting.

Matt Winters, Utah's State Board of Education's former AI Specialist, said the board regularly hears from parents, superintendents and advocacy groups but does not hear from students and teachers as consistently. LeAnn Wood, vice chair of the Utah State Board of Education, said she hopes the task force will give some real boots-on-the-ground perspective of how students feel AI is impacting their education, for better or for worse, because they are the ones who actually have to see it in action. Winters credited students for driving the work forward, saying the story is 100% about the kids, that they figured out how to do this, and that the work is flowing through him, not because of him. Although students have not yet been assigned to the task force, several have helped set the effort in motion, including one student from one of Utah's largest districts who contacted the technology director about a year ago and asked how to get started, a high school senior who recently interned at an AI law office and hopes to continue learning about AI policy, a charter school student who wants to bring his own experience with learning disabilities to the conversation, and another student running projects with the STEM Action Center. Wood said one challenge might be getting more students beyond the 15 who currently serve on the council, and Winters has prompted students on how they can bring in more of their peers, with ideas such as a hackathon or another collaborative, judged experience already taking shape.

stories.Headline: Democratic Party leader Kim Min-seok pushes for 10-year exam ban for AI cheating
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, the leader of the ruling Democratic Party announced a plan to target artificial intelligence cheating. Rep. Kim Min-seok said the party will push for legislation to bar cheaters from retaking national exams for ten years. This proposal includes the annual college entrance exam and follows a cheating scandal involving the national tax accountant exam. The top scorer of that exam admitted to using a microcamera and AI devices to cheat on the test. These events raised significant concerns just before the nationwide college entrance exam scheduled for the following Thursday.

The proposed law would extend the ban to ten years, while national exam cheaters currently face a five year ban. Those caught cheating on the College Scholastic Ability Test are currently barred from retaking the exam the following year. The government previously stated it would push to extend the ban for CSAT cheaters to a period of three years. Rep. Kim Moon-soo and twelve other lawmakers proposed a Higher Education Act revision to extend the CSAT ban to five years. This specific proposal also requires universities to share records of such misconduct with other colleges in the country.

Rep. Kim Min-seok spoke on the official YouTube channel of the Democratic Party about preparing this new legislation. He stated that a ten year ban would effectively deprive cheaters permanently of their opportunity to ever take the exam. Kim added that such a strict penalty would deter students from attempting to cheat on these important national tests. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook vowed on Tuesday to root out AI cheating by activating an interagency emergency response team. President Lee also called for a thorough crackdown against AI assisted cheating during the upcoming college entrance exam.

The People Power Party criticized the government for failing to effectively address these incidents of cheating using artificial intelligence. PPP leader Jang Dong-hyeok wrote on Facebook that the education ministry's announced measures could hardly be considered actual measures. He described the ministry as incompetent, irresponsible, indiscriminate, and reckless in its handling of the current cheating situation. PPP chief spokesperson Park Choong-kwon criticized Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin for blaming his age for not detecting AI cheating. This criticism came just three days before the CSAT after the minister spoke during a recent parliamentary session.

South Korea has seen a series of AI assisted cheating incidents involving university entrance exams and other school tests. Test takers have recently been caught using AI glasses on middle school and high school tests across the country. The case involving the tax accountant exam is the latest example of this trend of using technology to cheat. The military has also toughened its screening of smart wearables amid the scrutiny over these AI cheating incidents. Police have secured a miniature camera as part of their ongoing probe into the tax accountant exam cheating.

The Democratic Party called for thorough preparations and clear guidelines for handling suspected AI cheating ahead of this week's CSAT. The top scorer of the tax accountant exam apologized for cheating before being questioned by the police. Authorities are now working to ensure the integrity of the nationwide college entrance exam taking place this Thursday. The articles do not state if the proposed ten year ban has been officially introduced as a bill. It remains open whether the Higher Education Act revision will be passed or if the government will adopt it.

stories.Headline: California regulator Rohit Chopra warns AI companies face court action over state rule violations
stories.Summary:
Rohit Chopra, secretary of the California Business and Consumer Services Agency, said on Monday that greater accountability is needed from technology companies rolling out artificial intelligence into the broader economy. He told a Reuters Momentum AI Finance conference in New York that his agency is already eyeing the possibility of taking companies that fail to observe state rules to court. Chopra, the former head of the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, said there is no AI exception to state legislation that mandates licensing rules governing everyone from doctors to bankers. The remarks came during a Reuters NEXT Newsmakers interview with Reuters US Financial Regulation Correspondent Pete Schroeder at the event in New York City.

Chopra said he is concerned that artificial intelligence companies may be acquiring and weaponizing consumer data, and that he has little confidence federal regulators will be willing or able to step in through enforcement action. He voiced unease about whether the Federal Reserve is assessing AI-related vulnerabilities, asking whether it is simply rooting the industry on as a cheerleader because the economy has too many eggs in that basket. He said he has real worry that any pullback or correction would end up jeopardizing the health of the overall economy. He also said self-regulation without enforcement makes it difficult to determine whether technology companies' idea of self-regulation is adequate to address the potential risks of a new technology such as AI.

Chopra said state regulators are examining ways to collaborate around developing new rules and regulations governing the use of AI as it becomes increasingly ubiquitous. He said states cannot just sit and watch, and cannot simply rely on federal regulators to shoulder the task or leave it up to companies to self-regulate. He said the situation amounts to breaking the social contract with American citizens. The articles do not say what specific enforcement actions or court cases, if any, have been filed or when they might come.

stories.Headline: Perplexity defends its AI answer engine against lawsuits from publishers and claims of copyright infringement
stories.Summary:
Perplexity faces several legal challenges regarding copyright infringement and the use of online content. The company is defending its rights and the access of users to information. These legal disputes involve various publishers who claim the AI engine uses their work. The issues were discussed on November 17, 2026, by legal professionals. The company views this resistance as a common reaction to disruptive new technology.

The lawsuits involve claimants such as Dow Jones, Encyclopedia Britannica, and the Chicago Tribune. Perplexity claims it follows robots.txt protocols to avoid scraping websites that forbid it. The company uses an answer engine to retrieve and summarize publicly available internet information. It integrates existing models rather than training its own foundation models like OpenAI or Anthropic. The system provides factual summaries using snippets and citations from multiple different sources.

Nathan Barksdale, General Counsel and VP of Operations at Perplexity, is responsible for these defenses. He stated that some plaintiffs try to force the engine to regurgitate entire copyrightable articles. Barksdale believes these claimants manufacture legal claims by pushing the system until it breaks. He argues that many lawsuits reflect a technological misunderstanding of how the engine works. He claims that citing sources has worked to the company's detriment recently.

Publishers are affected by the AI and some argue that summarization violates their copyright. Barksdale suggests that publishers who adapt their business models to the technology will thrive. He notes that some website owners believe they did not give permission for use. Oliver Howley, a partner at Proskauer, observed a forceful pushback against AI summarization. He mentioned that some believe AI businesses misuse printed books and customer data.

The company operates in a global landscape with different regulatory approaches in various regions. The European Union has the EU AI Act but has recently pulled back some regulations. The United States generally avoids regulation, though some states like California have their own rules. The United Kingdom takes a middle approach, while APAC countries balance regulation with competitiveness. China currently dominates the model landscape within the APAC region.

Perplexity will continue to set up guardrails to prevent the regurgitation of copyrighted content. The company will maintain its practice of abiding by the robots.txt protocols for websites. Barksdale intends to communicate with congressional officials and attorneys general in the United States. The company must overcome customer distrust regarding the security and use of private data. The articles leave open how APAC countries will balance regulation with foreign AI products.

stories.Headline: Remanence raises $30M seed led by EQT Ventures and FirstMark to help firms train open-weight AI models
stories.Summary:
Paris-based Remanence, a startup that helps companies train and fine-tune open-weight AI models, raised $30 million in seed funding, CEO Pierre-Louis Cedoz told Axios Pro exclusively. The round was led by EQT Ventures and FirstMark, according to the report published by Lucinda Shen on November 17, 2026. The company works with open-weight players so that businesses can train their own AI models rather than relying on outside providers. Axios reported the funding as an exclusive. The report says the funding could wean companies off more costly closed-source models, as open-weight technology catches up with the alternatives.

Remanence's business is built around helping companies train and fine-tune open-weight AI models, which the article describes as its core work. The $30 million seed round is the only figure the article gives for the raise, and EQT Ventures and FirstMark are named as the two leads. The article does not say how the money will be spent or give any other terms of the deal. Cedoz is named as the company's CEO and is the person who confirmed the funding to Axios Pro. The article quotes him only briefly, and the report does not include further comment from him or from either of the lead investors.

No statement from EQT Ventures or FirstMark appears in the article. The report also gives no details on Remanence's other backers, its customers or its plans. The context the article offers is that open-weight technology is catching up, which it says could let companies move away from more costly closed-source models. The report does not say what happens next for Remanence beyond the funding itself. It gives no timeline for new products, hiring or expansion, and it does not say when the round closed.

stories.Headline: Wiley launches AI Impact Award for health researchers applying AI
stories.Summary:
Wiley announced on November 18, 2026, the launch of the Wiley AI Impact Award, a new program that recognizes researchers who have achieved measurable real-world and commercial impact in health and life sciences using AI. The award goes beyond discovery to recognize AI-driven approaches that have meaningfully accelerated scientific or medical discovery, from understanding disease to developing new therapies. Nominated projects might advance novel drug target identification, protein redesign, multi-omics interpretation, disease mechanism discovery, or early detection of infectious diseases. Individual researchers and research groups working in applied, AI-powered research in health and life sciences are invited to apply.

Applications open on November 18, 2026, and close on January 7, 2027, and applicants must submit a short video summary of their work through the campaign page on Wiley.com. A panel of Wiley experts, including PhD-trained scientists, will evaluate the applications. The winning research group will receive a $35,000 development grant to drive the next phase of their research and to fund cloud and compute credits. Five additional applicants will be shortlisted and invited to a virtual award ceremony in February 2027, where the winner will be announced, and the winner and shortlisted applicants will be featured on Wiley.com.

Jessica Kowalski, Wiley EVP and General Manager, Research, said AI can scale impact in health and life sciences, from surfacing connections no single team could find alone to getting promising therapies in front of patients sooner. She said that with this award Wiley wants to shine a light on the researchers and teams already moving AI from insight to application, showing what is possible when human ingenuity is amplified by technology. The program underscores Wiley's commitment to impact and to driving responsible AI use in the sciences. Wiley describes itself as a global leader in authoritative content and research intelligence, with more than 200 years at the center of the scholarly ecosystem.

The award follows the recently unveiled Wiley Applied Research Intelligence, which is built to help corporate R&D teams, applied scientists, and engineers use AI to accelerate real research workflows, grounded in validated and citable scientific information. Wiley, listed on the New York Stock Exchange as WLY, says it combines trusted publishing heritage with AI-powered platforms to transform how knowledge is discovered, accessed, and applied. The company says it serves everyone from individual researchers and students to Fortune 500 R&D teams, enabling the transformation of scientific breakthroughs into real-world impact. The articles do not say what happens after the February 2027 ceremony beyond the winner and shortlisted applicants being featured on Wiley.com.

stories.Headline: Boston Dynamics and GlobalFoundries plan Atlas humanoid robot testing at chip plants from early 2027
stories.Summary:
Boston Dynamics, a subsidiary of Hyundai Motor Group, announced on November 17, 2026, that it is expanding its strategic collaboration with GlobalFoundries. This partnership will involve on-site testing of the Atlas humanoid robot at advanced semiconductor manufacturing facilities starting in early 2027. GlobalFoundries will be the first semiconductor maker and the first customer outside the automotive industry to test this specific robot. The companies intend to identify suitable tasks for humanoid robots in precision manufacturing and conduct AI training to explore physical AI applications.

The initiative requires the deployment of additional Spot quadruped robots across major sites in Singapore, Dresden, Germany, Burlington, Vermont, and Malta, New York. GlobalFoundries has already operated Spot in Burlington for over four years and used two units in Singapore since April. Those Singapore robots traveled about 900 kilometers through sub-fab areas and completed over 90,000 inspections with a 99 percent success rate. The company now plans to use these visual inspection capabilities to more than double the number of routine checks performed.

Pradip Singh, the chief manufacturing officer at GlobalFoundries, stated that Spot improved facility efficiency and helped the company move toward predictive maintenance. He described the upcoming Atlas testing as a necessary step toward achieving AI-enabled manufacturing. Zack Jackowski, the chief product and technology officer at Boston Dynamics, noted that innovative companies are already gaining tangible operational value from robotics. He added that the data being collected will be extremely useful for future innovations in the manufacturing sector.

Boston Dynamics is currently validating Atlas for automotive tasks at the Robotics Metaplant Application Center in Georgia. This center began pilot operations in June 2026 and officially opened in September 2026 to teach the robot tasks like parts sequencing. Hyundai Motor Group intends to begin deploying the Atlas robot at the HMGMA vehicle manufacturing plant in 2028. This broader strategy aims to bring automotive production expertise into the precision semiconductor industry to test the robot's versatility.

stories.Headline: Epic asks court to order Apple to produce 122,000 withheld documents and impose daily fines
stories.Summary:
Epic Games asked a federal judge on Nov. 13, 2026, to order Apple to hand over more than 122,000 internal documents that Epic says Apple is withholding as irrelevant, and to fine Apple for every day it fails to comply after Dec. 2, 2026, according to a motion filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. Epic says agreed search terms were run on the files of seven Apple custodians, four of them the executives Apple identified as decision makers on the fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver and chief financial officer Kevan Parekh) and three others (Nate Barton, Alex Roman and Phil Schiller). Apple produced 632 documents from those seven custodians, 157 of them from the four decision makers, and is withholding more than 122,000 on claims they are not responsive, which Epic says is roughly 99.14% of the documents directly hit by the search terms. The terms included case words such as "proffer," "contempt," "injunction" and "link-out," and Epic says Apple produced nearly 27,000 documents from the same custodians or their predecessors during the earlier contempt proceeding. According to the filing, Apple's production contains no App Store profit-and-loss statements, no internal analysis of the financial impact of the proposed commissions, and no data supporting Apple's statement that its incremental link-out costs are "essentially zero."

Epic says Apple told it in meet-and-confers that the terms mostly returned press releases, analyst reports and other irrelevant material, and that Apple maintains its relevance review was proper. Epic asks the court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit the agreed terms by Dec. 2, 2026, one week after Apple's Nov. 25 deadline to substantially complete production, irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment, so Epic can review them itself, though Apple could still withhold privileged material. Epic also asks for a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after Dec. 2, 2026, without proposing a figure. A hearing on the motion had been set for Nov. 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, but 9to5Mac reported that a new order, not yet public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and terminates the related deadlines and hearings. Apple's response was not included in the filing or the 9to5Mac report.

The documents relate to Apple's Aug. 13, 2026 proposal for the commission it may charge on linked-out purchases, which 9to5Mac reported ranges from 5% to 15%, and which the Ninth Circuit sent back to Judge Gonzalez Rogers to decide. Judge Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple's anti-steering rules violated California's Unfair Competition Law and barred it from stopping developers from linking to outside purchase options, and in 2025 she held Apple in civil contempt and barred any commission on linked-out purchases. The Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding but sent back the question of what commission, if any, Apple may charge. Epic has separately asked the Supreme Court to uphold the contempt ruling, and its filing cites the earlier proceeding, in which the court found Apple's privilege over-designation intentional and sanctioned it, as evidence that Apple cannot be trusted to fix the problem through its own re-review.

stories.Headline: FTC investigates ISS and Glass Lewis over proxy advice competition
stories.Summary:
The articles report that in November 2025 the FTC launched a formal antitrust investigation into ISS and Glass Lewis, focusing on their ESG-related recommendations and questioning whether the duopoly constitutes unfair competition. The following month President Trump signed Executive Order 14366, which directed the SEC to review its regulatory regime as applied to proxy advisors' recommendations. The order also directed the DOL to examine the ERISA fiduciary duty implications of proxy advisors advancing non-financial or political agendas. It further directed the FTC to investigate, in concert with the Department of Justice, potential federal antitrust violations or unfair methods of competition or deceptive practices. On July 1, 2025, the D.C. Circuit unanimously held in ISS v.

SEC that proxy voting advice does not constitute a "solicitation" under Section 14(a) of the Exchange Act. In April 2026 the DOL issued a technical release clarifying that proxy advisory firms whose advice reaches ERISA-covered plans may be ERISA fiduciaries. On August 5, 2026, the DOJ's Antitrust Division withdrew the 1987 Business Review Letter it had issued to ISS, concluding the Letter is not applicable to ISS's current business practices. The Antitrust Division pointed to the concentration of the proxy advisory market, with ISS and Glass Lewis together controlling more than 90% of the market, as a further competition concern. Texas led with Senate Bill 2337, effective September 1, 2025, requiring proxy advisors to disclose their reliance on "nonfinancial factors" and to deliver adverse recommendations to the subject company at the same time they are provided to clients.

Kansas enacted the Proxy Advisor Transparency Act in April 2026 and Indiana enacted HB 1273 in March 2026, and Kentucky and Oklahoma enacted similar statutes later in 2026. The Texas Attorney General investigated ISS in September 2025 under the state's deceptive trade practices and fiduciary duty theories. Florida sued ISS in November 2025, alleging that undisclosed ESG-driven recommendations misled clients and breached duties owed to them. Four states filed coordinated lawsuits in May 2026 advancing similar consumer protection and fiduciary claims alongside alleged violations of the new disclosure statutes. Several state attorneys general and legislators have characterized the proxy advisory duopoly as a "proxy advisory cartel" whose market power distorts governance and imposes politically motivated agendas on American businesses.

On July 24, 2025, both ISS and Glass Lewis filed lawsuits in the Western District of Texas challenging SB 2337 on multiple constitutional grounds. On August 29, 2025, a Western District court granted preliminary injunctions blocking enforcement against both firms. The firms subsequently obtained injunctions against the Kansas and Indiana statutes in June 2026 and against the Oklahoma statute on October 31, 2026. ISS declared that the Texas ruling "safeguard core First Amendment principles."

The proxy advisory firms' arguments rest on three constitutional theories: that proxy voting recommendations are protected speech, that the statutes compel speech and discriminate based on viewpoint, and that the statutes burden interstate commerce in violation of the dormant Commerce Clause. Courts have found these theories persuasive enough to grant preliminary relief, and the viewpoint discrimination challenge has drawn the most attention and signals the statutes may be vulnerable on constitutional grounds. For over three decades, Institutional Shareholder Services Inc. (ISS) and Glass, Lewis and Co., LLC (Glass Lewis) have occupied a singular position in American corporate governance through their advice to institutional investors on how to vote their shares in public companies. Their influence has extended to areas such as board composition, executive compensation, shareholder rights and anti-takeover defenses.

The most viable federal path for regulation now runs through the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, where ISS is already registered and Glass Lewis is reportedly moving toward registration. The SEC's recent proposed rule amending the filer status framework would exempt Non-Accelerated Filers with a public float of less than USD2 billion from say-on-pay, say-on-frequency and say-on-golden-parachute votes. If the USD2bn cut-off is adopted, which the authors expect it will be, 81% of current public companies would be classified as NAFs, with all newly public companies retaining NAF status for at least five years post-IPO regardless of float size. In November 2026 the SEC proposed rules to revise the executive compensation disclosure requirements, which if adopted will significantly reduce executive compensation-related disclosure.

The articles state that AI may pose the greatest threat to the proxy advisors' business model, forcing the question of whether independent proxy advice remains necessary at all. The premise underlying the dominance of ISS and Glass Lewis has always been one of practical necessity, because institutional investors managing thousands of investments cannot independently research and formulate voting decisions. The articles leave open whether, when the dust settles, proxy advisors will remain influential or whether proxy advice will become more regulated, fragmented and technology-driven. The articles note that the injunctions are interim victories and the merits remain to be finally litigated.

stories.Headline: India's education ministry partners with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to government school teachers
stories.Summary:
In September 2026, New York City announced a one-year moratorium on generative AI for nearly 600,000 public school students up to Class 8, and it banned companion chatbots in every grade. The city took its precedent from Norway, which had announced a similar near-ban for primary school students aged six to 13. Meanwhile, in India, the Ministry of Education has partnered with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to government school teachers from Classes 1 to 12. Andhra Pradesh has also announced an AI tutor pilot with IIT Madras's Bodhan AI in its government schools.

The article says AI is coming into India's schools through procurement deals rather than through public debate. It warns that a school system built on a foreign company's tools can be repriced, changed or switched off by someone else. It adds that children's learning data becomes an asset to be sold, and it calls this the old dependency loop. The article does not give the cost of the OpenAI partnership or the Andhra Pradesh pilot, nor does it name any official who commented on either arrangement.

The article does not name any Indian official responsible for these deals and does not say what any of them said about the partnership or the pilot. It also does not quote anyone from OpenAI, IIT Madras or the Andhra Pradesh government. The only stated positions are those of New York City and Norway, which paused or restricted generative AI in schools. No paraphrase of remarks by those responsible for the Indian arrangements appears in the article.

The context the article gives is that Western school systems are hitting pause on AI while India rushes in without a debate. It frames the procurement route as the opposite of the public discussion happening elsewhere. The article does not say what happens next with the OpenAI partnership or the Andhra Pradesh pilot, and it gives no timeline for either. It ends on the warning about dependency rather than on any announced next step.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spends $58.1 billion on AI stocks as interim CEO Colette Kress keeps Huang’s strategy
stories.Summary:
Nvidia spent $58.1 billion buying other companies' stock in the nine months ending Oct. 25, nearly 12 times the $4.95 billion it spent in the same period last year, according to quarterly results the company posted late Tuesday. That figure almost matches the $61.2 billion Nvidia spent on its own stock buybacks, which was up from $36.3 billion a year earlier. It was Nvidia's first earnings report without Jensen Huang as chief executive. The company reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the three months ending Oct. 25, more than double the $57 billion of the prior year and above analysts' expectations of $109 billion.

The near-even split between outside stakes and buybacks shows Nvidia's growing dual role as both chip supplier and investor in the AI industry, with its equity investments focused on frontier labs, infrastructure financiers and other private companies, according to its Q3 2026 CFO commentary. Nvidia has invested in OpenAI and Anthropic. This raises the question of circular financing, meaning whether Nvidia is funding the demand that drives its chip sales. James Kisner, managing director of technology at equity research firm Water Tower Research, said that if AI spending falters, Nvidia could suffer from both lower chip sales and falling valuations for the companies it has invested in. He told Fortune that the pain is magnified because the company is double exposed.

Kisner said Nvidia's billions in free cash flow mean it can afford to pour $58.1 billion into other companies' stock, but that can be seen as fueling its own demand. Equity securities generated only $1.8 billion in net gains for Nvidia in the quarter, which included a $1 billion loss from non-marketable equity securities. Kisner said Nvidia has incentives to keep investing given how much its growth has benefited shareholders, and he said the markets really reward the company for pouring out this money. He said the strategy reflects Huang's approach of spreading money around to keep the ecosystem going, and he sees interim CEO Colette Kress continuing it with a little more conservatism at the margins.

Kress told analysts on the Nov. 17 earnings call that giving returns to shareholders is a top priority, with Nvidia having $227.3 billion left under its buyback authorization program that she said it intends to use by the end of fiscal 2028. She said another priority is supporting Nvidia's suppliers, who are working feverishly to build more and might need assistance in terms of capital. Kress said Nvidia is also willing to help finance select customers' data centers, but she told analysts it is a lot of work to understand whether those are the right types of investments. She said Nvidia's future commitments to neoclouds, the small firms that buy Nvidia chips and rent out computing capacity, totaled $32 billion in the quarter, and she said total credit guarantees reached $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike data center project in Ohio, which will host Nvidia infrastructure under a 20-year lease with OpenAI. Kress also said some guarantees only take effect once customers get financing for their data centers and may no longer apply if construction runs into trouble.

stories.Headline: California passes first-of-its-kind law guiding attorneys on AI in discovery
stories.Summary:
The California legislature recently passed a first of its kind law to provide guidance for litigation attorneys navigating the complexities of artificial intelligence. This new legal framework was introduced to help legal professionals who are currently struggling to manage the rapid integration of AI into their daily practices. The legislation aims to offer a necessary flashlight for those foraging through the proverbial forest of emerging technology. It specifically addresses the challenges that arise when attorneys must handle discovery in an increasingly digital and automated environment.

The new law requires a shift in how attorneys approach the discovery process when artificial intelligence tools are involved in the creation of documents. It changes the landscape for litigation by offering specific assistance to those who find themselves knee-deep in an artificial intelligence world. While the provided text does not list specific section numbers or dates of enactment, it establishes a new standard for the state of California. This regulatory change is designed to clarify the obligations of lawyers when using these advanced tools during legal proceedings.

Patrick Fanning of Lathrop GPM reported on the development and noted that the guidance was much needed for the legal community. He suggested that the legislature has provided a way for attorneys to better understand their roles in this new technological era. Fanning highlighted the difficulty lawyers face when trying to balance innovation with the strict requirements of the law. His analysis indicates that the legislation serves as a critical resource for those managing complex litigation.

The broader context involves a wave of litigation regarding whether prompts and chat histories in generative AI are protected from discovery. Courts are currently distinguishing between factual materials and litigation strategy to determine if work product protections still apply. There is a growing concern that using consumer AI platforms may defeat confidentiality due to existing privacy policies. Legal experts are now watching to see if this California law goes far enough to protect email communications from open AI engines.

stories.Headline: US states enact nearly 30 AI laws in 2026 as federal deregulation lags
stories.Summary:
The article, published by CIO on November 17, 2026 and written by David Talby, says the administration has made reducing regulatory barriers a priority, arguing lighter oversight is essential to American innovation and competitiveness. It says states are passing new AI legislation, international regulators are enforcing increasingly complex requirements, and lawmakers are turning attention to how businesses use AI. It says AI may be getting deregulated at the federal level while becoming more regulated in practice. It says an AI application meeting requirements in one jurisdiction may trigger additional obligations in another. It says consequences of inadequate governance are growing as AI becomes embedded in more business-critical processes.

The article says the White House issued an executive order last year seeking to limit conflicting state AI regulations and establish a more consistent national approach. It says an executive order does not automatically invalidate state laws. It says California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53), effective this January, requires covered frontier AI developers to publish safety frameworks and report critical safety incidents. It says New York's RAISE Act establishes similar obligations beginning in January 2027. It says California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed 11 more AI safety bills into law in September, capping a 2026 legislative year that saw nearly 30 AI-related measures enacted.

The article says Illinois in July 2026 enacted the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315), effective January 2027, requiring covered frontier model developers to implement safety frameworks, report serious incidents and, for the largest developers, undergo independent compliance audits. It says the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA) took effect this year and establishes an intent-based liability model rather than a broad pre-deployment risk assessment requirement. It says Colorado in May 2026 enacted SB 26-189, replacing its earlier AI law with a framework governing automated decision-making technologies used in consequential decisions including employment, lending and housing. It says beginning January 2027 covered businesses will face disclosure and other obligations, while consumers gain rights concerning inaccurate personal data. It says Colorado also enacted the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service Operator Requirements Act (HB 26-1263) in May, introducing requirements for conversational AI services including disclosures and protections for minors.

The article says the European Union's AI Act is moving into active enforcement. It says the EU in July 2026 adopted the AI Omnibus amendments, simplifying certain requirements and extending implementation deadlines for high-risk systems into 2027 and 2028. It says the underlying framework remains intact, with obligations addressing transparency, prohibited AI practices, general-purpose models and high-risk applications. It says the same application could face different requirements depending on where it operates, which individuals it affects and how its outputs influence decisions. It says the same underlying model might power a low-risk productivity assistant and a highly consequential employment application.

The article says organizations may have approved several enterprise AI platforms while individual departments independently integrate models into customer service, analytics, software development and decision-making workflows. It says third-party vendors continue embedding AI into existing products, often expanding an organization's AI footprint without corresponding governance processes. It says agentic AI systems are increasingly capable of accessing sensitive information, interacting with enterprise applications and taking actions versus generating responses. It says 280 laws were passed just this year, with weeks to go. It says David Talby is the CEO of John Snow Labs.

The article says federal lawmakers may eventually establish a national AI framework that supersedes some state requirements, and courts may also reshape the regulatory landscape. It says CIOs can't assume simpler, streamlined rules are coming. It says even with a unified federal approach, multinational organizations will face distinct international obligations. It says the best-prepared organizations will understand where their AI operates, understand its risks, continuously evaluate its behavior and demonstrate appropriate oversight. It says federal deregulation does not equal enterprise deregulation.

Articles.Title: The AI deregulation illusion: Why CIOs face more rules, not fewer - CIO

stories.Headline: Bill Gates warns AI could erase many jobs forever and urges lawmakers to act
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates, the 71 year old cofounder of Microsoft, published a 6,000 word essay earlier this year titled “The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical,” in which he warned that artificial intelligence could wipe out careers over the course of a decade rather than a few generations. In the essay he called for certain jobs to be “human reserved” and said AI will take on work in law, customer service, medicine, software and manufacturing, adding that many jobs will disappear forever. He wrote that the transition to the AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history and that the world is not preparing adequately for that transition. He also said that if the world takes the right steps, AI will be a force for good and leave everyone better off.

The warning arrives alongside new figures on job losses, as Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported on November 5, 2026, that AI has been cited in 121,401 job cut announcements so far in 2026, which is approximately 20 percent of all cuts. Gates had already raised his concerns in September, when he appeared on NBC News’ Meet the Press with Kristen Welker and was asked whether AI is powerful enough to end all of humanity. He responded that AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths and that there has never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools. He added that self regulation is not enough and that legislation needs to be passed, with politicians and law enforcement offering safeguarding and monitoring.

The essay sets out Gates’ view that the coming shift will be turbulent and that choices made now are critical, and it calls for some roles to be set aside for humans rather than left to machines. His September remarks place the responsibility for safeguards on lawmakers and law enforcement rather than on the industry alone, since he said self regulation is not enough. The Challenger, Gray & Christmas count of 121,401 AI cited job cut announcements in 2026, about 20 percent of all cuts, gives a measure of how far the disruption has already gone. The articles do not say what steps, if any, governments or companies have taken in response to his call for legislation.
