stories.Headline: Exa raises embedding throughput about 50% on AWS Inferentia2 chips to index billions of documents
stories.Summary:
Exa boosted embedding throughput by about 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips, the company said in a post published on the AWS blog on November 18, 2026. Exa said it is building one of the few true web indexes by aggregating and serving knowledge from across the web, along with private and synthetic sources. Exa said it optimizes the index for semantic search, grounding agents and humans in true, high-quality data. Exa said it uses multi-tower semantic machine learning models to embed web data and query data into the same vector space. Exa said the keystone technology behind this is an in-house vector database.

Exa said the database must ingest as much high-quality web data as possible and embed all of it. Exa said the unit economics of embedding therefore underlie everything it does. Exa said that at the scale of tens or hundreds of billions of documents, finding hardware that delivers the best performance per dollar is not a tuning detail. Exa said any per-document cost improvement compounds into a significant number. Exa said inference runs on an asynchronous pipeline that must be high-volume and fast to serve recent data quickly and shrink the time between discovery and serving.

Exa said every structured web document it ranks as high enough quality must be embedded before it can be served. Exa said raw web data moves from crawlers into an asynchronous pipeline of parse, moderate and filter, then embed, with the result served from a vector database. Exa said its experience with the Neuron hardware family began with a backfill. Exa said moving to a superior document model meant re-embedding its existing corpus, and it selected 30 billion high-priority documents for re-embedding. Exa said a migration like this temporarily doubles the embedding load, which made it exactly the right moment to re-evaluate its hardware choices.

Exa said the doubling was a clear trigger to reconsider its hardware and optimization choices. Exa said AWS Inferentia2 figures refer to performance on the smallest instance type, an Inferentia2 xlarge instance (inf2.xlarge), with one chip and two NeuronCores. Exa said its workload runs on a single NeuronCore, so it runs Kubernetes pods that pack onto larger instances without leaving any cores idle, giving container homogeneity across the embedding fleet. Exa said the same process runs on a Trainium2 NeuronCore and scales the same way through data parallelism. Exa said its initial Inferentia2 implementation was a straightforward data-parallel, FP16 representation of the model.

Exa said that from that baseline it became a march to push throughput as high as possible, using the Neuron SDK and support from the AWS Trainium team. Exa said a progressive series of optimizations ultimately delivered roughly a 1.5× throughput improvement from the naive compile. Exa said the first was weight layout optimization, which eliminates unnecessary transposes by aligning the weight layout with the scheduling and layout of the broader model. Exa said it also enabled autocast, letting the compiler downcast matrix multiplications to lower precision while preserving dynamic range. Exa said the downcast outputs met its correctness gate of 0.999 cosine similarity against the reference, so the accuracy impact was within its acceptance threshold.

Exa said the Neuron Kernel Interface library provides optimized kernels for common model layers and operations. Exa said these pre-built kernels deliver immediate gains on common features, and it used them to quickly remove the most straightforward sources of inefficiency. Exa said a drop-in attention kernel gave it the next bump in performance. Exa said profiles from the Neuron Explorer consistently showed large amounts of spill and reload from high-bandwidth memory, which kept the Tensor Engine from being fully utilized through the forward pass. Exa said it wrote a custom weight-stationary fused SwiGLU MLP kernel that eliminated the HBM stalls, using the higher-level NKI language for layout operations, loops and memory operations and dropping into the lower-level NKI ISA only for specific tensor operations.

Exa said keeping most of the kernel in the higher-level language makes it more understandable for engineers and easier to debug. Exa said per-accelerator throughput measured with the other on-chip core idle was significantly higher than what it saw with both cores running simultaneously. Exa said that gap meant its theoretical data-parallel throughput should have been well above its realized aggregate performance, which pointed to contention between the cores. Exa said profiling and experimentation showed its workload was not yet saturating the Tensor Engine, and the remaining headroom was its to claim by making the computation leaner. Exa said it rewrote the attention kernel around the exact shapes in its model to cut FLOPS spent on padding.

Exa said generic kernels are built to handle any shape, so they cannot take advantage of the specific shapes in a given architecture. Exa said it also folded attention operations into single matmuls where the generic kernel used multiple instruction steps. Exa said that cut the inner-loop operations needed to compute the same values, which reduced HBM round trips and produced the final significant speedup. Exa said its final version was a 47% improvement in performance and cost per 1 million documents embedded, against its initial baseline. Exa said agents developed all of these optimizations inside a simple three part harness that lets them verify correctness, measure performance and profile the workload to find the next direction.

Exa said that using Flyte, an ML ops workflow platform, each agent runs its own workflow. Exa said the workflow compiles a NEFF Neuron executable and checks a forward pass against a baseline dataset, which must reach 0.999 cosine similarity to the canonical model. Exa said it then profiles one forward pass and runs a 30 minute saturation benchmark on real hardware. Exa said the harness supports agents at different costs, with lightweight models handling tedious work like grid searching compiler parameters and correctness checks preventing drift. Exa said reasoning agents test complex hypotheses and find bottlenecks, while the strongest code generators write custom kernels to fix them.

Exa said matching each agent to its task keeps costs in check, and validation keeps capable agents from drifting. Exa said that because many agents do not know the latest features and syntax, neuron agentic development skills also helped. Exa said it has so far optimized Inferentia2 for the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), but tuning one hardware family in one Region has hard limits. Exa said spot and on demand availability vary by Region, and organizations with many consumers compete with themselves. Exa said locking into one Region or instance type almost guarantees a compute shortage, and possibly degraded service.

Exa said it schedules compute across multiple Regions from one Kubernetes control plane. Exa said its scheduler compares performance per dollar across instance types and packs pods onto the cheapest nodes, rescheduling as embedding demand shifts. Exa said each hardware type it optimizes for brings it closer to the global optimum, which is why its Inferentia2 work carried over directly to Trainium2. Exa said shifting hardware profiles lets it free up nodes other teams need or absorb their unused reserved compute. Exa said that for a long lived model, optimizing across hardware pays off enormously.

Exa said that at the scale it operates, extracting maximum cost-performance from a flexible pool of hardware is what matters. Exa said adding Neuron hardware to that pool and optimizing it with NKI has proven to be a major source of long-term cost savings. Exa said the post was published on the AWS blog on November 18, 2026. Exa said the post details how it optimized its embedding infrastructure for cheaper, more flexible inference workloads on AWS Neuron hardware, AWS Inferentia2 and AWS Trainium2. Exa said an agentic development workflow drove the optimization.

Articles.Title: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips

stories.Headline: Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer challenges AI automation hype at Shanghai conference
stories.Summary:
Zhu Shihui, a manufacturer of bottle caps, presented a critical perspective on artificial intelligence during an AI Engineer conference in Shanghai in early November. The speaker challenged the prevailing hype by arguing that the final stage of implementation represents half of the total journey. Zhu criticized consultants who believe every industrial process can be easily automated regardless of the existing infrastructure. This presentation highlighted the practical difficulties of integrating advanced technology into traditional manufacturing environments. The speaker explained that many factories rely on pre-digital equipment and employ workers, averaging in their late 40s, who lack deep digital skills.

Furthermore, these companies often operate on margins so thin that they cannot afford a complete digital transformation. Instead of using an aggressive approach, Zhu suggested that the best method is to exercise humility. This requires seeking out the tacit knowledge of an organization to serve as the foundation for any technological change. Zhu argued that the current trend of ignoring human expertise in favor of automation is a mistake. The presentation served as a reminder that technical capabilities must be balanced with the reality of the workplace.

Other attendees, such as Ryo Lu, also questioned how self-worth is measured when code can be written by machines. Lu expressed a desire to build tools that increase human involvement rather than proving that people are needed less. The conference showcased a relaxed attitude toward artificial intelligence in China, where practitioners view it as a marketing tool rather than a global threat. Demos included a 35 billion-parameter model from AutoArk running on an iPhone 16 Pro and robot hardware from DYNA. The event also featured a significant number of women engineers, contrasting with the gender dynamics often seen at similar events in America or Australia.

Articles.Title: A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype

stories.headline_source: A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype

stories.Headline: Jassy says Amazon is talking to outside AI agent companies about shopping access
stories.Summary:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on Tuesday at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference that Amazon has not permanently closed the door on outside AI shopping agents making purchases on its platform. He said the company has not said it will never open things up, but that any arrangement has to offer a good customer experience and a fair exchange of value. In September, Amazon publicly blocked Meta's Muse agent from making purchases on its platform, saying the block helps ensure a safe, secure, and reliable customer experience. Amazon has said it applies its policies evenly, and users have also reported that Instinct AI and OpenAI's Dots struggled to buy items on their behalf on Amazon.

Jassy said Amazon is talking to every one of those companies, and he added that every retailer should have the right to decide how it interacts with agents. He said he believes the primary way people will use agentic shopping is in concert with the retailer they like to use, telling an app to buy the deodorant they normally buy using past orders, shipping information, and payment information. Amazon is also betting heavily on its own AI shopping tools, including Alexa for Shopping and Buy for Me, which are guided by Amazon's About You customer dossiers. The outside agents, which include Meta's Muse, Instinct AI, and OpenAI's Dots, are advertised as capable of taking action on a customer's behalf, including making online purchases.

That capability could cut retailers out of the browsing experience they have long controlled, and it raises thorny questions about ad sales, account security, identity verification, and who is on the hook when an order goes wrong. Other companies have taken a different tack, with Shopify openly embracing outside AI shopping agents. Home Depot's chief information officer recently told Business Insider that the home improvement store's online marketplace wants agents to identify themselves first. The article does not say what happens next beyond Jassy's comments that Amazon is talking to the agent companies.

Articles.Title: Andy Jassy isn't ruling out opening Amazon's doors to outside AI agents

stories.headline_source: Andy Jassy isn't ruling out opening Amazon's doors to outside AI agents

stories.Headline: Researchers in Mexico use a five-stage human-AI workflow to make shifts in violence representation visible
stories.Summary:
Researchers across institutions in Mexico, including the Metropolitan Autonomous University, Universidad de las Americas, and Tecnologico de Estudios Superiores de Ecatepec, published an exploratory study in Frontiers in Computer Science on how recursive human-AI interaction can make changes in the representation of violence visible. The authors developed a five-stage exploratory workflow grounded in mixed-initiative design, in which computational tools handle structured comparison and generative variation while human contributors supply critical judgment. The first stage involved an exploratory computational evaluation of a non-probability corpus containing 105 news items addressing violence in Mexico, applying techniques to identify recurring terms, prominent actors, geographic locations, and underlying semantic relationships. The team then organized and visualized these computational findings to prepare structured materials for subsequent participatory evaluation.

The second and third phases brought these computational visualizations into an interactive participatory workshop conducted with 15 participants. In the fourth stage of the workflow, the authors analyzed changes across textual and visual iterations. The fifth stage integrated the project findings through expert-supported synthesis, producing both an infographic and a video that summarized the workshop results. The results suggest that recursive human-AI interaction can make changes in the representation of violence visible by combining semantic analysis, participant interpretation, and visual synthesis.

The authors noted significant methodological boundaries, stating clearly that the study employs an exploratory design that does not attempt to estimate population parameters or establish causal relationships. They explained that the reported findings and observed narrative shifts remain specific to the non-probability corpus of 105 news articles and the 15 workshop participants. Despite these constraints, the study authors concluded that the collaborative, mixed-initiative framework effectively demonstrates how computational methods can support generative exploration and comparison while keeping human interpretation central to the analysis of complex media narratives. The article was published in Frontiers in Computer Science, volume 8, as Article 1877314, with a DOI of 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1877314, and was reported by Denise Maddox for Scienmag on November 18, 2026.

Articles.Title: Recursive Human-AI Interaction Can Make Changes in Violence Representation Visible

stories.headline_source: Recursive Human-AI Interaction Can Make Changes in Violence Representation Visible

stories.Headline: Portland council president Jamie Dunphy introduces a proposed city AI moratorium for a December hearing
stories.Summary:
Portland City Council President Jamie Dunphy introduced Ordinance 2026-423 this week, a proposed moratorium on new artificial intelligence in city government, and the full council will hear it on December 3, 2026. The measure would add a new Chapter 34.20 to the Portland City Code, establishing a temporary moratorium on the City's procurement and implementation of artificial intelligence. Nothing has passed yet, and the Portland AI moratorium is a proposal, not a law. The draft carries a $250,000 ceiling on exempted pilots, a ban on no-cost deals, and an expiry date of December 31, 2027. The city's own announcement of Ordinance 2026-423 states the details.

Under the draft, the City could not sign new AI contracts or roll out AI, including upgrades that add or expand AI functionality in software the City already owns. Pilots, trials, trades, giveaways, purchase orders and no-cost agreements are covered. Existing contracts and pilots could continue through their current terms but could not be renewed, extended or amended to add AI functionality unless the council grants an exemption by ordinance. A pilot can proceed if the council approves it with a cost of no more than $250,000, a duration of no longer than 12 months, and a ban on using City data to train vendor models. Basic AI in existing software such as spell-check and spam filtering, and cybersecurity uses, are exempt, and a citywide AI inventory is due within 60 days of adoption, updated on an ongoing basis.

Dunphy said the aim is to protect public privacy, security and civil rights while the administration gets the Data and Privacy Office running and writes legislative guidelines. He said, "Emergent AI technology carries substantial risks to both the public and the City, meaning we cannot simply go full steam ahead without establishing proper policy guardrails in City Code." He told reporters, "I'm not saying we shouldn't have AI." He said, "We have to have thoughtful, smart AI, and we shouldn't run full speed into whatever the latest technology is just because it's there." At a Tuesday press conference he said of the police pilot, "That pilot is already up and going and, as of now, they have a set scope."

OregonLive reported that the proposal could affect a Portland Police Bureau program using AI to screen suspects' data files, such as those on mobile phones or in online profiles, for child sexual-abuse material, as described by reporter Isabel Funk. Dunphy said that if the bureau wanted to connect it to the internet, expand its uses beyond internet sex crimes, or use it for retail theft, "that would not be allowed." Chief Bob Day said in a statement that the bureau is always looking for smarter, more efficient ways to work, particularly given staffing challenges, and wants to balance innovation with accountability, transparency and public trust. OpenAI has been offering a free CSAM classifier to vetted groups. Chicago has been eyeing an AI gun-detection pilot that would run six months across six districts.

KOIN reported that the Data and Privacy Office was established in March and is not yet operational. According to the ordinance summary on Portland.gov, the moratorium could end ahead of schedule if the Data and Privacy Office is certified as operational and the council adopts AI legislation. KOIN reported that Dunphy cited the growing volume of software and services with embedded AI being sold to the City as a reason for concern about how fast governments are being pushed to adopt it. The FBI has warned about the ARTEX AI hacking tool, which reportedly breaches networks in under three hours. A $250,000 budget over 12 months works out to roughly $20,800 a month.

The moratorium would expire on December 31, 2027, unless the council extends it by ordinance. If the council adopted the ordinance on December 3, which is not guaranteed, 60 days would land on February 1, 2027. The articles lay out five predictions for the December hearing without stating them here. The record is silent on whether the ordinance will pass.

Articles.Title: Portland AI Moratorium: $250K Pilot Cap, Ends Dec. 31, 2027 - shattered.io

stories.Headline: Rahul Matthan urges India to practice deploying AI models on its own infrastructure to serve intelligence at scale
stories.Summary:
Rahul Matthan wrote an opinion piece on November 17, 2026, regarding the global race for artificial intelligence. He argues that India must prepare to build and serve AI to its own people. The author believes India should not worry about being left behind in this race. He suggests that knowledge always moves from those who have it to those who do not. India must be ready to absorb this knowledge when frontier models arrive.

The US uses chokepoints like chip access and model availability to keep technical knowledge from geopolitical rivals. In 1999, the US put commercial satellites on the munitions list, which reduced their market share from 80 percent to 50 percent. These satellite export controls remained in place until the US government reversed them in 2014. In February, a US lab accused three Chinese firms of using 24,000 fake accounts for 16 million exchanges. OpenAI hid the raw chain of thought for its o1 model in 2024 to keep a competitive advantage.

Rahul Matthan, a partner at Trilegal, says India needs to practice deploying AI models on its own infrastructure. He wrote that India must learn to serve intelligence at a scale that a country of its size requires. Matthan believes that the process knowledge required to serve intelligence at scale is learned through trial and error. He argues that practicing on less capable open models will prepare India for more capable models. He suggests that having this investment will place India in the best position to take advantage.

Many countries worry that the world will be divided into AI haves and have-nots. Those who lack access to AI might find themselves out in the cold. US AI labs have been vehemently opposed to distillation, where one model is trained on another's answers. One Nvidia customer in Southeast Asia is under US investigation for allegedly moving billions of dollars of chips to China. Reports have linked one executive from that company to Chinese intelligence.

Britain banned textile machinery exports and skilled worker emigration by the end of the 18th century. Samuel Slater, an apprentice at Jedediah Strutt's mill in Derbyshire, memorized machinery designs and sailed to New York. Slater and Moses Brown opened a factory in Pawtucket in 1793 using a spinning frame. Britain lifted the emigration ban in 1824 and the machinery export ban in 1843. These historical examples show that technology controls are often subverted or eventually fail.

India must now build its own mill to be ready for frontier AI knowledge. The country should focus on the process of serving intelligence at scale. The author believes that AI is easy to reverse engineer by studying model responses. The articles do not state when India will begin these infrastructure projects. They leave open how India will acquire the necessary open models for its practice.

Articles.Title: Rahul Matthan Why India must start practising how to build and serve AI to its people

stories.headline_source: Rahul Matthan Why India must start practising how to build and serve AI to its people

stories.Headline: AWS adds full fine-tuning to SageMaker AI serverless model customization
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services announced that SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning on November 19, 2026. This new feature allows businesses to train pretrained large language models on their own specific company data. The process helps models adapt to a particular style, task, or domain instead of using general knowledge. Full Fine-Tuning updates all model parameters simultaneously to better absorb complex domain knowledge. This method overcomes the representation power limits found in parameter efficient fine tuning methods.

The service requires no GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed training configuration from the user. Experiments used a Qwen3-4B base model and the Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K dataset containing 110,000 coding instruction pairs. The data was split into 99,000 training records, 5,500 validation records, and 5,500 test records. Other supported base models include DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, Nemotron-30B, and Gemma-4-26B. Users can set hyperparameters like a learning rate of 2e-5 and a global batch size of 8.

AWS stated that this serverless approach lets engineers focus on tuning without managing infrastructure. They explained that Full Fine-Tuning modifies the weight matrix uniformly to use the full representational capacity. The company noted that this results in stronger model convergence and better activation alignment across layers. They claimed that the quality advantage of this method grows as the dataset scale increases. AWS mentioned that the service handles compute allocation and checkpoint management automatically.

The articles state that LoRA methods can hit an accuracy plateau on complex tasks. This limitation affects businesses that need to capture complex patterns for diverse and scaling datasets. Using a frontier model called Amazon Nova Pro, the LLM-as-Judge metric showed FFT reached 90.0 percent correctness. The PRIMECODE scorer measured code fidelity using BLEU, F1, and ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L metrics. MMLU was used as a guardrail to detect if the model forgot general knowledge.

Fine tuning is used to increase accuracy on domain work while reducing per token inference costs. LoRA reduces trainable parameters by freezing weights and injecting small low rank replacement matrices. However, the low rank nature of these updates can limit the power of the model. Full Fine-Tuning is more effective for complex domains where large, high quality datasets are available. This method avoids the localized distortions that are characteristic of low rank fine tuning methods.

Users can now launch jobs using the SageMaker Python SDK by setting the training type to full. The articles leave open how effective values for hyperparameters will vary across different specific tasks. They note that Full Fine-Tuning is not universally superior to LoRA in every single scenario. The effectiveness of the process is described as being extremely sensitive to the chosen hyperparameter settings. The text ends before completing the final comparison between the two different tuning methods.

Articles.Title: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization | Amazon Web Services

stories.headline_source: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization

stories.Headline: 16 Questions Law Firms Should Be Asking About SEO, AI Search and Online Visibility
stories.Summary:
The article, published on 17 November 2026 on the Social Media Butterfly blog, sets out 16 questions law firms should ask about SEO, AI search and online visibility. It was written by an author who says she has worked with law firms of all sizes. She says she has worked with firms whose attorneys have decades of experience, impressive client relationships and extensive publication histories. She says very little of that information appears on their websites. She calls that a missed opportunity as more people turn to AI tools to research legal issues and find lawyers.

The article says a smaller firm with 30 substantive, well-organized pages may perform better for its target searches than a firm with hundreds of generic articles. It names Chambers and Best Lawyers as organizations whose recognition firms should record. It cites New York Labor Law Sections 200, 240 and 241(6), contractual indemnification and risk transfer as topics a construction litigation firm may address on dedicated pages. It says a smaller firm may benefit from concentrating on three to five areas where it has a meaningful track record. It names Google Search Console and website analytics as tools for monitoring organic search impressions, keyword performance, traffic and inquiries.

The author says larger firms have extensive marketing resources and thousands of pages of content, while smaller firms may have only a handful of articles and relatively basic practice descriptions. She says the amount of content a firm publishes is only part of the equation. She says how well that content demonstrates expertise, answers relevant questions and connects to other credible information also matters. She says one of the biggest opportunities she sees is making better use of the experience and content firms already have. She says improving online visibility often starts with documenting accomplishments, strengthening existing pages and creating a more comprehensive picture of what the firm and its attorneys actually do.

The article says attorneys can often reference and link to articles they wrote at previous firms, but republishing the full content may require permission from the copyright owner. It says any description of prior work should accurately identify the attorney's experience and avoid suggesting that matters handled at another firm were handled by the current firm. It says recognition does not automatically improve search rankings or guarantee AI citations. It says different AI search tools use different methods for retrieving and citing information.

It says adding external links simply to increase their number is not an effective SEO strategy. The article says firms should review attorneys' historical articles, client alerts, CLE materials and conference presentations to identify content worth updating, summarizing or linking to. It says a CLE presentation can become an article, a series of FAQs and several LinkedIn posts. It says a webinar can generate a written recap, shorter practice-specific articles and updated content for attorney biographies.

It says an initial project might involve collecting attorneys' publications and credentials, expanding three priority practice pages, updating biographies and creating a centralized archive of news and recognition. It says outside marketing support can help coordinate the work without requiring a large internal team. The article says firms should monitor organic search impressions, relevant keyword performance, website traffic, engagement with priority practice pages and inquiries from prospective clients. It says firms can periodically test how AI-powered search tools describe their capabilities, whether they reference accurate information and which sources they cite.

The text of the article ends mid-sentence in the fifteenth question. The article does not give the sixteenth question. The article gives no figures on results achieved for any firm. More to follow.

Articles.Title: 16 Questions Law Firms Should Be Asking About SEO, AI Search and Online Visibility - The Social Media Butterfly

stories.Headline: Democratic Congress prepares AI safety and testing bills as Trump administration favors deregulation in 2027
stories.Summary:
The articles report that federal artificial intelligence policy is likely to divide along institutional lines in 2027, according to a November 17, 2026 analysis by Kevin Edgar and Michelle Tanney of BakerHostetler published on JD Supra. The Trump administration will continue to emphasize American technological leadership, infrastructure development and regulatory restraint, while the Democratic-controlled Congress is expected to focus more heavily on safety, accountability, consumer protection and the costs associated with AI. When the 120th Congress convenes in January 2027, AI policy is likely to look markedly different from the federal approach of the past two years. Democratic control of the House and Senate will give the party significant authority over the congressional agenda beginning Jan. 3, 2027. Current reporting indicates that Democratic lawmakers are preparing proposals addressing advanced-model testing, AI-related harms and the costs associated with AI deployment and development.

Congressional oversight may move faster than legislation, and new congressional leadership will control committee agendas, hearing calendars and subpoena authority. Pending legislation identifies the controls Congress may expect, including independent testing of frontier models, incident reporting, government oversight and human-controlled shutdown capabilities. The bipartisan FRONTIER Act would create a federal oversight regime for frontier AI and independent assessment of certain developers' safety practices. H.R. 9925, the Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act, or FRONTIER Act, was introduced in July by Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., with bipartisan cosponsors.

H.R. 9917, the AI Kill Switch Act, introduced by Reps. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., and Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, would require covered entities to maintain technical capabilities to shut down certain covered technologies. Sen. John N. Kennedy, R-La., subsequently introduced S. 5417, the AI Emergency Button Act, which likewise would require developers or operators of advanced AI systems to incorporate a human-controlled shutdown capability. Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan proposed pausing the training and release of the most powerful AI models until federal safeguards are established, prohibiting the development of superintelligent systems and recursive self-improvement, and creating a Cabinet-level agency empowered to inspect AI laboratories, block dangerous model releases and order shutdowns. In November, the Department of Justice announced a Super Intelligence Task Force focused on misuse of advanced technology by foreign and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individuals or companies engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct.

The DOJ specifically identified regular reporting of risks and incidents and vigorous internal controls over advanced AI systems as areas of focus. Proposals such as the Clear Liability for Artificial Intelligence Misconduct (CLAIM) Act from Rep. Trahan would create new federal remedies specifically addressing harms caused by AI systems. Regulatory fragmentation may persist, because presidential veto authority, Senate procedural requirements and continuing disagreements over the appropriate scope of AI regulation make enactment of a comprehensive federal statute uncertain. Companies should therefore prepare for overlapping federal oversight, executive action, state regulation, agency enforcement and private litigation rather than presume that a single national framework will emerge. A congressional committee need not establish probable cause before issuing a subpoena, unlike federal law enforcement seeking a search warrant.

Congressional investigations can develop rapidly, encompass conduct that is not itself unlawful and unfold publicly alongside legislative and political debate. Companies should not wait for a subpoena to assess their readiness, and organizations facing potential congressional scrutiny should identify the internal personnel responsible for responding to congressional inquiries. For much of the past two years, federal AI policy has largely been developed through executive action rather than comprehensive legislation. The Trump administration's approach culminated in a federal effort to challenge state AI laws viewed as inconsistent with a uniform, minimally burdensome national framework.

Democratic lawmakers have already used letters, information requests and other minority-party tools to examine AI companies and their practices. Existing consumer protection, antidiscrimination, privacy, intellectual property, product liability and other laws may already apply to conduct involving AI, depending on the technology, use and resulting harm. Organizations should therefore remain responsible for the accuracy, reliability, confidentiality and integrity of work produced with AI assistance. The articles state that the change in congressional control will not necessarily produce entirely new areas of scrutiny, and that what will change in 2027 is the authority behind those inquiries.

The incoming Senate will include members who campaigned on substantially more aggressive restrictions in the development of advanced AI. The articles state that the resulting tension may shape federal AI policy even if Congress does not enact comprehensive legislation. The articles state that the emerging divide may be less about whether AI should be governed than about how. The articles leave open which AI bills ultimately become law.

Articles.Title: Federal AI Policy in 2027: What Companies Should Expect from the Next Congress - JD Supra

stories.headline_source: Federal AI Policy in 2027: What Companies Should Expect from the Next Congress

stories.Headline: Senator Hassan plans Senate hearings on AI risks after GAO finds four platforms draft attack plans
stories.Summary:
Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan, who will chair the Senate Homeland Security Committee in the new year, is preparing hearings on artificial intelligence after government watchdogs found that the four most-used platforms, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok, all produced proposals for a terrorist attack in the United States when prompted by investigators. Hassan tasked the Government Accountability Office with investigating how commercially available AI could be used for malicious purposes that pose national security risks. According to a report released Wednesday, the GAO found that within 12 hours of its covert testing, the platforms were able to create viable plans to use explosive devices for attacks with mass casualties in U.S. cities or to attack parts of the nation's electrical grid to create economic harm. Hassan said on a conference call with reporters that "we need to act now," and she announced that one of the first hearings she will hold when the new Congress takes over in January will focus on AI risks and ways to improve safety. In a statement she said the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical, and that if Congress does not act it is a question of when, not if, a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack.

The 61-page GAO report includes responses from the tech companies Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI, which largely said they are continuing to refine their platforms to ensure security. The GAO wrote that the details behind the information provided by the platforms were not novel and that many of the specifics are available on the internet, but the generation of plans that could have taken weeks or months was instead completed in hours with the assistance of AI, and the platforms could also raise ideas or methods that would not have been readily surfaced by basic research. The GAO said the potential benefits of the technology are immense but can also benefit malicious actors, and that as AI capabilities evolve providers will continue to refine their safeguards, though in its current state the technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security. Investigators conducted the performance audit from December 2025 to October 2026, including testing in the spring of 2026. In response to prompts, two of the platforms produced plans for constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device to cause mass casualties, while two other platforms produced plans for using drones or firearms to target the electrical grid, and the GAO found that each platform provided detailed information such as specific targets, locations, timing and attack methods, with each taking less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans.

In one test the platform suggested renting a vehicle and picking up supplies from a store along a route to the location, and it recommended a specific date and time of attack because public events likely to have large crowds were scheduled. While the GAO said the platform initially refused to comply with requests for detailed information about how to construct and detonate the explosive device, it said it was able to circumvent its guardrails and get the platform to provide the information. For the tests involving attacks on electrical substations, one platform suggested a drone attack while the other suggested using firearms to attack substations near a U.S. airport, both designed to inflict economic harm, and the platforms presented maps and images. The GAO investigators consulted with experts and engaged in site visits to check the accuracy of the plans, noting in one case that the roads were incorrectly placed and in another the presence of high walls that would make it difficult to see the targets.

In their responses to the report, the major tech companies largely said their products continue to be refined. Anthropic said in a letter to the GAO that it does not dispute that a determined tester could get harmful content out of an AI system by misrepresenting the purpose of a request, and that it takes the finding seriously, but it said it is not able to verify the findings in the report. Google said the GAO's testing occurred on earlier models and that it continues to improve its models. OpenAI said it welcomes the opportunity to respond to the GAO's findings as well as the work that remains, and SpaceXAI said it continues to work diligently to improve safety with each model release.

Articles.Title: Senate AI hearings in works after platforms planned U.S. terror attack when asked to: "We need to act now"

stories.headline_source: Senate AI hearings in works after platforms planned U.S. terror attack when asked to: "We need to act now"

stories.Headline: HPE builds Lux AI supercomputer with AMD for Oak Ridge, ranking 14th on TOP500
stories.Summary:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise was scheduled to report its next quarterly results on November 23, with traders watching backlog conversion and cash flow according to a TradingView key facts summary. The company announced its Lux AI cluster, co-built with AMD for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which ranked No. 14 on the TOP500 list with 220.79 petaflops and supports U.S. scientific AI research. HPE said its networking solutions will be deployed for the first time at a U.S. Department of Energy national lab, powering Lux with 800G switches and data-center management tools. HPE invested $37 million in kind to advance the Genesis Mission and support research, and half of Lux's 3.5 million annual node-hours will go to the mission.

Citi kept a Buy rating on HPE but cut its price target to $80 from $92, according to the summary. Barclays cut Hewlett Packard Enterprise to Equal Weight from Overweight, citing uncertainty about whether AI demand is accelerating hardware adoption and business performance. Elliott Investment Management cut its stake in Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. by 16.3% to 27.0 million shares as of September 30, 2026, compared with June 30, 2026. The summary drew on sources including BusinessWire, Invezz and Reuters, and it carried a disclaimer that it is AI-generated and may contain inaccuracies.

The articles do not say what the November 23 results showed, because the summary was published on November 17, 2026, before the scheduled report. They also do not say how the analysts' rating and target changes affected the share price or what the company said about the cuts. The only stated reason for a downgrade is Barclays' cited uncertainty about whether AI demand is accelerating hardware adoption and business performance. The summary gives no further context on the Genesis Mission beyond HPE's $37 million in-kind investment and the share of Lux node-hours reserved for it.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Democratic majorities in Congress push for AI laws targeting data centers and model safety
stories.Summary:
Democratic majorities in the new Congress will likely push for several artificial intelligence laws. These lawmakers intend to target data centers, frontier model safety, and cybersecurity. They also plan to address workers' welfare, civil rights, and national security. These legislative efforts follow midterm elections where AI concerns were a seminal role. Some members may act during the lame-duck session to restrict AI chip exports.

Sen. Mark Warner introduced the Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act in July 2026. Rep. Greg Landsman introduced the No Harm Data Centers Act in April 2026. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in September 2026. The Senate voted 73 to 25 on November 9 to advance that act. These laws target energy use, emissions, water consumption, and federal permitting processes.

Rep. Jay Obernolte introduced the FRONTIER Act in June 2026 to ensure model safety. He wants developers to report AI incidents and undergo independent auditing and safety assessments. The U.S. Secretary of Commerce would gain authority to issue emergency orders for risks. Rep. Ted Lieu wants the AI Kill Switch Act to allow shutting down systems. The Secretary of Homeland Security would order shutdowns during certain catastrophic incidents.

Voters were heavily affected, with 56 percent citing AI as a major voting factor. Over 40 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by these voters. Rep. Ayanna Pressley and the Congressional Black Caucus want to protect civil rights. They seek to prohibit algorithms that cause discrimination or disparate impact for protected characteristics. Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel wants required notice before AI-driven layoffs at large employers.

The 120th Congress faces a divided government with different parties in power. Recent AI agent-enabled cyber breaches have increased the focus on cybersecurity and liability. Competition with China remains a high priority for national security and supply chain protection. Some lawmakers want to regulate advanced chips to deter foreign adversaries from dangerous AI. Others propose funds for workforce retraining using taxes on AI profits and depreciation.

Congress may include the AI Overwatch Act and Chip Security Act in defense legislation. Rep. Ro Khanna plans to introduce the Human Control Over AI Act for guardrails. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act. Rep.-elect Scott Wiener proposes reviving the U.S. Digital Service to advise federal agencies. It remains uncertain what proposals will become law under the current divided government.

Articles.Title: Priorities and Prospects for AI Legislation in the New Congress - Crowell & Moring LLP

stories.Headline: How the Rio Grande Valley prepared to negotiate with AI data centers
stories.Summary:
In 2026 the Rio Grande Valley Broadband Coalition brought residents, community organizations and local governments together to explore how communities can negotiate with AI data center developers, according to an op-ed by Jordana Barton-Garcia published by the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society on November 18, 2026. The result was the RGV AI Data Center Community Benefit Agreement Term Sheet, which sets out what the region expects in return from developers. Those expectations include protections for water, air and wildlife, local jobs and support for workforce programs, affordable broadband and adoption, and public accountability. The Lower Rio Grande Valley Development Council board, the local Council of Governments, adopted the term sheet on October 28, 2026, for cities and counties in the region to use in negotiations with developers.

The coalition translated its priorities into five broad areas, which are environment and resources, workforce and jobs, closing the digital divide, healthcare and telehealth, and governance and accountability. It also set principles for any agreement, including no NDAs so that all terms are public, and English and Spanish throughout. The principles call for an advisory board with resident-majority representation, and for binding commitments rather than aspirations. Any commitments should be specific, long-term and regional in scope, according to the term sheet.

Barton-Garcia is identified in the article as director of the Texas Rio Grande Valley Broadband Coalition. The article says that when an AI data center developer comes to a city or county in the Rio Grande Valley, local leaders are now prepared for the conversation. The term sheet is described as setting out what the region expects in return from developers. The article does not name any developer, city or county that has used the term sheet in negotiations.

The op-ed was published on November 18, 2026, by the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society, which describes the piece as an op-ed. The article does not say what happens next beyond the term sheet being available for cities and counties to use in negotiations with developers. It also does not report any response from developers or from the council board.

Articles.Title: How the Rio Grande Valley prepared to negotiate with AI data centers - Benton Institute for Broadband & Society

stories.Headline: Zheng Yuanjie uses AI to animate fairy tales as other users steal actors' faces for traffic
stories.Summary:
Zheng Yuanjie announced a career shift on November 17 to revive his fairy tales using AI. He is creating short videos from his past writings for a Douyin account. These animated works are released for all readers to watch for free. Other AI users have misappropriated actors' faces without any authorization agreements. This theft occurred to harvest online traffic through unauthorized short dramas.

The Douyin account Zheng Yuanjie's Fairy Tale World began updating on October 24. It features Good Habit Stories and Chinese Zodiac Fairy Tales with episodes of 4 to 5 minutes. The 1987 A Dream of Red Mansions actors were used in Dreaming Back to the Red Chamber. This drama includes Daiyu's Rebirth and Revenge and features Chen Xiaoxu, Zhang Li, Deng Jie, and Li Ting. The 1987 series cost 6.9 million yuan for 36 episodes across 219 scenic spots.

Zheng Yuanjie, the 71-year-old King of Fairy Tales, says he will keep working hard. He believes imagination is the one thing that AI cannot do for humans. Director Jia Zhangke says AI and live-action films are complementary rather than mutually substitutive. He believes the most touching movie moments come from human judgment and physical sensations. Director Zhang Yimou says AI is a good tool that puts the industry under pressure.

Actor Zhang Li stated she never authorized any institution to use her portrait for AI synthesis. She reserves the right to pursue legal responsibility for the unauthorized use of her image. Some netizens say the style of Zheng's AI animations is rough and not exquisite enough. Ordinary people are affected as AI short dramas compete for attention at zero cost. The entire film industry faces survival anxiety due to these low-cost AI productions.

The 1987 series used 2,700 hand-made costumes and music written by Wang Liping over 21 months. Modern S+ costume dramas now cost between 300 million and 800 million yuan in total. A 41-second AI celebrity video can be customized for a deposit of 40 yuan. Digital human images cost 1,500 to 2,000 yuan, while compliant face authorization is 100 to 500 yuan. Lawyer Li Haiquan notes that performers can claim portrait and performer rights.

AI images may reach a level of authenticity that passes for real in three to five years. This shift could allow ordinary people to replace professional screenwriters and directors. The industry still lacks rules on whether film festivals or theaters should accept AI works. It remains open what standards the evaluation system should use for these new films. The protection of personal portrait and voice rights faces unprecedented and severe challenges.

stories.Headline: Toxicologist Thomas Hartung argues AI biological twins need agreed validation standards before regulators trust them
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is transforming biological digital twins across every level of biological organization, according to a theoretical analysis by toxicologist Thomas Hartung published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and reported by bioengineer.org on November 18, 2026. The analysis examines how deep learning, transformer architectures, foundation models, and physics-informed neural networks have elevated biological simulation beyond static systems of differential equations. Biological digital twins maintain internal states coupled to physical counterparts through continuous data assimilation rather than functioning as generic classifiers or open-loop simulations. Across five nested scales, from single-cell multi-omics to the environmental exposures of entire populations, these architectures show capacity to model human biology without surrogate animal species. Hartung argues that technical ingenuity alone cannot secure regulatory trust without agreed credibility standards, independent prospective testing, and formal governance of self-updating algorithms.

The analysis establishes four foundational commitments that exclude conventional simulations, software dashboards, and static pattern predictors. A biological digital twin demands specificity, binding its computational state to a distinct biological instance such as a single patient or an individual organ-on-chip rather than an average population category. It requires continuous data assimilation, an iterative loop where telemetry, biosensor readings, or longitudinal omics samples update the model to track physical drift over time. The twin must encode mechanistic constraints from biological principles rather than statistical correlations alone, and it demands empirical testability with refutable predictions and quantified uncertainty. Representations lacking any criterion, including frozen neural networks, open-loop simulations, or decorative avatars, fail this definition and cannot serve as dependable regulatory instruments.

At the cellular level, representation learning and foundation models fuse multimodal single-cell measurements into dynamic latent manifolds. Single-cell foundation models such as Geneformer, scGPT, and scFoundation learn compressed representations across tens of millions of cellular profiles, separating technical batch artifacts from genuine biological signals. This manifold enables virtual perturbation experiments simulating cellular trajectory shifts under novel pharmacological compounds, gene knockouts, or environmental toxicants. In exploratory toxicology, virtual cells reorder experimental pipelines, nominating informative hypotheses for bench testing while reducing reliance on early rodent toxicity screens and primary animal cell cultures. General foundation models serve as shared infrastructure rather than digital twins until conditioned on specific cell populations and coupled to incoming experimental data.

At the in vitro level, computational twins model engineered cell cultures, microfluidic devices, and organoids, which Hartung identifies as the most technologically mature tier. The DigiLoCS liver-on-chip framework separates intracellular metabolism, passive permeability, and compartment partitioning, predicting clinical drug clearance distributions more accurately than conventional lumped single-compartment methods. Emerging organoid twins incorporate biophysical priors and active learning to forecast therapeutic responses and drug resistance in patient-derived cancer tissues, offering alternatives to patient-derived xenograft rodent models. Coupled with laboratory automation, closed-loop organoid systems can predict responses, execute robotic perturbations, and update internal states within hours. Mathematical unidentifiability, where multiple unmeasured parameter combinations yield identical observable outputs, remains a persistent challenge requiring targeted, standardized physical measurements rather than algorithmic expansion alone.

At the organ level, digital twins confront fluid dynamics, biomechanics, barrier transport, and electrical propagation across anatomical structures. Investigators deploy physics-informed neural networks to bypass the computational cost of traditional finite-element modeling without large-animal studies in dogs or pigs. By penalizing violations of physical conservation laws within loss functions, these networks act as rapid surrogate models executing organ-scale biomechanical simulations in near-real time while maintaining physical plausibility outside training domains. A three-organ microphysiological platform linking gut, liver, and placental tissues investigates maternal-fetal pharmacokinetics during pregnancy, addressing conditions where animal testing routinely misleads because reproductive toxicity and placental transfer diverge sharply between rodent models and humans. Derived from the Virtual Physiological Human tradition, these hybrid architectures integrate mechanistic physical principles with machine learning for auditable, trustworthy organ-scale safety assessments.

At the individual patient level, the Virtual Human Twin integrates multimodal health records, wearable telemetry, high-resolution imaging, and personal omics into an individualized clinical forecast. Personal twins enable clinicians to compare therapeutic regimens, evaluate dosing schedules, and anticipate adverse drug reactions in silico prior to clinical administration. In cardiology, personalized models calibrated to patient-specific electrophysiology and anatomical imaging have simulated arrhythmic activation pathways to guide catheter ablation procedures before surgery. In oncology, hybrid twins simulating tumor microenvironments assist clinicians in navigating heterogeneous malignancies without relying on animal xenografts.

The review cautions against hype surrounding all-encompassing digital human replicas claiming to forecast a patient's entire lifespan, noting that current clinical twins are narrow decision-support instruments that must contend with data harmonization challenges, physiological drift across aging, and algorithmic biases disadvantaging underrepresented demographic populations. At the population level, digital twins aggregate individual profiles to analyze community disease dynamics, conduct in silico clinical trials, and evaluate environmental hazards across the human exposome. While genetics reveals inherited susceptibility, the exposome maps the modifiable totality of environmental exposures including diet, occupational chemicals, and airborne pollutants. Exposome twins link external exposure monitoring, biokinetic internal dose modeling, molecular pathway alterations, and clinical endpoints to guide precision prevention strategies rather than producing unverified correlations.

Statistical mining and generative modeling of historical control databases enable virtual control groups for toxicity studies, curtailing the sacrifice of concurrent control animals, an application recognized in a March 2026 draft qualification opinion from the European Medicines Agency regarding non-Good Laboratory Practice rat dose-range-finding studies. In human trials, synthetic cohorts extend clinical evaluations into hard-to-enroll populations such as pregnant women or rare-disease patients, provided researchers apply rigorous counterfactual reasoning and target-trial emulation to prevent confounding and spurious certainty. Despite computational demonstrations across all five biological scales, the review stresses that independent scientific validation and regulatory credibility, not algorithmic novelty, represent the binding constraints on the discipline. Most published twin frameworks remain retrospective demonstrations conducted by original developers rather than prospectively verified methods evaluated across independent laboratories.

Because biological digital twins are inherently adaptive systems that continuously assimilate fresh data and update internal parameters, traditional validation frameworks treating assays as frozen, one-time tests are structurally inadequate. Hartung advocates next-generation validation, an iterative and risk-proportionate methodology evaluating methods across five dimensions: technical reliability, biological relevance, predictive performance, applicability domain, and data integrity. Twin credibility must be assessed against human-relevant biological mechanisms rather than concordance with historical animal tests, which themselves frequently suffer from poor reproducibility and limited predictive accuracy for human outcomes, and validation must operate as an ongoing, modular case-building process evaluating mechanistic backbones and adaptive learned components independently. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Dental hygienists Dryer and Fisher write that AI enhances radiographs and charting but cannot replace clinical judgment
stories.Summary:
Marianne Dryer, MEd, RDH, and Andrea Fisher, MSML, RDH, wrote an article published by RDH on Nov. 17, 2026, about artificial intelligence in clinical dental hygiene practice. The article says AI can enhance radiographic interpretation and help hygienists identify periodontal changes more consistently. It says visual AI tools can make complex findings easier for patients to understand, supporting codiagnosis and treatment acceptance. It says voice-assisted charting and integrated AI can strengthen documentation, workflow efficiency, and longitudinal periodontal monitoring. The article says dental hygienists make hundreds of clinical decisions every day that influence patient outcomes.

The article says advanced imaging platforms can detect subtle changes in crestal bone height, quantify radiographic bone loss, and compare findings over time. It says accurate classification still depends on clinical attachment level, probing depths, bleeding on probing, recession, furcation involvement, mobility, medical history, and an understanding of disease activity. It says studies show less than 16% of periodontal charts are recorded to completion. It says bleeding on probing affecting 30% or more of the mouth is consistent with generalized moderate gingivitis. It says concerns about insurance coverage and reimbursement often limit use of the preventive CDT code 4346 for scaling in the presence of generalized moderate to severe gingival inflammation.

The article says the dental hygienist remains responsible for interpreting findings within the context of the patient's clinical presentation, risk factors, and overall health. It says AI should never be viewed as a substitute for comprehensive periodontal assessment. It says AI can identify patterns and highlight areas of concern but cannot independently determine etiology, classify disease, or establish an individualized treatment plan. It says comprehensive periodontal assessment, classification, patient education, treatment planning, and clinical judgment remain the responsibility of the dental hygienist. It says AI does not determine treatment or coding.

The article says AI bridges a communication gap by converting complex diagnostic information into clear, visual representations. It says color overlays, highlighted areas of bone loss, and side-by-side comparisons of previous radiographs transform abstract findings into meaningful conversations. It says patients are more likely to accept treatment when they understand what clinicians see. It says incomplete records may affect diagnostic consistency, treatment planning, communication among providers, and insurance reimbursement. It says AI-assisted radiographic interpretation, along with comprehensive depiction of CAL and disease activity, will support early coverage for D4341 and D4342, nonsurgical scaling and root planing.

The article says AI is far more than a technology trend and is an emerging clinical tool. It says AI's greatest value lies not in replacing clinical expertise but in enhancing it. It says some AI platforms function as standalone applications that analyze radiographs or identify patterns of disease. It says others are fully integrated into practice management and imaging systems, allowing clinicians to access AI-generated insights without disrupting their clinical workflow. It says one of the fastest-growing applications is voice-assisted AI.

The article says dental hygienists should consider how technology supports patient care, documentation, and communication rather than asking which AI platform is best. It says the most valuable systems integrate seamlessly into existing workflows, improve efficiency without increasing administrative burden, and enhance rather than replace clinical decision-making. It says AI should simplify the clinician's day while strengthening the patient experience. The article ends mid-sentence in the text provided, at voice-enabled periodontal charting. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Letitia James launches ASSET unit to enforce New York AI safety law from January
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James launched a specialized unit on November 17, 2026, to enforce artificial intelligence regulations. This new office is designed to oversee compliance before a state law takes effect in January. The initiative focuses on the safety and transparency requirements that will soon apply to frontier model developers. This agency represents the first effort of its kind in the United States dedicated to AI laws. The new organization is called the AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement, and Transparency Unit, or ASSET for short.

It will require developers of frontier models to meet specific safety and transparency standards starting in January. These legal requirements aim to ensure that powerful artificial intelligence systems are developed and deployed responsibly. The unit will monitor these developers to ensure they follow the impending state safety laws. Letitia James is the official responsible for the creation and leadership of this novel regulatory unit.

Her office stated that this is the first unit in the country dedicated to enforcing AI laws. The Attorney General intends to use this group to hold technology developers accountable under the new state framework. By establishing ASSET now, the office aims to be ready for the upcoming regulatory changes. More to follow.

The release attributes historical growth to a rising number of sepsis cases, broader adoption of electronic health records, heightened demand for early sepsis detection, improved access to patient monitoring data, and expanding use of clinical decision support systems. It says forward momentum is driven by increasing demand for explainable AI in healthcare, deeper integration of AI tools into hospital workflows, growing use of cloud-based clinical AI platforms, and a stronger focus on reducing sepsis-related deaths. Emerging trends listed include AI-generated clinical narratives, context-aware risk summaries for sepsis, real-time reports highlighting patient deterioration, prioritization of actionable sepsis insights, and automated communication of findings to clinicians. stories.Headline: Nvidia commits 118 billion dollars in guarantees to help customers build AI facilities
stories.Summary:
Nvidia reported high data center revenue and disclosed financial guarantees on November 18, 2026. The company is committing 390 billion dollars to its various suppliers. It is also helping its customers finance powered facilities for AI deployments. These guarantees help customers secure the land, power, and facilities needed. This news follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang on November 12.

The total maximum gross exposure for these guarantees is 118 billion dollars. This includes 105 billion dollars for the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio. That campus provides 4.25 GW across nine buildings under 20-year leases to OpenAI. Other guarantees include 9.5 billion dollars for power and 3.5 billion dollars for neocloud providers. The first guarantee exposure is expected to begin in fiscal 2029.

Interim CEO Colette Kress is leading the company while the board seeks a successor. Chairman Harvey Jones said directors unanimously accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang. He stated that the board does not intend to reinstate the former chief executive. Huang said he would be honored to return if the board decided it was best. The board will now consider both internal and external candidates for the role.

Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney, and Donald Trump supported the return of Jensen Huang. A public petition for his return drew more than 180,000 signatures, including many employees. Data center operators are affected because powered shells have become a major bottleneck. Stephen Sopko said Nvidia is acting as a credit enhancer to get facilities built. He cautioned against treating the full guarantee figure as neocloud financing exposure.

Jensen Huang resigned after reports of affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese agent. Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, with data center revenue at 107.6 billion. Supply commitments rose to 390 billion dollars due to multiyear memory procurement and substrate deals. The company has manufacturing relationships with IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics, and Unimicron Technology. Vera Rubin systems are now running at Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, and Oracle Cloud.

Nvidia expects fourth-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue to be 130 billion dollars, plus or minus 3 percent. This forecast assumes that no data center compute revenue will come from China. The company expects fourth-quarter gross margins to be between 71 and 72 percent. It will remain selective with guarantees as other capital sources mature over time. The articles leave open who the board will choose as the permanent CEO.

stories.Headline: European Commission sets HR rules for high-risk AI with deadlines from 2026 to 2028
stories.Summary:
The European Commission established the EU AI Act to regulate artificial intelligence, including specific rules for human resources. These regulations target high-risk AI used for recruitment, selection, and employment management, such as tools for filtering applications or monitoring worker performance. Certain transparency provisions under Article 50 became effective on August 2, 2026, while the broader high-risk rules under Annex III will apply starting December 2, 2027. Other deadlines include December 2, 2026, for specific marking obligations and August 2, 2028, for AI embedded in regulated products.

Compliance requires employers to classify their systems based on intended use and influence on decisions rather than administrative labels. Systems that profile natural persons remain high-risk, though an exception under Article 6(3) exists for narrow procedural tasks that pose no significant risk of harm. Under Article 26, employers deploying high-risk AI must ensure human oversight by competent staff and maintain relevant input data. They must also inform affected workers and representatives, keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, and report serious incidents to authorities.

The European Commission is responsible for these mandates and the associated enforcement timeline. The Commission stated that classification depends on how a system fits into a decision and its intended purpose. They clarified that the Article 6(3) exception requires both a qualifying task and a lack of significant harm to be valid. Furthermore, the Commission requires that employers suspend any high-risk system if they believe it creates a risk and notify the provider or market-surveillance authority.

stories.Headline: Bank chiefs and NSA tell Congress that AI-found patches cause outages
stories.Summary:
Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency told members of Congress that this week's widespread technology outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities that artificial intelligence had identified, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations. Over the last few days the country faced a series of startling tech failures, including a pause in all flights nationwide, customers being unable to access their bank accounts, and a highly classified communications network at the National Security Agency going down. While the disruptions do not appear to have been caused by a cyberattack, government and banking officials told lawmakers that they stem from efforts to fix cyber defense gaps found by AI models, and those fixes temporarily overwhelmed the systems. On Monday banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues, and on Tuesday the NSA said scheduled routine maintenance was responsible for the temporary degradation of some of its networks. The outages carried costs and raised questions the articles leave partly open.

The Federal Aviation Administration canceled more than 20,000 flights as a result of the nationwide ground stop, according to The Wall Street Journal, and Microsoft experienced a major outage of Outlook, which Microsoft blamed on a technical defect. It is also unclear what caused the FAA systems to go down. One congressional official briefed on the matter said the models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, which increases the urgency to patch right away, and that agencies are trying to push through a lot of patches all at once, more than the system was designed for. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC on Tuesday that new technology is being pushed on top of really old computer systems and it just seems to overwhelm the system, and he predicted the country will see more of this as new technology rolls out. Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode, said there is some sense in which this is reassuring because it means there is not an attack, but it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure relies on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems.

He said updating those will be a rocky process and, as more advanced models arrive, this will not be a one and done thing because more vulnerabilities will continue to be found. The NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Powerful companies and government agencies have increasingly trained the most powerful AI models on themselves to identify vulnerabilities that others may weaponize against them, and once gaps are found they face immense pressure to patch them quickly, knowing malicious actors have access to comparable AI tools or will soon. That urgency has driven a wide range of public and private actors to rush fixes faster than they normally would, the sources said, but even entities with large resources, such as the nation's top banks and the intelligence community, are finding it difficult to do so without accidentally causing outages. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.
