stories.Headline: US restricts advanced AI chip exports to Southeast Asia and Brazil to prevent diversion to China
stories.Summary:
The United States Department of Commerce announced tighter controls on the export of advanced artificial intelligence chips on Monday, November 16, 2026. These new restrictions target Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brazil because Washington believes there is a higher than normal risk of these chips being illegally diverted to China. The move follows a scandal involving the Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed, which was accused of funneling Nvidia chips to China. This regulatory shift comes as President Donald Trump travels to China to meet with President Xi Jinping.

Under these rules, companies must obtain a US license to export, re-export, or transfer advanced semiconductors to the four listed Southeast Asian nations. Overseas data centers providing significant computing power to companies headquartered in China must secure US export licenses by mid-February 2027 to maintain their services. While US-headquartered companies are exempt if they report shipments, non-American regional AI cloud companies and data center operators will need licenses for new advanced chips. Operators serving Chinese customers at scale will face the hardest challenges, as they require separate licenses for those specific clients.

Josh Gilbert, a lead analyst for Asia Pacific at eToro, stated that these restrictions act as a speed bump for the AI ambitions of Singapore. He noted that investors will now seek more clarity because the Nvidia-Megaspeed situation increased political pressure on Washington to limit China's access to computing capacity rented overseas. Matthias Hendrichs, an advisor to AI companies, explained that the rules highlight gaps in current checks since most chips reaching China recently passed through Southeast Asia. He warned that uncertainty regarding chip delivery could cause financing delays of several months for new projects.

Dr. Maria Monica Wihardja from the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute observed that Southeast Asian governments have tried to remain neutral during the rivalry between the US and China. She pointed out that while Singapore and Malaysia have export control laws, Thailand has not fully implemented its framework and Indonesia lacks a dedicated regime. This lack of oversight in some countries may increase the perception that the region is helping enemies of the United States. Experts suggest that these curbs could eventually push the region to toughen its own regulatory oversight to attract more stable AI investments.

stories.Headline: Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion Series C to advance its AI drug design engine
stories.Summary:
Isomorphic Labs, the UK-based AI drug research company founded by Nobel laureate Demis Hassabis, announced on November 17, 2026 that it had completed a $5 billion Series C financing round, equivalent to about 33.3 billion yuan, which was oversubscribed. The round was jointly led by Greenoaks and HSG (Sequoia Capital), with participation from a16z and multiple new investors, while Alphabet continued to make large-scale investments. All existing investors also took part, including Thrive Capital, MGX, GV, CapitalG, Temasek and the UK Sovereign AI Fund. According to the article, the round refreshed the company's previous single-round financing record and may set a new global record for single-round financing in the AI pharmaceutical sector. The financing brings Isomorphic Labs' total publicly disclosed funding to $7.7 billion, about 51.3 billion yuan, after a $600 million first external round in March 2025 and a $2.1 billion Series B in May of that year.

The company, founded in 2021 and headquartered in London, plans to use the new funds to upgrade its proprietary drug design engine IsoDDE, expand its self-developed and partnered drug candidate pipelines, and build a globally AI-driven bioengineering infrastructure. It said positive preclinical results have been achieved in its internal oncology and immunology projects and in cooperative projects, and that preparations are underway to advance them into clinical trials. The article adds that the use of the financing has extended from model research to drug pipelines, translational research and clinical development infrastructure. Hassabis, who is founder and CEO of Isomorphic Labs, co-founder and Chairman of Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist of Alphabet, and who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction work with AlphaFold, said the team believed at founding that biology could be understood and modeled at the most fundamental molecular level and that AI could significantly accelerate this process. He said the company's drug design engine is generating molecules with higher precision and speed, and that the financing will help the team build fundamental biological models, deepen understanding of disease mechanisms and push the first batch of therapeutic projects to clinical trials.

Max Jaderberg, the company's President since January 2026, who holds a doctorate from the University of Oxford and previously led the DeepMind Open Learning Research Team and served as Chief AI Officer, said the team achieves reproducible scientific progress with models every week and converts it into better molecular properties. Isomorphic Labs was incubated by Google DeepMind and operates independently under Alphabet for external financing, and its core technology is the IsoDDE engine, which integrates fundamental simulated AI models covering multiple therapeutic areas and drug types and is described as exploring the vast chemical space to help design, optimize and screen molecules with ideal druggable properties. The company has also developed proprietary Agents for exploring complex biological systems and conducting reasoning, and says the combination of its models and Agents has driven progress across multiple candidate drug pipelines. After this round, the company will continue to improve IsoDDE, explore new biological fields with more advanced models, build a partner ecosystem and construct a scalable, AI-centered translational research and clinical development system. The article notes that most of the company's major achievements remain in the preclinical stage, and that as the first projects advance to clinical trials, the safety, effectiveness and development progress of its candidate drugs will become an important basis for verifying AI drug design capabilities.

stories.Headline: Judge Wise lets memory price collusion lawsuit against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron proceed
stories.Summary:
A class action lawsuit over memory price manipulation will proceed after Judge Noel Wise of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California dismissed the joint motion to dismiss filed by Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron on November 14. The ruling, a 20-page document, rejected the three manufacturers' attempt to end the case. The lawsuit was first filed on June 25 this year. Mark Garciagire, an ordinary consumer living in Pasadena, California, joined 16 other plaintiffs and entrusted the boutique law firm Bathaee Dunne to sue the three major memory manufacturers in federal court. The 17 plaintiffs include ordinary consumers who buy RAM modules from Amazon and Micro Center, as well as small distributors such as PC assembly stores in Florida.

The three parties must submit an official response before December 7 and are required to hand over internal production capacity schedules, executive correspondence and meeting minutes during the subsequent discovery phase. The plaintiffs accuse the three giants of colluding to control production since October 2022, leading to a 697% surge in the price of regular DRAM contracts within 18 months. They presented shopping receipts in the 118-page indictment. The three companies together hold over 91% of the global DRAM market share. This is the first time in DRAM history that a class action lawsuit over price hikes during the AI cycle has crossed the motion to dismiss stage and entered the evidence discovery phase.

Judge Wise became a federal prosecutor through the U.S. Department of Justice's Honors Program in her early years and later spent ten years presiding over complex civil litigation trials in California courts. In response to the claim that the old case would repeat itself, she only replied: "This court does not think so." Facing the defense lawyers' "eagles watching each other" theory, Judge Wise refuted along the same metaphor: in nature, eagles may watch each other when hunting, but they will never fly together in a neat formation. She dismissed the motion to dismiss because the plaintiff presented "additional factors" sufficient to meet the threshold at this stage. The plaintiff's lawyer Brian Dunne's team was also prepared early.

The defense lawyers referred to the period from the end of 2022 to the beginning of 2023 as the "DRAM Winter". In the first quarter of 2023, Samsung's semiconductor division suffered a huge loss of 3.51 billion U.S. dollars, SK Hynix lost 2.61 billion U.S. dollars, and Micron posted a net loss of 5.833 billion U.S. dollars for the entire 2023 fiscal year. The lawyers argued that production cuts were for self-rescue, and shifting production to HBM was to chase the AI trend. They cited the Chicago School's "oligopoly interdependence theory", which successfully convinced judges in a similar lawsuit back in 2018. The plaintiff pointed out that on October 26, 2022, SK Hynix took the lead in cutting DRAM production capacity, and only three weeks later, Micron followed suit immediately.

In January 2023, Samsung executives even publicly stated that "we will never artificially reduce production of memory chips", but on April 7, 2023, Samsung suddenly made a 180-degree turn and joined the production cut camp. According to TrendForce's calculation, by the first quarter of 2026, the output value of a single wafer for DDR5 64GB RDIMM has surpassed that of HBM, and its profit margin is also higher than HBM. In the third quarter of this year, the global total DRAM revenue soared to nearly 200 billion U.S. dollars, a year-on-year surge of 369%, but the actual total shipment capacity of the entire industry only increased by 4%. The lawsuit revealed that Samsung and SK Hynix forcibly raised the price of server memory sold to Google and Microsoft by 60% to 70% within one quarter, and refused to sign long-term multi-year contracts. By the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026, Micron's single-quarter revenue surged to 54.23 billion U.S. dollars, and its Non-GAAP gross profit margin soared to 87%, surpassing NVIDIA in one go; its full fiscal year net profit reached 84.97 billion U.S. dollars.

In the second quarter of 2025, the three parties all shut down or significantly cut the production lines of low-cost DDR4 for regular PCs; Samsung and Hynix also simultaneously stopped selling old DRAM manufacturing equipment to the second-hand market. On December 3, 2025, when consumer-grade memory prices hit a record high, Micron suddenly announced the shutdown of Crucial, its well-known consumer brand that had been in operation for 29 years. stories.Headline: Han Seong-sook bans smart devices and deploys extra staff to stop AI cheating in college entrance exam
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said Tuesday that the government would activate an interagency emergency response team, ban the possession of smart devices during the exam and deploy additional personnel to test sites to root out AI cheating in this week's college entrance exam. She made the remark during a Cabinet meeting, as concerns deepened that AI-assisted cheating could be used in this year's College Scholastic Ability Test, which is set for Thursday. The concerns followed the confession by the top scorer of this year's certified tax accountant exam that he cheated with the help of AI. Han called such cheating a social evil and said the government would root it out completely.

Han said all smart devices, including smartphones, must be powered off and turned in, and that authorities would thoroughly inspect all glasses and watches worn by test takers. She said items such as collars, sleeves and buttons would also be carefully checked. The government will tighten the management of Wi-Fi networks around the test sites, and all bags belonging to examinees must be stored outside the examination rooms, such as in hallways. Checks will be conducted to ensure that no smart devices are active among the personal belongings stored outside the examination rooms.

Han said the government would deploy additional proctors and apply a zero-tolerance policy to strictly penalize any instances of cheating. She said any suspected case would be thoroughly investigated and met with stern action, including invalidating the exam, revoking eligibility and filing criminal complaints or requesting police investigations. President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday ordered additional measures to curb AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's exam, including a proposed reward of at least 100 million won, or about $75,000, for tips. The article did not say what happens next beyond those measures.

stories.Headline: Ha Jung-woo tours Daejeon AI research sites to discuss K-Moonshot and K-Factory industrialization
stories.Summary:
Standing vice chairman Ha Jung-woo of the National AI Strategy Committee visited several research sites in Daejeon on November 17, 2026. He toured the National AI Science Research Center, Daejeon Tipstown, and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology to discuss industrialization. This trip followed previous regional visits to Daegu-North Gyeongsang and Gangwon that took place during October. Ha met with various officials from academia, industry, and research to review ways to apply artificial intelligence in the field.

The committee is focusing on the K-Moonshot project, which uses AI across twelve mission areas including nuclear fusion, semiconductors, and new drugs. This effort is supported by the National AI Science Research Center, which was established in May to integrate AI into the entire research process. Additionally, the government is promoting K-Factory, an intelligent unmanned factory system that utilizes digital twin technology and robots. Ha reviewed the KAIROS platform at KAIST, which is an unmanned operating system built with domestic technology to control logistics and humanoid robots.

Ha Jung-woo and other officials discussed the necessity of strengthening industrial competitiveness to help South Korea become one of the top three AI powers. During a talk concert at Innovate Korea 2026, Ha exchanged views with Yoon Kuk-jin, Jin Yohan, and Hong Won-hwa regarding corporate survival and future talent. He also spoke with investors and startups at Daejeon Tipstown, a facility established in 2021 that currently hosts thirty companies. The participants focused on the tasks required for entering global markets and exporting the K-Factory system overseas.

stories.Headline: McKinsey and BCG say banks must adopt AI fast and at scale to capture $370 billion in annual profit by 2030
stories.Summary:
McKinsey and Boston Consulting Group released reports in November 2026 about the urgent need for banks to adopt artificial intelligence. These firms state that banks must implement AI quickly and at scale to remain competitive in the global industry. The reports warn that there is no grace period for financial institutions to integrate these new technologies. This push comes as AI agents are being rapidly adopted by the banking client base. The goal is to capture significant profit potential before competitors secure an enduring advantage.

Boston Consulting Group estimates retail banks could gain US$370 billion in annual profit potential by 2030 and beyond. This figure is over 30 per cent higher than potential gains from business as usual. McKinsey notes the industry reached a record net income of US$1.3 trillion in 2025. Retail bank revenue growth is expected to slow to 2 to 4 per cent annually through 2029. Savings revenues already fell by almost 35 per cent year on year in 2025.

McKinsey says the AI disruption dividend will go to banks that move with precision and speed. They claim that young and old people are adopting AI at nearly the same rate. Boston Consulting Group states that becoming an AI first organization is now a mandate rather than aspirational. They argue that AI reduces client acquisition and servicing costs significantly for wealth management firms. These firms can now grow without primarily poaching relationship managers or pursuing acquisitions.

Retail banking customers were surveyed by McKinsey, and 46,000 people showed almost universal awareness of generative AI tools. Nearly a quarter of these customers already use these tools to manage their personal finances. S&P Global analysts Miriam Fernandez and Nicolas Charnay say the next three to five years are critical. They believe AI adoption will differentiate leaders from laggards and affect credit quality assessments. Neobanks and fintechs are mentioned as efficient new entrants that increase pressure on traditional banks.

Banks began using AI more than a decade ago to improve fraud detection and operational efficiency. Recent advancements are now underpinned by deep pocketed banks that are willing to commit significant capital. S&P Global notes that efficiency gains only become substantial at very high levels of investment. Larger banks have an advantage due to their sizeable cost bases and larger customer pools. However, smaller entities might find it easier to adopt AI because they have less legacy infrastructure.

S&P Global expects management teams to prudently allocate budgets and monitor returns to avoid poor investment decisions. Praveen Raina of OCBC says AI must make banking easier for customers and people more effective. He argues that adding another system to run is overhead rather than true innovation. The reports leave open how banks will navigate power constraints and sustainability targets. It remains to be seen which firms will successfully scale these solutions without falling for hype.

stories.Headline: New Zealand Commerce Commission issues AI guidance for businesses
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Commission of New Zealand released new guidance for businesses on November 18, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence. This regulatory framework helps companies understand how existing consumer protection and competition laws apply to their modern technological tools. The commission issued these instructions because businesses are increasingly using AI to conduct transactions, engage with consumers, and support commercial decision-making. These guidelines aim to clarify the legal landscape as AI continues to change the way various businesses operate.

The new guidance specifically explains how the Commerce Act 1986 and the Fair Trading Act 1986 apply to AI systems. It highlights potential legal risks and provides practical steps that companies can take to manage those risks effectively. The framework requires that businesses remain fully accountable for all outcomes, regardless of whether decisions are made by people or algorithms. Companies must ensure that the information they provide is accurate and that all consumers are treated fairly.

Deputy Chair Anne Callinan stated that using artificial intelligence does not shift the legal accountability or responsibility of a business. She explained that the commission is not focusing on regulating the technology itself, but rather its impact on markets and competition. Callinan urged boards and senior leaders to treat AI as a governance issue that requires constant monitoring. She emphasized that leaders must ensure sufficient safeguards are in place to oversee how the technology influences corporate decisions.

More to follow.

He believes that the current era is being defined by these major transformative technologies.

The strategy requires banks to align their technological advancements with their existing organizational structures to ensure efficiency. Financial institutions must also coordinate their investment cycles to keep pace with the rapid speed of technological change. Furthermore, the Chairman stated that banks must find a careful balance between pursuing innovation and managing potential risks. These three pillars are intended to guide banks as they move from pilot programs into full production.

Liao Lin explained that the Asia-Pacific region offers unique opportunities for AI due to its diverse financial services and vast markets. He also pointed to the highly interconnected industrial and supply chains within the region as a primary driver for growth. The Chairman described artificial intelligence as one of the most significant transformative technologies of the modern time. stories.Headline: China-linked threat actors use autonomous AI tools to breach ten organizations
stories.Summary:
China-nexus threat actors used autonomous AI tools to breach ten organizations between August and September. These attackers targeted advanced manufacturing, defense sectors, and civil and human rights organizations. The malicious activity was tracked as CL-STA-1238 by researchers at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42. This campaign represents the second documented attack where China-linked actors used the Cairn penetration-testing framework. The actors conducted twenty-five operations against at least nineteen organizations during this specific time period.

The attacks targeted seven semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain firms and three US defense and defense policy organizations. Attackers used Chinese large language models Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro. Victims included a semiconductor-lithography manufacturer, an industrial-automation manufacturer, an education nonprofit, a US teacher's union, and an industry standards body. One organization suffered a mass exposure of personal data that exceeded one million records. Other targets included a defense policy think tank and various human rights and civil society organizations.

Unit 42 researchers stated that the attackers supplied a target and goal for the AI to execute. They noted that Cairn planned, executed, and recorded results on its own using a shared blackboard. The researchers explained that AI model agents write findings back as a fact-intent graph. They also observed that human operators could inject hints to guide the operations if needed. Unit 42 reported that the attackers obtained dozens of valid credentials and retrieved military identities.

Tyler Oliver of Huntbase said it does not matter to a victim if AI or humans are attacking. Rickard Carlsson of Detectify noted that Cairn builds on earlier findings without a person reviewing every result. John Strand of Black Hills Information Security suggested that organizations use continuous attack surface management. He also recommended using cyber deception by setting up tripwires to detect attackers during reconnaissance. These experts highlighted that the victims were affected by known security gaps and dated public CVEs.

The articles state that the attackers exploited authentication bypasses and insecure direct object references. They also used mass-assignment privilege escalation, exposed cloud APIs, and weak or default credentials. The Cairn framework allows for simultaneous operations against multiple organizations to reduce dependence on human operators. Individual operations lasted anywhere from twenty minutes to more than fifty hours. The background shows that another AI penetration-testing framework called Artex is also being weaponized.

Defenders can still use identity hygiene, attack-surface reduction, and software patching to remain effective against these tools. Organizations are encouraged to identify all services exposed to the internet and restrict access wherever possible. The articles leave open how these AI-driven attacks will evolve in future offensive operations. They do not specify which particular military or government identities were retrieved during the successful breaches. It remains unclear how many other organizations may have been targeted beyond the nineteen identified.

stories.Headline: Researchers describe technique to hide malicious payloads in open-weight AI models
stories.Summary:
Researchers described a technique called Lazarus last week to hide malicious payloads in open-weight AI models. This method allows an attacker to poison a model using a few near-imperceptible neurons. Microsoft described this specific process as turning an AI model into a sleeper agent. These poisoned models can grant an attacker access to the environment of the user. The attack targets models downloaded from the open Internet that users often trust.

The technique requires targeting fewer than 10 dormant neurons late in a model's processing cycle. These neurons are arranged to fire sequentially and stay inactive until they receive a specific trigger. Triggers can be user inputs, tool outputs, or a date read in a user's terminal. The payload can be any small, correctly formatted command that does not impact normal functioning. This differs from MaleficNet, a 2022 technique using code division multiple access to spread binaries.

Briland Hitaj of Confidencial said that people download models from strangers and give them system access. He explained that neural networks have more parameters than needed, allowing weights to be nudged unnoticed. Hitaj noted that while malicious models appear on Hugging Face, they usually abuse Python's Pickle format. He stated that no scan proves a model is clean because testing rarely finds triggers. He advised limiting agent access and requiring human approval for all consequential actions.

Luigi Vincenzo Mancini of Sapienza University of Rome advised organizations to take a defense-in-depth security approach. He suggested that users download models from official sources and compare them against a trusted baseline. Mancini noted that detecting these modifications requires diffing deployed weights against the original, unmodified weights. He said that monitoring for unusual shell commands or network connections is a more actionable technique. Users and organizations using open-weight AI models are the primary parties affected by these risks.

Open-weight models are popular because they are cheap, auditable, and liked by developers. McKinsey found that 63 percent of organizations used them early last year. Additionally, 76 percent of those survey respondents expected to use these models more in coming years. Qwen 3.8-Max is an example of an open-weight model with 2.4 trillion parameters. This model likely contains around 100 million neurons, providing ample cover for secret payloads.

Users should treat model weights like source code or binaries rather than ordinary data files. Organizations must monitor system boundaries for unexpected agent behavior to detect potential malicious intent. They should also keep production systems and credentials out of reach from AI agents. The articles leave open whether anyone has hidden payloads in weights outside of research. They do not specify if any real-world attacks using the Lazarus technique have occurred.

stories.Headline: NTT Data CTO Vikram Bharwani argues banks must control data and decisions to use AI
stories.Summary:
Vikram Bharwani, CTO for Banking and Financial Services at NTT DATA in the UK and Ireland, published an article on November 13, 2026, arguing that every major bank will need sovereign AI. He defined sovereign AI not as a bank-owned frontier model or a warehouse full of GPUs, but as the ability to use powerful AI while retaining control of knowledge, actions and decisions. The article appeared on nttdata.com at 06:00:00Z on 2026-11-13, and a second version appeared on 2026-11-14 at 06:00:00Z. Bharwani wrote that banking has spent half a century digitalizing how money moves and how financial services operate. He said AI is now beginning to digitalize something far more complex, namely the judgment behind banking decisions.

Bharwani cited a 2024 survey by the Bank of England and the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, which found that 75% of responding firms were using AI, up from 58% in 2022. He described the reverse information paradox as framed by Satya Nadella, who said that in the AI age the buyer risks giving away knowledge just to use what they bought. Bharwani said a bank's knowledge includes the credit officer's correction, the fraud analyst's rejected lead and the exception an experienced underwriter accepted, with the reasons for those decisions. He said the knowledge layer is more valuable than the model itself, and that a bank can use external models while owning its private evaluations, approved knowledge, feedback and orchestration. He said data residency is important, but a model can run in a bank's own building and still leave the bank unable to explain a decision or switch suppliers.

Bharwani said sovereignty comes down to whether a bank controls its data, can explain decisions, retains what the system learns and can keep operating when something fails. He said an agent's permissions, network access and spending limits need to sit outside the model, and critical actions need approval and an effective way to stop them without it. He said these controls can exist in a public cloud and can also be missing from a private deployment. He said the FCA expects firms to apply existing duties and governance to AI, including consumer outcomes and senior accountability. He said a decision passport should capture inputs, permissions, policy and model versions, tool actions, human interventions and the final explanation, and a bank must recreate that record after changing models.

Bharwani said a mortgage application from someone with irregular income shows what the architecture must do, with AI reconciling payslips and bank statements, finding policy, flagging conflicting evidence and preparing an affordability recommendation. He said the underwriter should see conflicts and assumptions rather than a confident paragraph that hides them, and a declined customer deserves a clear reason and a way to correct the record or seek review. He said an upheld appeal may expose a faulty interpretation, arrears may show whether affordability assumptions reflected risk, and a complaint may reveal that the explanation failed the customer. He said learning should stay in a sandbox, tested against unseen cases, before release under control, and historical lending data can reflect past exclusions while declined applicants create gaps in outcome data. He said the same principle applies to fraud, customer service and operational resilience, and the test is fewer avoidable referrals, lower false positives, faster resolution, sounder decisions and better customer experiences.

Bharwani said banks do not need to own every part of the AI stack but must control their data, knowledge and evaluations, with freedom to change models without losing context. He said banks need clear controls over what agents can do, decision records that survive each technology change and, for critical services, a tested fallback. He said some tasks warrant private inference while others are better served by a smaller model or a clear deterministic rule. He said a bank should start with one material process, establish what a good decision costs today, how long it takes, where it goes wrong and what customers experience, then measure whether AI improves those outcomes. He said cost per token means little if the result is a faster, cheaper mistake.

Bharwani said banks should consider what happens to human judgment as work is automated, asking how junior underwriters learn to challenge AI in five years if it builds every first-pass credit pack. He said they should be given supervised exceptions, simulated cases and access to model traces, and human oversight is meaningless if a person clicks approve without the chance to investigate the evidence. He said powerful AI will be available to everyone, and the real difference will be whether banks turn it into a governed extension of institutional judgment without giving up control. He said a bank can rent a model but cannot rent accountability, and he expects sovereign AI to become part of core banking infrastructure. The articles leave open which specific process a bank should choose first and what the IDC InfoBrief sponsored by NTT DATA concludes.

The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority is examining the third parties that banks, super funds and insurers rely on as it deals with the risks of artificial intelligence, according to Law360 Australia. APRA Chair John Lonsdale said those third parties are a focus for the regulator, the report said. The report was published on November 18, 2026, and was written by Antony Scholefield. The report described APRA as being at the edge of its mandate in scrutinising third parties on AI. The report did not give any further numbers, dates or names beyond those of Lonsdale, Scholefield and the regulator itself.

It did not say what the scrutiny requires of the third parties or what changes it might bring for the banks, super funds and insurers involved. The report also did not set out a timeline for any action by APRA. The available article was a preview that stopped before the full text. The report said Lonsdale made the comments about the third parties being a focus for the regulator.

It did not give further detail of what he said beyond that. The report did not say who else was responsible or what other officials said. The report did not give the context behind the comments or say what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: DDN offers software-defined EXAScaler deployment for enterprise AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
DDN announced a new software-defined deployment option for EXAScaler on November 17, 2026, in Santa Clara, California. This new option is enabled by the upcoming EXAScaler 7 release for enterprise AI infrastructure. The company allows customers to run high-performance data infrastructure software on qualified industry-standard servers. This change provides an alternative to using purpose-built systems or cloud partners for deployment. A limited beta for this software-defined deployment is planned for early 2027.

The software will start on DDN AI2200 servers, with qualified third-party appliances following later. This makes both EXAScaler and DDN Infinia available in software-defined formats for various customers. Hyperscalers and NCPs with established storage infrastructure can now deploy EXAScaler on industry-standard hardware. This model allows AI platform teams to select hardware suited to their specific requirements. DDN will continue developing purpose-built systems for those preferring integrated performance and reliability.

Omer Asad, the Chief Product Officer at DDN, is responsible for this product direction. He stated that AI infrastructure is becoming more diverse and customers want more freedom. Asad explained that making EXAScaler available as software extends flexibility across the company portfolio. He noted that customers can choose integrated systems or deploy software on third-party hardware. This approach maintains the core capabilities that customers depend on from the EXAScaler platform.

The new model affects organizations that bring AI and HPC workflows together in one environment. In life sciences, researchers use AI surrogate models on molecular dynamics simulation outputs to predict protein behavior. Software-defined EXAScaler on qualified hardware allows simulation and training to run on the same data. This removes the need for copying data between different environments during the research process. These capabilities help researchers avoid repeating every computationally intensive simulation during their work.

DDN has provided AI data storage and management platforms for over 20 years of innovation. The company serves national labs, research institutions, financial firms, and autonomous vehicle innovators. Its platforms support next-generation AI factories, hyperscale clouds, and Sovereign AI initiatives. DDN is recognized as a leading provider for the largest AI deployments on Earth. The company offers EXA, Infinia, and various intelligent data management platforms to its customers.

DDN is developing enhancements for multi-tenancy, performance, and data protection for the EXAScaler platform. These specific enhancements are targeted for general availability in the first half of 2027. The company will share validated performance data as it becomes available to the public. The articles leave open the specific dates for general availability, as they may change. It remains unclear which third-party appliances will be qualified for the software-defined deployment.

stories.Headline: NTT Data launches generative AI service to rebuild COBOL systems in Java and targets ¥50 billion in revenue
stories.Summary:
NTT Data said on November 17 that it has begun offering a service called Clean Modernization, which uses generative AI to analyze core systems built in COBOL and other legacy languages and redesign them into highly maintainable Java systems. The company applies generative AI across processes that run from recovering business specifications to testing, and it expects to cut project timelines by about 40% compared with manual work. It will target financial institutions and government agencies, aiming for cumulative revenue of ¥50 billion, or approximately $313.9 million, over the three years starting in fiscal 2027. The service migrates existing core systems in stages to a state that is easier to maintain and modify over the long term. The service covers four domains, which are applications, infrastructure, operations and organization, and it reviews existing systems from two angles.

The first is visualization, which documents the current state to make it easier to understand, and the second is change enablement, which restructures systems to make it easier to limit the scope of change impacts. In the core application overhaul, generative AI recovers business specifications from COBOL and other programs and design documents, organizes intricately intertwined processing into functional units, and then redesigns the system into highly maintainable Java. The AI models used can be selected from multiple frontier AI options depending on the customer's environment and policies. At companies and local governments across Japan, core systems written in COBOL remain in operation, and the aging and retirement of engineers who understand the specifications has become a serious problem.

Against this obsolescence risk, known as the 2025 cliff, the approach of recovering specifications with generative AI could help compress modernization costs and timelines. At the same time, how to verify the accuracy of specifications recovered by generative AI is an important consideration for adopting companies. NTT Data has indicated a policy of advancing visualization and change enablement in stages, aiming to reduce migration risk by avoiding wholesale replacement. Demand for core system modernization is expected to remain at a high level, and the company's order trends are likely to affect the competitive environment in Japan's IT services market.

stories.Headline: Asia-Pacific university leaders urge redefining core missions as AI reshapes knowledge delivery
stories.Summary:
University leaders from the Asia-Pacific region met during the APEC meetings week in November 2026 to discuss how artificial intelligence is challenging traditional knowledge delivery. These educators believe that institutions must redefine their core missions to foster humanistic judgment and bridge the digital divide to ensure education equity. They argue that universities should transition from being the sole providers of teaching to becoming hubs for the co-creation of validated knowledge. This shift requires universities to reform teaching methods by using AI for content delivery while reserving class time for critical discussions and case studies. Angelo Jimenez of the University of the Philippines suggests establishing jointly recognized doctoral programs in bioscience and engineering to retain highly skilled talent.

Tatacipta Dirgantara from the Bandung Institute of Technology emphasizes the need for professor-to-professor partnerships and shared resources to foster intercultural understanding. These changes aim to strengthen foundational literacy and numeracy so that humans maintain control over advanced technology. Angelo Jimenez stated that humans must control legitimacy and validity because AI cannot replace the responsibility of human judgment. Tatacipta Dirgantara noted that while AI is an enabler like the calculator, it cannot replace empathy or the responsibility educators have toward the people. Yang Bin of Tsinghua University observed that some faculty are moving to industry for better computing resources and real-world data.

He believes that sustained dialogue during events like the APEC University Leaders Forum will help build consensus on academic credits and quality assurance. The academic community expects the center of gravity for global higher education to shift toward the Asia-Pacific region as it grows as an innovation hub. Many institutions used the recent APEC gatherings to sign new partnership programs or expand existing collaborations to address the revolutionary impact of AI. These leaders believe that mutual benefit and shared research interests will make these cross-border connections sustainable for the future. Future efforts will focus on mutual recognition of degrees to support the region's expanding role in global economic development.

stories.Headline: Dell adds Nvidia and AMD systems to its AI Factory to move agentic AI into production
stories.Summary:
Dell announced new additions to its Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA on 16 November 2026, according to IT Brief Australia, extending a portfolio it says now includes more than 420 offerings and serves more than 6,500 customers. Dell Technologies also expanded its Dell AI Factory with new AMD-based infrastructure products spanning servers, modular platforms and rack-scale systems, IT Brief Asia reported on 17 November 2026. The Nvidia announcements focus on four areas: data preparation for AI, management software for AI infrastructure, partner-built validated solutions, and new storage options for large AI workloads. The AMD update includes the Dell PowerEdge M8825 server, new configurations for the Dell AI Platform with AMD, and the AMD Helios Rack-scale Solution from Dell. Dell says the changes are intended to help companies move agentic AI projects from pilot stages into production.

The PowerEdge M8825 is an air-cooled server based on AMD EPYC processors, offering up to 512 cores and 1,024 threads per node for agentic AI and other compute-intensive workloads. Dell expanded its Dell AI Platform with AMD by adding modular configurations built on the PowerEdge XE7745 and R7725 servers, which use AMD Instinct MI350P PCIe GPUs. The AMD Helios Rack-scale Solution can deliver up to 2.9 exaflops of performance with 72 AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs, paired with Dell PowerRack for networking and storage. Dell added Agentic Data Gateway, which in internal testing reduced token consumption by as much as 76% and increased answer accuracy from 60% to 94%. Dell introduced Dell OpenManage Rack Scale, which can manage up to 100,000 devices, up from 8,000 in the previous generation.

Arthur Lewis, President, Infrastructure Solutions Group, Dell Technologies, said AI outcomes do not come from models alone and take data with the right context, infrastructure that scales and solutions validated to work together. Lewis said the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA is that full-stack foundation, one you own and control, with 6,500 customers already proving it works. Dell said Dell and AMD are giving customers more ways to deploy AI with confidence, whether they are starting small, scaling fast, or going all-in on frontier infrastructure. Dell describes the liquid-cooled storage platform as a 2OU platform supporting up to 32 NVMe drives and designed for file, block, object or parallel file storage. Dell says the 1U platform offers 67% higher drive density per rack unit than the previous generation.

Ashish Nadkarni, Group Vice President and General Manager, Global Domain Lead, Enterprise Infrastructure, IDC, said success increasingly depends on combining trusted data, scalable infrastructure, operational simplicity and ecosystem integration into a repeatable model for AI deployment. Nadkarni said vendors like Dell that help reduce complexity and accelerate time to value will be well positioned to support enterprise AI adoption. Dell says software-defined PowerScale on Dell Exascale has achieved NVIDIA-Certified Storage validation at the Foundation level. Dell says Dell Fabric Manager, in internal lab analysis, could cut Day-2 operational effort by up to 80% while maintaining a fully accurate device inventory. Partners in the latest wave include F5, JFrog, DataRobot, Dynatrace, Ipsotek, Iternal Technologies, Teradata, Aible, Atolio, Maven AGI, OpenAI and ClearML.

Dell is also adding hybrid data pipeline orchestration so pipelines can run where data already sits, including on-premises private clouds, Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA environments, non-Dell systems and public clouds. Other changes include Storage Intelligence and Data Intelligence tools to show data provenance, quality and usage across large file environments, along with a unified data access layer for tables, images, video and documents. Dell says the system can route vectors to existing databases without requiring migration, and cited indexing speeds of up to 12 times faster based on external benchmark data. The platform is also being linked with tools from LangChain, OpenAI, Codex and Unstructured.io. The Enterprise SONiC Distribution by Dell Technologies is being extended to support additional platforms, including the Z9964F-ON and NVIDIA Spectrum SN4700 switches.

The broader architecture also includes modular infrastructure built around Dell PowerStore, Dell PowerEdge XE9785 systems with NVIDIA HGX B300 GPUs, and Dell-supported NVIDIA AI Enterprise software. The expanded AMD platform will include validated support for AMD Enterprise AI Suite, Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform and Red Hat AI Enterprise. Dell says its AI Factory Engineers model brings together teams across platform design, workload delivery, data, governance and security, while its data centre services focus on power, cooling and space planning for AI deployments. Dell says the modular approach lets customers start with a single compute node and add GPUs, nodes, storage or networking as demand grows. Dell said the AMD package is backed by deployment and lifecycle services, giving customers a single supplier for integrated AI infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Port Washington mayor Ted Neitzke leads tours of a $15M AI data center site as residents raise concerns
stories.Summary:
A $15 million artificial intelligence data center is under construction in Port Washington, Wisconsin, developed by Vantage in partnership with Oracle and OpenAI, and it is drawing both community curiosity and criticism. The 672-acre site, with an additional 1,000 acres reserved for expansion, is larger than the entire Village of Whitefish Bay, and the construction site sees 3,500 workers daily. Port Washington Mayor Ted Neitzke has been leading van tours of the site to engage locals and address their concerns about the project. The first phase includes four data center buildings, each with a footprint of 800,000 square feet, large enough to hold two Lambeau Fields.

Vantage says the center will be operational by early 2028, providing internet and cloud services while storing, processing, and distributing data. The project is expected to bring significant tax benefits by transforming agriculturally zoned land assessed at a few million dollars into a site valued at $120 million, which is anticipated to support the majority of city services. Construction on the data center began in December 2022 and is scheduled to be completed by 2028. Neitzke said almost everything visible at the site is manufactured, made or fabricated in Wisconsin, so it is not just a Port Washington thing but a statewide one.

Neitzke said he was surprised and caught off guard by the unexpected backlash, saying he did not see that coming. He has emphasized transparency during the tours, addressing concerns about water usage, power supply and electricity rates, and he said the center does not use a lot of water and that power is protected and rates do not go up. He believes data centers are the newest of all the utilities, something everyone needs alongside clean water, clean sidewalks and electricity, and now information. He has also been advising elected officials across the country on how to navigate similar projects, saying local communities are in an amazing position to negotiate.

Clean Wisconsin and other groups have raised concerns about the environmental impact of AI data centers and the power plants required to support them. A Clean Wisconsin representative said Wisconsin is incredibly vulnerable right now to AI data centers, and that a project as large as the one in Port Washington will be vastly bigger in terms of energy needs than anything the state has ever seen. The representative said those are resources everyone relies on and that the conversation needed to happen well before now, when construction is going on and almost done. One contentious meeting resulted in the arrest of three women, and Al Poull, whose family has lived on a nearby farm for 126 years, acknowledged the changes, saying things change and it is just the way it is.

stories.Headline: Israeli study finds 78% use AI for health questions but only 38% verify answers
stories.Summary:
A new Israeli study found that 78% of respondents have used artificial intelligence for health-related questions, while only 38% verify its answers against additional sources, raising questions about public trust in the technology. The study was published Thursday by the Samuel Neaman Institute for National Policy Research at the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology, Shenkar, Wikimedia Israel, and the Israel Internet Association. It found that 85% of Israelis have used AI to satisfy their curiosity, and 78% used AI to get answers to health-related questions. Only 38% of respondents said they verify AI-generated answers against additional sources, even as 53% acknowledged that the technology can produce incorrect information. The study, which examined information consumption habits and public trust in Israel in 2026, also found that 73% of respondents described AI's impact on their search and learning habits as positive.

Beyond health-related questions, 71% reported using AI to understand concepts, 70% sought tips and advice, 55% used the technology for news and current affairs, and 25% used it to write computer code. According to the data presented, 63% use algorithmic information sources at least four days a week, compared with 29% who use traditional information sources such as television, radio, print newspapers, and other internet sites including Wikipedia. The gap is largest between the 25-34 year-old demographic, where it reaches 50 percentage points, gradually narrowing with age. When comparing information appearing on Wikipedia and information provided by AI, 28% of Israelis said they tended to prefer Wikipedia, while 29% said they tended to prefer AI tools. Among daily users, the research showed that trust levels are close, with 53% of users trusting Wikipedia and 49% trusting AI tools.

The study found that about half of Israelis believe AI responses are based on up-to-date information, and 41% believe the information AI provides is generally accurate and factual. On the other hand, 53% were aware that AI models may generate incorrect information, with 61% of the 18-34 year-old demographic being aware of this compared to 41% for those aged 55 and older. A notable gap was also found between Jews and Arab Israelis surveyed, with 59% of Jews being aware of this issue as compared to 29% of Arab Israelis. Researchers found that 55% of Israelis regularly read AI-generated summaries and then consult additional sources, while 28% rely solely on the summaries and do not do further research. Among those who read Wikipedia daily, 55% said they verify AI responses against additional sources, compared with 33% of those who do not read Wikipedia at all.

As part of the study, researchers asked 1,226 respondents open-ended questions examining how the use of AI had changed search and learning habits. Of these, 73% said they had experienced a positive change, while 2% said they had experienced a negative change. Exploring the changes, 28% of respondents mentioned the speed of finding information, 26% cited ease and convenience, and 20% cited new learning opportunities, while 14% explicitly stated that AI had replaced search engines for them. iPanel conducted the survey using an online panel and quota sampling of Israel's adult population, aged 18 and older, in Hebrew and Arabic. The full findings of the study will be presented on Thursday at a conference at Shenkar, with the participation of Prof. Sheizaf Rafaeli, president of Shenkar, Michal Wander Schwartz, CEO of Wikimedia Israel, and Dr. Eran Leck, senior research fellow at the Samuel Neaman Institute for National Policy Research at the Technion.

stories.Headline: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress oversees a cautious shift in AI funding strategy
stories.Summary:
Nvidia is likely to recalibrate its aggressive financing strategy following a change in leadership. Former CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, 2026, leading to this shift. Colette Kress has served as interim CEO since the resignation of Huang. The company is now expected to take a more cautious investment approach. Financial partners continue to discuss funding arrangements for various artificial intelligence companies.

The $500 billion initiative announced August 10 involves Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR. Nvidia may backstop 25 percent of transactions, which equals 125 billion dollars. An OpenAI data center in Ohio saw guarantees reduced from 250 billion to 105 billion dollars. Apple data center guarantees were cut from 500 billion to under 250 billion dollars. These specific guarantees are separate from the broader third-party capital initiative.

Interim CEO Colette Kress has overseen finances since 2013 and maintains a cautious stance. Former CEO Jensen Huang stated that the days of acting as a blank check are over. Huang told partners in Berlin they must build structures to raise their own funding. He suggested that companies seeking GPUs should collect upfront payments from their own customers. This approach aims to reduce the industry's total dependence on Nvidia's financial support.

UBS estimates that over 50 billion dollars in liquidity could disappear from the market. AI startups and neocloud companies with limited financial resources are directly impacted by this shift. These companies rely on guarantees to secure data centers and AI chips upfront. Low profitability and rising interest rates could make it harder for them to operate.

Morgan Stanley expects future capital to concentrate on large customers with stronger credit profiles. PitchBook reports Nvidia made 129 global investments this year, compared to 49 in 2023. This activity accounted for 27 percent of all global venture investment activity this year. The company projected 70 percent revenue growth for fiscal 2028 during a presentation in August.

Previous adjusted gross margins were 75 percent, with third quarter guidance set at 74 percent. Wall Street expects third quarter revenue of 109.1 billion dollars and earnings per share of 2.47. Nvidia will release fiscal 2027 third-quarter results on November 17 and hold an earnings call. Investors will watch the rollout of the Vera Rubin platform and its revenue contribution.

The company will provide written commentary on results at 6:20 a.m. Korea time, November 18. A $3 billion investment in Perplexity and talks with other startups remain under consideration. The articles leave open how rising memory prices will impact the company's gross margins.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO amid scandal and allegations of chip diversion to China
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia chief executive and board member on November 12. He stepped down following an infidelity scandal and allegations of diverting AI chips. These accusations involve relationships with Kimberly Powell and Alice Huang, a suspected spy. Alice Huang allegedly used the former leader to send chips to China. The diversion involved at least 7.5 billion dollars worth of Nvidia technology.

Interim CEO Colette Kress now leads the company and its financial operations. She previously lowered an OpenAI data center guarantee in Ohio to 105 billion dollars. On August 10, Nvidia signed a 500 billion dollar memorandum with six firms. These partners include BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, KKR, and Apollo Global. The company's market value fell to 3.7629 trillion dollars, placing it third overall.

Colette Kress is responsible for management and is known as a finance executive. She has previously stopped several large transactions from moving forward at the company. Elon Musk stated that Huang led supply chain management brilliantly through verbal agreements. Musk warned that the company will lose key contracts without Huang's personal trust. Sam Altman called Huang his hero but noted that heroes have flaws.

Shareholders Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker sent a formal letter requesting Huang's reinstatement. A petition titled Stand With Jensen gathered about 160,000 signatures from employees and investors. Many startups may struggle because Nvidia participated in 129 venture capital investments this year. UBS warned that 50 billion dollars could leave the market if funding scales back. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia should look outside the company for leadership.

Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 after mapping it out at a San Jose Denny's. He previously worked as a dishwasher at that restaurant while living in Oregon. He married Lori Huang in 1985 after meeting at Oregon State University. His daughter, Madison Huang, served as a chief of staff and pushed marketing. Biographer Stephen Witt described Huang as an arrogant man who could not tolerate dissent.

The Nvidia board is not currently discussing bringing Jensen Huang back to power. A war room of executives is reportedly lobbying the White House for his return. Denny's will reinstall a plaque marking the birthplace of the trillion dollar company. Bitdeer plans to open an AI data center in southern Malaysia next year. The articles leave open whether the 500 billion dollar financing project will collapse.

stories.Headline: US senators urge White House to launch national effort against AI enabled cyber threats
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 18, 2026, Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota urged the White House to launch a national effort against AI-enabled cyber threats. The lawmakers sent a letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warning that artificial intelligence is rapidly increasing the ability of attackers to discover and exploit software weaknesses. They noted that current defenses are not keeping pace with these threats, which have already powered cyber intrusions in Japan. The senators also highlighted concerns from banks regarding AI agents and the widespread use of Chinese-developed AI models for nefarious purposes.

The proposal requires the White House task force on AI, chaired by Clayton, to accelerate the deployment of defensive AI tools and establish security standards for autonomous agents. This effort would involve a meeting between AI developers, cybersecurity firms, critical infrastructure operators, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The lawmakers want CISA to lead the adoption of tools that can continuously identify vulnerabilities and block attacks across hospitals, utilities, banks, and government agencies. Additionally, they requested a national cyber defense grand challenge to demonstrate how AI can reduce the time between discovering a vulnerability and implementing protection.

Senator Rounds, who chairs the Senate Armed Services subcommittee on cybersecurity, has repeatedly called for more action to confront the risks posed by AI. The senators stated that while the United States possesses the necessary technological expertise, it currently lacks a coordinated national strategy to implement effective defenses. Director Clayton has not officially commented on the letter, but he recently told Fox Business that AI scanners are helping defenders identify and patch vulnerabilities faster than ever before. He explained that recent technology outages at airlines, tech companies, and banks resulted from these large-scale system upgrades and patching efforts.

This request follows an urgent FBI warning about a Chinese tool that automates cyber intrusions in the United States, South Korea, and Japan. Furthermore, a Government Accountability Office investigation from the spring found that Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok all provided terrorist attack plans during safety tests. The senators believe that without a coordinated strategy, the time required to test and install patches across interconnected systems could disrupt essential services for weeks or months. They argue that a unified approach is the only way to ensure that national security and critical infrastructure remain resilient against evolving AI threats.

stories.Headline: Nvidia outlines AI-defined model for chip fabrication using simulation and digital twins
stories.Summary:
Nvidia outlined what it calls an AI-defined model for semiconductor fabrication on 17 November 2026, combining accelerated computing, physics-based AI, AI agents and digital twins. The company said the approach focuses on using AI tools to shorten engineering analysis in chip manufacturing, where assessing process changes, materials interactions and defects can take days. It noted that physical experiments on production lines are costly, and that manufacturers face rising demand for advanced chips and increasingly complex processes. Nvidia said even small errors in yield or process quality can have significant commercial consequences in that environment.

The model relies on faster simulation so engineers can test more alternatives before deciding which changes to try in physical production. Software provider COMSOL is using Nvidia's cuDSS library to speed up semiconductor manufacturing simulations by up to 10 times, and Applied Materials is working with Nvidia on atomic-scale materials discovery and process development. Nvidia said Applied's Ginestra platform runs up to 10 times faster than CPU-only approaches with cuDSS, while its ACE+ multiphysics platform delivers topography simulations up to 35 times faster with Nvidia PhysicsNeMo. Siemens is integrating Nvidia cuLitho into its Calibre lithography software, which Nvidia said delivers up to 17 times acceleration on key simulation workloads.

Nvidia also cited Lam Research, which it said has shown that the PhysicsNeMo framework can predict plasma behaviour in milliseconds compared with days for a full simulation. Nvidia said engineers still make the decisions in semiconductor production, but many intermediate steps can consume hours, and it highlighted AI agents as a way to automate sequences of tasks traditionally handled manually. It said Advantest is using Nvidia NeMo Switchyard AI agents to automate the selection of which AI model to apply to a particular task, cutting response times from hours to minutes. Applied Materials uses Nvidia Omniverse libraries to build physically accurate digital twins of entire fabrication plants, according to Nvidia, and those models simulate material movement, identify bottlenecks and assess layouts, throughput, cost and process control.

Nvidia argued that these technologies become more useful when linked in a closed engineering loop, where production data informs simulations and AI models that are then used to test alternatives before engineers decide on the factory floor. Nvidia presented the closed loop as a way to shorten feedback cycles across semiconductor manufacturing, helping engineers identify problems earlier, evaluate more options and act on production insights sooner. The push comes as chipmakers and their suppliers look for ways to manage greater process complexity without relying solely on slower, more expensive physical trials. Nvidia said the aim is to extend simulation beyond individual manufacturing steps to the operation of the factory as a whole, which it said is increasingly relevant as fabrication plants become more complex and the cost of unsuccessful process changes rises.

stories.Headline: Atturra forum speakers urge schools to set clear AI boundaries and limit data exposure
stories.Summary:
Atturra hosted an education forum in Sydney on the use of technology in schools, and speakers said schools need to adopt digital tools carefully as AI and cyber risks reshape teaching, administration and parent engagement. The forum focused on how schools are managing rising expectations from teachers, students and families while under pressure to improve efficiency and protect sensitive data. Discussion covered AI in classrooms, cybersecurity, administrative systems and the challenge of ensuring smaller schools can keep pace with change. Brett Auton, Director of Scholarion at Atturra, said schools were being forced to think more strategically about technology decisions across teaching, risk management and communication. The forum was reported by IT Brief Australia on 18 November 2026.

Speakers said institutions should not treat AI as a neutral tool and must set clear boundaries around its role in learning. Dr Joseph Sweeney, Adviser at IBRS, said some schools may increasingly consider replacing large external technology platforms with sovereign AI tools built for their own environments, although he suggested that option would be more realistic for better-resourced institutions. According to the Australian Education Technology Industry Association, K-12 schools spent an estimated AUD $3.2 billion on education technology products and services in 2025, up 28 per cent since 2023. Barrett said Microsoft's data shows more than 15,000 emails containing malicious QR codes are aimed at the education sector every day. Auton said schools needed to examine what information they hold, who can access it, how long it is retained, and their exposure to third-party providers.

Auton said school leaders need to understand the strategic implications, teachers need to understand how technology will support their work, and students and parents need confidence that information is being handled appropriately. Sweeney said schools must keep teachers firmly in charge rather than letting software act as a moral authority or companion, and must safeguard kids against manipulative, addictive algorithms. Sweeney said AI should prompt students to think rather than simply hand over answers, and that if ungoverned it has the potential to be even more damaging to children's cognitive development and learning than social media has been. Lee Barrett, AI Education and Advocacy Lead at Catholic Education Network, said teachers are entitled to ask for the evidence and parents are entitled to understand what their children are using and why.

Vivek Puthucode, General Manager of Microsoft Elevate Asia, said the question is no longer whether students should learn to use AI but how we equip them to use it wisely, safely and creatively. Barrett said schools are working incredibly hard but are up against a lot, and that education is consistently among the most targeted sectors. Puthucode said success in the age of AI won't be measured by how much technology we put into classrooms but by how much more time educators have to teach and how well we protect the trust that students, families and communities place in schools. Auton said knowing and limiting your exposure is becoming the main game in town, which means understanding what information you hold, reducing unnecessary duplication, reviewing who has access to it, challenging how long you retain it, and being much more deliberate about the systems and providers you use.

Auton said simplifying admissions, improving communication with families, removing duplicate data entry and making student information easier to access can deliver significant value across a school. Barrett said when a new staff member logs in on day one and everything they need is already connected, that is back-office technology doing its job well, and when a teacher in a remote school gets the same reliable network and tools as one in the city, that is equity. Auton said strong core platforms, reliable data, cybersecurity, integration capabilities and the skills needed to use technology effectively are the foundations that allow schools to take advantage of new capabilities as they emerge. Puthucode said the real value of AI in education isn't simply about saving time but about how we reinvest that time, and that by reducing administrative burdens we can help educators focus more of their energy on improving learning, supporting student wellbeing, and helping young people thrive.

Speakers warned that smaller schools may struggle to keep up with emerging technology because of cost and limited internal expertise. Sweeney said pooling resources lets schools access sovereign AI platforms, negotiate better vendor terms and share specialist teachers remotely across campuses so students don't miss out. Auton said schools shouldn't need to become technology companies to operate effectively, and that standardised platforms, cloud-based services, shared capabilities and repeatable implementation approaches can all help reduce the cost and complexity of adopting modern technology. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a November 2026 public offering using a governance structure to protect its public benefit mission
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to launch an initial public offering on Wall Street during this current month of November in the year 2026. The San Francisco startup intends to go public while maintaining a pledge to prioritize the benefit of humanity during AI development. This transition to a public company will test a commitment the firm has held since the time of its founding. The company wants to balance the new pressure to deliver profits with its original mission to help the general public. This move marks a significant shift as the startup prepares for its official debut on the American stock market.

The company is a public benefit corporation, which is a legal designation used to balance shareholder interests with the public good. Anthropic has sketched out a governance structure that it says will protect its broader mission against various financial interests. This legal status is also used by its rival, OpenAI, to manage the tension between profit and social benefit. Experts say the described mechanisms give the company wide leeway to decide how it measures its benefit to society. The company is operating in uncharted territory as it reaches a potential valuation of many trillions of dollars.

The company is responsible for creating a governance structure that protects its mission from the pull of financial interests. Anthropic says this structure will ensure that the company continues to prioritize humanity as it develops its artificial intelligence. The firm claims that its legal status as a public benefit corporation helps it maintain this specific social balance. These internal mechanisms are designed to keep the company focused on the public good during its growth. The startup maintains that its mission remains central even as it seeks to attract new public investors.

Sarah Kreps is a professor and director at Cornell University who provided an expert perspective on the company's new filing. She stated that the real test emerges if the question of public benefit becomes costly for the business. Kreps believes a conflict may arise when the public benefit clashes with the need to make a profit. Other experts are affected by these developments as they monitor how trillion dollar AI firms handle social responsibilities. These observers are concerned that the company has too much wiggle room in its official IPO filing.

Anthropic was founded as a startup in San Francisco with a core mission to develop artificial intelligence for humanity's benefit. The company chose to incorporate as a public benefit corporation to legally embed this social mission into its structure. This background mirrors the approach taken by OpenAI, which also uses the public benefit corporation legal designation. The firm has spent its early years developing AI while promising to avoid prioritizing profits over the public good. This history sets the stage for the tension expected during its upcoming transition to a public company.

The company will now move forward with its initial public offering to begin trading on the Wall Street stock exchange. This process will determine if the firm can actually prioritize humanity while meeting the demands of its shareholders. The articles leave open exactly how the company will measure whether it is successfully benefiting the global society. It remains unclear if the governance structure will be strong enough to resist the pressure for higher financial returns. The final outcome of this experiment in corporate governance will be seen after the IPO is complete.

stories.Headline: Google warns that hackers use AI agents to accelerate and scale cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
Google warned that artificial intelligence is now doing more heavy lifting in hacking during a third quarter analysis. This report identifies a trend toward automation where hackers use AI agents to accelerate their cyberattacks. These actors are using autonomous tools to scale their intrusions and exploit flaws much faster than before. The shift toward machine speed allows for the automated chaining of complex attack paths to scale operations. This trend has reached a critical inflection point according to the analysis provided by the company.

Hackers use autonomous workflow multi-agent frameworks including Artex, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions. Between August and October, threat actors used a customized PentAGI platform to scan organizations in Asia for vulnerabilities. A Chinese-speaking actor used the open-source Cairn attack on more than a dozen organizations, per Palo Alto Networks. Google researchers observed a threat actor using a framework to breach companies in the U.S. aerospace sector. These tools allow attackers to automate the reverse engineering of patches to weaponize n-day vulnerabilities.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant are responsible for the findings regarding the shift toward autonomous hacking frameworks. They stated that the speed and scale of these frameworks introduce a new defensive challenge for security teams. The researchers noted that a lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of non-working LLM-generated exploits. They also found that financially motivated actors are using LLMJacking to hijack AI systems and resell usage tokens. Google first noted an increase in these LLMJacking incidents earlier in November 2026.

Defenders are affected by the additional verification work created by the wave of fake exploits generated by LLMs. However, Google noted that unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic and leaves behind distinct code-level traces for defenders. The report mentions that attackers still rely on compromised credentials and target unpatched systems to gain access. Other affected entities include the U.S. aerospace sector and various organizations located across Asia. These groups face intrusions occurring at machine speed due to the new paradigm shift in hacking.

The articles provide background on a new method called Self-Improvement Memory, or SIM, developed by Google and other researchers. This research involved Google Cloud AI, Google DeepMind, and the Pennsylvania State University, led by doctoral student Xin Yu. SIM organizes reasons for code modifications and results into memory to enable continual recursive self-improvement across tasks. Tests in programming, text classification, office tasks, and engineering design showed that SIM improved performance in most cases. In one office task test, the SIM scheme scored 84.75 points compared to 73.42 points without it.

Threat actors will likely keep using these frameworks because of the low barrier to entry and massive scale. Future attacks could become more autonomous, which would compress timelines for the hackers to achieve their goals. Attackers will likely become stealthier and more sophisticated, meaning they may no longer trade stealth for operational speed. The articles leave open how defenders will adapt to AI attacks that no longer leave noisy forensic traces. It remains unclear how the SIM research will specifically impact the ongoing battle between AI attackers and defenders.
