stories.Headline: Africa Tech Festival opens in Cape Town to advance AI development across the continent
stories.Summary:
The Africa Tech Festival 2026 officially opened on Tuesday in Cape Town, South Africa. Organizers launched the event to advance digital transformation across the African continent. The festival aims to position Africa to seize opportunities in the age of artificial intelligence. This event brings together leaders from the technology and telecommunications industries. It also includes entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers, and innovators to explore emerging technologies.

The 29th edition runs through Thursday at the Cape Town International Convention Centre. It features more than 13,500 attendees and 2,000 companies from over 130 countries. There are more than 450 speakers and 350 exhibitors under the theme Powering Africa's Digital Transformation. Six pillars include Telecoms and Connectivity, Data Centers, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Startups, and Digital Transformation. The schedule includes keynote speeches, panel discussions, technical masterclasses, investment forums, roundtables, and networking.

South African Deputy President Paul Mashatile delivered a virtual opening address to the attendees. He stated that African countries must take a more active role in shaping the global AI landscape. Mashatile argued that the continent should become a developer and exporter of emerging technologies. He claimed that digital transformation is fundamentally about human development rather than just technology. He urged the continent to build its own capabilities by drawing on local talent.

Mashatile warned that millions could be left behind by high connectivity costs and skills shortages. He noted that inadequate broadband access and infrastructure gaps also threaten inclusive digital transformation. The African Continental Free Trade Area was highlighted as a way to establish a single digital market. This market would require trusted data flows, interoperable payment systems, and harmonized regulations. He believed closer regional integration would drive innovation, investment, and inclusive growth for the people.

The festival covers key areas ranging from digital infrastructure to the growth of the digital economy. It features an exhibition with startups and providers of artificial intelligence solutions. Mashatile outlined five priorities to translate digital potential into broad based prosperity for the continent. These priorities include building future ready infrastructure and investing in digital skills and human capital. He also emphasized strengthening innovation ecosystems, building cybersecurity trust, and deepening regional continental cooperation.

The event seeks to turn discussions into tangible progress through bold investment and stronger partnerships. Mashatile called for decisive action to ensure people benefit from technological advancement for generations. The articles do not state the specific outcomes of the investment forums or roundtables. They leave open how the continent will specifically implement the five outlined digital priorities. The text does not mention the specific names of the 2,000 attending companies.

stories.Headline: Applied Materials posts record quarterly revenue as AI chip demand outpaces supply
stories.Summary:
Applied Materials released fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter results, for the year ended Oct. 25, on Nov. 12, and its revenue jumped 53% from the year-ago period to a record $10.41 billion. The quarterly revenue growth was significantly higher than the annual revenue increase of 21% to $34.45 billion. Applied Materials' non-GAAP earnings per share increased 92% year over year to $4.16 in the previous quarter, well above the company's fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS growth of 37% to $12.89. The semiconductor sector saw turbulence in the second half of 2026, with a 28% drop in the PHLX Semiconductor Sector since the beginning of July. Shares of Applied Materials have retreated 46% since the beginning of July.

The pullback was triggered by factors including a September rate hike by the Federal Reserve, the possibility of further hikes to keep inflation under control, and the viability of robust artificial intelligence infrastructure spending amid a high-interest rate environment. Applied Materials sells wafer and fabrication equipment used by semiconductor foundries, integrated device manufacturers, and memory manufacturers to make chips. Applied Materials expects the momentum to continue in 2027, predicting a 30% increase in wafer and fabrication equipment demand next year. Industry association SEMI predicts the wafer and fabrication equipment market could clock 23% growth in 2026 and expects a 21% increase in wafer and fabrication equipment sales next year. Applied Materials expects $11.1 billion in revenue in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, implying a 58% increase over the prior-year period, and forecasts non-GAAP EPS of $4.35, an 83% increase over last year.

Management noted on the latest earnings call that demand for advanced semiconductors remains much higher than supply, and multi-year investments in new fab capacity are needed for the industry to close this supply-demand gap. Applied Materials is confident it can grow faster than the wafer and fabrication equipment market by gaining more share in this space. Applied Materials is more confident in this market's growth due to the construction of new semiconductor fabs worldwide. Consulting firm McKinsey recently raised its 2030 global semiconductor industry revenue forecast to $2.3 trillion, up from $1.6 trillion, noting that demand for advanced chips to support the AI build-out will be a tailwind for the sector. Applied Materials' revenue fell slightly in the same quarter last year, while its EPS was flat on a year-over-year basis.

Each share of Applied Materials trades at just under $400, as of this writing, so $500 in investable cash after meeting expenses, saving for difficult times, and clearing high-interest debt can be considered for the stock. Applied Materials trades at just 21 times forward earnings, a discount to the iShares Semiconductor ETF's price-to-earnings ratio of 39. Assuming Applied Materials trades at even 30 times earnings after three years and its EPS reaches $29.49, the stock could jump to $885, implying a potential 145% increase. Harsh Chauhan has no position in any of the stocks mentioned, and The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Applied Materials and iShares Trust - iShares Semiconductor ETF. The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team identified 10 best stocks for investors to buy now, and Applied Materials was not one of them.

The Motley Fool cites Netflix, which made the Stock Advisor list on December 17, 2004, when $1,000 invested at the time of the recommendation would have grown to $327,620. It cites Nvidia, which made the list on April 15, 2005, when $1,000 invested at the time of the recommendation would have grown to $959,410. Stock Advisor's total average return is 802%, compared to 205% for the S&P 500, per returns as of November 18, 2026. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy. The article was published by Harsh Chauhan on Nov 18, 2026.

The article states that healthy investments in AI data center infrastructure are now driving stronger growth, and that the trend seems sustainable given the semiconductor industry's long-term growth potential. It states that Applied Materials' EPS is poised to grow at a healthy rate over the next three years. It states that the company's earnings per share are poised to increase at a healthy clip over the next five years, paving the way for a big jump in the stock price. It states that Applied Materials is poised to win a bigger share of the semiconductor equipment market. It states that Applied Materials is benefiting from the growth in wafer and fabrication equipment spending, which explains the company's impressive revenue and earnings growth.

The article leaves open whether Applied Materials will trade at 30 times earnings after three years and whether its EPS will reach $29.49. It leaves open whether the stock will jump to $885 and deliver the potential 145% increase. It leaves open whether the 30% increase in wafer and fabrication equipment demand and the 58% and 83% first-quarter fiscal 2027 increases will materialize. It leaves open whether the wafer and fabrication equipment market will grow 23% in 2026 and 21% next year, and whether McKinsey's $2.3 trillion 2030 forecast will hold. It leaves open whether the sell-off is overdone and whether the stock is a top buy right now.

stories.Headline: AI analysis of one echocardiogram clip plus H2FPEF score identifies 78% of hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF cases
stories.Summary:
Researchers applied an artificial intelligence model called EchoGo HF to resting echocardiograms from 280 outpatients who had been referred for suspected heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and each patient also underwent exercise hemodynamic testing as the diagnostic gold standard, according to research published in the November 2026 issue of the Journal of Cardiac Failure. Adding the AI analysis of a single routine echocardiogram clip to the H₂FPEF clinical score identified 78% of patients with hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF, compared with 48% using the score alone. The AI model added the most value for patients with low or intermediate H₂FPEF scores, the group where diagnosis is hardest, so the authors tested a two-step strategy of calculating H₂FPEF first and then applying AI only when the score is inconclusive. An AI-detected HFpEF result also independently predicted elevated filling pressures and reduced exercise capacity, which suggests the model reflects disease severity as well as diagnosis.

The November issue, focused on artificial intelligence in heart failure, also includes a study in which investigators used clinical notes from 599 patients seen in cardiology clinics to optimize a large language model, OpenAI's o1, that classified the documented reason for non-prescription of SGLT2 inhibitors with 84.7% accuracy. Physician-attributed factors were the most common theme at 28.7% of notes, and the leading specific reasons were deferring the decision to a future visit at 15.4% and the physician judging the patient low-risk or unlikely to benefit at 7.4%. A review in the same issue maps current AI applications across the heart failure care continuum, including AI-enabled ECG and imaging for opportunistic detection of low ejection fraction, HFpEF and structural heart disease, risk stratification based on electronic health records, clinician decision support, remote medication titration and wearable monitoring. The review's authors conclude that the strongest evidence favors AI built into active clinical workflows that guide targeted testing, treatment optimization and follow-up, rather than AI used only to send passive alerts.

In their Editor's Page, guest editors Jonathan W. Cunningham of Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School, Elena Donald and Nir Uriel of Columbia University Irving Medical Center, and Ankeet S. Bhatt of Kaiser Permanente San Francisco Medical Center wrote that heart failure's population burden is growing and outcomes are worsening while the number of heart failure physicians is flat and training spots go unfilled, and that AI could help close that gap. They wrote that promise alone is insufficient and that AI, like any innovation intended to change clinical care, must be rigorously studied to understand where it adds value, where it does not and how it can be implemented safely and effectively. The editors called on the heart failure community to move past retrospective and in silico demonstrations of model performance and instead want prospective studies, including randomized trials where feasible, that test whether AI tools improve clinical decisions, treatment delivery, outcomes, equity and clinician workload. They wrote that AI researchers will continue to advance these tools but that clinicians and patients must lead their translation into care, and the complete November 2026 issue is available online now.

stories.Headline: Singapore deploys AI missions to fight scams, widen lending and test agent payments
stories.Summary:
Singapore is setting out three artificial intelligence missions covering financial crime, business lending and AI-agent transactions as it expands the technology's use in finance, deputy prime minister Gan Kim Yong said in his keynote address at the Singapore FinTech Festival on Wednesday. Five banks are already pooling transaction data so that AI can spot scam patterns that individual lenders may miss, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore plans a study early next year for a shared detection system. Gan, who also chairs the MAS, said scams are not confined within the boundary of one bank and that a victim's money can pass through several institutions within minutes. The finance industry accounts for about 14 percent of Singapore's economy and employs roughly 200,000 people, making it a test case for how far AI can be built into a major financial centre without undermining jobs, operations or trust.

The financing mission will test whether more data can help lenders assess smaller companies and startups that may lack long credit histories or assets to use as security. AI could eventually identify when a viable business needs funding and alert it to suitable options before it applies. Singapore will also test AI agents that can make payments or purchases on behalf of people and companies, which could speed up transactions and enable new forms of machine-led commerce. Gan said greater autonomy must come with clear responsibility and accountability, and that the systems would operate within defined limits, with firms remaining accountable for actions taken on their behalf. For financial crime, MAS plans to use lessons from the five-bank trial to design a shared system that can identify suspicious activity across institutions, with the first phase focused on Singapore, though Gan said there may eventually be opportunities to work with other jurisdictions as scams cross borders.

Gan also addressed new US rules on remote access to advanced chips, which require licenses to export them to five countries, including Singapore. He said the government is working with affected companies to assess the impact and is engaging US authorities on how to maintain access. Gan said Singapore values its international reputation and does not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries in their international business activities, and that it will act against those who flout its laws. The initiatives are part of National AI Missions announced by prime minister Lawrence Wong in February, with financial services among four areas targeted for wider use of the technology. Twenty-three banks, insurers and asset managers have pledged to train more than 80,000 Singapore employees in AI skills by 2028 as firms study how jobs and tasks will change.

stories.Headline: Toobit launches SmartK and AI Trading Assistant for futures traders
stories.Summary:
Toobit, the global cryptocurrency exchange based in George Town in the Cayman Islands, announced on November 18, 2026 that it is showcasing two trading analysis tools available through Toobit Futures. The tools are called SmartK and AI Trading Assistant, and the company says they help traders assess market conditions, explore trading opportunities and plan potential positions. SmartK focuses on chart-based technical analysis, while AI Trading Assistant provides AI-generated market insights and structured trade references. Both tools are designed to complement traders' existing analytical approaches rather than replace them.

SmartK features five proprietary indicators covering market signals, entry scoring, multi-timeframe positioning, volume-price relationships and momentum divergence. Traders can pair main-chart and lower-panel indicators to compare technical signals, examine price trends and assess potential entry conditions. AI Trading Assistant offers AI crypto market analysis and AI trading opportunities, providing potential trade setups for scalp and swing trading. Its analysis includes directional signals, entry zones, take-profit targets, stop-loss levels and adjustable risk-to-reward ratios to support trade planning and risk assessment. Both offerings support independent trading decisions, allowing traders to incorporate technical analysis and AI-generated insights into their existing strategies while retaining control over their trades.

Toobit describes itself as an award-winning cryptocurrency derivatives exchange that provides zero-fee spot trading, AI trading tools and high leverage for both crypto and TradFi markets. The company says it maintains a fair, secure and transparent environment for traders to navigate digital asset markets. The announcement cites eToro's September 2026 Retail Investor Beat, which surveyed 11,000 retail investors across 13 countries, finding that 56% already use or are open to using AI tools to select or adjust investments. Among those respondents, 41% believe AI can save time on research, which the announcement presents as reflecting interest in AI-assisted investment analysis.

The announcement was distributed through GlobeNewswire and carried by outlets including markets.businessinsider.com and the Manila Times, and it includes a contact named Davin C. along with the website www.toobit.com. Both versions carry disclaimers stating that the content is sponsored and does not necessarily reflect the views of the media platform or its publisher. The disclaimers say the information is for general informational purposes only and should not be considered financial, investment or trading advice, and they warn that cryptocurrency activities carry risks including the potential loss of capital. stories.Summary:
Various artificial intelligence applications were showcased during the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit from November 2 to 5. This event took place in Wuzhen, Zhejiang province, and featured a wide array of robots and software agents. One notable example included an AI robot named Xiaomai who recommended coffee to visitors near Andufang Wharf. Other displays included a bionic hand and a platform for creating short dramas. These demonstrations suggested that AI is moving from simple technical displays into everyday human activities.

The transition to practical AI requires international standards organizations and technology companies to create ways for agents to communicate. These systems must be able to recognize one another to perform complex tasks like checking inventory and verifying purchase authorizations. In Jiaxing, Zhejiang, a media company showed a platform that uses open-source models to generate a 15-second video from one sentence in three minutes. This specific tool integrates scriptwriting, storyboarding, and sound production on a single computer. Meanwhile, a Hangzhou company called Brain-Co developed a bionic hand that translates nerve signals into finger movements.

The media company from Jiaxing stated that their open-source platform could significantly lower the barriers for people creating digital content. Experts at the summit discussed how the internet could evolve from a source of information into a tool for AI agents to complete tasks. The bionic hand from Brain-Co allowed a young man to play the piano, demonstrating a path toward greater independence for users. These various developers aimed to show that the true value of AI lies in its practical utility. They believe the technology should be judged by how it improves the daily lives of people.

The event highlighted that AI applications are currently at many different stages of development across various industries. The integration of open-source technology and neurotechnology suggests a future where complex creative and physical tasks are more accessible. By moving beyond the exhibition stage, these tools may soon allow more individuals to pursue personal interests and perform routine chores. The summit served as a glimpse into a world where AI agents handle logistical burdens and restore physical capabilities. Future progress will likely depend on the ability of different AI systems to work together seamlessly.

stories.Headline: AdMaven launches Mave AI assistant that prepares campaign changes for advertiser approval
stories.Summary:
AdMaven introduced an AI assistant called Mave that is built directly into its advertiser dashboard, letting advertisers launch pop campaigns, adjust settings, analyze live account data and get platform help in their own language, according to a company announcement dated November 18, 2026. The company said media buyers often spend roughly 26 percent of a campaign manager's time, or over 10 hours a week, on a tedious weekly checklist of monitoring results, tweaking bids, reallocating budgets and pausing underperforming ads. Mave was designed to handle that post-launch daily grind so media buyers can focus on strategy rather than repetitive tasks, and it never acts on its own. Whenever an advertiser asks to create a campaign, adjust a bid or change a budget, Mave prepares a confirmation card showing every detail, nothing happens until the advertiser clicks Approve, and cards expire after 10 minutes. With Mave, advertisers can set up to 5 pop campaigns at once through guided, clickable prompts, with support for CPM, Smart CPM, Smart CPA and Pure CPA where enabled, plus country, OS and device targeting and an optional daily budget before creatives go into standard review.

They can pause or resume up to 20 campaigns at once, update bids for one country or all countries, or adjust daily budgets with a $10 minimum, and they can ask in plain language for daily check-ins, weekly summaries, campaign comparisons and period-over-period breakdowns by day, country, device, OS, browser and source, with data refreshing roughly every 10 minutes. Mave can also identify sources that spend without converting or convert at a much higher CPA than average so advertisers know which ones to block, show running and paused campaigns, creative approval status, current bids by country, source lists and available balance plus credit line, and answer questions from AdMaven's help center of 35 articles, including setup guides for 13 trackers, tracking macros and policy rules. When an issue needs a person, such as a payment or creative-review dispute, Mave prepares a pre-written message so the advertiser can contact support in one click. Noam Cohen, Co-Founder at AdMaven, said most of what advertisers do in the dashboard is not launching something new but the same daily questions about how campaigns are doing, where they are overpaying and what should be paused.

He said Mave lets them ask those questions directly and get an answer or a change ready to approve, but it does not make the call for them, and the budget and judgment stay with the advertiser while Mave removes the clicking in between. AdMaven describes itself as a performance-driven global advertising network delivering over 1 billion daily impressions worldwide, specializing in Pop, Push, In-page Push and Interstitial ads, and offering publishers a brand-protected ecosystem with no minimum traffic barriers. Mave is currently rolling out on an invite-only basis, enabled account by account inside the AdMaven advertiser dashboard's chat panel, and read-only Q&A access is also available through the AdMaven API for pulling account answers without making changes. Advertisers interested in early access can reach out to their account manager, and the company invites interested advertisers to sign up as an AdMaven advertiser to get started.

stories.Headline: Family physician Mara Gordon uses an AI scribe on her phone to draft notes but reviews and signs each one
stories.Summary:
Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., wrote in a piece published November 17, 2026, that a reader asked whether to worry about an artificial intelligence scribe recording private medical conversations. The reader said her doctor had started recording office visits with an AI scribe and that she said yes when asked if she was comfortable. The reader said that in hindsight she felt a little freaked out. Gordon wrote that AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Gordon wrote that doctors use them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.

Gordon wrote that she first asks the patient if they are comfortable using the service. Gordon wrote that if the patient says yes, she starts recording using an app on her smartphone, usually set down on the desk in the exam room. Gordon wrote that the scribe uses "automatic speech recognition," which records the conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. Gordon wrote that sometimes, when a family member accompanies the patient, the app needs to distinguish between three or more voices. Gordon wrote that when the visit ends, the recording is transcribed and a large language model geared toward medicine converts the raw transcript into a medical note.

Gordon wrote that the notes follow a standard format specific to the specialty and the type of visit. Gordon wrote that the notes reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making. Gordon wrote that she is ultimately responsible for the content of the AI-generated note and always reads them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Gordon wrote that most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them. Gordon wrote that when the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, she almost always ends up editing them to make her clinical decision-making more clear.

Gordon wrote that she talked to Dr. Eileen Kim, an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego who specializes in clinical informatics. Gordon quoted Kim saying that an overburdened doctor seeing too many patients has an AI tool offered that seems like a great solution but no time to adequately review everything. Gordon quoted Kim saying the note goes into the chart and another AI tool reading the notes propagates errors throughout the chart. Gordon wrote that she comes across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time and that it is hard to know how much is related to AI and how much to human error. Gordon wrote that many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients, and that health equity advocates fear this means unequal access that could further widen health disparities.

Gordon wrote that she has been an eager adopter in her own primary care practice. Gordon wrote that she uses an app on her phone that records her conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record. Gordon wrote that it saves her time and helps her focus more fully on her patient, so she can make eye contact rather than stare at the computer screen. Gordon wrote that she shares her patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship. Gordon wrote that she worries corporate health systems will pressure doctors to use time saved with an AI scribe to squeeze in even more patients, and that artificial intelligence might one day put her out of a job.

Gordon wrote that there are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Gordon wrote that most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, though some use a desktop computer or a separate recording device. Gordon wrote that she uses her personal smartphone, as do many physicians she knows, and that she once got notification pings from her book club's group chat while recording a patient visit, which made her put the phone in "do not disturb" mode. Gordon wrote that conversations are not stored on her device but uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud, where the data is transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note, and that most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time. Gordon wrote that HIPAA means the program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy, and that the software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step, encrypting it, controlling access, protecting against data breaches, and being liable if data is leaked.

Gordon wrote that she recently saw a patient with metastatic cancer who did not believe he had cancer despite multiple conversations with her, his oncologist, and his surgeon, and that she had even, with his permission, called his spouse. Gordon wrote that the AI scribe did not get this tricky situation right and that the note simply said the patient had been misdiagnosed rather than reflecting the nuances of the conversation. Gordon wrote that she often catches other errors, like mistaking a patient's gender or age, and that the scribes are known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not," where the difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death. Gordon wrote that most AI scribe companies delete recorded conversations within a set period of time as a security feature, to protect patient privacy and protect doctors from lawsuits, and that there is widespread concern the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits. Gordon wrote that some researchers call the recordings "digital gold" that could assess the quality of AI-generated notes or study physician-patient communication, and that for now recordings of regular appointments, unless a patient is enrolled in a research study, are not used for research.

Gordon wrote that most of her patients readily agree to the AI scribe, but occasionally patients worry the data isn't really secure or could be used to identify them in the future. Gordon wrote that if a patient doesn't want the AI scribe, she just takes notes on the computer while they talk, as she did for years before the scribes became available. Gordon quoted Kim saying AI is "just everywhere" and it would be impossible to separate it, and that software relying on machine learning is used for billing, clinical decision-making, and communication between the doctor's office and patients. Gordon wrote that AI is often used in risk calculators, like tools that estimate a patient's risk of heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure, and in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis based on vital signs and lab values. Gordon quoted Kim saying it is basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you."

Gordon wrote that she asked Kim, a primary care doctor like her, whether AI would replace them in the coming years, and whether an AI scribe that could ask the same questions she does could generate a treatment plan as good or better than the one she recommends. Gordon wrote that Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care, possibly for the better if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer. Gordon wrote that the article ends there, leaving Kim's ultimate answer about replacement unstated. Gordon wrote that readers can send health questions to thrive@npr.org. Gordon wrote that she is happy to have robots help with her administrative tasks but still takes pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence.

stories.Headline: Marsh's Schnur links AI tools to a doubling of client cyber incidents
stories.Summary:
Marsh reported that its clients filed 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October, which is more than double the 48 incidents recorded in the final two weeks of May, according to data the insurance broker released and Reuters reported on November 17, 2026. Meredith Schnur, who leads the US and Canada cyber practice at Marsh Risk, told Reuters in an interview this week that attackers are using AI enabled and agentic tools to identify vulnerabilities, and she said AI could be attributed to a significant number of the incidents. She said the speed and scale of AI tool adoption, combined with organizations taking longer to contain attacks and respond to incidents, were the main factors driving the recent increase in cyber incident volumes. Schnur said AI is not a peril but an amplification of risk in all areas, and she said the technology lets attackers find and exploit longstanding vulnerabilities such as unpatched software, exposed systems and weak identity controls at a much faster pace. The rise in reported incidents requires businesses and their insurers to contend with attacks that spread faster and reach more targets, because AI tools that are becoming more widely accessible let attackers scale their operations with fewer resources.

GlobalData expects global cyber insurance premiums to rise 6.9% to $16.6 billion in 2026, before growth accelerates to 10% in 2027 to reach $18.3 billion, as businesses respond to rising attack frequency. The Marsh figures compare the final two weeks of October with the final two weeks of May, and the 105 incidents more than double the 48 recorded in the earlier period. The report ties the increase to AI adoption and to slower containment and response times, and it says the wider availability of AI tools is widening the pool of potential targets and putting pressure on businesses. Schnur, the US and Canada cyber practice leader at Marsh Risk, is the person the articles identify as explaining the data, and she attributed a significant share of the incidents to AI in her interview with Reuters this week. She said the signs that attackers are using AI enabled and agentic tools to identify vulnerabilities are happening, and she described AI as an amplification of risk in all areas rather than a peril in itself.

She said the speed and scale of AI tool adoption, together with organizations taking longer to contain attacks and respond to incidents, were the main factors behind the recent increase in cyber incident volumes. The reporting was by Noor Zainab Hussain and Manya Saini in Bengaluru, with editing by Shilpi Majumdar, and the story was published by Reuters and carried by Insurance Journal. The context the articles give is a cyber insurance market that GlobalData expects to grow faster over the next two years as businesses respond to rising attack frequency, with premiums reaching $16.6 billion in 2026 and $18.3 billion in 2027. The articles do not say what Marsh or insurers will change in response to the data, and they do not describe any new policy terms or claims figures beyond the incident counts and the premium forecasts. What happens next, according to the articles, is continued growth in cyber insurance premiums at a faster pace over the next two years, driven by the rising frequency of attacks that the Marsh data shows.

stories.Headline: Nvidia pledges disciplined support for AI infrastructure and raises fiscal 2028 sales forecasts
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on Tuesday that it will continue supporting AI infrastructure through investments and credit guarantees. The company reported third quarter results that beat expectations and raised its fiscal 2028 sales forecast. This news eased investor concerns following the recent exit of former CEO Jensen Huang from the firm. Neocloud and chip stocks rallied after the company disclosed its plans for selective and disciplined support. Nvidia stock rose 1.2 percent in overnight trading following the release of the quarterly financial report.

The company disclosed 32 billion dollars in neocloud commitments, which is down from 36 billion in Q2. Total guarantees reached 118 billion dollars, while 390 billion dollars were committed toward future supply and capacity. Revenue for the third quarter more than doubled to 115.8 billion dollars, beating expectations of 109.3 billion dollars. Data center sales rose 110 percent to 107.6 billion dollars, and current quarter revenue is forecast at 130 billion. Fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecasts were raised from 70 percent to 75 percent by interim CEO Colette Kress.

Interim CEO Colette Kress stated that neocloud operators are an important part of the global AI infrastructure chain. She explained that credit backstops only activate if partners can successfully build and deliver the necessary computing infrastructure. Kress noted that the company remains thoughtful and disciplined regarding how it commits capital to the AI ecosystem. She added that Nvidia is rigorously evaluating future investments as the market matures and more capital sources become available. Kress emphasized that neoclouds provide more customers with access to compute and expand the reach of the platform.

Analyst Daniel Newman called neoclouds the biggest sustained bet for Nvidia to create an ecosystem of powered hyperscalers. Wharton professor Mohamed A. El-Erian noted that the earnings highlight Nvidia's expanding role as a major AI creditor. Hedge fund manager Eric Jackson said the push into physical infrastructure for AI compute was the earnings highlight. Nebius and IREN rose over 10 percent, while CoreWeave gained 9 percent and Marvell Technology gained 5.7 percent. Arista Networks rose 3.7 percent, and chip heavyweights Intel, AMD, Micron, and Broadcom rose between 2.7 and 4.7 percent.

The company recently cut ties with 63 year old co founder Jensen Huang following a scandal involving extramarital affairs. One of these affairs allegedly involved a woman who is a Chinese spy, leading to his sudden departure. Huang previously played a central role in the deals that made Nvidia a de facto financier of AI infrastructure. The uptick in supply commitments was primarily related to the multiyear procurement of memory supply for the company. Shares of Nvidia had fallen 16.5 percent year to date as of the most recent market close.

Chairman Harvey C. Jones stated on an analyst call that Nvidia is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. The iShares Semiconductor ETF rose 3.8 percent as retail sentiment on Stocktwits climbed into the extremely bullish zone. One trader suggested that Elon Musk should act soon if he wants to buy shares of the company Nebius. The articles do not state when the current quarter ends or the specific dates for fiscal 2028 targets. It remains open whether other capital sources will reduce the need for Nvidia to provide these credit guarantees.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and over 40 partners launch AI Transparency Initiative to set open standards for accountable AI
stories.Summary:
At Microsoft Ignite on Tuesday, Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella announced the AI Transparency Initiative, a collaborative effort with customers and partners. The initiative is a common, open approach to security and governance across models and providers. Microsoft launched it with organizations across industries to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents. The announcement came from Redmond, Wash., on Nov. 17, 2026. The initiative reflects a principle that greater AI autonomy requires greater transparency.

The initiative has three parts, the first being that Microsoft will expand its participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology's SI Agent Standards Initiative and draw on its research. Second, Microsoft is collaborating with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to help develop open standards for AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Third, Microsoft will incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot, enabling customers to use the resulting evidence with their security and compliance tools, whether from Microsoft or other providers. The initiative is designed to work across models and providers, including closed and open-weight models, so developer teams can change or update the models powering their agents without compromising IT and security teams' ability to govern them securely or compliance teams' ability to audit their actions. Organizations interested in helping shape the initiative or following its progress can learn more and sign up at aka.ms/learnmoreAItransparency.

Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security, said every organization needs greater transparency into the model itself for security controls to be effective. Gallot said the work will bring more transparency to all models and called it a critical step in making containment smarter and stronger, allowing better accountability and traceability. Aanchal Gupta, Chief Security Officer, Adobe, said security teams need clear visibility into what agents are accessing, what actions they are taking and how those actions can be verified. Gupta said building a common approach to AI transparency across the industry is essential to strengthening trust and helping organizations innovate with confidence while maintaining security and accountability. John Israel, Global Chief Information Security Officer, KPMG International, said clients want to move faster with AI and should not have to choose between innovation and safety.

Israel said trust in AI requires transparency, explainability and responsible oversight, and that KPMG is proud to work with Microsoft on the initiative to help establish open, industrywide standards. Harpreet Sidhu, global cybersecurity lead, Accenture, said organizations taking the next step in their AI reinventions need a solid foundation of trust and confidence to build from. Sidhu said initiatives like this from Microsoft to take an open, industry-driven approach to AI transparency can help as Accenture secures AI models and fits them with controls and governance. Enterprises are connecting AI models to data, tools, credentials and infrastructure, enabling agents to take actions without human approval at every step. Agents with access to data, tools and credentials carry the risk profile of a privileged insider but operate at machine speed and scale, making independent oversight essential.

Existing controls can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they cannot see what happens within them or independently verify their accounts of their own behavior. This limits organizations' ability to understand the context behind an agent's actions, and that evidence gap creates security, compliance, audit and accountability risk. Security teams need a new trust architecture to address the growing insider risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents. Accountability stays with the organization, and when something consequential happens, leaders answer to customers, employees, boards, auditors and regulators.

Blaming the AI isn't an answer, and "trust the model" isn't a control. Microsoft believes every organization should be able to see what AI systems access and do, verify their actions independently and control what they are permitted to do. On seeing, organizations should know what the AI was asked and authorized to do, which model and runtime were used, what data and tools it accessed, and what actions it took, and monitor agent activity and risk signals continuously against policies and thresholds. On verifying, agents cannot be the sole source of truth about their own behavior, and frontier models cannot be trusted to govern themselves.

Evidence covering agent identity, delegated intent and actions should identify its source, the model, the runtime around it, or independent systems such as identity and policy, so model-reported signals can be checked against independently observed records. Organizations should be able to independently verify AI activity using their own security and compliance systems, without relying solely on the model provider's account of its behavior. On controlling, clear evidence of each workflow's purpose, owner, data and delegated authority helps organizations enforce their policies before consequential actions occur and reconstruct what happened during investigations, containment, recovery and audits. That evidence should stay with organizations when models and providers change, and organizations should retain control over what data their agents can access and how that access is governed, regardless of the model or provider.

Microsoft and industry leaders will share insights at Microsoft Ignite on how organizations can manage AI models and agents with confidence. More is available on the Microsoft Security blog, and press can contact Microsoft Media Relations, We. Communications for Microsoft, at (425) 638-7777. The articles leave open what the open standards will contain and when the work will reach Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot.

stories.Headline: Diligent Institute finds only 15% of APAC boards very confident in overseeing major risks
stories.Summary:
Diligent Institute published its APAC Governance Outlook 2027 report on Wednesday 18 November 2026, based on a regional survey in which Australian-headquartered organisations accounted for 63% of respondents. The study surveyed board members, C-suite leaders and general counsel across Asia-Pacific. It found that only 15% of respondents said they were very confident their board had the information, expertise and processes needed to oversee significant risks. The most commonly cited barriers were insufficient time, named by 26%, and a lack of relevant expertise, cited by 17%. The findings come as boards in Australia face regulatory scrutiny over operational resilience, cyber governance and executive accountability.

Cybersecurity, data protection and privacy were the leading strategic priority for 69% of respondents, while AI deployment followed at 54%, ahead of operational cost optimisation at 52%. Some 55% expected economic downturns to disrupt their organisations over the next 12 months, 53% named geopolitical events as a major threat, and 48% identified cyber and data privacy incidents as a likely source of disruption. Some 29% said AI adoption was outpacing governance, 25% said governance was keeping pace and 8% said it was ahead of adoption. A quarter of respondents said they used approved AI tools for governance workflows, 17% reported informal use of general-purpose or consumer tools, and another 25% said they had no foreseeable plans to use AI in those settings.

Dottie Schindlinger, executive director of Diligent Institute, said effective oversight is not about adding every emerging issue to an already full agenda. She said it is about understanding how risks intersect, identifying what matters most to the organisation's strategy and decisions, and ensuring management is taking action. She said boards can start by asking for clear, integrated reporting that connects emerging risks to business priorities. She also said boards should dedicate time to challenging assumptions and gain a clear understanding of where and how AI is being deployed, including in their own governance processes.

When asked about the main opportunities from AI, 78% pointed to improved data analysis and reporting, and workflow automation was the next most common response at 58%. Security and privacy were cited by 66% as the leading concern linked to AI, while half of respondents also named hallucinations, misinformation or disinformation. Digital technology, including AI and data management, was the most frequently cited board skills gap at 62%, more than double the 29% who named cybersecurity as a board skills gap. Some 65% said more time for strategic planning or dedicated planning meetings would improve the boardroom, while 26% said their board lacked time to discuss emerging risks. Mandatory director training or continuing education was selected by 49%, while 48% wanted greater access to outside parties or experts on specific issues and risks.

The survey was conducted online during August and September and included respondents from public and private organisations across the Asia-Pacific region. Participants included board members, C-suite leaders, general counsel, company secretaries and other governance leaders. The concentration of Australian respondents gives the findings particular relevance for local boards as organisations deal with cyber threats, data governance questions and pressure to demonstrate clearer oversight of AI use. The results suggest boards are managing immediate operational concerns while also trying to respond to rapid changes in technology use. Among the report's core findings, just 15% of respondents said they were very confident their board was equipped to oversee major risks.

The articles do not state what actions boards, regulators or Diligent Institute will take next. They leave open how the 26% who cited insufficient time and the 17% who cited a lack of relevant expertise would address those barriers. They do not say whether the 49% who wanted mandatory director training or the 48% who wanted greater access to outside experts will receive either. They do not state how the 29% who said AI adoption was outpacing governance would close that gap. They also do not say what the regulatory scrutiny facing Australian boards over operational resilience, cyber governance and executive accountability will require.

stories.Headline: Nokia leads AIGF Northern consortium to build AI computing network across four Nordic and Baltic sites
stories.Summary:
A consortium led by Nokia, named AI Gigafactory Northern (AIGF Northern), plans to develop a network of AI computing facilities across the Nordic and Baltic region. The founding partners Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda announced the formation of the consortium on 16 November 2026. The group intends to submit a bid under a call for tenders for AI Gigafactory consortia published by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU). The project seeks to select and establish AI Gigafactory consortia, aligning with European efforts to expand domestic artificial intelligence infrastructure. The announcement was published by Nokia on 16 November 2026 at 08:00 AM Europe/Amsterdam and carried by GlobeNewswire the same day.

The proposed network would span four locations: Oulu in Finland, the Iru site in Estonia, Valmiera in Latvia, and a site in Sweden yet to be determined. Operating as a federated AI Gigafactory under European governance, the sites will combine large-scale AI computing infrastructure with sovereign cloud and AI platform services, high-capacity connectivity and decarbonised energy. The model would distribute computing capacity across multiple countries, linking data centers, cloud platforms and telecommunications networks under European governance. Through InvestAI, the EU aims to mobilise €30 billion for AI investment, combining €20 billion in private-sector funding with €10 billion from EU and national public sources. Distributing capacity across these locations will allow the consortium to draw on multiple sources of decarbonised energy, expand computing infrastructure where capacity is available and reduce reliance on any single site or supplier.

Mikko Hautala, Chief Geopolitical and Government Relations Officer at Nokia and Chairman of Nokia Defense, said Europe's AI ambitions depend on infrastructure it can trust, control and scale. He said AIGF Northern brings together the connectivity, computing, cloud and energy capabilities needed to turn that ambition into reality. He added that by linking strengths across borders, the partners can build a more resilient foundation for European innovation, competitiveness and technological sovereignty. Markus Päivinen, Managing Director of Nscale Finland, said scaling AI infrastructure in Europe requires the right foundation of partners and experience in deploying large-scale AI computing infrastructure for customers. He said Nscale's role is to ensure the AI solutions delivered are enterprise-grade, flexible and ready to support organisations across Europe as demand accelerates.

Taavi Madiberk, CEO and co-founder of Skeleton Technologies, said building lasting AI capacity requires more than compute alone, including energy and power infrastructure using technologies developed and manufactured in Europe. He said Northern Europe brings together abundant decarbonized electricity, strong engineering capabilities and an advanced industrial base, and that Skeleton contributes power systems so AI infrastructure wastes less energy and gets more compute power from every GPU. Anders Olsson, Executive Vice President and Head of Telia Sweden, said customers and the continent have a rapidly increasing need for scalable and trusted AI services, and that Telia's connectivity and systems integration skills make it a natural fit. Michael Champion, Chief Information Security Officer at Verda, said it is essential that Europe has its own strong infrastructure to support research, the public sector and wider industry. The consortium aims to create value for industry, start-ups, research organisations and the public sector across Europe.

Nokia will supply network and connectivity technology, while Nscale and Verda will provide AI computing and cloud platforms. Telia, with its subsidiary Telia Cygate, will support connectivity, data transmission, infrastructure operations and cloud solutions. Skeleton Technologies will provide high power systems designed to improve data center efficiency and electricity grid stability, reduce strain on the electricity grid and support lower-carbon operations. Research organisations VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland and KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Sweden are also supporting the initiative. VTT brings capabilities in quantum computing, semiconductors, physical AI and photonics, and KTH, Sweden's largest technical university, contributes multidisciplinary expertise in AI research, education and skills development.

The Nordic and Baltic region offers suitable conditions for sustainable AI infrastructure, combining reliable, decarbonised energy supply, advanced digital networks and a cool climate that reduces cooling demand. These advantages enable data centres to deliver more computing capacity from existing grid connections while supporting lower-carbon operations. By distributing capacity across borders, the federated AI Gigafactory will reduce concentration risk and strengthen the resilience of Europe's AI ecosystem. The consortium is being developed as the EU steps up investment in European AI capacity. AIGF Northern is described as a European-led consortium built across the Nordic and Baltic region to serve customers throughout Europe and the world.

Partners are engaging European and national stakeholders to refine the model and identify next steps for growth. The partners intend to submit a bid to build and operate AIGF Northern under the EuroHPC JU call for tenders for AI Gigafactory consortia. The location of the Swedish site remains to be determined. The articles do not state when the bid will be submitted or when the tender decision is expected. The articles also do not state the cost of the proposed network or the timing for building the facilities.

stories.Headline: Nebius shares rise 3.0% as Nvidia results revive AI infrastructure sentiment
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group shares rose 3.0% on November 18, 2026, according to Quiver Quantitative, which attributed the move most likely to a rebound in AI infrastructure and neocloud shares after Nvidia's latest earnings renewed confidence in demand for GPU capacity. The stock also retained support from Nebius's own recent results, which showed very rapid revenue growth even though investors had been worried about timing delays tied to third-party data center capacity. On November 12, Nebius said third-quarter revenue rose to $980.8 million, with AI Cloud revenue of $973.8 million, showing that customer demand remains strong. Nebius said four new sites began generating revenue across the U.S. and Europe, and additional capacity was delivered in New Jersey during the quarter and through November. The company said prepayments on third-quarter agreements covered more than 100% of associated capex, which may have helped reassure investors about funding for expansion.

The report said the rise could also reflect a relief rally, because the stock had sold off sharply after management moved its 2026 revenue outlook to the low end of its prior range, leaving room for improvement as sentiment across the AI compute group recovered. Quiver's price movement analysis was generated with the help of AI and carried a disclaimer asking readers to double-check the information for mistakes. The same article reported that Nebius insiders traded the stock on the open market 119 times in the past six months, with 11 purchases and 108 sales. It listed sales by COO Ophir Nave of 500,000 shares for an estimated $117,765,467, by CEO Arkadiy Volozh of 84,405 shares for an estimated $19,824,423, and by Chief Infrastructure Officer Andrey Korolenko of 62,961 shares for an estimated $14,786,641, among others, while Arne Grimme made 11 purchases of 2,014 shares for an estimated $330,439.

It said Wall Street analysts had issued eight buy ratings and one sell rating on the stock in the last several months, with Citigroup, Truist Securities, Rosenblatt and Baird among the recent buy or outperform ratings and Rothschild & Co issuing a sell rating on September 21. stories.Headline: Norwegian researchers develop an AI model that generates foot x-rays preserving skeletal structure
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology in Ålesund have developed an artificial intelligence model that generates x-ray-like images of the foot while preserving the actual skeletal structure, according to Di Wu, an associate professor at the university's Department of ICT and Natural Sciences. The method is called a skeletal-constrained conditional diffusion model, and it is designed specifically to produce anatomically accurate images of hallux valgus, the misalignment of the big toe commonly known as bunions. Wu and her colleagues also created two measurement methods to check whether the generated images are anatomically accurate, and they tested the approach against other methods used to generate new digital images. The work lies at the intersection of medical imaging and artificial intelligence, and the technology is similar to that used by many AI tools that generate images.

The method could in the long term mean that patients avoid some x-ray examinations and that diagnostic imaging becomes more accessible where equipment is unavailable or unaffordable, since images of hallux valgus must be taken while the patient is standing and bearing weight. Wu said the results also suggest that an ordinary photograph of the foot could serve as an additional source of information for AI-assisted screening, medical assessment and treatment planning, and some doctors have suggested the approach could be used for early-stage screening rather than clinical diagnosis. The technology remains at the research stage, and the AI-generated images are not intended to replace actual x-rays or clinical assessments, at least not yet. Wu said more work involving larger and more diverse patient groups will be needed before that can happen.

Wu is responsible for the research and described the method as a machine-learning approach that makes it possible to preserve the actual skeletal structure of the foot when the model creates an x-ray-like image. She said tests showed the method produced both better image quality and a more accurate representation of the foot skeleton than other methods used to generate new digital images. She also pointed to a 2023 meta-analysis based on studies involving more than 186 million people, which estimated that 19 per cent of people worldwide have hallux valgus, with 24 per cent among women and 11 per cent among men. Among people aged 20 to 60, 12 per cent have the condition, compared with 23 per cent of those over 60, and Wu said various studies suggest it may be under-researched in many regions.

Hallux valgus has a long history, with one of the earliest anatomical descriptions provided by the physician Galen of Pergamon, who lived from AD 129 to 200, and the first book on the condition published in 1781 by Nicholas-Laurent Laforest, personal chiropodist to King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette. Archaeologists in England found an unusually high number of misaligned big toes in skeletons from the 14th and 15th centuries, when tight, almost carrot-shaped shoes were fashionable, and among 177 skeletons the highest prevalence was at an Augustinian friary, where as many as 43 per cent of those buried had the condition. By 1463, shoes had become so pointed that King Edward IV introduced a law prohibiting anyone below the rank of lord from wearing shoes with toes extending more than two inches beyond the foot. Toes that point inwards can range from a cosmetic issue to causing considerable pain, problems with footwear and changes in the way people walk, which can place uneven strain on the knees, hips and back, and surgery can correct the deformity.

stories.Headline: Everpure raises full-year forecast as AI demand lifts quarterly revenue 51% to $1.5 billion
stories.Summary:
Everpure Inc. reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that surpassed analysts’ expectations on November 18, 2026, and its stock gained just over 4% in after-hours trading that day. The data center infrastructure company also raised its full-year forecast for the third successive quarter. It reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 86 cents per share, beating Wall Street’s consensus estimate of 77 cents. Revenue for the period rose 51% from a year earlier to $1.5 billion, surpassing the analyst’s target of $1.33 billion. Chairman and Chief Executive Charles Giancarlo said the results reinforce the company’s status as a trusted partner for enterprises.

Adjusted operating income reached $345 million, $70 million above prior guidance. Product revenue came to $948 million, up 77% from a year earlier, while subscription services revenue was up 20%. Net income for the quarter came to $100.4 million, up from $54.8 million in the same period one year ago. Remaining performance obligations ended the quarter at $4.2 billion, up 44%. The company raised its full-year revenue guidance from a prior range of $5.03 billion to $5.07 billion to a new range of $5.2 billion to $5.21 billion.

Giancarlo said organizations are working to break down data silos and modernize their data estates, and that growth across core and new, high-growth markets shows the company is uniquely equipped to solve their most complex data challenges at scale. He said on a conference call that much of the momentum has to do with AI. During the quarter, Everpure won a design contract with one of the top five largest hyperscale cloud companies, he added. Everpure rebranded in February 2026 from Pure Storage as part of an effort to emphasize its vision of “data primacy.” The company claims its Data Intelligence software and FlashBlade servers can prepare data, speed up inference and lower GPU and storage costs.

NAND Research analyst Steve McDowell told SiliconANGLE that a primary reason for Everpure’s growth is the rising cost of memory and flash storage, which has allowed the company to bump up prices of its storage products substantially this year without any negative impact on demand. He said Everpure continues to outperform the broader storage market and the numbers suggest it is taking market share away from its rivals. McDowell said the only real blot on the results was a slight drop in subscription margins, which was more than offset by increased product margins, and that this was not addressed on the conference call. He said Everpure has spent the last year expanding its offerings without showing any material impact on its bottom line from those efforts. He said its hyperscale business is only just starting to impact revenue, so most of the growth has been from its traditional products.

Everpure’s growth has been accelerating for more than two years, and in August the company said its revenue had grown for eight successive quarters. Over the last five quarters, it has grown by 16%, 20%, 35%, 38% and 51%. McDowell said it is the third consecutive quarter of growth above 35%, and that the company has been growing product margins even in the face of rising component costs and supply chain challenges. Everpure provides enterprises and cloud infrastructure providers with high-speed, cost- and power-efficient data storage and management solutions for AI workloads. It integrates closely with Nvidia Corp.’s graphics processing units.

For the current quarter, Everpure is forecasting sales of between $1.5 billion and $1.52 billion, which would amount to growth of between 42% and 43%. The forecast is ahead of the Street’s target of $1.49 billion in sales. To keep accelerating its growth, it would need fourth-quarter revenue of at least $1.6 billion, about $83 million higher than the top end of its forecast range. Everpure beat the top end of its range by $125 million in the quarter just gone. Wall Street analysts are modeling full-year sales of $5.06 billion.

stories.Headline: Cardiologists in the Driver’s Seat for AI-Echo Success
stories.Summary:
David Ouyang, MD, a cardiologist at Kaiser Permanente Northern California, built an interactive echocardiography training website called intro2echo. Ouyang was also an investigator in the AI echo INSIGHT study, presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026. That study compared AI-, cardiologist-, and sonographer-generated preliminary echo reports. Medscape interviewed him about both, and the interview was edited for length and clarity. Ouyang said the intro2echo tool is valuable for trainees and for practicing cardiologists as a reference guide.

Ouyang built the website with Claude, as a chance to play with AI and better understand it. He said you give it feedback and it gradually builds a bigger website, essentially from text messages. It is all synthetic data, with no patient data or real ultrasound data. Similar training tools for angiography and ECG were released around the same time. Ouyang said he believes the author of one mentioned being inspired by what he did.

The AI echo INSIGHT trial used the EchoPrime AI model, which uses computer vision, meaning having the computer analyze images to produce an interpretation. The trial found that AI-assisted preliminary reports were comparable to those prepared by sonographers and cardiologists. Using AI to generate preliminary interpretations almost halved the time cardiologists spent interpreting each scan, from 8.5 to 4.6 minutes. Keane K. Lee, MD, MS, presented the findings at AHA. Ouyang said the website is built with a different kind of AI and is strictly meant to teach the parts of an echo exam, what it takes to interpret one, and the caveats and challenges involved.

Ouyang said imaging use in the US keeps climbing as the population ages and standards of care rise. He said the number of images is going up while the medical workforce stays roughly the same size, so the backlog keeps growing. He said a key bottleneck in doing more echocardiogram studies is having expert sonographers perform the scans prior to interpretations. In the short term, he thinks the saved time is time cardiologists can spend with patients, handle urgent messages, and review ongoing care. He said Echo depends on skill in acquiring images as well as reading them, and that better reading alone cannot overcome poor images.

Ouyang said he and colleagues are discussing with internal stakeholders to get approval from the cardiovascular service line, IT, and AI leaders for a broad deployment. He said the technology would need FDA clearance, and they are preparing to submit the initial inquiries and eventual submission package. He said the FDA reviews software as a snapshot in time rather than a continuously learning system, and that in the short term he expects clinical AI to be most commonly fixed, regulated software products. He said he has no interest in commercializing the website and is not sure there is a huge business case for commercialization. He said he hopes it could be integrated into a medical school curriculum, partly why he hopes it stays free.

Ouyang is a deputy editor at NEJM AI, and JAMA will launch an AI journal in 2027. He said journals are recognizing that AI needs more rigorous testing and evaluation. He said many of his patients already use chatbots for a first-pass interpretation of what is happening, and he thinks that elevates conversations in clinic. He said clinicians who know AI will be faster, more accurate, and able to see more patients. David Ouyang reported receiving consulting, equity, or honoraria for lectures from AstraZeneca Alexion, EchoIQ, Ultromics, Pfizer, InVision, Dandelion Health, Johnson and Johnson, and Abbott.

stories.Headline: Cardinal Czerny says humans must stay accountable for violence unleashed by AI
stories.Summary:
Cardinal Michael Czerny, the Prefect Emeritus of the Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development, spoke in Sofia on November 17, 2026, at a gathering co-hosted by the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences and the Apostolic Nunciature in Bulgaria. He was there to present Magnifica humanitas, Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, with a particular focus on war and peace. In his remarks, the Cardinal said that humans must remain directly responsible for any violence and destruction which their technologies unleash. He also said that decisions about lethal force must remain in human hands and that it must always be possible to identify the people who made them. Cardinal Czerny drew on two biblical building projects, Babel and the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem after the exile, to show that the difference between them lies in the desire that guides the act of building.

He applied the same question to artificial intelligence, asking what kind of world and what kind of civilization these tools help to build. He warned that the term "just war" is often used loosely to justify aggression, even as weapons have become more destructive. He said Pope Leo upheld the right to self-defense in the strictest sense while declaring that the just war theory is outdated, pointing instead to dialogue, diplomacy and forgiveness as ways to resolve conflicts. The Cardinal set out three criteria from the encyclical, the first being that the chain of responsibility must be identifiable and verifiable, from those who design and train a system to those who authorize and use it. The second is that those deciding whether to use lethal force must have time to exercise judgment, because speed and efficiency cannot determine an irreversible decision.

The third is that civilians must be distinguished from combatants and protected, along with the infrastructure they need to survive. He also recalled the encyclical's warning that a culture of power pushes the suffering of people at war into the background as governments pursue strategic interests, and that this outlook takes hold when societies regard war as inevitable and dismiss those who seek peace through dialogue as unrealistic. For Cardinal Czerny, that responsibility also has a personal dimension, since Pope Leo's call for the disarmament of heart, mind and life reaches into ordinary encounters where the words and images people choose can themselves do harm. As the Cardinal put it, the roots of both war and peace are within, and everyone needs to pacify the belligerence at work in each one's heart.

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches initial public offering as token usage emerges as a key investor metric
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is launching an initial public offering on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The company is moving toward the public markets to attract new investors. Industry watchers are focusing on how the company measures its success. They believe token usage will be a key metric for AI investors. This measure is compared to subscriber counts for video streaming services.

The company reported 33.2 billion dollars in revenue for the first nine months of 2026. This grew from 16.3 billion dollars earned during the first half of the year. Consumption based revenue accounted for 80 percent of sales in those first six months. Subscription based revenue made up the remaining 20 percent of the total sales. Anthropic faces long term infrastructure spending commitments of nearly 900 billion dollars.

Anthropic describes its pricing as metered in tokens and priced by the selected model. The company says business customers have signed multiyear contracts with locked in pricing. These contracts include minimum spend commitments that customers cannot cancel. Anthropic stated it only books revenue as tokens are actually consumed. A token is a small chunk of text that a model reads or generates.

Sarah Friar of OpenAI said usage grew ten times after cutting Luna model prices. JPMorgan analysts say Chinese frontier AI models tend to be cheaper than US labs. Claire Husson Citanna says labs that disclose token math could borrow money more cheaply. Ilan Strauss and Tim O Reilly argue the filing omits total token volume. They believe these missing building blocks are necessary for investors to understand growth.

The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index measured the most powerful models as of July 14, 2026. Open weight rivals and quantum computing advances threaten to lower token prices. The AI Disclosures Project is calling for more transparency regarding costs per token. Many investors want to know how much customers prepaid in token credits. This visibility helps distinguish between discounted enterprise commitments and steady demand.

The filing will establish a precedent for other AI labs preparing to go public. The first lab to disclose these figures could set the industry roadmap. Investors still cannot tell how much committed spending remains unused by customers. The articles leave open whether Anthropic will eventually disclose its total token volume. It remains unclear if the company will reveal its exact cost per token.

stories.Headline: Investment experts advise diversification as AI stocks decline and Nvidia shares drop
stories.Summary:
Investors are currently feeling uneasy because shares of Nvidia have dropped 35 percent since October 6. This decline followed the resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO after reports of his romantic ties to a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Technology companies within the S&P 500 have fallen nearly 17 percent from their peaks in early October. These events have led many market participants to wonder if the artificial intelligence bubble is finally popping.

The current market structure requires a careful look at diversification because the ten largest S&P 500 companies command 37 percent of the index. As of November 17, technology stocks also represent 37 percent of the benchmark weighting. This concentration exists even before the initial public offering of Anthropic, which targets a valuation that would make it the tenth largest public firm in the United States. Experts suggest that nervous investors should evaluate their exposure and consider equal weight indexes or international stocks.

Dan Lefkovitz of Morningstar Indexes says that exiting the market is an extreme option that could cause investors to miss tremendous gains. Anthony Saglimbene from Ameriprise notes that market capitalization weighted funds do not work well when technology stocks experience a sell off. Jamie Cox of Harris Financial Group believes younger investors should focus on long term opportunities rather than short term volatility. Ryan Detrick from Carson Group explains that broad market pullbacks of 5 percent or more happen more than three times per year on average.

The broader context involves a persistent demand for data centers and microchips that may benefit megacap firms like Microsoft and Alphabet. While short term drawdowns are possible, the historical trend of the United States stock market has generally moved upward. Investors are encouraged to talk with financial advisors before making wholesale changes to their portfolios. The goal is to participate in the market without being overly reliant on a single theme or the top end of the market.

stories.Headline: Microsoft releases seven AI models it says beat rivals on price and performance
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI released a family of seven new models on November 18, 2026, saying it wanted to keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability while offering price points that let agents run around the clock on real engineering work. The company said MAI Cyber 2 Flash beats GPT-6 Astra's quality at less than 2% of the cost per task on the CyberGym-E2E benchmark. MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of the coding quality of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 40% of the price, and against Opus 5.5 it reaches 96% performance for just 5% of the price. MAI Code 2 Flash matches GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price and Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the price.

MAI Image 2.7 is ranked first on Artificial Analysis image editing, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst at its maximum setting at just one-fifth of the price. MAI Realtime 1 outperforms GPT-Realtime 2.1 and starts at just $0.01 per audio minute. Dragon Copilot Transcribe is built on MAI Transcribe 2, described as the world's fastest and most accurate multilingual transcription model, and already powers 10 million patient encounters a month with multilingual error rates halved. Decision 1.1 is the latest decision model from Microsoft, 50 times faster and 79 times cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol.

Maia 200, Microsoft's second-generation AI accelerator, is now in production running the company's largest models and achieving 1.7 times more tokens per watt. Microsoft AI said its mission is to build the very best models in the world, and that as token spend skyrockets it knows customers also want models at a price point that lets them run agents 24-7 doing real engineering work. The company framed the seven releases as a family of world-class models at what it called a truly exceptional price-performance. The announcement did not say when the models would become generally available beyond the release itself, or give further details on access.
