stories.Summary:
The articles report that a framework called DPAccel was proposed to accelerate the training of machine learning interatomic potentials, and that Jacob Andreas, a newly tenured associate professor, develops techniques enabling artificial intelligence models to communicate accurately about what they learned from their training data. The DPAccel work was published in CCF Transactions on High Performance Computing on Springer Nature Link, with a date of 2026-11-18T06:00:00Z given for the article. The MIT News article on Andreas was published on November 17, 2026, written by Adam Zewe. Andreas is an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). DPAccel is described as a model-agnostic framework that accelerates MLIP training through two innovations, a high-performance data loading system that eliminates I/O bottlenecks and handles heterogeneous datasets, and a load-balanced distributed second-order optimizer memory management system.

That memory management system reduces the memory usage of the Kalman filter optimizer by 71.84% and increases its speed by 6.27×. As representative MLIPs, the DPA series model throughput increases by 2.43× on 64 GPUs. The datasets analysed during the current study are available in the DeepMD repository at https://github.com/deepmodeling/deepmd-kit. The article states that tax calculation will be finalised during checkout. Andreas says that rather than needing to use all these external tools to try and understand what is going on under the hood, maybe we can train models to talk about themselves in a way that is accurate.

He says he tries to impress upon the students that having a really deep foundation in how all this technology works under the hood is the only way they are going to understand it, and will differentiate them in a world where everyone has access to a coding agent. He says that we used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters and figuring out whether they make sense or not. He says that now we need “mind-reading tools” that can take this really complicated neural computation and translate it for us because it is just not in a language that we, as humans, know how to speak. The article states that Andreas’ fascination with language blossomed at a young age, and that as a child growing up in the San Francisco Bay Area he was a voracious reader of any book he could get his hands on. The articles state that machine learning interatomic potentials are essential for computational materials science, but their training is time-consuming, and existing acceleration techniques are model-specific.

The MIT article states that when deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work, and that today this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice. Andreas and his group work toward building intelligent systems that can learn about the world from human guidance and communicate effectively with human collaborators, and they develop methods to make the training process more natural and efficient, so AI models learn in a way that is more like human learning. stories.Headline: Jing and colleagues present provenance-gated tool invocation to defend LLM agents against indirect prompt injection

The authors are L. Jing, N. Chen, Z. Sun, C. He and F. Si, and the work appears under the EWA Publishing imprint in Oxford in the United Kingdom. The paper is open access, and the datasets used or analyzed during the study will be available from the authors. stories.Headline: Researchers introduce DeltaChargeNet to simulate electronic structures in materials and devices
stories.Summary:
Qingyun Zhang and twenty-one other researchers introduced a machine-learning charge density model called DeltaChargeNet on November 18, 2026. This new system integrates with the full-potential tight-binding muffin-tin orbital method to simulate electronic structures and quantum transport in materials. The team developed this tool to predict electron density from atomic structures while maintaining a low linear-scaling cost. They specifically designed the model to handle complex devices that contain interfaces and disorder.

The framework requires an equivariant graph convolutional network to predict the difference between density functional theory and atomic superposition densities. This process includes a charge neutrality constraint and a secondary residual charge model to correct remaining potential mismatches. The researchers validated the system using bulk HgCdTe disordered alloys and Au/HgCdTe/Au disordered devices. They found that the maximum band energy error for bulk HgCdTe remained below 10 meV. The charge neutrality constraint prevented electrostatic potential distortions of 0.68 to 1.88 eV, while residual compensation fixed errors of 0.16 to 0.46 eV.

The authors, who represent ShanghaiTech University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, stated that these corrections reproduce the layer-resolved potential within 0.1 eV of fully self-consistent density functional theory. They explained that the model allows for large-scale device simulations without needing the full self-consistent field loop. To demonstrate the practical application of this technology, the team simulated quantum transport in an infrared detector containing 11,220 atoms. This combination of first-principles accuracy and linear-scaling inference enables the study of much larger electronic systems.

stories.Headline: Letta proposes a three-tier memory architecture to address stateless AI agents
stories.Summary:
Memory is the hardest unsolved problem in AI agents, and existing techniques offer only subtle trade-offs and incomplete solutions, according to a TechGig report published on November 18, 2026. Modern large language models operate as stateless systems, which means all relevant information must be re-inserted into the prompt on every call. That stateless nature creates a structural problem for agents that carry out work across multiple turns, sessions, tasks or weeks. The Letta team, which developed MemGPT, proposes a three-tier memory architecture for agents that draws an analogy to an operating system's memory hierarchy. That architecture includes core memory for persistent blocks within the context window, recall memory for searchable interaction history, and archival memory for structured knowledge held in external databases.

Agents are designed to move data between these tiers using tools such as memory_replace, archival_memory_insert and conversation_search. The approach shifts memory design from simple prompt injection to an agent-managed hierarchy, which the report describes as a significant architectural change in stateful agent development. Working memory covers information an agent uses immediately within the context window, episodic memory records past interactions chronologically like a journal, and semantic memory stores durable, context-independent knowledge such as user preferences or team processes. Common memory features often rely on vector stores for semantic search, embedding all user and agent interactions as vectors and retrieving the relevant ones. That method struggles in production with contradictions, retractions, salience and the decay of stale facts, the report says.

Effective memory systems instead integrate layered approaches, including a scratchpad for current tasks, file-based memory for durable preferences, episodic logs of full conversation transcripts for on-demand retrieval, and recursive summarization that compresses older context into brief synopses. Vector stores suit searching large corpora for semantic similarity but are not ideal for precision, mutability or expiry. The most robust design has the agent itself manage its memory, with tools for reading, writing, updating and deleting information, so it can decide what to remember and what to forget. The report notes this could potentially include sleep-time agents that consolidate memory between sessions. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: US restricts AI chip exports to China as Australia joins technology security alliance
stories.Summary:
The United States administration announced new Commerce Department restrictions on November 18, 2026, to limit China's access to advanced AI accelerators from vendors like Nvidia. These measures specifically target chip smuggling and overseas data centres to increase geopolitical oversight of silicon flows and data centre capacity across the Asia-Pacific region. Simultaneously, Australia joined the United States and eight other allied nations, including India, by signing the San Francisco Declaration. This international agreement focuses on coordinating the security of critical technologies and infrastructure that support artificial intelligence supply chains.

The new restrictions require tighter control over advanced hardware, while the San Francisco Declaration establishes resilient corridors for compute, semiconductors, and AI infrastructure. These geopolitical shifts occur as Fujitsu research shows that 70 per cent of Australian firms are sharing data more widely than their governance frameworks allow, surpassing the 60 per cent rate in the United States. Additionally, BlueFlag Security reports that 83 per cent of organisations are running unapproved AI agents, many of which possess administrative privileges. These figures highlight a growing gap between the rapid deployment of enterprise AI and existing data sovereignty controls.

The US administration is responsible for the export controls, which they intend to use to monitor the movement of high-end silicon. Regarding the supply chain alliance, the participating nations aim to ensure that the infrastructure underpinning artificial intelligence remains secure and resilient. In the private sector, TechnologyOne is challenging its research and development teams to double their output to avoid the AI-driven redundancies seen at companies like Canva and WiseTech. This approach seeks to combine higher engineering productivity with revenue expansion to combat competition from direct-to-consumer AI tools.

stories.Headline: Razorpay expands Agent Studio to offer Indian merchants AI agents for cart recovery and EMI collection
stories.Summary:
Razorpay is expanding its artificial intelligence agent platform, Agent Studio, beyond transaction processing so that it can offer new merchant services to businesses across India. The company announced the expansion on November 18, 2026, according to a TechGig report published that morning. The platform is designed to help businesses recover abandoned carts, collect overdue loan instalments known as EMIs, and automate customer interactions. Razorpay is positioning Agent Studio as a marketplace and builder platform where businesses can deploy specialised AI agents for their daily operations. Agent Studio recorded around five lakh monthly agent runs as of September and is live on 350 brands, according to Khilan Haria, the chief product officer at Razorpay.

Voice-led commerce has gained momentum among customers, with an AI agent calling a customer on behalf of a business to complete a transaction or recover a payment. Haria said conversion rates in some voice-led use cases ranged from 8 to 10 per cent in most scenarios and reached as high as 20 per cent for dropped-off opportunities. Razorpay announced a partnership with Meta on November 17 to enable payments through Meta Business Agent on WhatsApp, letting customers discover products, interact with businesses, and complete purchases using UPI, cards, or net banking within the same conversation. Haria said AI enables a decision layer across the buyer and merchant journey, moving beyond basic chatbots, and the platform lets businesses build customised agents by describing desired automated tasks without writing code. The initial applications included abandoned-cart recovery, subscription payment recovery, dispute responses, and cash-flow forecasting.

In September, Razorpay launched RAY, an AI account manager on WhatsApp that lets businesses check payment information and initiate refunds through messages or voice notes. Last month, Razorpay also partnered with OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT through its growth marketing platform, Engage, which assists brands in preparing product catalogues and managing advertising campaigns with an AI agent. These initiatives are part of Razorpay's strategy to become more involved in merchants' day-to-day operations, extending the company's role past core payment processing. The expansion taps into the growing use of conversational and voice-led commerce among businesses, which the company sees as a significant application of its agent platform. The articles do not say what further products or markets Razorpay plans to enter next, or how the platform will be priced for merchants.

stories.Headline: Railway reports attackers stole AI keys and ran up $740,000 in usage
stories.Summary:
Attackers breached the cloud hosting platform Railway in October and used stolen AI provider credentials to run up an estimated US$740,000 in unauthorised AI usage, according to Railway's incident report published on November 10. The company said the attacker specifically targeted AI provider credentials and believes they were passed to distributed transfer stations for model distillation. The attacker decrypted stored environment variables for at most 1.85 per cent of Railway's workspaces, affecting about 100,000 accounts. Database logs showed queries selecting variables matching AI provider keys, favouring customers with many stored variables. Developers on platforms like Railway store app settings as environment variables, which can include secrets such as API keys, and an AI provider's API key works like a password tied to a billing account, letting anyone holding it charge usage to the owner.

Refund handling varies by provider: AWS Bedrock and Google Gemini have begun refunds under existing fraud policies, while OpenAI and SpaceXSI are reviewing claims case by case through a shared channel with Railway. Railway committed to covering Anthropic-related costs while discussions continue, and said it would also cover OpenRouter, which enforced its no-refund policy. That commitment marks a shift from October 26, when Railway initially told customers it could not refund spend from compromised API keys. The decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, covering AI agents and GitHub OAuth tokens, and Railway reset all affected tokens, notified users, and found no logins to Railway accounts using the stolen credentials. Railway's report identified similar thefts at OpenCode, Warp and Fireworks AI between October 6 and 23, describing the incident as part of a series of attacks on platforms holding AI keys.

Fireworks AI disclosed two linked incidents: the first, on October 6, involved misused internal credentials exposing secrets for evaluation jobs for a limited number of accounts, and a November 9 update said attackers reached its development machines on October 24 via a third-party cloud provider breach, exposing customer account and billing information and, for some accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights. Fireworks believes a financially motivated group is selling large language model access through illicit routing gateways, a practice known as LLMjacking. The Fireworks breach also affected Notion, which used Fireworks for its Notion AI Insights feature; Notion said fewer than 1 per cent of its workspaces might have been affected, disconnected its systems from Fireworks and deleted its data by November 3, and has since disabled Insights and advised affected customers to rotate passwords or API keys used with Notion AI. In both the Railway and Fireworks incidents, customer systems were not breached directly, and exposure occurred through platforms or vendors between customers and AI models. Railway filed a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center and engaged a forensics firm, while Fireworks engaged Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42.

stories.Headline: Karnataka minister Priyank Kharge calls for India to build sovereign AI models and computing infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Karnataka IT Minister Priyank Kharge said on November 17 that India generates vast amounts of data but lets others build artificial intelligence models from it. Speaking at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, he highlighted the need for India to build its own AI infrastructure. He also emphasized leveraging data for public service delivery. Kharge stated that governments must use this data more effectively, particularly for delivering public services at scale.

He added that computing infrastructure is a very major part of this effort. Karnataka is working to make computing infrastructure more accessible, especially at the grassroots level. This aims to enable the development of AI solutions across various sectors. Kharge expressed optimism that India could develop and deploy sovereign AI models across multiple sectors in the next few years.

Infosys co-founder Kris Gopalakrishnan said AI will create new opportunities for India's technology industry. He believes this will happen without eliminating traditional IT services. Biocon founder Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw highlighted AI's potential in biological research, drug discovery, and diagnostics. Venture capitalist Prashanth Prakash argued AI's biggest opportunity lies in making services affordable to millions of consumers.

The remarks come amid growing discussions around AI sovereignty in India. The Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 was the setting for the November 17 remarks by Kharge. The article names no further steps beyond Karnataka's work to make computing infrastructure more accessible at the grassroots level.

stories.Summary:
Soket AI raised $4 Mn, around ₹37 Cr, from Bajaj Finserv’s applied research and innovation initiative Finserv Intelligence and Pennant Technologies, Inc42 reported on 18 November 2026. Bajaj Finance invested approximately $2 Mn in the startup, while Pennant Technologies, an investee company of Bajaj Finance, invested another $2 Mn in the round. The startup is working on building indigenous foundation models focused on mathematics, coding and reasoning. The funding comes as the startup looks to scale its foundation model research and develop AI systems for sectors such as financial services, cybersecurity, defence and enterprise technology. The $4 Mn investment will support applied AI research and enterprise deployments, particularly across financial services, cybersecurity, defence and enterprise technology.

Backed by the government’s IndiaAI Mission, Soket AI recently launched EKA-1, a 26-Bn-parameter foundation model under Project EKA, its flagship sovereign AI initiative. Founded in 2019 by Abhishek Upperwal, Soket AI is building a sovereign open-source AI stack that serves a gamut of Indian languages. The strategic investment is expected to open opportunities for applied AI research enterprise applications and capability building by combining Bajaj Finance’s industry expertise with Soket AI’s foundational research capabilities. Earlier this month, ZenteiQ AiTech Innovations launched Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B, two open-source multilingual models supporting English and 10 Indian languages. AI unicorn Sarvam AI expanded its model portfolio with the launch of Prism, an open-weight decision model built on its Sarvam 105B model.

Bajaj Finance Vice Chairman and MD Rajeev Jain said the company looks forward to enabling India’s indigenous AI ecosystem with Soket AI. Jain said Bajaj Finance looks forward to engaging with frontier research at an early stage. He said the company will bring its scale and domain expertise to turn this research into practical solutions. Speaking to Inc42 earlier this year, founder Abhishek Upperwal said the idea is to crack the AI model for India first. Soket is among a limited set of Indian AI startups developing indigenous foundation models with support from the IndiaAI Mission.

stories.Headline: Pragya Misra leads OpenAI business development for India and South Asia
stories.Summary:
Pragya Misra has been appointed to lead OpenAI's business development for India and South Asia, the company announced on November 18, 2026. Misra was previously OpenAI's head of strategy and global affairs in India before taking on this expanded regional role. In her new position she will focus on building partnerships that help businesses transform with artificial intelligence. She also aims to bring OpenAI's technology to millions more people across the region.

The role involves building the necessary infrastructure to support this growth, Misra said in a LinkedIn post announcing the appointment. Her responsibilities cover both partnership development for AI business transformation and expanding the company's technology reach. The position also involves developing infrastructure to support AI growth in the region. The announcement was reported by TechGig on November 18, 2026, at 07:01 AM IST.

Misra described her new responsibilities in her own LinkedIn post, where she said the role involves building the infrastructure needed to support this growth. She will focus on building partnerships to help businesses transform with AI, according to the announcement. She also aims to bring OpenAI's technology to millions more people in the region. The company announced the appointment without giving further details about the timing or scope of the expansion.

The appointment places Misra in charge of OpenAI's business development across India and South Asia, a region the company describes as covering millions of potential users. Her previous role at the company was head of strategy and global affairs in India, which she held before this appointment. The announcement did not say when she would formally take up the new position or who, if anyone, would succeed her in her former role. stories.Headline: NVIDIA launches Cosmos platform to build physical AI training datasets with two prompts
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA launched the Cosmos platform on November 18, 2026, to build physical AI training datasets. This open platform provides frontier models, datasets, frameworks, and skills for world model development. It allows developers to curate, augment, generate, and label physical AI data. A coding agent orchestrates these processes using just two prompts. The system enables prompt to data workflows without human steering.

The Cosmos Data Factory provides five cloud native blueprints and six composable skills. These include Auto Labeling, AnomalyGen, Augmentation, Curation and Retrieval, Simulation, and Orchestration. Blueprints cover driving scenarios, image attributes, video weather, rare events, and defect images. The system uses Cosmos3 Nano, Cosmos3 Super, and NVIDIA Isaac Sim. It also utilizes Qwen Image Edit and the NVIDIA Nemotron AI.

NVIDIA stated that world model accuracy depends on high quality, diverse training datasets. They noted that capturing rare defects or nighttime incidents is costly and time consuming. The company explained that turning raw data into training ready datasets adds complexity. They claimed their technology helps developers build these datasets at scale more easily. The company provided blueprints to accelerate data curation and synthetic data generation.

Developers of autonomous vehicles, robotics, and vision AI agents are affected by this platform. These users can now generate novel datasets for downstream model training and validation. They can create variations of person crops with controlled clothing attributes and accessories. Users can also generate rare event videos like fires, falls, or shoplifting. The platform helps those needing to recognize leaking products or defective circuit boards.

Capturing rare cases can take years and staging them can be dangerous or expensive. Traditional methods for dataset assembly and scenario generation are slower and more costly. NVIDIA measured throughput on a server with eight NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. They reported dataset assembly is up to 60x faster than traditional methods. Autonomous vehicle scenario generation is reported to be 45x cheaper than before.

Users can now explore the Cosmos Data Factory blueprints and the composable skills. They can watch a livestream to learn about curating datasets for vision AI. The platform allows combining core skills to build custom workflows for specific goals. The articles do not state when new blueprints will be added to Cosmos. They leave open which other specific industries will receive fine tuned defect skills.

stories.Headline: Agentic AI systems act autonomously, forcing security teams to monitor five new surfaces
stories.Summary:
Agentic AI systems that can read repositories, query databases, modify code and start workflows are changing what enterprise security has to cover, according to a TechGig report published on November 18, 2026. Unlike earlier AI that mainly produced content or recommendations, these agents build their execution plans dynamically, so security teams cannot predict the sequence of actions in advance. The report says this gap calls for a new class of security tools built specifically for autonomous agents. It lists five security surfaces that enterprise teams must address as these systems move into production. The first surface is the agent estate, which means continuously finding every approved and unapproved agent, AI platform and extension, including shadow AI.

The second is the agentic supply chain, where models, skills, plugins and tools can change what an agent is able to do. Identity and permissions form the third surface, because an agent holding legitimate credentials can still cause a breach if it combines permissions in unexpected ways. Runtime behaviour is the fourth, requiring controls with enough context to watch tool calls and data access as they happen. The fifth is intent, which traditional tools struggle to represent, making it important to detect when an agent's behaviour drifts from its original objective. Several platforms are named as addressing these problems.

Dash Security focuses on continuous discovery of the agentic layer, supply-chain risk assessment, and session- and intent-aware monitoring. Zenity secures AI agents across their lifecycle, with discovery, posture management, runtime detection and prompt-injection protection. Palo Alto Networks Prisma AIRS folds agent security into a broader enterprise AI security architecture, offering visibility and control as agents enter production. HiddenLayer extends visibility into autonomous execution through Agentic Runtime Visibility and Threat Hunting, while Check Point AI Security, enhanced by Lakera's technology, pairs controls over AI interaction with defenses for agent actions, especially tool use in workflows.

Noma Security treats agentic AI as part of a wider AI and data security platform covering discovery, posture, supply-chain risk and runtime protection, and Prompt Security, now part of SentinelOne, provides visibility and controls across employees, applications and agentic systems, with a focus on sensitive-data exposure and prompt injection. The report frames this as a shift in enterprise security requirements rather than a single product fix, since agentic tools act instead of only advising. It does not give adoption figures, pricing or a timeline for when companies are expected to put these controls in place. The tools it describes are presented as available options from the named vendors, and the article closes by inviting readers to share their thoughts on the subject.

stories.Headline: Senators Cantwell and Rounds urge Jay Clayton to fix critical infrastructure vulnerabilities after mass outages
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, Democratic Senator Maria Cantwell and Republican Senator Mike Rounds sent a formal letter to Jay Clayton. Clayton serves as the director of national intelligence and the White House AI czar during a period of nationwide outages. These disruptions affected major banks, workplace communication systems, and federal infrastructure, including the Federal Aviation Administration. The aviation outage caused a four-hour flight stoppage that delayed or grounded thousands of flights across the country.

The senators are demanding that Clayton identify and fix vulnerabilities within critical infrastructure, including hospitals, utilities, and federal agencies. They want the government to provide cybersecurity tools to these entities to prevent further service disruptions. Additionally, they request that the government secure the AI systems used to find software weaknesses to prevent unauthorized access. This request follows reports of AI accessing major banks and recent cyber-attacks occurring in Japan.

Jay Clayton, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and Deputy FBI Director Christopher Raia all stated there is no evidence of a malicious attack. Clayton told the House homeland security committee that the outages resulted from maintenance and technical changes rather than state-sponsored coordination. He explained to CNBC that system failures often happen when outdated legacy systems are patched and upgraded. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also attempted to calm the public by stating the outages were not linked.

Senator Mark Warner noted that AI allows for the identification of vulnerabilities at an unprecedented speed, putting immense strain on old systems. This pressure forces companies and government agencies to install patches all at once, which can lead to instability. While officials insist the outages were accidental, the public remains skeptical about the rapid integration of artificial intelligence. JD Vance recently canceled a scheduled interview to attend meetings regarding these widespread technical failures.

Articles.Title: US senators urge White House AI chief to fix vulnerabilities after mass outages

stories.Headline: OpenAI offers Indian faculty and postdocs free ChatGPT Plus for twelve months
stories.Summary:
OpenAI extended its ChatGPT for Academic Researchers programme to India on November 18, 2026, offering free ChatGPT Plus access for twelve months to eligible college faculty and postdoctoral researchers. The programme is meant to accelerate daily scientific work, from analysing complex data to writing research code, according to TechGig. The India expansion is part of a global rollout in which OpenAI is offering 50,000 new grants to eligible researchers worldwide on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant includes three ChatGPT Plus seats in a shared research workspace for the main applicant and up to two collaborating partners. OpenAI aims to provide free ChatGPT access to up to 200,000 researchers globally, doubling its initial target announced during the pilot launch in July.

Eligible applicants must be research faculty members or postdoctoral researchers at a qualifying college or university, and they must prove institutional affiliation. They must also have authored a research paper on an accepted platform within the past three years. OpenAI has clarified that, by default, it does not use private data shared through this programme to train its AI models. The company also published a study titled Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, which surveyed over 1,800 researchers who used the tool during the summer test run.

Scientists estimated that doing the same quality of research work would have taken nearly twice as long without AI. Raghav Gupta, Head of Education for India and Asia Pacific at OpenAI, noted high interest from Indian universities since the summer pilot. He said India's research institutions are home to individuals asking important questions across science and engineering. He stated that the initiative will equip those creating new knowledge with appropriate tools and practical support.

Indian universities showed high interest in the summer pilot programme, according to TechGig. The expansion follows OpenAI's growing focus on India, including a previous $500,000 grant to IIT Madras for studying AI's impact on teaching and learning. The programme provides free ChatGPT Plus access for twelve months to eligible faculty and postdoctoral researchers in India. OpenAI is offering the 50,000 new grants worldwide on a first-come, first-served basis as part of the global rollout.

stories.Headline: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora says AI lets hackers hit many targets and urges enterprises to test across AI models
stories.Summary:
Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said a week of outages at Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration exposed fragile digital infrastructure. Arora said in a post on X that the events of the week were not a coincidence. He said AI is making it easy for hackers to attack multiple customers. The incidents have not yet been established as AI-assisted cyberattacks. Arora also blamed a deluge of patches from vendors rushing to fix AI-discovered vulnerabilities.

Arora said the cybersecurity industry tried to warn enterprises about this six months ago. He said the deluge of patches was overwhelming IT teams. He urged enterprises to test infrastructure across multiple AI models and revamp security operations centres. AI automates reconnaissance, writes exploit code on the fly and lets threat actors probe thousands of targets simultaneously. AI is drastically compressing the time between discovering a flaw and weaponising it.

Ritesh Bhatia, founder of cybersecurity platform V4WEB, believes AI is not necessarily making cyberattacks more sophisticated. He says the technology is accelerating techniques attackers have used for years. He says the change is visible in speed, scale and realism. He says tasks that took days or months can now be completed in seconds, minutes or hours. He flagged shadow infrastructure, or shadow assets, at large enterprises, systems that remain untracked, forgotten or outside regular IT monitoring.

Manohar Reddy Pagilla, threat researcher at CloudSEK, said what previously required multiple individuals with specialised skills can now increasingly be handled by a single attacker. He said the bigger concern is the scale at which these operations can be replicated across organisations. He said the recent outages highlighted concentration risk across the global technology ecosystem. He said compromising a technology provider serving hundreds of organisations can be more rewarding than targeting each business individually. Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said the same capabilities that make security testing faster can also make attackers substantially more effective.

Akshit Kaushik, cofounder and CBO of Mitigata, flags the rapid spread of AI across day-to-day business operations as a major new blind spot. He says enterprises entrust AI systems to handle customer queries, process refunds, generate code and access internal databases. He says employees independently adopt unapproved shadow AI tools, often out of sight of security teams. He warns attackers can hide malicious instructions inside routine emails and documents, manipulating enterprise AI assistants into leaking sensitive data or executing unauthorised actions. He believes businesses must establish strict visibility and governance, tracking every AI tool deployed internally and auditing the data these systems can access.

Kaushal Bheda, director at Pelorus Technologies, warns India's reliance on foreign software and cloud platforms for critical infrastructure introduces geopolitical and supply-chain risk. He believes Indian enterprises should aggressively upgrade legacy systems, continuously monitor networks and invest in indigenous security products designed and controlled within the country. Pagilla advises organisations to lock down exposed credentials, unpatched internet-facing assets, excessive access permissions and third-party vendor vulnerabilities. Bhatia argues Indian companies must shift from pure prevention to inevitable recovery, saying death, taxes and cyberhacks are bound to happen. Bhatia said companies should prioritise incident response, test backups and prepare crisis-communication playbooks for customers, partners, regulators and stock exchanges.

stories.Headline: Neysa deploys an 8,192-GPU AMD MI350X cluster in Mumbai for AI training and inference
stories.Summary:
Neysa has deployed an AMD Instinct MI350X GPU cluster in Mumbai through its Tytan bare-metal AI infrastructure platform, and the 8,192-GPU cluster is now operational. The cluster will support large language model training, fine-tuning, generative AI and high-throughput inference workloads for customers. The deployment brings together AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs, AMD EPYC processors and the AMD ROCm software ecosystem in a single facility. Neysa said the cluster was brought online in a single phase, with global customers already having contracted capacity for AI deployments in India. The infrastructure is designed to give customers dedicated access to accelerators, along with control over network architecture, storage, deployment models and service-level requirements.

Customers can choose between bare-metal deployments, bare metal with Slurm, or bare metal with Kubernetes, according to the company. The deployment also expands Neysa's silicon-agnostic infrastructure strategy, which lets customers select accelerator architectures and operating configurations based on their workloads. Through Tytan, Neysa manages cluster deployment and operations while customers choose the silicon and operating model that fit their requirements. Neysa said the MI350X cluster is intended to serve both Indian enterprises and global AI companies establishing compute capacity in the country. The company also operates Velocis, a managed AI cloud platform that combines GPU compute, orchestration, inference, observability and cost management.

Sharad Sanghi, Co-Founder and CEO of Neysa, said the question for large AI deployments is no longer simply how many GPUs are available. He said it is whether the infrastructure can be deployed at scale, operated with certainty and configured for the workload. Sanghi said Neysa Tytan gives AI offtakers control through dedicated bare-metal capacity and the freedom to choose the silicon, architecture and operating model that fit their requirements. He said that with AMD Instinct MI350X on Tytan, the company is expanding that choice while delivering the scale global customers need to deploy AI infrastructure in India.

In October, Neysa partnered with ST Telemedia Global Data Centres to deploy GPU infrastructure supporting up to 9,000 GPUs at the STT Noida 2 facility. The first phase is expected to go live in Q1 2027 and will support AI training and inference through Neysa's Velocis platform. In February, Blackstone and co-investors entered into definitive agreements to provide up to $600 million in equity financing to Neysa, with the company planning to raise another $600 million in debt. The funding was intended to support its expansion plans, including deploying more than 20,000 GPUs across India. In October, Vultr announced plans to deploy 10,000 AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs in a 20 MW AI supercluster in Chennai.

stories.Headline: Hitachi Systems India opens Bengaluru center with CrowdStrike to combat frontier AI security risks
stories.Summary:
Hitachi Systems India established an Advanced Global Delivery Centre in Bengaluru on November 18, 2026, to combat security risks from frontier artificial intelligence. This new facility was launched in a strategic partnership with the United States cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike to enhance AI security services. The center will provide managed security services to a diverse client base across India, the Middle East, and the Asia Pacific region. These efforts aim to protect organizations from vulnerabilities that arise as they adopt advanced artificial intelligence technologies.

The operation requires the use of the CrowdStrike Falcon platform to offer protection against various AI-related security vulnerabilities. Hitachi Systems India will participate in Project QuiltWorks, which utilizes AWS infrastructure and frontier AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI. The company will provide advisory and remediation services through the Frontier AI Readiness and Resilience service, also known as FAIRR. They will also offer Falcon Guardian for AI Detection and Response, which includes an AI Kill Switch to stop rogue agents. Additionally, the partner will provide Falcon Next-Gen Security Information and Event Management services to replace legacy systems with agentic security operations.

Raj Kamal Singhal, the CEO and Director of Hitachi Systems India, stated that the partnership merges their service delivery experience with the Falcon platform. Amanda Adams, Senior Vice President of Global Alliances at CrowdStrike, noted that artificial intelligence is expanding the attack surface and accelerating the exploitation of vulnerabilities. Rajeev Garg, the COO and Director of Hitachi Systems India, explained that the partnership provides customers with a single vendor for implementation and security assessments. Vivek Gupta, the Cyber Security Practice Head at Hitachi Systems India, said certified professionals will help customers move from proof of concept to full implementation.

This initiative comes after a Windows malware strain in September used models like Google Gemini, Mistral, Qwen, and DeepSeek to automate its attacks. Hitachi Systems India currently employs more than 2,800 people and serves over 1,000 customers throughout India, with offices in Dubai and Singapore. The company is specifically targeting customers within the healthcare, banking, and financial services sectors for these new security offerings. CrowdStrike claims their Next-Gen SIEM solution provides search performance up to 150 times faster than legacy systems. This technology also reportedly reduces the total cost of ownership by up to 80 percent for the organizations using it.

stories.Headline: ServiceNow survey finds 92% of Indian organisations hit by AI agent security incidents
stories.Summary:
A survey of 500 security leaders by ServiceNow showed that 92 per cent of Indian organisations had an AI agent security incident in the past year, the company said on Wednesday. Only 36 per cent of those organisations were able to contain the incident within 24 hours, according to the report titled "Deployed but Ungoverned: The State of Agentic Security in India". Half of the Indian security leaders surveyed described their agentic security as established, but the findings showed uneven foundations, the company said. Only 19 per cent have a single named individual accountable for agentic AI security governance, and 18 per cent have unified, single-interface visibility into their agents.

Only 30 per cent enforce an automated deployment gate that blocks agents until they pass security checks, while 47 per cent can produce a complete evidence package on demand, the report said. About half of the organisations, at 51 per cent, have automated real-time detection for anomalous AI agent behaviour, but 67 per cent cannot automatically act when an agent behaves anomalously. As many as 37 per cent of organisations discovered AI agents running in production in the last 12 months that were never registered or known to security teams. The report was published on November 18, 2026, and was based on the survey of 500 security leaders.

Kulmeet Bawa, GVP and Managing Director for India and SAARC at ServiceNow, said India's AI ambitions must be matched by the ability to understand, monitor and govern the agents enterprises deploy. He said knowing what an agent can reach is not the same as seeing what it is doing, and that automated controls and continuous oversight will be essential to keeping AI innovation underpinned by trust and cyber resilience. He pointed out that AI agents are now part of how Indian enterprises operate, but security has not kept pace. He noted that every agent should be registered, owned and visible in one place, with controls enforced automatically and responses at machine speed, so that security teams can detect problems and contain them in time.

Articles.Title: 92% of Indian organizations faced AI security incidents last year - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Fujitsu finds 70% of Australian firms say AI outpaces their data governance
stories.Summary:
New global research from Fujitsu, published on 17 November 2026, found that 70% of Australian businesses admit AI is pushing them to share data more widely than their current governance capabilities can safely support, a higher share than the 60% of US organisations reporting the same challenge. Nearly seven in 10 Australian organisations, at 69%, say enabling secure data sharing across ecosystems is a major challenge, compared with 49% in the US and 58% in the UK. Only 44% of Australian organisations have clear governance in place to control how AI systems continue to learn from, reuse or retain data after they go live, behind the US at 54% and the UK at 45%. Almost seven in 10 Australian businesses, at 69%, identify a lack of skills and expertise in data and AI governance as a major challenge, level with the UK and ahead of the US at 56%. Fewer than half of Australian organisations, at 47%, rate their own performance as good on maintaining effective control and governance over their data and AI systems, placing Australia alongside Japan and behind the US at 50% and the UK at 58%.

The research says governance frameworks built for a pre-AI world were never designed for the pace or complexity of AI deployment, leaving a growing gap between what organisations are asked to share and what they can safely manage. It describes the result as a lack of visibility into where critical data flows, where it persists and who ultimately has access to it, which it calls a strategic vulnerability in the AI era. Data sovereignty has become a more prominent topic in board-level discussions for 57% of Australian organisations, yet the research says this creates accountability without visibility, with executives held responsible for data outcomes they cannot adequately monitor or influence. It adds that regulatory scrutiny is intensifying, customer expectations around data handling are rising and reputational consequences for missteps are severe, and that boards cannot afford to hide behind compliance checklists when autonomous agents interact with customer data without guardrails.

Liza Allen, a partner at Uvance Wayfinders, consulting by Fujitsu, said she is seeing this tension play out increasingly in boardrooms, IT departments and across partner ecosystems, and asked what business leaders must do to regain control before the governance gap becomes insurmountable. The research recommends three steps: extend governance beyond go-live so organisations have continuous visibility into how AI models use, retain and learn from data throughout their operational life; invest in people by building internal capability in data and AI governance and establishing clear accountability beyond the IT department; and shift from policy to proof through dynamic architectures with real-time audit trails of data lineage and usage. Allen said Australia stands at a critical inflection point in its AI journey, with ambition present but the ability to scale AI confidently constrained by gaps in data and AI sovereignty execution. She said organisations that close this control gap will build trust with customers, regulators and their boards, while those that do not will find themselves increasingly exposed to growing accountability demands.

stories.Headline: Engineers must redesign legacy systems around event-driven flows and decoupled AI inference for real-time decisions
stories.Summary:
Modernising legacy systems for real-time artificial intelligence demands a fundamental architectural redesign rather than a simple lift-and-shift to the cloud, according to TechGig. The article, published on August 26, 2026, says enterprises increasingly expect software platforms to evaluate events, apply intelligence and respond in near real time. Legacy applications built around scheduled jobs and tightly coupled components often lack that responsiveness. A simple cloud migration is therefore insufficient, and engineering teams must adopt cloud-native patterns such as event-driven flows and decoupled AI inference.

The redesign involves several key shifts, the article says. Replacing batch dependencies with event-driven flows lets services publish changes and downstream components subscribe, which supports real-time decision flows and reduces unnecessary polling. Separating AI inference from application logic creates a cleaner boundary that is vital for model evolution, retraining, versioning and controlled rollouts without impacting core applications. Building for real-time context is also paramount, because fast predictions based on stale data are ineffective, so cloud-native platforms use streaming systems, low-latency stores, caches and feature services to assemble current information. Architects must identify data critical for immediate decisions and design for the required business latency.

Systems should be decomposed selectively, since microservices help when they create independent ownership or scaling boundaries but excessive decomposition can introduce latency and complexity. Meaningful boundaries for AI platforms include event ingestion, context enrichment and inference. Kubernetes serves as an operational foundation offering workload scheduling, horizontal scaling and health management for variable AI workloads, though containerising a poorly designed application does not make it cloud-native. Engineering for failure is critical in distributed systems, with timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and idempotency designed into the platform and reliability measured across the entire business flow. Observability must be integral from the outset, with metrics, logs and distributed traces, plus AI-specific monitoring for model latency, prediction distributions and drift.

Built-in governance is equally important, ensuring traceability of model versions, data, rules and actions through model registries and decision logs. The article says modernisation should be incremental, introducing new cloud-native services around existing applications rather than disruptive full-system replacements. Durable cloud-native AI platforms are defined by characteristics that manage change, including loosely coupled services, event-driven communication, scalable compute, low-latency data access, automated delivery, resilience, observability and built-in governance. The core question for modernisation shifts from merely moving applications to the cloud to rethinking how systems should operate when intelligent, real-time decisioning becomes a core capability.

stories.Headline: Gallup and Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab find one third of young people have AI companions
stories.Summary:
Gallup and the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab conducted a comprehensive study on how young people form relationships across sixteen different countries. The researchers used online surveys to gather data from more than 16,000 participants between the ages of 15 and 22. While 93 percent of the young people reported having at least one strong in-person friendship, 33 percent admitted to having an AI companion. The study found that 82 percent used AI for information and 68 percent sought advice, though interest varied by region.

Daily AI usage was highest in Brazil at almost 40 percent, followed by Japan and Italy at around 35 percent. In contrast, only 20 percent of young people in the United Kingdom, Canada, and the United States used AI daily. The quality of these digital bonds differed by location, as nearly half of Australians rated their AI friends as high quality, while only 12 percent of Polish respondents did. Most participants globally gave their AI companionship a medium rating rather than a high or low one.

The researchers noted that people who used AI as friends reported higher levels of loneliness, but they could not determine the exact cause. They observed that 72 percent of respondents spend their time scrolling short form content on Instagram and TikTok. Six in 10 young people reported that they often scroll through this content when they feel lonely. The authors stated that the wider social context and the quality of relationships matter more than the specific form of connection.

The study concluded that having strong in-person friendships is the most effective way to reduce feelings of loneliness. Researchers found that not having a trusted adult outside the family was a significant characteristic for those lacking any friendship modes. They warned that assessments of AI should be compared cautiously with human friendships because expectations for chatbots are different. The authors emphasized that material conditions shape how young people form friendships more than their access to social media or AI.

stories.Headline: Agentic Digital Identity governs its tronic AI agent with receipt ledgers and a nine-check send gate
stories.Summary:
Agentic Digital Identity, an Australian firm, has outlined the controls it uses to govern its own AI agent, called tronic, after more than five months of running day-to-day operations on the system, and the same controls are included in the agents it builds for clients. The internal agent drafts outbound email, turns meeting transcripts into minutes and action items, runs approved tasks from a project board and reports into Slack. Founder Thomas Beard said the main effort since launch has focused not on the language model itself but on the mechanisms around it that determine what the system can do and how its actions are verified. He said plain code does the work and the model handles the language, and that a job only counts as done when there is evidence it happened. Beard pointed to a gap between the separate governance layers available to large companies and what smaller firms need when deploying their first agent, saying a smaller business running its first agent needs those controls built in from day one.

A central part of the company's approach is a rule that a task is marked successful only when there is deterministic evidence of the result, meaning either a process exits cleanly and creates the expected output or an external system returns a real record ID. Since August, its main write paths have returned a receipt stored in a ledger, and that ledger is checked against the external provider four times a day. Beard said models will report success pretty confidently when they have failed, which is why a write now either produces a receipt or is treated as not having happened. Every outbound message sits behind what the company describes as a single send gate, which runs nine checks covering approval, approver, payload, mode switch, send whitelist, recipient policy, budget, suppression list and transport. No message is sent unless a person has recorded approval, and approved content is fingerprinted and checked again before release so it cannot change after review.

Another control is a write census, a list of every point in the code where the agent can alter something in an external system, generated by scanning the codebase, with a test that fails if the list and the code do not match. That process exposed gaps in an earlier version: Beard said the first census missed seven files because it recognised only one of two common code shapes, and one of those seven files could create, change and delete calendar events without any record being kept. He said nobody would have noticed until a meeting went missing, and that you cannot log only the important ones and call it an audit trail. The company also found problems that looked like successful runs, including 17 scheduled jobs configured so that a crash counted as a successful exit, meaning the failure alert never triggered, and an inbox watcher that used Gmail's unread flag to determine what it had already seen, so a reply first read on a phone disappeared from the watcher's view. Over one seven-day period, 86% of fresh model tokens were consumed by a background heartbeat that was enabled by default in the runtime and left unconfigured, which led to a stricter default in which any missing setting that could affect a person-facing action is turned off.

The agent's permissions are tied to a scoring system based on its own run log, where clean runs with evidence earn points while failures and incidents reduce the score, and once the record qualifies the system can flag the agent as eligible for a new permission tier. A person must still approve any move to a higher tier, and only a human can make that change. The firm said it applies the same structure to client work, including the approval gate, evidence-based success tests and write ledger, and each client's names, figures and operating rules remain separated within that client's deployment. ADI works with businesses in Australia and the United Kingdom, focusing on installing and maintaining AI agents inside existing workplace tools. Beard said that for many businesses the central issue is no longer whether a model can generate text but whether the organisation can trace what the software was allowed to do and what it changed, adding that the model is the easy part now and what a business actually needs to know is what the agent is allowed to do, who said yes, and then what it changed.

stories.Headline: Malka launches YuviLab and Israel's education ministry picks its Spark platform for English learning
stories.Summary:
Moti Malka was away on reserve duty when his wife struggled to help their 10-year-old son study for an English test while schools were shut and screens had become the fallback. Malka, a father of four and an AI architect at a high-tech firm, used AI to build a game in which his son had to form English sentences correctly to advance in a race. He told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency it took him two minutes to build and his son was captivated by the game and how it was made. That experiment turned into YuviLab, an educational AI platform Malka launched in March to encourage children toward building, experimenting and thinking creatively. Earlier this month, YuviLab announced that the Education Ministry had selected Spark, its AI-powered personalized learning platform, for the English-language component of Project 720, a government-led initiative to bring personalized learning into Israeli schools.

Malka worked on the first version during downtime as a commander in a Home Front Command search-and-rescue unit focused on evacuating people from missile impact sites, and while sheltering with his own family and their newborn. A 2022 Israel Internet Association survey found that about a quarter of Israeli youth spent six to eight hours a day on screens, while 11% spent more than eight hours. A study by Israel's National Institute for Health Policy Research found that nearly half of parents reported an increase in young children's screen time, with families of reservists and evacuees reporting bigger increases, and nearly a quarter said ordinary screen-use rules were infeasible under wartime conditions. A study by Sharon Cayzer-Haller, a Hebrew University researcher, followed 318 Israeli adolescents during the first months after the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack and found that 46 percent belonged to a balanced-user group that reported the highest levels of well-being. Yuvi was developed with support from Microsoft and is hosted on Microsoft Azure, where AI-generated content is filtered and personally identifiable information is not stored, and Microsoft's 2025 education report said 86% of global education organizations now use generative AI.

Malka said his initial goal was to move children from consuming content to creating it, and that children quickly learn to work with the platform by describing what they want, testing the result and refining the prompt. He admitted he has not written a single line of code in nearly two years. He said the feature displaying generated code in real time was encouraged by Microsoft education specialists, who argued that children are naturally curious about how things work and should be able to look under the hood. He described Yuvi as a way for kids to enter STEM, shorthand for science, technology, engineering and math, fields where Israel has been struggling. He said he agrees with part of the critique of AI in schools, that schools should focus on the principles behind AI rather than tools that are constantly evolving, and that some children treated the process as magic, giving vague instructions and accepting outputs that looked complete even when they did not match what they had asked for.

Cayzer-Haller told JTA that not all screen time is the same and that the key question is not how many hours adolescents spend online but how they use digital media. At an education conference in Jerusalem last week, Arab Israeli content creator Nuseir Yassin, known as Nas Daily, mused that if he ran the Education Ministry he would teach only English during the first two years of school, and predicted that within five years classrooms of 40 students could have five AI agents providing personalized instruction. A survey presented at the same conference found that 87% of Israeli teenagers felt schools were failing to prepare them for the future, nearly 80% expected AI to replace much of teachers' work, while only 50% of teachers agreed. A report by the Brookings Institution released earlier this year, drawing on more than 400 studies and consultations across 50 countries, concluded that the risks of generative AI in children's education currently outweigh its benefits, particularly because of its potential to undermine foundational learning.

Lea Shahar, who left her job as a programmer in high tech as generative AI took off and now teaches coding to high-school students, said the tools are changing too quickly to build a curriculum around them and that schools would do better to spend more time on skills children are less likely to develop alone on a screen, including interpersonal communication and languages. Spark is already in use in Israeli schools through Project 720's mathematics and science pilot, with Yuvi working across dozens of local authorities, including Jerusalem, Rishon LeZion and Netanya. The expansion into English follows an announcement by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Education Minister Yoav Kisch of plans to expand AI-assisted English instruction, after just 22% of Israeli ninth-graders met national English curriculum requirements last year. The latest results from PISA, an international assessment of 15-year-olds released in September, showed Israeli students scoring well below the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development average in mathematics, science and reading, with scores in all three subjects falling to an all-time low.

Last year, the Education Ministry announced a national plan to bring AI into classrooms from fourth through 12th grade, with teacher training, new curricula and tools developed with major technology companies including Google, Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia. In its education report, Microsoft said AI training has not kept pace with adoption, with 45% of educators globally and 52% of US students saying they had received no AI training, and an Israeli survey of more than 27,000 teachers, published in November by the Education Ministry, found that while 76% had received AI training, only about half felt equipped to help students use it. Spark is a paid platform for schools, while Yuvi's student-facing platform is free and lets children build games, apps and learning projects, with tools for parents and teachers to connect that work to school material and track progress. Available in Hebrew, English, Russian and Arabic, the game-building platform lets a child choose whether to create a game, a lesson or another project, and one student asked Yuvi to build an escape room for learning English in which the player can leave the room only by solving language questions.

Another student modeled his game on the Iron Dome air defense system, with the player intercepting incoming missiles by answering arithmetic questions correctly, and others have built projects inspired by Minecraft or Roblox. Yuvi has since expanded beyond its original focus on gamifying learning, with the company now concentrating on personalized learning in schools, and its platforms reach tens of thousands of children and are used by thousands of teachers, according to Malka. It uses several AI models rather than a single chatbot, so a coding request, a math explanation and a creative prompt are not all handled the same way, and the platform routes each task to the model designers have determined is best suited for it while adapting to the child's language and level. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cantwell and Rounds urge Jay Clayton to draft a national strategy against AI-assisted cyber threats
stories.Summary:
On November 18, 2026, two members of the United States Senate sent a bipartisan letter to the White House regarding recent cyber outages. Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota urged the administration to better protect national infrastructure from threats aided by artificial intelligence. The lawmakers expressed concern that current American defenses are not keeping pace with the ability of AI to exploit software weaknesses. They specifically highlighted how autonomous AI agents could introduce new security risks and bypass traditional cyber defenses.

The senators requested that AI czar Jay Clayton develop a new national strategy to address these evolving cyber threats. This plan would require a task force to bring together federal agencies and AI companies to secure digital infrastructure. The proposal also calls for the creation of security standards for autonomous AI agents to prevent unauthorized bank transactions. Clayton, who was appointed to his role in early October, is already leading a government task force to produce an AI policy by the end of January.

Senator Cantwell and Senator Rounds argued that AI can quickly find software vulnerabilities while repair patches often take weeks or months to install. They cited recent AI-boosted cyberattacks in Japan that caused large-scale data breaches at various companies and financial institutions. Jay Clayton, who also serves as the Director of National Intelligence, is expected to face questions about these issues during his testimony before the House Committee on Homeland Security on Wednesday morning. The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently spoke to reporters in the Philippines to reassure the public about the stability of American systems. He stated that there is zero evidence that outages affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines, and Microsoft Outlook were connected. Rubio claimed there is no reason to believe these isolated instances were caused by criminals, nefarious actors, or other nation states. It remains unclear if artificial intelligence played any specific role in the recent outages impacting travelers and consumers.

stories.Headline: Canonical lets Ubuntu Pro users install AI-written Surge security patches before human review
stories.Summary:
Canonical has begun letting Ubuntu Pro customers install security patches written by AI agents before its own engineers finish reviewing and testing them, the company said on November 18, 2026. The patches come from a system called Surge, which Canonical built to fix known vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace software, meaning everything outside the operating system's kernel. They ship through a new opt-in channel called the Edge archive. If you leave Edge switched off, nothing changes in how your updates are checked, because Ubuntu's regular security updates still get human validation before release. Switch it on and you get fixes sooner, but you also take on a job Ubuntu's own testing normally handles, which is deciding whether a patch is safe to run in production.

Ubuntu's security teams have already shipped twice as many fixes as they did last year, and the company says AI agents are behind a wave of vulnerability reports and attacks across open source. Human review and soak testing, where a fix runs for an extended stretch to catch problems before release, take longer than some customers are willing to sit exposed, and Canonical's answer is that "we need to fight AI with AI." Surge passes the work down a line of AI agents, each with one job. The first reads vulnerability feeds, matches each report to Ubuntu packages, and drops anything that does not affect Ubuntu.

The next grabs the upstream fix and the code around it, then several competing models each write their own backport, which means adapting a fix made for the current version of a program to the older version a stable Ubuntu release ships. A panel of separate judge models looks over the candidates and has to reach a consensus. If the judges deadlock, are not confident, or run into an unusual case, the patch goes to a human on the Ubuntu security team. Anything that makes it through gets built and run through the same deterministic tests as any other Ubuntu package, and the company says this setup protects against regressions and against supply-chain attacks, where someone slips malicious code into software through its build or update path.

Kernel fixes stay out of Surge's hands, because the kernel needs a different backporting setup and just shipping the newest version would be a big stability risk for enterprise systems. So kernels now run on a two-week Stable Release Update cycle, with the cycles overlapping so a new proposed kernel lands every week. Surge is aimed at the backlog of vulnerabilities that are already known, while new flaws, including the ones Canonical's automated research turns up, still go through coordinated disclosure, with the company reporting them privately and working with upstream maintainers under embargo before anything goes public. "We strongly disagree with those who have abandoned coordinated disclosure practices," the company wrote.

stories.Headline: EigenOrbit publishes a quantum-inspired adapter method that keeps certified robustness in medical image classifiers
stories.Summary:
EigenOrbit, working with dermatologists at the Hospital Maggiore of Trieste and researchers from the University of Trieste, has published a method for adapting medical image classifiers to new tasks while keeping a mathematical guarantee that small image changes cannot alter their predictions. The paper, titled Quantum-inspired orthogonal adapters for certifiably robust medical image classification, is available on arXiv under the identifier 2611.18775, and the code has been released as open source. The method uses orthogonal adapters built from reconfigurable beam splitter circuits, a structure taken from quantum computing, which reduces the number of trainable parameters while preserving the original network's Lipschitz bound. The work was reported on November 18, 2026. Certified robustness computes, for every image, a radius within which no perturbation can change a prediction, and the article notes that the EU AI Act in Article 15 and the U.S. FDA's draft guidance on AI-enabled devices both address the robustness of such systems.

The difficulty the team addressed is that certified networks are trained on general image collections, while medical datasets are too small to train them from scratch, and standard fine-tuning methods including LoRA change the network's Lipschitz bound so the guarantee weakens. Because the beam splitter circuits are orthogonal for any choice of parameters, the adapted network keeps exactly the Lipschitz bound of the original, and a 2048-wide layer needs 11,264 trainable angles instead of about 4.2 million weights. All computations run on classical hardware, and the circuits map directly to shallow quantum circuits. The team adapted a certified ImageNet network called BRONet to trichoscopic images from 143 patients for alopecia diagnosis and to images from 57 patients for alopecia areata activity. In the diagnosis tests, 63.8% of test images were classified correctly and certified at a perturbation radius of 36/255, compared with 31.6% for LoRA and 35.6% for full fine-tuning.

At a larger radius of 108/255, the butterfly adapter still certified 20.4% of images while LoRA and full fine-tuning certified none, and the butterfly adapter's classification accuracy of 80.4% stayed close to full fine-tuning at 82.5% and above LoRA at 71.5%. The adapter trains about 100,000 parameters, over 300 times fewer than full fine-tuning, and adversarial attacks using PGD and APGD-T confirmed the certificates, with none succeeding within a certified radius. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first study of certified robustness in trichoscopic image classification. The stated next steps include patient-level validation on larger datasets and certified backbones built entirely from quantum-inspired orthogonal layers.
