stories.Headline: HHS publishes an eight-page clinical AI roadmap proposing state sandboxes and risk-based FDA review
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services published a federal roadmap for clinical artificial intelligence, hosted by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and dated Friday 13 November 2026, according to Nextgov. The roadmap proposes state sandboxes, risk-based FDA review, outcomes-based Medicare payment and post-market monitoring. It sets a "better than today" safety bar that clinical AI researchers, academic medical centres and research offices will need to plan around. The document is titled "A Clinical Super Intelligence Roadmap: Better Answers, Faster Care, and Lower Costs" and runs eight pages. It uses the term clinical Super Intelligence (SI) throughout and states that SI is the former "AI," while Nextgov reported it on 16 November 2026 as a roadmap to boost clinical AI.

The PDF is hosted on cms.gov and says it "does not mandate SI adoption," "does not create a new agency or duplicate an existing regulator," and does not authorize autonomy that has not cleared the "better than today" bar for its risk tier. The document is organised around four priorities: earn public trust, build the data foundation, establish clear rules of the road, and pay for what works. It cites OpenAI's o3 model ranking the final diagnosis first in 60% of complex cases against 15.9% for internal medicine physicians, and Microsoft's MAI-DxO diagnosing 85.5% of challenging cases against roughly 20% for practising physicians. The roadmap's "rules of the road" section lists a continued rapid path to market for consumer wellness and clinical decision support software, consistent with FDA guidance it dates to 2026. It lists FDA regulation aligned to risk, "potentially anchoring around a novel competency-based approach, similar to how physicians are evaluated for their credentials," for certain SI-enabled devices.

Nextgov reports that an FDA discussion draft would require chatbots and generative AI to pass doctor-like competency tests before marketing. The roadmap lists real-world surveillance and predetermined change control plans, with FDA and CMS collaborating on surveillance infrastructure. It lists partnership with states on SI sandboxes in areas of state-only regulation, and clearer regulatory pathways that it says will lead to clearer ownership of liability, with federal guidelines aiming to offer best practices for de-risking innovation. CMS anticipates extending its ACCESS model to primary care, creating structures for SI-led solutions to join CMS Innovation Center primary care and total-cost-of-care models, exploring outcomes-based payment in Original Medicare, and working with states, including in Medicaid, on alternative payment tests. SI-led solutions would need partnerships with clinicians and facilities for escalation to human clinicians.

The roadmap builds on the White House AI Action Plan of July 2025, OMB memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22, and an HHS strategy in December 2025 followed by a request for information. It says the CMS Health Tech Ecosystem grew from more than 60 initial company commitments to over 800, and that patient digital data access rose from roughly 5% to 60% in a year. The Medicare App Library launched in 2026. The roadmap points to FDA's TEMPO pilot and a January 2026 clinical decision support guidance. FDA's December 2025 announcement describes TEMPO as a voluntary pilot from its device centre in which manufacturers may request enforcement discretion for certain requirements, such as premarket authorization, in exchange for collecting and sharing real-world performance data, and it runs alongside the CMS ACCESS model.

CMS describes ACCESS as a voluntary 10-year Innovation Center model that pays for technology-supported chronic care based on outcomes; it began on 5 July 2026 and adds heart failure, COPD, substance use disorder and tobacco cessation tracks on 1 April 2027. The roadmap also cites FDA work with ARPA-H on the ADVOCATE programme to develop ways to evaluate highly autonomous systems. FDA has separately adopted the Super Intelligence terminology. Nextgov reports that the roadmap says the federal government wants to work with states on "areas of clear state regulation" without defining that phrase, and notes that states regulate the practice of medicine and license clinicians.

It points to Utah, which is testing through phased pilots whether AI can safely issue initial prescriptions and refills, and reports that the roadmap does not say whether FDA oversees those pilots. Utah's Office of AI Policy told Nextgov it "remains dedicated to actively coordinating with federal partners." The roadmap says it "will not wait for flawless evidence to open pathways, but it will require evidence to keep them open." The roadmap does not specify a reporting mechanism for monitoring data, so any institutional monitoring plan should anticipate the FDA and CMS surveillance infrastructure it describes rather than a fixed template.

Where tools reach patients through ACCESS and TEMPO, organisations must be Medicare Part B-enrolled and name a medical director, per CMS. The roadmap names patient control of health data and consent to its use in SI as a core principle. HHS has also filed a final HIPAA rule changing patient record access. The roadmap says some FDA actions may trigger express preemption of differing state requirements, and ACCESS accepts applications on a rolling basis and adds new clinical tracks on 1 April 2027.

Articles.Title: HHS Clinical AI Roadmap: What Researchers Face

stories.Headline: Colleges should set course goals first to decide AI licensing and budgets
stories.Summary:
The article is a guidance piece from EdTech: Focus on Higher Education, published on November 18, 2026, and written with CDW experts as part of its UniversITy blog series, so it reports no single event or actor but instead lays out how colleges should license and budget for AI in teaching. It says AI literacy and technology job skills are quickly becoming an employer requirement across industries, and that institutions are responding by building AI literacy into coursework. It adds that many faculty now see an outright ban on AI as no longer constructive, and that students must instead understand appropriate uses and be able to document and explain their prompts and choices. The piece frames the operational question for IT leaders as how to fund and manage AI in the classroom.

The article says budgeting starts with determining exactly what a course needs by setting goals, such as what students should be able to do with AI by the end, what they should understand about how the tool works and what demonstrable skills they will learn. Those answers can set the level of access, from basic chat to advanced analytics or specialized computing resources, and can decide whether a course needs a consistent university-provided tool or lets students choose their own platforms. It notes that institutions already using Microsoft or Google products likely have some AI features, but capabilities and access depend on the licensing agreement, and that a shared platform gives IT greater control over security. It also warns that students may bring their own subscriptions, which offer flexibility but are harder to manage, so guardrails, clear policies, detailed guidance and training are vital. The article stresses distinguishing usage from licensing, since basic chat typically falls under a basic license or defined usage parameters while data analysis and different models consume more tokens and cost more, and it notes that courses vary in length while licenses are typically annual.

On responsibility, the article assigns institutions the task of reviewing academic goals as an institutional priority to earn buy-in from university leadership, and of connecting proposed investments to overall institutional goals to build a case for ongoing budget prioritization. It says usage forecasting can help predict costs, but actual demand can be unclear because a small number of users might account for a large share of activity when advanced features are available, so institutions should monitor usage and adjust access or budgets. It adds that a license does not ensure effective use, that faculty and students need support, and that institutions need a way to assess whether the investment meets goals, with a pilot able to reveal real usage patterns, unexpected costs and support needs before expansion. It states there is no single licensing or funding model that fits every institution, and that CDW can work with institutions to shape a plan around workforce development goals, identify programs and students who would benefit most, match tools and licensing to course needs, explore funding opportunities and think through sustaining long-term access.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices IPO on Nov 18 and begins Nasdaq trading Nov 19 under ticker ANT
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is expected to price its initial public offering on Nov. 18, with shares set to begin trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19 under the ticker ANT, as the company gears up to go public this week. The company is offering 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece, with up to 20% of the offering allocated to retail investors, according to its amended S-1 document. According to reports last week, the Dario Amodei-led company is considering pricing its IPO above the $70 to $78 range amid strong investor demand, potentially pushing its valuation above $1.5 trillion and proceeds beyond $100 billion. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering, while the company is reportedly prioritizing funding its computing needs over maximizing its valuation, and the IPO is nearly seven times oversubscribed.

Jake Behan, Head of Capital Markets at Direxion, told Benzinga via email that he is watching market breadth and relative strength across AI stocks as traders assess whether recent weakness reflects broad risk reduction or a rotation within the sector. He said Anthropic rising alongside Nvidia, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices in the first few sessions post IPO could suggest that recent selling reflects risk-off positioning ahead of a major week for markets rather than a fundamental unwind. He said Anthropic holding its gains on strong trading volume, alongside a broader advance in AI stocks, is a much healthier signal for the overall trade than a big Anthropic rally in isolation. By contrast, he said Anthropic climbing while weakened AI leaders continue declining would scream rotation, wherein traders might be financing new Anthropic positions by selling existing holdings elsewhere in the AI trade.

Dr. Chan Ahn, CEO of Tessera PE and a former Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan executive, told Benzinga previously that Anthropic's biggest post-IPO risk is a mismatch between fixed infrastructure costs and usage-based revenue. The company reportedly faces a $1.25 billion monthly commitment through May 2029, equivalent to nearly 30% of estimated 2026 revenue, tied to Space Exploration Technologies Corp. following its acquisition of xAI. Ahn cautioned that falling AI capacity prices or weaker demand could turn these commitments into stranded costs. He said Anthropic's S-1 disclosure on contracted enterprise revenue versus on-demand usage will be critical to assessing this risk, and Kevin O'Leary warned Anthropic IPO investors to understand what they are betting on, saying the company may not make money until 2030.

stories.Headline: Alphabet spends $159.8 billion on data centers and halts buybacks as free cash flow falls 73.2%
stories.Summary:
Alphabet bought back $5.5 billion of its own stock in the twelve months to September 30, 2026, down 90.1% from $55.8 billion a year earlier, Trefis reported on November 18, 2026. In the first nine months of 2026, Alphabet bought back nothing at all. Its last buyback quarter in the data was the fourth quarter of 2025. The cash went into data centers, with capital spending up 105.2% in a year to $159.8 billion over twelve months. Free cash flow fell 73.2% to $19.7 billion.

The earlier year's buybacks were $36.0 billion more than this year's entire free cash flow. Alphabet raised $42.9 billion from new common shares in the first nine months of 2026 and another $19.1 billion from preferred stock. Net new debt came to $76.3 billion in those nine months, and total debt rose about 4.2 times in a year. New debt and new shares brought in $138.3 billion in nine months, while capital spending in the same nine months was $132.0 billion. Alphabet's diluted share count rose 1.4% from the third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026.

On the second-quarter call in July, the finance chief was asked about the recent equity and debt raises. She said Alphabet funds its investment first from operating cash flow, then from debt, and most recently from an equity raise. Buybacks are not on that list. Alphabet has not announced a pause in buybacks, and the pause shows up only in the cash flow numbers. Alphabet first guided 2026 capital spending to $175 billion to $185 billion, and by July the range was $195 billion to $205 billion.

The October call kept that range and said spending is expected to increase significantly in 2027. Alphabet had $924 billion of future purchase commitments at the end of the third quarter, when free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion, which the company tied to capital spending, a build-up of chip inventory and the payment of a European Commission fine. Microsoft spent $135.9 billion on capital projects over the same twelve months and still had $60.0 billion of free cash flow, paid 80.1% of that to holders in buybacks and dividends, and repaid more debt than it issued. Meta bought back no stock in the fourth quarter of 2025 or in the first nine months of 2026, and its net new debt over twelve months was $51.3 billion.

Amazon's free cash flow was negative $46.9 billion over twelve months, and its net new debt over the same twelve months was $124.1 billion. Together, the four companies' twelve-month free cash flow fell 70.3% in a year. Alphabet closed at $280.20 on Tuesday, Nov 17, which is 14.6 times its twelve-month earnings per share and below every year-end multiple from 2020 to 2025, the lowest of those being 19.3 times in 2022. Alphabet held $265.1 billion in cash and short-term investments at the end of September. Over twelve months, net income was $78.7 billion more than operating income, and in the third quarter other income was negative $8.2 billion, mainly a paper loss on Alphabet's SpaceX stake.

In 2020 Alphabet averaged 13.7 billion shares, and by 2025 it was down to 12.2 billion after years of large buybacks that peaked at $62.2 billion in 2024. The stock closed 30.4% below its May 13 high and 17.7% below its October 16 close. After its 2012 peak, Apple first closed 27% below its high in December 2012, and from there it fell another 23.4%. Trefis said the Apple case shows only that a deep fall could go deeper, not that this one will. Trefis said the change that matters is in the cash, and that if you owned Alphabet for steady buybacks, that part of the story has stopped.

Trefis said the test that would prove its view wrong is simple: if free cash flow climbs back while spending keeps rising, and buybacks restart, the cash squeeze is over. Trefis said it thinks that is unlikely soon, given the 2027 outlook and the purchase commitments. Trefis said owners have already sat through a drop of about 30% from the May high, and the company bought back no stock while it fell. Trefis said to base any decision to sell on the business, not on the chart, and to size the position to the fall you could live with. Trefis said its High Quality Portfolio lost about 81 cents for every dollar its benchmark lost, holding 30 quality stocks in equal weight.

Articles.Title: Is AI Costing Alphabet Holders Their Buybacks?

stories.Headline: Tencent profits drop as company increases AI infrastructure spending sixfold
stories.Summary:
Tencent Holdings experienced a decline in adjusted net income during the third quarter ending September 30, 2026. The Chinese technology giant saw its profits drop by 6 per cent year on year to 66.5 billion yuan, which equals 10 billion US dollars. This financial dip occurred because the company significantly increased its spending on computing power to remain competitive in the artificial intelligence race. While revenue grew by 8 per cent to 207.3 billion yuan, this figure failed to meet the market expectation of 210.5 billion yuan.

The company expanded its computing capacity by increasing capital expenditure to 81.4 billion yuan, representing a 527 per cent jump from the previous year. This spending increase was 54 per cent higher than the amount spent during the second quarter and exceeded 12 billion US dollars. Such massive infrastructure outlays pushed the firm into a negative free cash flow of 69.1 billion yuan. These investments required the company to sacrifice its profit margins to build the necessary hardware for AI development.

The company is responsible for these financial shifts as it prioritizes long term technological growth over short term gains. By ramping up spending more than sixfold, the firm aims to catch up in a cutthroat domestic market for artificial intelligence. Analysts polled by Bloomberg had predicted the adjusted net income figure, though the overall revenue missed their targets. The company continues to pour money into infrastructure to ensure it possesses the computing power required for future AI competition.

Articles.Title: Tencent profit dips on sixfold increase in AI infrastructure spending

stories.Headline: Wall Street analysts see 160% upside for Sandisk and 130% for CoreWeave amid the AI sell-off
stories.Summary:
Wall Street analysts identified two AI stocks with high upside on November 18, 2026. This analysis followed a market correction that hit the Nasdaq Composite earlier that month. The Nasdaq Composite closed at 24,328.38 during this period of AI boom concerns. Sandisk and CoreWeave are the two companies highlighted for potential growth. These stocks are seen as buying opportunities despite the current market sell-off.

Sandisk shares are 809 dollars with a median target price of 2,100 dollars. CoreWeave shares are 50 dollars with a median target price of 115 dollars. Sandisk will split its stock 8-for-1 on November 19. CoreWeave reported a contracted revenue backlog of 132 billion dollars. Sandisk reported 11 billion dollars in revenue for the first quarter of fiscal 2027.

Sandisk CEO David Goeckeler said NAND flash is the only economically viable solution for real-time inference. He stated that product differentiation is strongest as the critical nature of the technology is understood. Dylan Patel of SemiAnalysis called CoreWeave the benchmark for AI cloud performance. He praised the company for technical execution and operational maturity in managing large-scale solutions. These leaders highlighted the technical strengths of their respective AI infrastructure companies.

SemiAnalysis recognized CoreWeave as the best AI cloud for the third consecutive time in September. Investors are affected by the cyclical nature of the memory industry and rising interest rates. Sandisk faces competition from Samsung and SK Hynix in the storage device market. CoreWeave competes with general-purpose clouds operated by Microsoft and Amazon. The Nasdaq Composite has historically returned 21 percent in the year after a correction.

Sandisk focuses on consumer products like SD cards, USB flash drives, and portable solid-state drives. It uses a joint venture with Kioxia to purchase NAND flash memory wafers at cost. CoreWeave rents large clusters of GPUs for training and running artificial intelligence models. Sandisk reported triple-digit sales growth in its edge segment and quadruple-digit growth in data centers. CoreWeave reported third-quarter revenue of 3.6 billion dollars, which rose 168 percent.

Sandisk earnings are forecast to grow at 40 percent annually over the next three years. CoreWeave revenue is expected to increase at 96 percent annually through 2028. A memory supply glut could develop by 2029 and drive profits lower. CoreWeave must still prove its debt-fueled expansion can generate sustainable profits. The articles leave open the timing and severity of the next industry downturn.

Articles.Title: Stock Market Correction: 2 AI Stocks With 130% and 160% Upside, According to Wall Street.

stories.Headline: Civil servants pitch AI and data ideas for £50,000 prize by 10 December
stories.Summary:
The fifth Civil Service AI & Data Challenge opened for entries on 18 November 2026, inviting civil servants of any role or grade to pitch ideas for using AI and data in public services by 10 December, with £50,000 of investment and senior support going to the winner. Global Government Forum reported the launch on 17 November. Entries can be written in plain English and no technical background is needed. Senior digital and data officials shortlist the best ideas, and each shortlisted entry is worked up by a volunteer team drawn from different departments and disciplines. Those teams pitch at a semi-final in a Dragons' Den-style format, after which four go through to a further development stage and a final.

The competition is run jointly by Global Government Forum, the Cabinet Office, DCMS and the IT services company NTT DATA. Past winning ideas include a service to support peatland restoration and a project to improve how the NHS and the Department for Work and Pensions share data after a death, to spare bereaved families some paperwork. The organisers say departments and agencies are progressing at least seven of last year's entries. Last year's winner, DWP verification assurance officer Marlon Woodley, is now working on his idea to improve the tools benefits caseworkers use, aimed at fewer errors and faster decisions.

Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said civil servants see first-hand where technology could make a real difference. Government chief data officer Aimee Smith described the challenge as a way for staff at every grade to put good ideas in front of people who can deliver them. The article's own view is that the scheme's value lies in its pipeline more than its prize, and that at least seven ideas in progress from a single round is a useful signal that bottom-up suggestions can reach delivery. It says the test for this round is whether winners move from pilot to service at a pace that keeps frontline staff entering.

stories.Headline: Payhawk raises US$280m in Goldman Sachs-led Series C at a US$2bn valuation
stories.Summary:
Payhawk announced on November 18, 2026 that it raised US$280m in Series C funding led by Growth Equity of Goldman Sachs Alternatives, bringing its valuation to US$2bn and its total funding to more than US$515m. The AI-native spend management platform was founded in 2018 and now operates across 33 countries and 12 offices. Payhawk reported positive cashflow in Q3 2026 and said 70% of the capital raised in its 2022 Series B round is still held. Co-Founder and CEO Hristo Borisov told FinTech Magazine that the money will help the company scale globally.

Payhawk said the capital will be used to build what it calls the global Finance Operating System for the AI era, built around three interconnected layers. These are AI agents that perform financial work, payments infrastructure that lets agents safely interact with money, and enterprise controls that give finance teams governance over what agents can do and when human help is needed. Borisov said fintech represents only a small percentage of the global payments market, which he and the investors see as an incredible growth opportunity. He said the company aims to bring finance teams AI-native products that combine agents, payments infrastructure and enterprise controls.

Borisov said Europe does not need to build local versions of categories invented somewhere else, and that Europeans should build categories the rest of the world follows. He said being born in Europe exposed Payhawk to complexity from day one, and that the window to define the category is open now. James Hayward, Managing Director within Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, said Payhawk's growth reflects the strength of its engineering DNA, global footprint and clear vision for modern spend management. He said payments, AI and enterprise software are increasingly converging, and that Goldman is excited to partner with the team as it scales globally. Hayward is set to join Payhawk's Board of Directors following the round.

Payhawk said its independence will let it scale its predictable subscription pricing model and develop its AI-native finance suite beyond its own cards. Visa is Payhawk's card network, with Payhawk operating as a Visa principal member under EU and UK electronic money institution licences. Oracle NetSuite integrates with Payhawk through a native connector, and Payhawk reports that 99.7% of transactions sync with zero manual intervention and that customers close their books 50% faster. Sage Intacct lists Payhawk as a recommended solution following an integration launched on 10 September 2024.

stories.Headline: ECB warns AI debt boom echoes subprime bubble risks in November review
stories.Summary:
The European Central Bank released its November Financial Stability Review on November 18, 2026, to warn about the current artificial intelligence borrowing boom. The bank stated that the rapid shift toward debt finance resembles the mechanics of the dotcom and subprime bubbles. This trend could lead to financial spillovers that threaten the stability of the euro area. The report highlights that the way these projects are funded creates risks for lenders and investors.

The review estimates that big tech firms held more than $4 trillion in off-balance-sheet commitments by the second quarter of 2026. Major US technology companies are projected to reach $5.5 trillion in cumulative capital spending by 2030. European insurers hold approximately €211 billion in private credit, which represents 2.3 percent of their total assets. Looser capital rules could potentially increase demand for securitized debt by another €10 billion to €20 billion.

Vice-President Boris Vujcic stated that the financing needs across the AI supply chain are unprecedented. He noted that heavy borrowing by private firms creates competition for capital with governments that already carry high debt. President Christine Lagarde elevated these warnings to a political signal during a G7 summit in Évian. The bank cautioned that a market reassessment could trigger abrupt repricing and significant valuation losses for investment funds.

The bank is specifically concerned about circular financing and opaque private markets where risk is repackaged and spread. These structures make it difficult to trace who owns the debt if a data center developer fails. The ECB is not predicting an immediate crash but has placed the debt-fueled buildout on its stability watchlist. The next Financial Stability Review is scheduled for publication on May 26, 2027.

Articles.Title: ECB says the AI borrowing boom has echoes of the subprime bubble

stories.headline_source: ECB says the AI borrowing boom has echoes of the subprime bubble

stories.Headline: Ukraine’s chief AI officer says war accelerates the country’s AI rollout and offers lessons for Europe
stories.Summary:
Roman Kyslyi, Ukraine’s chief AI officer, told Euronews in an interview published on 18 November 2026 that Russia’s war is accelerating the country’s rollout of artificial intelligence, because the need to keep essential public services running has driven rapid technological innovation. Ukraine has become a testing ground for AI-powered military technologies, including self-guided drones, while also pioneering the use of artificial intelligence in public administration, according to the article. Kyslyi said Ukraine is among the first countries to start an AI assistant for citizens, referring to the digital government app Diia, which offers advice and access to public services. The country is also developing its own national AI language model, drawing on locally gathered data that includes cultural and scientific material, while partnering with the US technology giant Nvidia to build its sovereign AI infrastructure.

Kyslyi said Europe could learn from Ukraine’s experience of deploying technology rapidly while maintaining services under extraordinary pressure, and he explained the speed by saying the country has no other choice. He said Ukraine has to continue to provide the services because they are essential for its citizens, according to the interview with Euronews. Ukrainians can even get married or divorced through the app, he said, highlighting its importance for soldiers on the front lines and for the millions of Ukrainians living abroad. The article was published by Leo Cendrowicz on 18 November 2026 at 9:29 GMT+1, and it describes the wartime push as offering lessons for Europe.

The article does not name any other officials, does not give figures for the rollout, and does not say when the AI assistant or the national language model was first launched. It also does not describe the terms of the partnership with Nvidia or say how far the sovereign AI infrastructure has been built. The context it gives is Russia’s war in Ukraine, which it says has made the country a testing ground for AI-powered military technologies such as self-guided drones. The article does not say what happens next beyond describing the work already under way and the lessons Kyslyi says Europe could draw from it.

stories.Headline: AMD executive warns against using data center GPUs in radio access networks
stories.Summary:
Piotr Weglicki of AMD warned against using data center GPUs in radio access networks on November 18, 2026. He spoke during a recent AI-RAN symposium organized by the company Omdia. Weglicki promoted AMD CPUs as a power efficient answer for telcos. He predicted a big backlash against using power hungry GPUs in these networks. This position follows three years of Nvidia promoting a GPU based RAN vision.

AMD suggests using general purpose CPUs instead of GPUs or custom silicon for the RAN. The company is based in Santa Clara and rivals Intel in x86 architecture CPUs. AMD offers a model with 84 cores, which exceeds the 72 cores in Intel's Granite Rapids. This approach avoids the T2 Telco Accelerator Card and Xilinx FPGAs acquired in early 2022. It targets the L1, L2, and L3 categories of the RAN function stack.

Piotr Weglicki said that general purpose compute is now absorbing the RAN acceleration. He claimed that CPUs provide telcos with data center economics and faster development cycles. Weglicki stated that software based forward error correction on general purpose cores has huge consequences. He argued that operators can then decide how to allocate compute between different workloads. This flexibility allows for better distribution between network tasks and edge applications.

Alok Shah of Samsung Networks said his company has done work with the AMD platform. He noted that the 84 core platform can support meaningful multicell capacity for operators. Nokia is currently using Nvidia GPUs to develop its future 5G and 6G products. Ericsson remains heavily invested in custom silicon, though it has some hardware independent products. Most networks today use custom silicon because it is as energy efficient as possible.

Nvidia helped set up the AI-RAN Alliance nearly three years ago to promote GPU based networks. Intel integrates a hardware accelerator for forward error correction, which AMD called vendor lock-in. AMD previously tried using separate FPGA cards, but telco executives found them too power hungry. Custom silicon is expensive to develop and cannot be sold outside the RAN sector. This makes the return on investment for custom silicon less attractive than CPUs.

AMD needs big RAN vendors to adopt its CPU strategy to make visible progress. Samsung is currently the most likely avenue to market for these AMD processors. Other vendors must develop software only forward error correction to allow a wider rollout. The industry still seems to look at Nvidia for any GPU based RAN needs. It remains open if AMD will develop a lightweight GPU for mobile energy constraints.

Articles.Title: AMD telco chief says GPU 'backlash' is coming in AI-RAN

stories.Headline: Samsung executive Kim says neoclouds hold about 8% of the AI market and pose no major threat to growth
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics, the world’s top maker of memory chips, on Wednesday downplayed concerns that highly leveraged neocloud providers could fuel a broader AI bubble, saying they account for only a small share of the overall market. Kim Yong-kwan, president and head of corporate management, strategy and operation at Samsung’s component business division, spoke at a Morgan Stanley conference in Singapore. The story was refiled to correct an image, with no changes to text, and was reported by Miyoung Kim in Singapore on Nov 18. Shares of neocloud firms including CoreWeave, which rents out computing capacity to tech firms, have been hit by concerns that their debt-fuelled data center expansions could backfire if AI demand slows. The departure of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia this month could also tighten funding for smaller, highly leveraged neocloud companies that have helped fuel the industry’s rapid expansion, analysts and investors have said.

Kim said neoclouds represent a relatively smaller and limited portion of the overall market, approximately 8%. He said Samsung does not expect these concerns to pose a significant threat to the broader AI growth trajectory. Kim said the current AI investment boom was structural rather than cyclical, with long-term contracts between chipmakers and customers providing greater visibility over demand and supply. He said the current boom differed from previous cycles in which speculative investment ultimately led to overcapacity. Kim said today’s investment is not a result of speculation, but actual tangible demand.

Kim also reiterated Samsung’s previous statement that it would carry out its remaining shareholder returns through a mix of cash dividends and a substantial share repurchase and cancellation program. He said the company had a number of factors to consider, including capital expenditures, before announcing details on its shareholder return package in January. Samsung Electronics shares were up 2.31%, and CoreWeave shares were up 0.02%. The conference was a Morgan Stanley event held in Singapore. Kim is president and head of corporate management, strategy and operation at Samsung’s component business division.

stories.Headline: DXC adds AI tools to its insurance software in Australia and New Zealand
stories.Summary:
DXC Technology has expanded its insurance software business in Australia and New Zealand with new investment and product changes across life insurance, broking, claims and reinsurance, according to an announcement dated 19 November 2026. The update includes new uses of artificial intelligence in insurance operations and covers additions to the company's Assure Platform and related software. These include a new Regulatory Assistant feature for the Australian workers' compensation market, AI-assisted changes to Assure Risk Management, and broader reinsurance functions for life and general insurers. The work is intended to help insurers modernise core operations without replacing existing systems, with DXC focusing on areas where insurers still rely on manual processes and where regulated workflows can slow product changes and upgrades.

One specific addition is a PIAWE Calculator within Regulatory Assistant, designed to calculate pre-injury average weekly earnings in the Australian workers' compensation sector, where detailed rules and documentation requirements apply. DXC describes the calculator as an early example of applying AI to regulated insurance tasks while retaining human oversight. The company also disclosed early figures from a customer engagement tied to Assure Risk Management, projecting that an AI-assisted approach to moving a major custom enhancement will cut required work by half, from about 1,400 hours to 700 hours, and reduce delivery time from roughly eight months to three months. The figures come from a live engagement rather than a completed broad market rollout. The Assure Platform combines data, integration, security and cloud elements so insurers can connect existing systems with newer applications, and Assure Smart Apps apply workflow, automation and AI to specific insurance processes while maintaining governance and controls.

Dr Michael Neary, Managing Director of Insurance Software and Business Process Services at DXC Technology, said transformation has to deliver value today while creating flexibility to adapt tomorrow. He said that for customers this means connecting existing technology and operations with new capabilities, including AI, rather than forcing unnecessary disruption, and that DXC brings together industry expertise, technology and operational scale to help customers make that transition practically. Another part of the announcement centres on reinsurance in Australia and New Zealand, where DXC is extending its customer base and broadening software support for both life and general reinsurers. New investment in Assure Reinsurance includes added life insurance functions that automate manual work across cession and retrocession orders, deductions and reinstatement conditions, and the system can allow valid records to continue through processing when individual exceptions arise while giving authorised users more control over life-specific business rules.

The changes are intended to reduce delays caused by manual intervention and fragmented workflows, and they support a common platform for life and general reinsurance, removing the need to maintain parallel systems for different lines of business. The regional insurance technology market has become increasingly focused on practical modernisation projects rather than full platform replacement, especially as firms seek faster returns on technology spending. In that environment, suppliers that can show lower implementation effort, shorter timelines and fewer process bottlenecks are likely to attract attention from insurers balancing cost control with compliance demands. DXC's latest move suggests it sees the strongest demand in operational areas that are complex, repetitive and rule-heavy, including claims-related calculations, custom system enhancements and reinsurance administration, and its broader strategy gives insurers options to protect systems that still work, extend them with new functions and transform selected areas where larger change is justified.

stories.Headline: Baidu CEO Yanhong Li urges AI industry to prioritize applications to ensure financial returns
stories.Summary:
Yanhong Li, the co-founder and CEO of the Chinese technology giant Baidu, shared his assessment of the artificial intelligence industry on November 18, 2026. He spoke during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, where 2,000 delegates from 21 member states gathered as Presidents Trump and Xi prepared to meet. Li expressed optimism that AI is an inevitable trend, but he warned that the industry faces an urgent situation because the return on investment for use cases has fallen short of expectations. He cautioned that if companies do not see higher revenues or increased profits after adopting the technology, the concern that AI is a bubble could become a reality.

To avoid this outcome, Li argues that the industry must shift its emphasis toward applications, which he considers the most critical of the four AI tiers alongside GPU chips, cloud infrastructure, and large language models. He believes that without practical applications, the other components of the AI ecosystem are useless because long-term competitiveness depends on delivering measurable productivity gains and meaningful business outcomes. Baidu has implemented an application-driven approach by creating a portfolio that includes the general work agent DuMate, the digital human agent Yijing, the self-evolving agent Famou, and the content creation platform KuKu. The company has also integrated internal tools like the AI coding assistant Comate, the workplace agent Dodo, and the vibe coding platform Miaoda to help users complete complex tasks.

Li stated that users are willing to pay for products that consistently save time and solve problems, which creates a significant monetization upside as applications handle higher-value work. He pointed to DuMate as a success story, noting that its monthly active users increased more than 30-fold quarter-over-quarter in September without large-scale marketing campaigns. Regarding the Yijing digital human agent, Li claimed the technology matches or exceeds human hosts in e-commerce live-streaming while reducing production costs by approximately 80 percent. He noted that production time has also decreased by more than an order of magnitude, making these digital humans more scalable for customers.

This push for application-driven value comes as Baidu reports its sixth consecutive quarterly revenue drop amid a global struggle for AI domination between the United States and China. The company continues to optimize specialized agents like KuKu, which was rebranded from GenFlow and utilizes resources from Baidu Drive and Baidu Wenku to help users create high-quality artifacts. By focusing on real-world use cases, Baidu aims to prove that AI can generate actual financial value for enterprises and individual users alike. The company expects that as AI agents take on more complex scenarios, the adoption rate and willingness to pay will continue to grow.

Articles.Title: "The value of AI has to come from applications" - where Baidu's CEO reckons the emphasis needs to be placed to encourage user adoption

stories.Headline: Paul Bainsfair says agencies must make AI deliver real business value
stories.Summary:
IPA Director General Paul Bainsfair addressed the evolving challenges of artificial intelligence in the November 2026 edition of the IPA AI Magazine. He explained that the industry has moved past the initial stages of experimentation and building capability over the last two years. The current focus must shift toward ensuring that these technological tools provide meaningful value for businesses, clients, and agencies. AI is already being used to optimize media buying, generate research, and support account management teams.

This transition requires agencies to resolve practical issues regarding costs, measurement, and commercial return. The latest magazine examines how AI affects talent, workload, and mental health while analyzing the limitations of synthetic audiences. It also explores the economics of deployment and how AI-mediated customer journeys change the way consumers discover products. These changes force a reevaluation of daily workflows and the overall accountability of agency operations.

Paul Bainsfair stated that putting AI to work is now the easy part of the process. He argued that the real challenge lies in making the technology work for the business. According to Bainsfair, the next phase of adoption depends on how technological promises meet the realities of budgets and data. He noted that AI is no longer on the edges of operations but is actively influencing brand interactions.

The industry is now looking toward how conversational AI and digital sales agents might reshape the entire role of advertising. The IPA AI Magazine intends to provide expert guidance and real-world insight to help leaders create sustainable business value. Future efforts will focus on turning these technological opportunities into practical tools for long-term growth. Agency leaders must now navigate the intersection of innovation and commercial reality.

Articles.Title: IPA Director General Paul Bainsfair Outlines Pressing AI Challenge for Agencies — LBB - LBB

stories.Headline: Fitch Ratings says AI-driven bond issuance will intensify market concentration and raise volatility for exposed issuers
stories.Summary:
Fitch Ratings said on November 18, 2026 that the growth of AI-related bond issuance is likely to boost bond market volatility as the market becomes increasingly tied to the fortunes of hyperscalers. Through the first 10 months of 2026, investment-grade corporate bond issuance in the U.S. reached US$940 billion for non-financial sector companies, which was up 33% from the same period a year ago, driven largely by AI-related issuance. The rating agency said it expects new issues of AI-linked investment-grade corporate debt to continue in the year ahead. Fitch said it does not expect the increase in regulatory uncertainty around data centre development in the U.S. to lead to a major pullback in capex in 2027.

As a result, the bond market's concentration around the AI boom will likely continue to intensify, potentially tightening funding conditions and raising volatility for AI-exposed issuers, Fitch said. It said increased volatility could lead to tighter funding conditions for some issuers, especially if Treasury yields remain elevated and hyperscaler credit profiles or equity valuations weaken, causing spreads to widen. In turn, increased market volatility and tighter funding conditions will raise the risk profile of the overall market, the agency noted. Fitch said issuers in sectors such as health care, technology and utilities that have significant upcoming maturities could face tougher financing conditions, due to higher borrowing costs and the need to time issuance opportunistically when refinancing this debt.

James Langton, a senior reporter with Investment Executive, wrote the article, which was published by Investment Executive on November 18, 2026. The article attributes the outlook and the warnings about funding conditions and volatility to Fitch Ratings, which it describes as a rating agency. The article does not say what Fitch or any other party plans to do next beyond expecting AI-linked investment-grade corporate debt issues to continue in the year ahead. It also does not give any further dates or figures beyond the US$940 billion and 33% figures for the first 10 months of 2026.

stories.Headline: Generali raises its 2027 AI earnings target above €350 million and expects to beat all plan targets
stories.Summary:
Generali raised its artificial intelligence earnings target at its investor day in London on 18 November 2026, confirming it expects to exceed all financial targets from its current strategic plan. The group's current FY2027 AI ambition stands at more than €350 million on its operating result, up from an initial target of approximately €300 million when the plan launched. Generali said it already expects to exceed €200 million on a cumulative run-rate basis by the end of 2026, ahead of that ceiling. The revised 2027 figure came at the FY2025 earnings call in March 2026, when group CEO Philippe Donnet said execution was running ahead of original assumptions, according to a conference call transcript published by Generali. The 16 AI use cases the group is scaling span pricing, underwriting, claims and operations.

Generali's global corporate and commercial business, which serves brokers and medium-to-large corporate clients across more than 180 countries, has already deployed AI in cyber underwriting submissions and multinational programme governance. Its AGORA platform, built in partnership with Capgemini, reduced pre-bind underwriting activity completion time by 80% across 25 countries, according to Capgemini. Faster submissions processing and reduced back-and-forth on multinational programmes are the practical outputs of that investment for the brokers placing business with Generali GC&C. On the underwriting side, Generali said it expects P&C gross written premium growth at a compound annual rate of 6.6% for the first two years of the plan, with the P&C operating result growing at 12% over the same period. In its third-quarter results, Generali absorbed €1.1 billion more in nat cat and large man-made losses than a year before and still kept the P&C combined ratio at 92.8%, while the P&C operating result grew 4.5% to €2.86 billion over the same period.

The life segment's operating result is projected to grow at a 5% compound annual rate between 2024 and 2026, with the new business margin expected to reach approximately 5.9% at year-end. Net inflows reached €25.2 billion cumulated in the period from FY2025 to the first nine months of 2026. Adjusted earnings per share growth is expected to exceed 14% year-on-year by the end of 2026, well above the original 8% to 10% target range. Cumulative net holding cash flow is projected to surpass €7.6 billion for the first two years of the plan, putting the group on track to exceed its more than €11 billion target by the end of 2027.

The investor day sits against the backdrop of a structural shift that takes effect from January 2027, when Generali is consolidating its global insurance markets into five regional clusters, folding its GC&C book under Italy governance and reducing a layer of senior management. The changes were framed as preparation for the final year of the current plan and the cycle that follows. That combination of target-beating financial performance and a leaner operating structure gives Donnet room to set more ambitious targets in the next plan. It also positions Generali to press harder in multinational and commercial lines, where it has been building broker relationships and underwriting capability for the past several years.

Articles.Title: Generali raises AI target as group expects to beat all plan targets

stories.Headline: Nicolas Bouliane says AI Overviews cost All About Berlin 70 to 75 percent of its traffic
stories.Summary:
Nicolas Bouliane, who has run the website All About Berlin since 2017 and has lived from it since 2020, wrote on November 18, 2026 that artificial intelligence is killing his site. After seven years of growth, the website has lost 70 to 75 percent of its traffic to Google AI Overviews, according to his post. When people used to search Google, they got a link to his website, but now they get a page of ads, then an AI-generated answer trained on his content, and only then a link to his site. He described the impact on his traffic as devastating and said it is hard to fund his work with only a quarter of his audience remaining. The change means Bouliane will soon need another way to pay his rent, and he already spends his days preparing for that future instead of writing new guides.

He said he has poured eight years of his life into making something good and useful, and that strangers' faces light up when they learn he runs the site. Local and federal government offices refer people to his guides, the Berlin immigration office uses his data about itself, and his work inspired two government portals and a few similar websites in other cities. If his work just gets mixed into an AI-generated answer, he said, he loses his voice and his audience, his carefully chosen words lose their meaning, and no one shakes his hand, buys him a beer, or tells him how their citizenship application went. Bouliane said this is not an isolated case, because many website owners have reached out in private to commiserate with him. Some of them have paywalled their work, while others have given up and moved on, keeping their websites online but no longer updating them because it is just not worth it.

He said it will get worse, noting that Google made two announcements last week: AI-generated answers will replace search results entirely, and they have ads in them. He called that the future of the internet, with no websites, just a chat box with ads, and said he does not know where All About Berlin fits in that future. The post said the situation was also discussed on Mastodon, Hacker News, LinkedIn and Twitter, and it invited affected people to reach out and let him know how they are doing, because they are not going through this alone. The article listed mentions in The Telegraph, Forbes, The Indicator by NPR, Deutschlandfunk, The Ringer, OMR, PPC Land, Handpicked Berlin, NDTV, Stockhouse, Clarin, Press.pl, H7O magazine, Root.cz, Adevarul and Pineberry. It also linked to similar stories about StackOverflow's traffic being down 99 percent from its peak, about how Google and AI are killing travel blogs, and about what is happening with Liliputing, and it cited Techcrunch as a source.

Articles.Title: AI is killing All About Berlin

stories.Headline: Gallup and Boston Children’s survey finds over a third of young people use AI for companionship
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children’s Hospital and Gallup conducted a survey between May and August. They sampled 15,925 people aged 15 to 22 across 16 countries to examine how Gen Z forms connections. The findings reveal that more than 33 percent of these young people rely on artificial intelligence for companionship. This figure rises to 50 percent among those who use AI daily and reaches 42 percent for those with online-only friends.

The report indicates that while in-person friendships provide the most positive emotional experiences, digital bonds are common. Nearly half of young people in the United States have at least one close friend they have never met in real life. Instagram and Discord are the primary platforms used in the US to maintain these online-only affiliations. Men often find digital acquaintances through gaming, whereas women typically use social media to cultivate their connections. The study suggests that those relying on AI or online-only friends may face higher odds of loneliness.

David Bickham, the research director of the Digital Wellness Lab, stated that adolescents seek various contexts to socialize. He explained that young people growing up with AI are simply more engaged with its social capabilities. Bickham noted that while AI can fill a social gap, it cannot fully compensate for loneliness. Andrew Dugan, a principal researcher at Gallup, suggested that AI companionship will likely become more common over the next five years. He questioned whether AI reinforces lonely feelings or serves as a necessary tool for those who feel isolated.

This research arrives as countries like Australia and the UK implement social media bans and age restrictions for minors. In the United States, many citizens support banning social media for children under 16, and some legislators want to curb addictive design features. Experts like Jon-Patrick Allem argue that measuring total screen time is a deficient approach to understanding youth mental health. Instead, they advocate for investigating the actual content consumed and the quality of the relationships formed online.

Articles.Title: A Gallup survey of 15,925 people aged 15 to 22 across 16 countries finds that more than 33% rely on AI for companionship, rising to 50% among daily AI users (Jason Parham/Wired)

stories.Headline: Constantine Kontokosta says biased data makes AI worsen city service inequalities
stories.Summary:
Constantine Kontokosta wrote in Vital City on Nov. 18, 2026, that biased data will cause artificial intelligence to amplify problems in city services. He said AI boosterism has woven itself into targeted advertising, credit scores, medical triage and automated vehicle controls. He said AI integration into city management and planning has been slower, first emerging with the smart city narrative almost 20 years ago. He said technology offers a chance to improve urban public services but raises concerns about data and algorithmic bias. He said city government provides basic necessities including protecting residents, water, energy, transportation, garbage removal, streetlights and safe homes.

He cited New York City Department of Environmental Protection smart water meters tracking near-real-time usage and air quality monitors identifying particulate concentrations. He said administrative records include building permit applications, traffic tickets and building violations. He said AI covers large language models such as Claude or ChatGPT and methods in machine learning, network science and spatial analytics. He said New York City's 311 system, run through the Office of Technology and Innovation, receives about 37 million contacts per year. He described a hypothetical example of 1,000 pothole complaints and five repair crews.

Kontokosta, a professor of urban science and planning at NYU who directs the Civic Analytics program at the NYU Marron Institute and the Urban Intelligence Lab at NYU CUSP, said cities are not a single thing but a cacophony of groups, interests and communities. He said the smart city folks failed by treating the city as a system to optimize toward universal efficiency. He said city agencies first need to hear from residents to provide services fairly. He said having more data does not mean having the right data. He said data provenance means understanding how data were collected, for what purpose and by whom.

He said his lab's research focused on biased data as another aspect of the AI bias problem. He said people do not complain at the same rate, due to differing trust in government, doubts about government response and cultural or personal aversion to complaining. He said households without heat or hot water in winter are probably not going to complain about a pothole. He said his team's research found predictive algorithms trained on 311 data overestimated repair needs in wealthier Kansas City neighborhoods with objectively better street conditions. He said vulnerable and underrepresented groups often bear a disproportionate burden when a failure occurs.

He said machine learning algorithms can identify gamblers most likely to lose money and direct behavioral prompts and game designs to keep them betting. He said 311 requests, GPS traces from vehicles and connected devices, smart water meter data and bikeshare usage each carry potential biases from reporting bias, coverage issues or representativeness bias. He said public-sector decisions require accountability, and it is not sufficient to say a building was left without heat for weeks because an algorithm did not see it as a problem. He said the trade-off is weighing the likelihood an algorithm will fail versus the likelihood of the status quo failing. He said predictive modeling can be effective in identifying risk.

He said AI can add efficiency to city service resource allocations, and even baseline data analytics can help make more informed decisions. He said cities need expertise in how models work, understanding of data provenance and guardrails ensuring human knowledge is prioritized. He said without these, cities seeking efficiency through AI risk making existing inequalities worse. He said city governments exist to balance, respect and incorporate residents' differing needs, priorities and values. He said AI can help deliver better services but not without recognizing data bias and embedding fairness into data-driven decision-making.

Articles.Title: If Data Are Biased, AI Will Only Amplify Problems

stories.headline_source: If Data Are Biased, AI Will Only Amplify Problems

stories.Headline: Texas environmental regulators grant SpaceX an air permit for a 750-megawatt gas plant at Starbase
stories.Summary:
The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued an air permit on Monday, Nov. 16, for a gas-fired power plant that SpaceX plans to build to run a supercomputing data center in the Rio Grande Valley, Politico reported on Nov. 17. TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez confirmed the issuance and said the agency had resumed its normal permit review process. The plant would generate 750 megawatts from 35 natural gas-burning turbines on a 444-acre site in the Brownsville area that was annexed to the city of Starbase in September, and it would not connect to the state grid. SpaceX did not respond to Politico's requests for comment. The permit allows the plant to emit up to 248 tons of nitrogen oxides a year, just below the 250-ton-a-year threshold that triggers a more extensive review, including a public hearing.

SpaceX filed for the permit on Sept. 8 under TCEQ's standard permit for electric generating units, with an initial set of 35 turbines from GE Vernova, Mitsubishi and Solar Turbines, later to be replaced by eight larger GE Vernova 7E units. The permit came three days after FracTracker Alliance and Public Citizen filed a complaint with TCEQ alleging that SpaceX had begun building at the site without a permit, in violation of the Clean Air Act, citing satellite and aerial images of cranes and gas turbines between Oct. 9 and Nov. 12. Kathryn Guerra of Public Citizen said the TCEQ is attempting to quickly and quietly move data center air permits forward, and Public Citizen has called on TCEQ's commissioners to resign. Gov. Greg Abbott ordered TCEQ in a Sept. 21 letter to stop approving data center permits until the grid operator, ERCOT, completed a review of data centers seeking grid connections. TCEQ received notice from Abbott's office on Friday, Nov. 13, that grid officials had finished gathering information on potential community impacts, one of several issues Abbott asked them to study, and it then resumed reviews, the Texas Tribune reported.

ERCOT plans to present its full findings to the Public Utility Commission on Dec. 10. Abbott's office did not respond to requests for comment from either outlet, and Abbott lost the Nov. 3 election to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who pledged during the campaign to keep data center approvals paused until the Legislature passes new state laws. SpaceX said on Nov. 12 that it plans to invest more than $24 billion in an AI supercomputing campus at Starbase and about $50 billion in a second campus in Cochise County, Arizona. Starbase has posted notice of a Dec. 9 hearing on SpaceX's request for a property tax abatement, which says the company plans to construct, own and operate a gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility, Politico reported. SpaceX's AI unit, the former xAI, has run into permitting fights over gas turbines at its Memphis-area data centers.

Articles.Title: Texas issues the air permit for SpaceX's 750-megawatt gas plant at Starbase as data center permits resume - MLQ.ai
