stories.Headline: Kyndryl finds 64% of leaders report positive AI returns as readiness for external risks falls to 24%
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl released findings from its third annual Readiness Report on November 10, 2026, in New York, showing a widening divide between AI returns and readiness to manage risks. The report found that 64% of leaders report positive returns on AI investments, up 10 points from 2025. Average readiness across external risks fell seven points to 24%, with the steepest declines in readiness for cyber threats and competitive disruption. The report captures the attitudes and actions of 3,700 senior business leaders across 21 countries. The data shows organizations racing to deliver returns on significant AI investments while feeling ill-equipped to navigate the implications for the AI era.

Significantly fewer leaders describe themselves as in the experimentation phase compared to a year ago, down 13 points from 2025 to 49%. Nearly half, 48%, substantially changed their AI strategies this year, with implications across tech, people and governance. About a quarter, 24%, saw an AI investment fail, and 21% canceled a major AI initiative. Just 27% have formally updated roles and responsibilities around AI, and 29% have fully implemented change management for AI adoption. Those who have done both are 28 points more likely to be completely ready for their AI implementation and 8 points more likely to report positive ROI on their AI investments.

Martin Schroeter, Chairman and CEO of Kyndryl, said that as AI creates significant opportunity, organizations are now focusing on how to make early returns sustainable. He said this year's Readiness Report shows a new kind of readiness gap, with AI ambitions moving faster than the systems needed to support them. He said the bar for readiness keeps moving as AI becomes more integrated in enterprises. He said Kyndryl's data shows that focusing on people, technology and governance can help organizations win with AI and keep the ability to adapt as opportunities evolve. Kyndryl is described as a leading provider of mission-critical enterprise technology services and trades on the NYSE under KD.

For the third year in a row, security concerns topped the list of external risks and contributed most to the overall decline in readiness. Just 26% of firms said they were completely ready for cyberattacks, a drop of 11 points from last year. Three in four leaders say AI helps their organizations identify threats faster, even as confidence in their ability to respond to cyberattacks has declined. The second-largest drop in readiness came from leaders' concerns about competitive disruptions outside of their industry, down 10 points from 2025 to 23%. Retailers are weighing how to benefit from AI shopping assistants without forfeiting direct customer relationships, software companies face questions about SaaS models as AI rebalances the build-versus-buy equation, and financial institutions are challenged by emerging lending models.

The research captures how leaders are considering digital sovereignty in a year marked by greater actions by governments, most visibly in the European Union. Leaders in the EU are slightly less likely to have taken sovereignty-related actions compared to those in the rest of the world. 68% say solutions offering full operational control, should they need it, are worth a premium of 10% or more, and 60% say greater control is worth slower deployment and adoption of advanced capabilities. For the third year in a row, leaders said upgrading their IT infrastructure was the number one action their organizations are taking to mitigate external risks, and 71% rate their infrastructure as mostly or fully modernized. Yet two-thirds of CIOs surveyed think their technology foundations need significant re-architecture before being fully ready for AI at scale.

The report is Kyndryl's third annual Readiness Report, and the 2026-27 Readiness Report is promoted on Kyndryl's site as exploring how organizations are navigating AI adoption, IT modernization and evolving business demands. Kyndryl's 2026 People Readiness Report is described as revealing a decline in workforce readiness as AI adoption surges, and what leading organizations are doing to prepare. The articles state that 66% of CIOs believe their infrastructure requires significant re-architecture before it can support AI at scale. The articles do not state what Kyndryl plans to do next with the findings, and they leave open which specific countries or industries drove the declines. More to follow.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave falls 6.12% despite earnings beat as Nvidia leadership change weighs on AI stocks
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave closed down 6.12% at $49.88 on the New York Stock Exchange on Nov. 16, despite reporting third-quarter results that beat market expectations, according to BigGo Finance. The pullback was driven not by weak earnings but by external variables, including the financing needed for data center expansion and the leadership change at Nvidia, which weighed on sentiment across AI-related stocks. South Korea's stock market also saw broad weakness, with the Kospi falling 3.60% and Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix plunging 4.47% and 7.89%, respectively. Still, some analysts say CoreWeave's results show that underlying AI demand remains solid.

Market participants are focused less on AI demand itself than on companies' ability to secure the capital needed to support large-scale infrastructure investment, since higher borrowing rates increase the interest burden on companies that must keep expanding data centers. Since founder Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO, questions are growing over whether Nvidia will maintain its existing strategy of extending funding to AI companies and data center customers to boost semiconductor sales. The Financial Times reported that this uncertainty is dampening investor sentiment toward AI-related stocks. Vladimir Oleinikov, a senior quantitative analyst at General Investments, said in an interview with the newspaper that while the Nvidia controversy has added uncertainty to AI investment, CoreWeave's results show that underlying AI demand remains robust.

The Kospi fell 190.23 points and the Kosdaq fell 34.02 points, based on closing prices on the Korea Exchange on Nov. 16. On the main Kospi market, foreign investors and institutions net sold 1.3838 trillion won and 459.9 billion won, respectively, while retail investors net bought 1.3484 trillion won, absorbing the supply. Samsung Electronics fell below the 200,000-won mark, and SK Hynix's decline approached 8%. Behind the selloff is also a warning from the U.S. Federal Reserve, which in its Financial Stability Report cited deteriorating profitability of AI investment as a potential vulnerability in financial markets. Adding to the pressure, litigation risk emerged over allegations that the world's three major memory makers, Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron, colluded on DRAM supply, further chilling investor sentiment.

Market attention is now turning to major events packed into this week, starting with Nvidia's earnings release on Nov. 17, followed by the release of the minutes of the October Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Nov. 18 and Anthropic's Nasdaq listing on Nov. 19. The question is whether this so-called AI Big Week will serve as a turning point for sentiment. Some analysts caution, however, that a stronger won could increase the incentive for foreign investors to take profits, limiting any recovery in sentiment. Park Sang-hyun, an analyst at iM Securities, said the won's relative strength appears to have created an environment favorable for foreign investors to lock in profits, adding that if Nvidia demonstrates sound business operations going forward and South Korea's semiconductor exports maintain strong momentum, a new trend could emerge. Some observers say that if Nvidia confirms the continuity of its funding strategy in this week's earnings, it could provide a short-term rebound catalyst for AI-related stocks that have entered oversold territory.

stories.Headline: Nebius meets Butler Township planners on data center plan as residents raise noise and payment concerns
stories.Summary:
Nebius AI representatives met with Butler Twp. planners on Monday evening, November 16, 2026, and received a chilly reception, according to the Republican Herald. A woman at the meeting asked whether Butler Twp. would get $15.5 million from Nebius, as Kline Twp. is getting from Amazon Web Services.

The Nebius representatives were noncommittal but felt reasonably certain negotiations on that subject were underway between the Netherlands-based data center developer and the township supervisors. In a 2-1 vote in September, the supervisors adopted an ordinance clearing the way for Nebius to build a data center complex on 600 acres next to the Walmart distribution center in Highridge Business Park along Interstate 81. Preliminary work has begun on the site, which was formerly approved for two warehouses. Nebius must submit a final plan to the planning commission, which recommends to the supervisors, and the supervisors make the final decision. Nebius bought the tract from Kansas City-based NorthPoint Development for a reported $187.5 million earlier this year.

Nebius has said publicly its total investment ranges from $13 billion to $15 billion for two data centers and possibly a third on the site. The ordinance sets noise levels at 65 decibels at the complex property line. The Highridge project is expected to provide 150 permanent jobs, and the target date for the first data center to come online is late 2027, with the second operational by mid-2028. Michael Crotty, Butler Township's special legal counsel on the project, said details would be spelled out in a community benefits agreement enacted before final approval of the Nebius AI project. Brett Ennis, a Nebius public affairs official for Pennsylvania and New Jersey, said the company is working with Schuylkill Technology Center and community colleges to develop training courses for prospective data center employees.

Nebius officials said a crash-rated 12-foot iron security fence will surround the property. Lisa Tarson, planning commission chair, said the commission would not act until all township residents' concerns were addressed, warning, "I don't want to be rushed." She added that the project is a very, very big undertaking for her township and that she needs time, clarity and transparency. Kevin Kresser, an engineer with AEI Affiliated Engineers, reviewed a noise study showing levels would fall beneath the ordinance limits 99.5% of the time, based on a computerized simulation of the region's highest temperatures over the last 20 years. Kresser said the study was based on temperature because the data centers' equipment is cooled with fans, which work harder and generate more noise as temperature rises.

A Nebius consultant said the closed-loop cooling system, which does not use large amounts of water, works on the same principle as a car radiator. Frank Zukas, Schuylkill Economic Development Corporation president, said the Schuylkill County Emergency Management Agency has been tasked with developing a training program for firefighters and first responders who could be called to emergencies at the complex. Butler Twp. planners George Leib, Lisa Tarson and Mike Hawranick are reviewing the plans, and concerns over noise levels, the impact on electrical rates and water consumption remain. In Kline Twp., where Amazon proposes to construct nine data center buildings on a tract bounded by Route 309 and Interstate 81, the supervisors approved an agreement on community benefits and taxes earlier this month.

Amazon will pay the township $5.5 million up front and $1 million each after receiving temporary occupancy permits on seven data center buildings. Amazon also agreed to pay the township $250,000 a year for 12 years, or $3 million, in taxes on top of the normal real estate taxes. Data center projects provide a potential windfall in tax revenue and community services to local municipalities, school districts and Schuylkill County. The meeting was held Monday evening, November 16, 2026, and the Republican Herald published its report on November 17, 2026. Nebius officials said they hoped the planning commission's concerns about noise levels, training and security could be resolved by its next meeting.

The planning commission is charged with making a recommendation to the township supervisors, and the final decision on the project lies with the supervisors. The articles leave open whether Butler Twp. will receive $15.5 million from Nebius, as the representatives were noncommittal and negotiations were only believed to be underway. The articles also leave open the terms of the community benefits agreement, which Crotty said would be enacted before final approval. The articles do not state when the planning commission will next meet or when the supervisors will decide.

stories.Headline: Nebius plans $40bn to $45bn 2027 infrastructure spend as CEO Arkady Volozh warns site delays hit Microsoft capacity
stories.Summary:
Nebius announced on November 12, 2026, a planned capital spending outline of $40 billion to $45 billion for 2027, according to CASRAI. The AI Insider reported on November 16, 2026, that the neocloud company warned delays at third-party sites are weighing on its AI infrastructure buildout. CEO Arkady Volozh said building at this scale is hard and that Nebius is not immune to industry-wide delays. Capacity for Microsoft at a Vineland, New Jersey, site run by DataOne has slipped, with just over half now due by year-end and the rest in Q2 2027. Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571%, but cut its 2026 forecast to $3 billion, and shares fell 17%.

The 2027 plan projects between $40 billion and $45 billion in infrastructure spending to expand global GPU clusters and data centre operations. The plan follows a revision of the full-year 2026 capital expenditure target to approximately $27 billion. Nebius aims to surpass one gigawatt of operational power capacity across its facilities. The Microsoft contract is worth up to $19.4 billion and allows Microsoft to terminate affected service and impose penalties for missed dates. A primary bottleneck occurred at a 300-megawatt data centre facility in Vineland, New Jersey, operated by partner DataOne.

Chief product and infrastructure officer Andrey Korolenko attributed the delay to DataOne winding down temporary generation faster than expected as it moves to Bloom Energy fuel cells. Volozh said Nebius is not immune to industry-wide delays. Nebius said Microsoft has been part of the planning. Chief revenue officer Marc Boroditsky said deals with Microsoft and Meta included large prepayments. CFO Maria Del Dado Alonso Sanchez said prepayments and contract-backed financing should cover up to 85% of 2027 spending.

CASRAI said management indicated roughly 75% to 85% of the projected capital outlay will be covered by customer prepayments on qualifying long-term contracts and asset-backed credit facilities secured against investment-grade commercial commitments. Site commissioning faced regulatory scrutiny from the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection regarding temporary natural gas generation units, prompting an accelerated transition to permanent Bloom Energy fuel cells. The resulting timeline revisions pushed commercial activation for certain capacity blocks from late 2026 into the first half of 2027. Nebius expects 2027 revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion. The neocloud commercial model is predicated on multi-year, multi-million-dollar take-or-pay agreements backed by substantial upfront cash prepayments.

Nebius operates within the rapidly expanding category of specialised GPU neocloud providers, offering high-density compute clusters distinct from traditional general-purpose hyperscale cloud architectures. Recent transactions with major industry partners, including multi-billion-dollar capacity agreements with Microsoft and Meta, underscore how hyperscalers are leasing wholesale capacity blocks from specialized operators. To mitigate counterparty and operational risks inherent in third-party development, Nebius is shifting future capacity additions toward owned-and-operated sites. The company's expansion roadmap focuses on scaling proprietary sites, including a second facility in Mäntsälä and new development in Lappeenranta, Finland, alongside domestic US campus developments in Missouri and Alabama. As facilities expand to multi-hundred-megawatt scales, the environmental footprint and power grid interactions become critical operational factors.

Very few academic institutions possess the balance sheet flexibility or procurement authority to enter into multi-year capacity prepayment arrangements, leaving research groups at a structural disadvantage when seeking direct access to leading-edge GPU architectures. As major hyperscalers contract large tranches of neocloud capacity wholesale to satisfy commercial enterprise commitments, spot and on-demand GPU capacity for academic researchers becomes increasingly scarce and volatile in pricing. Research teams undertaking compute FLOPs estimation for grant proposals must frequently adjust computing budgets upward to account for shifting cloud pricing tiers. For universities, managing access to scalable research data infrastructure increasingly requires hybrid strategies that combine campus-level clusters, national consortium allocations such as the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and structured institutional cloud agreements. Research computing administrators must ensure external cloud compute deployments comply with institutional research data management policies and data sovereignty requirements.

stories.Headline: Nebius reports record third quarter revenue of $980.8 million, up 571%
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group N.V. held its third-quarter earnings call, Tipranks reported on Sunday, November 15, 2026, and the call carried a strongly optimistic tone led by record revenue, improving profitability and intense demand for AI computing. Nebius reported record third-quarter revenue of $980.8 million, up 571% from a year earlier and 68% from the second quarter. Management said most of the growth came from capacity added during the past 12 months. Nebius AI Cloud generated $973.8 million in revenue, a 643% year-over-year increase, and the segment represented about 99% of group revenue. Group adjusted EBITDA reached $465.8 million, compared with a loss of $5.2 million a year earlier and $236.2 million in the second quarter.

Agreements completed in the quarter exceeded $25 million per megawatt, compared with $20 million to $25 million in the prior quarter. Nebius said it was signing multibillion-dollar AI cloud agreements in the fourth quarter, following its first contracts worth more than $1 billion announced three months earlier. Databricks, Datadog and Snowflake signed multiyear agreements with Nebius for the first time during the quarter, while Palantir also entered into a multiyear deal. More than 90% of third-quarter contract value included a prepayment, and the weighted average share of prepayments rose by about 20 percentage points from the second quarter. These payments covered more than 100% of the capital required to bring contracted capacity online, up from 50% to 60% previously.

The payback period for new capacity shortened to one year and seven months from one year and 10 months in the prior quarter. Nebius ended the quarter with $7.4 billion in cash and equivalents, alongside a $775 million asset-backed financing facility and a $5.75 billion convertible notes offering. It also raised about $1 billion through its share program, while management cited more than $40 billion of similar committed revenue available for future asset-backed financing. The adjusted EBITDA margin rose to 47.5% from 40.6%, while the AI Cloud margin increased to 53.2% from 50%. Nebius builds its own compute infrastructure, racks and storage while developing its software platform in-house.

Management said AI-native companies still accounted for most of the more than $12 billion in contract value signed since the start of the third quarter. Token Factory accelerated in the third quarter and early fourth quarter, and management said it is on track for annual recurring revenue in the hundreds of millions. The company integrated the Eigen, Clarifai and Inferize acquisitions, and Inferize adds model-loading capabilities designed to reduce cold starts and improve GPU use for workloads with uneven demand. Most of the company’s next gigawatt of capacity is expected to come from owned sites, and Alabama, Missouri, two Finland projects and Pennsylvania were identified as important capacity locations.

Token Factory has acted as a launch partner for models from Meta, Reflection, NVIDIA and other developers. Several colocation sites, including New Jersey, are behind schedule, although management said none of the affected capacity had been canceled. Some deployments have moved into 2027, shifting part of expected 2026 revenue into the beginning of the following year. Vineland was delayed after DataOne decided to wind down temporary generation sooner than expected, and management said the site would still experience a gap and a delay of roughly two months.

Nebius reduced its 2026 revenue outlook to $3.0 billion to $3.2 billion from $3.0 billion to $3.4 billion, attributing the change to the timing of third-party capacity. The company now expects 2026 capital expenditures of about $27 billion, above its previous range of $20 billion to $25 billion. Nebius recognized about $325 million of nonrecurring revenue in the quarter from an asset-light rollout in which partners fund capacity and deploy Nebius’ architecture and AI cloud platform. Management said quarterly EBITDA margins can move when new sites incur rent, power and staffing costs before generating revenue, and fourth-quarter results will include some of these early costs.

For 2026, Nebius expects an adjusted EBITDA margin of about 40%, more than $10 billion in customer prepayments, contracted power of 5 gigawatts by year-end and ARR to exceed $7 billion in February. Nebius expects 2027 revenue of $12 billion to $13 billion, with pretax breakeven targeted for the fourth quarter. It expects $40 billion to $45 billion of capital spending for more than one gigawatt of new capacity, with 75% to 85% funded through prepayments and asset-backed financing, while customer prepayments are expected to reach $17 billion to $20 billion. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Together AI researchers delete megakernels and build an AI agent compiler that beats them by 28 percent on B200
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Together AI developed the Together Compiler to optimize AI inference on GPU hardware. This new framework uses AI agents to rewrite and fuse GPU kernels during a model's forward pass. The team released this system on November 16, 2026, after two years of investigating next-generation optimization. They decided to delete the megakernels they had built during the previous year. This shift allows the system to handle increasingly heterogeneous model architectures and hardware platforms.

The Together Compiler beats hand-written megakernels by 28 percent on the B200 GPU. Specifically, it achieved 2,118 tokens per second compared to 1,649 tokens per second on Llama 3.2 1B. Using multi-kernels and agent loops, the system reached over 1,100 TPS for Llama 1B on H100. The researchers found that CUDA Graphs and PDL on default Torch Inductor kernels recovered 98 percent of megakernel performance. These improvements address the proliferation of different batch sizes and sequence lengths.

Authors Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, and Simran Arora led the research and development of the compiler. They stated that achieving peak performance across various regimes requires optimization frameworks that can keep up. The authors explained that megakernels were difficult to put into production for most customers. They argued that the space of possible optimizations is too large for guessing. Consequently, they believe the system should search for optimizations systematically instead of relying on heuristics.

The researchers found that Torch Compile's heuristics and benchmarking leave significant performance on the table. They noted that Inductor's greedy fusion algorithm often misses beneficial opportunities to merge kernels. This affects users of PyTorch 2.0, which uses the Inductor backend for operation fusion. The team observed that Inductor's isolated benchmarks overestimate kernel execution time compared to live inference. They also found that random inputs overestimate MoE grouped-GEMM latency by 4 to 21 percent on GLM 5.3.

The team previously built megakernels that executed an entire model forward pass within one fused GPU kernel. While these reached record speeds, they only worked for one model, one batch size, and one customer. The researchers investigated TorchDynamo, which uses fake tensors to capture operations into an FX graph. They analyzed 607 Inductor tuning flags, 198 of which were added in the past year. They discovered that enabling a freezing flag caused a 49 percent slowdown at batch size 1.

The Together Compiler now provides a framework for continual AI inference optimization. It replaces the need for specialized implementations like FlashAttention, ThunderKittens, and the original megakernels. The system aims to solve the problem of CPU launch overhead and underutilized GPU resources. The articles do not specify the exact release date for the agent-driven infrastructure. They leave open how the compiler will perform on future hardware beyond the B200 and H100.

Articles.Title: Last year we built megakernels. This year we deleted them: The road to Together Compiler - Together AI

stories.Headline: NTT DATA's Tulloch says AI threats push clients from annual audits to live risk scores
stories.Summary:
Ben Tulloch, executive managing director of advisory services for Asia Pacific at NTT DATA, said AI-driven threats are pushing companies from annual security audits to live risk scores that update whenever a company changes its software. He spoke to CRN Asia at the NTT R&D Forum 2026 in Tokyo and at a media roundtable there. He said each new feature or AI agent a company releases can open a fresh weakness or link systems in ways no one has checked. He said companies are producing software faster than ever, and a new agent built in one part of a business could expose a vulnerability elsewhere that the company did not know about. He said the traditional model, in which an outside firm spends several weeks reviewing a company and issues a grade for the year, had fundamentally changed in three months.

Tulloch said the traditional motion was to bring in someone to audit you, do a six-week assessment, get the stamp and come back next year. He described a live risk score, which tracks a company’s exposure as it changes, as a concept that was not around three or four months ago. He said a company could say its teams deployed more code today and that this increased exposures for reasons A, B and C, and therefore it needed to do something. He said NTT DATA had not found fewer than 100 vulnerabilities at any enterprise client in Asia Pacific, though the number varies with a client’s size, industry and exposure to the outside world. He said a medium-sized client would typically have hundreds, while one large client in Australia had more than 4,000 vulnerabilities.

Tulloch attributed the vulnerability counts to companies not assessing their software libraries, the ready-made blocks of code that developers borrow rather than write themselves, and said it is quite staggering. He said NTT DATA had been rethinking its approach to cybersecurity with clients since Anthropic announced its Claude Mythos Preview model in April. He cited a technical assessment published on 7 April in which Anthropic said the model could identify and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in every major operating system and web browser when directed to do so. He told reporters that AI can test every possible route into a system, so a collection of medium-risk weaknesses can now be exploited in ways that were not practical before. He said the first problem for many organisations is simply knowing where they stand, and that no one really knows whether you are being attacked or not until you are being attacked.

Tulloch said that once you understand your vulnerability, you cannot unsee that, and you are compelled to act. His roundtable presentation, citing CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report, put the average breakout time, meaning how long an attacker takes to move from a first foothold to other systems, at 29 minutes. He said the fastest was 27 seconds, and in one case data was taken out of a network within four minutes. He said this made the long-standing 1-10-60 benchmark, which gives security teams one minute to detect an attack, 10 minutes to investigate it and an hour to contain it, no longer workable. NTT DATA’s alternative is a machine-first response in which software takes the first containment step, such as cutting off a user session or stopping a compromised AI agent, and then passes the case to a person.

Tulloch said at the roundtable that this does not mean taking humans out of the loop, but that a machine has to be the first response to an AI threat. Asked who decides which actions a machine may take without approval, he said such decisions were moving beyond the chief information security officer to the CEO and the board. He said that if the CISO’s only metric was containment, that may be a great risk to revenue, so the CEO will be thinking about customer impact, revenue impact, people impact, as well as security. He did not say whether automated containment had ever shut down legitimate systems at a client, saying he was not sure he could answer that question. He said the attack surface, meaning the range of entry points open to attackers, had also grown as more staff across the business build their own AI agents, sometimes with low-code tools that require little programming.

Tulloch pointed to newer technologies such as MCP servers, which let AI agents connect to company applications and data, as changing what agents can reach. He said at the roundtable that this shift moves part of the problem out of the security team’s hands, because engineering flaws out is a software development problem and that is a different group of people. He noted that NTT DATA had formed partnerships with Google and cloud security company Wiz in recent months, and that Wiz’s code-scanning tool is used to flag weaknesses while software is still being written. He said that in regulated sectors such as banking and insurance, AI agents need to be highly accurate, and that you cannot be 30% wrong, you have got to be aiming for 98, 99%, and then bring the human in the loop for that. He said NTT DATA AIVista, the group’s AI firm in Silicon Valley, was working on neuro-symbolic AI, which pairs machine learning with rule-based logic, with the aim of keeping agents within defined limits and with insurance and banking as its main focus.

Tulloch said many of the agent-focused startups he saw at an event in Jakarta the previous week talked about productivity rather than quality. He said that in any regulated process it comes down to quality, that you have to be able to trust it, and that if you do not trust it, you will not deploy it, not at scale. He said clients are also asking for help managing the agents they already run, covering token costs, the usage charges for running AI models, access to data and the ability to show auditors what the agents have done. He said it is a sign of clients being serious about AI when they say they have these agents now and ask for help managing them, and that many software-as-a-service options for this are expensive, so clients are looking for lower-cost ways to do it. He said the last of the four areas in NTT DATA’s approach is preparing for post-quantum cryptography, encryption designed to withstand future quantum computers.

Tulloch told the roundtable that Singapore expects critical infrastructure operators to have migration plans by March 2027. He said that, as far as he was aware, no one can yet break current encryption with a quantum computer. He said the immediate risk is that attackers can steal encrypted data now and decrypt it once quantum computers are capable enough, a tactic known as harvest now, decrypt later. Asked about Malaysia, he said he was not personally aware of its plans, and he expected banks operating across both markets to follow Singapore’s timeline. He said most of the banks in Malaysia and Singapore are across borders, so they are probably more likely going to fall to the Singapore timelines, unless Malaysia is more stringent.

Articles.Title: AI pushes cybersecurity from annual audits to live risk scores, says NTT DATA - CRN Asia

stories.Headline: Indian AI stocks extend gains as ESDS Software Solution climbs 4.67 percent and E2E Networks rises 3.27 percent
stories.Summary:
Shares of ESDS Software Solution, E2E Networks and other artificial intelligence-related companies in India extended their gains on Thursday, following a sharp recovery in global technology stocks after a recent selloff on Wall Street. The Nasdaq 100 rose 2.5 percent in the previous session, and Nvidia shares gained 4 percent. Among domestic names, ESDS Software Solution was the top gainer, climbing as much as 4.67 percent, while E2E Networks advanced 3.27 percent. Netweb Technologies India traded 0.11 percent higher at Rs 4,157.50, MTAR Technologies gained nearly 2 percent, and Black Box rose close to 1 percent. Anant Raj also climbed 4 percent.

The rally extended beyond India, with CoreWeave Inc. surging 24 percent after issuing an upbeat outlook. Investor interest in AI-related stocks picked up again across markets, according to the report. OpenAI reported quarterly revenue of USD 10 billion, which the article cites as a sign of strong demand for AI services. Anthropic PBC's proposed initial public offering was also reported to be multiple times oversubscribed. Anant Raj has expanded into AI-ready digital infrastructure and data centres through its subsidiary, Anant Raj Cloud.

The article attributes the moves to market sentiment rather than to any single company decision, and it notes that the views and investment tips quoted from experts are their own and not those of the website. It advises readers to check with certified experts before making investment decisions. The article does not name any regulator or official response, and it does not describe any policy, filing or structural change tied to the gains. It also gives no forecast for how long the rebound will last.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO following a GPU cloud scandal
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO, and director of Nvidia on Thursday, November 14, 2026. This sudden departure followed reporting about a GPU cloud business and a specific partner program. The scandal involves the company's relationship with a Singapore based cloud provider called Megaspeed. These events led to the immediate resignation of the longtime leader of the chip company. The reporting focused on the risks associated with the Nvidia Cloud Partners program.

The company now has an interim CEO who previously served as the chief financial officer. The board of directors has named its first chair to oversee the current transition. They are currently searching for a permanent replacement among both internal and external candidates. The scandal involves Alice Huang, a former managing director of the GPU cloud firm Megaspeed. This firm is a member of the Nvidia Cloud Partners program based in Singapore.

The reasons for the resignation involve a private dinner in Taipei in May 2025. Reuters saw video of Jensen Huang meeting with Alice Huang during that specific event. Federal investigators looked into possible chip exports from Megaspeed to China in October. US intelligence officials expressed worry that Alice Huang was acting for Chinese intelligence. These investigations into the Singapore firm created the pressure that led to the resignation.

Indian startups like Gnani are affected because they rely on GPU clouds for AI. Gnani uses three specific clouds called Yotta, Neysa, and E2E Networks for compute. These three providers buy their chips from Nvidia and are Nvidia Cloud Partners. Tata Communications and Reliance Jio are the only two Indian firms with GH200 chips. The GH200 is the successor to the H100 chip used by many AI companies.

Nvidia chips are mostly made in Taiwan by a company called TSMC for global use. Jensen Huang previously told a head of operations not to consider Taiwan being cut off. He ran the company by deciding which risks to look at personally and exclusively. Employees were reportedly more afraid of his temper than of most other business risks. This centralized control defined how the chip giant operated for many years.

The company is now looking for a new permanent leader to replace the former CEO. The board must decide whether to hire an internal or external candidate for the role. It remains unclear how the investigations into Megaspeed will affect other Nvidia Cloud Partners. The articles do not state if federal investigators will take further action against Nvidia. The future of the sovereign AI infrastructure in India remains an open question.

stories.Headline: Linux Foundation finds 58% of development teams release code faster than security staff can review it
stories.Summary:
A Linux Foundation report published on November 16, 2026 found that 58% of software development teams are releasing code faster than their security staff can review it, according to DevOps.com. The report, State of AI Impact on Software Security and Cybersecurity 2026, surveyed 308 cybersecurity practitioners working in businesses and open source projects. It found that 60% of respondents said AI coding tools add external software dependencies to their applications, while just 16% reported fewer dependencies. Development teams review only 53% of indirect dependencies, leaving much of their software infrastructure without adequate scrutiny. Among experienced AI cybersecurity professionals, 93% expressed concern about software supply chain attacks, 90% about prompt injection attacks and 87% about the maintenance demands of frequent software updates.

Some 76% of experienced practitioners believe AI makes it easier for attackers to combine multiple vulnerabilities into more sophisticated exploits. Only 30% of surveyed teams have assigned specialized personnel to handle AI-related cybersecurity threats, a figure that rises to 35% among businesses but falls to 16% for open source projects. About one-third of organizations have adopted official security policies addressing AI, while 35% rely on informal guidelines, and while 76% identify approved AI tools, only 57% require human review of AI-generated code and just 36% include provisions for automated security scanning. Among teams with dedicated AI security personnel, 43% investigate and resolve most new security alerts immediately, compared with 23% among teams without dedicated AI security resources.

Practitioners credited AI-assisted security tools with identifying approximately 30% of the vulnerabilities they discovered during the previous year, and 69% of practitioners using these tools reported meaningful improvements in cybersecurity. Those tools helped practitioners complete security-related development tasks 17% faster on average, but inaccurate vulnerability alerts added an estimated 30% to workloads. Some 82% of respondents agreed that excessive dependence on AI tools weakens developers' fundamental security skills. The Linux Foundation recommends stronger controls over third-party software, formal AI security policies, continued developer training and greater use of automated security testing.

stories.Headline: InfoQ opens registration for six five-week online cohort workshops starting in January 2027
stories.Summary:
InfoQ opened registration on November 17, 2026, for six online cohort workshops that start between January 9 and January 22, 2027, the article by Artenisa Chatziou states. The six cohorts cover AI Engineering, Software Architecture, and High-Performing Teams, and each program runs five weeks. The workshops bring senior engineers, architects, and engineering leaders together to work through technical and organizational decisions with experienced practitioners. Participants apply frameworks from QCon and InfoQ to decisions from their own work and compare approaches with practitioners from other organizations. Working across different organizational contexts helps expose trade-offs and assumptions that may not emerge from an internal discussion alone, the article says.

Each cohort combines four hours of live facilitated sessions per week, independent application work, and a program-specific capstone, and participation costs USD 1,470 per person. The AI Engineering Program covers RAG architectures, agent design, platforms, and evaluation, and three January cohorts are planned. Hien Luu, an AI/ML leader and author of MLOps with Ray, starts January 9, with Saturday sessions at 09:00 PST. Adi Polak, Director of Developer Experience Engineering at Confluent, starts January 21, with Thursday sessions at 08:00 PST. Lan Chu, a principal engineer at Rabobank and author of Post-training LLMs, starts January 22, with Friday sessions at 14:00 CET, and her QCon London 2026 presentation examined a production RAG system built on more than 10,000 documents and used by more than 300 people.

The InfoQ Architect Program covers distributed systems, decentralized decisions, platform engineering, and AI architecture, and its capstone involves co-authoring a technical article examining AI's role in software architecture or platform engineering. Selected articles may be published on InfoQ. Both architecture cohorts start January 22 and are facilitated by Luca Mezzalira, an independent software architect and author of Building Micro-Frontends. Friday sessions are offered at 09:30 GMT and 10:00 EST. The High-Performing Teams Program examines team structure, ownership, delivery flow, AI responsibilities, and engineering metrics as one operating model, and its January 12 cohort is facilitated by Olimpiu Pop, an InfoQ Podcast co-host with experience in solutions architecture, engineering management, and CTO roles, with sessions on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 16:00 to 18:00 CET.

The article says faster coding does not necessarily improve delivery when reviews, approvals, or infrastructure dependencies become the constraint, and that AI agents change how responsibilities are divided and which work requires human judgment. Participants in the teams program evaluate constraints in their own team environments, compare approaches with peers, and develop a proposed target operating model covering responsibilities, workflow, and measurement. The live online workshops focus on discussion and application rather than recorded lectures, and participants work with an experienced facilitator and a small cross-company peer group. Sessions are not recorded, allowing participants to discuss organizational constraints more openly. Certification requires attendance, active participation, and successful completion of the program capstone.

The article lists related events, including QCon San Francisco from November 16 to 20, 2026, with early bird registration ending November 10, and QCon AI New York on December 15 and 16, 2026, also with early bird ending November 10. It lists QCon London from April 13 to 16, 2027, across 15 engineering tracks, with early bird ending November 10, and QCon AI Boston on July 8 and 9, 2027, with registration open. It also lists a High-Performing Teams Certification cohort on November 17, 2026, an AI Engineering Certification cohort on January 9, 2027, for the Americas, another on January 21, 2027, for the Americas, an AI Engineering Certification cohort on January 22, 2027, for EMEA, and an Architect Certification cohort on January 22, 2027. The article names InfoQ, C4Media Inc., and the author Artenisa Chatziou, and states that InfoQ.com and all content are copyright © 2006-2026 C4Media Inc. The article says the programs go beyond studying technical material, with participants returning to discuss what they tried and learned.

It says participants in the architect program apply the material to architecture decisions they currently own, compare trade-offs with peers, and practice communicating their reasoning to stakeholders. It says participants in the AI Engineering Program work through technical approaches and failure modes, applying them to AI systems or proposals from their own work. It says production AI involves decisions beyond model selection, including how context is retrieved and maintained, how much autonomy agents should have, and how reliability, latency, and inference costs are managed. It says architecture choices are shaped by system requirements, team boundaries, platform ownership, and organizational constraints. Full schedules, syllabi, and registration details are available on the InfoQ Online Certification Programs website, the article states.

The article gives no further information on the six January cohorts, on the facilitators beyond their stated roles, or on the capstones beyond what it describes. It does not say how many participants each cohort will take or where the live sessions will be held beyond being online. It does not say what happens to the co-authored articles that are not selected for publication on InfoQ. It does not give the dates of the five-week programs beyond their start dates.

stories.Headline: Opsera adds security and governance features to Forge for legacy applications
stories.Summary:
Opsera announced new capabilities for its Forge platform on November 17, 2026, from Palo Alto, California, to help enterprises understand, assess and secure legacy applications. The company said the additions give greater visibility, earlier risk detection, security assessments and built-in guardrails as AI accelerates discovery of vulnerabilities in legacy software. Opsera described Forge as its AI-native Software Factory for the enterprise. The announcement said organizations adopting AI across the software development life cycle find rewriting code easier, but understanding complex applications and controlling modernization remain significant challenges. The new capabilities are available today to Forge customers.

Forge now includes enhanced built-in security checks that help teams spot risks early, flagging known vulnerabilities, exposed credentials and outdated components and explaining each risk in plain business terms. An expanded ForgeScore assessment provides A, F grades aligned with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, and the 8-dimension scorecard now grades each application against that framework for a board-ready view. Enhanced Application Discovery maps each application's business rules and dependencies and shares a unified view for product, security and engineering leaders. Configurable Pipeline Controls let administrators set modernization stages, approvals and goal scope so teams follow a clear process. For threats like PHP2Shell, Forge shows which applications an upgrade will affect before it ships.

Vishnu Vasudevan, CPO of Opsera, said frontier AI has made finding vulnerabilities easier, but fixing them inside legacy code nobody understands is still expensive. He said Forge acts as the AI harness around the models and agents teams already use, so every modernization project becomes a security remediation project. He said leadership gets a NIST-aligned grade they can take to the board. The announcement said frontier models such as Claude Mythos Preview helped surface more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity vulnerabilities through Anthropic's Project Glasswing. That work shifted the bottleneck from finding flaws to fixing them, and legacy code is where fixes are hardest.

Across its customer base, Forge powers mission-critical initiatives in diverse sectors, including regulated industries, with a 99.8% success rate and token spend savings of over 60%. Forge works with the models and coding agents enterprises already use, including Anthropic, OpenAI, GitHub Copilot and Cursor. It connects to more than 150 development, security and delivery tools. Opsera directed readers to opsera.ai/forge/modernization to get a ForgeScore security and modernization assessment of their codebase. The announcement was issued through the SD Times Newswire.

The announcement said AI is being adopted across the software development life cycle, making code rewriting easier while understanding complex applications remains hard. It said identifying security risks and maintaining control over modernization are still significant challenges for organizations. It said AI accelerates the discovery of security vulnerabilities in legacy software. It said Forge provides visibility, risk detection and guardrails so enterprises address inherited risk as they modernize, not after. It said the new capabilities address security and governance throughout the modernization process.

The new capabilities are available today to Forge customers, and Opsera invited enterprises to request a ForgeScore assessment of their codebase at opsera.ai/forge/modernization. The articles did not say how many customers use Forge or which regulated industries they represent. They did not give pricing for the new capabilities or a date for wider availability beyond today. They did not say how many applications Forge has assessed or how the 99.8% success rate was measured. They did not say when Project Glasswing ran or which organizations received its vulnerability findings.

stories.Headline: OpenAI researchers report critical PHP vulnerabilities that attackers exploit before fixes are released
stories.Summary:
On August 11, 2026, researchers from OpenAI privately reported critical security vulnerabilities in PHP, a foundational technology powering much of the modern web, including millions of websites built on platforms such as WordPress and Drupal. Attackers targeted operational websites and critical systems supporting businesses, government agencies, and essential public services. Reported attacks included the theft of credentials and security keys, unauthorized access to vulnerable servers, installation of persistent malware, attacks against commercial and government systems, disruption of essential services, destructive file-wiping, and permanent loss of critical data. Security researchers reported millions of malicious probes and attempted exploits worldwide. Research published on November 12, 2026 confirmed that attackers exploited the PHP vulnerabilities to compromise production security gateways, install persistent malware, move into internal infrastructure, and conduct destructive attacks against victims.

One principal set of related fixes to PHP changed 423 files, adding 11,556 lines and removing 1,017. Developers spent more than two months developing and testing fixes for these vulnerabilities, while attackers began exploiting the weaknesses before the fixes were released and attacks continued afterward. Soon after the fixes were released, a verified crash resulted in new corrections. The available evidence indicates that PHP's automated regression tests are primarily designed, developed, and maintained by members of the open-source development community, rather than by a separate, independent professional software testing organization. The PHP Foundation describes its primary mission as funding PHP developers, rather than maintaining a separate professional testing organization.

Ed Kit, author of "Software Testing in the Real World" and CEO at Software Development Technologies, said he began his career developing software at Bell Laboratories and later worked at Tandem Computers. He said he knew some extraordinary developers and also saw extraordinary defects created by extraordinary developers, and that occasionally he was the developer. He said developers and professional testers bring distinct but complementary expertise, and that believing in your implementation influences what you think to test. He said professional testers are trained to challenge assumptions, asking what happens when a function fails halfway through, what survives into the next request, what breaks under load, and what hasn't been thought to test. He said he recognizes the PHP developers who added automated checks, used continuous integration and sanitizer builds, and worked with outside security specialists, but he has not found a comprehensive public, independently authored professional QA assessment of the broader release risks.

Kit said there is no publicly established evidence of a dedicated, independent team of professional test engineers responsible for test design and challenging developers' assumptions. He said that without an independent professional software testing organization there is no dedicated Test Manager to lead and coordinate testing, no independent Test Architect responsible for designing and maintaining a comprehensive test automation framework, and no separate team of professional test designers systematically identifying what needs to be tested. He proposed establishing an independent professional testing capability for significant changes to foundational open-source software, bringing experienced professional testers in early to challenge requirements and design assumptions, independently evaluate the test strategy, and address functional, integration, compatibility, performance, security, reliability, and regression risks. He said this would complement, not replace, the work of developers and security researchers, and that it needs funding, with corporate beneficiaries of open source supporting shared testing teams through foundations, grants, and sponsorships. He offered as a possible discussion point investing $1 in independent testing for every $2, $3 spent on open-source development, and said AI companies should also contribute.

Kit said the PHP vulnerability is much bigger than PHP, asking who independently evaluates the quality of foundational open-source software supporting businesses, hospitals, banks, governments, airports, space, and much of the internet, and citing Linux, OpenSSL, Apache, Python, and PostgreSQL as widely used projects. He said testing is risk management, that we can never test every combination of all possible feature variations, but that professional testers should be used to intelligently select the best combinations most likely to reveal the most significant failures. He said AI can now generate code at extraordinary speed, which makes designing the right tests more important, not less, and that developers, test designers, and test automation professionals are not competitors because critical software needs all three. He said he has long advocated Keyword Driven test automation because it separates the work of designing meaningful tests from implementing and executing them. He said emergency patching creates multiple obligations including eliminating the vulnerability and confirming that the service still works, and asked whether critical user functions were tested, whether the many PHP extensions were tested with the proposed changes, and whether there was a rollback plan.

The Software Development Technologies Board (www.sdtcorp.com) has committed to raising awareness of the urgent need for independent professional software testing and providing financial support to establish the Professional Independent Testing (PIT) Initiative, focused on foundational open-source software. The mission of PIT is to strengthen the quality of critical open-source technologies by establishing independent professional testing teams, led by experienced Test Managers and Test Architects, with dedicated professional Test Designers and Test Automation Engineers responsible for developing comprehensive, risk-based automated regression test libraries. The plan is to establish PIT as a private operating foundation and use Open Collective to help launch the initiative. Kit said we can debate the value of AI discoveries without a coordinated plan to fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them, but that the larger concern is that we depend on foundational open-source software without sufficient assurance that it has undergone comprehensive, independent professional testing. He said AI finds vulnerabilities, developers fix them, and independent professional verification and validation deserve equal attention.

stories.Headline: Secure Code Warrior finds budget AI models can produce safer code than premium versions
stories.Summary:
Secure Code Warrior released findings from its SCW AI Trust Index on November 18, 2026, regarding the security of AI-generated code. The research tested more than 30 AI models from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Alibaba, and Mistral to evaluate their safety. This study used AI systems to build over 15,000 applications and 41.3 million lines of code across 11 programming languages. The results showed a 15-fold gap between the best and worst performers, with vulnerabilities ranging from 0.24 to 3.66 per 1,000 lines of code.

The findings indicate that curated security rule sets can reduce measured risk by as much as 70 percent. While GPT-6-Astra-High led or tied for first in four frameworks, fifteen different models ranked first in at least one of the 11 frameworks. Budget models sometimes outperformed premium ones, such as GPT 6 Luna which cost USD $0.10 a run and had a risk score of 19.4. In contrast, Claude Opus 5.5 cost USD $8.17 a run and recorded a higher mean risk score of 43.6.

Pieter Danhieux, the Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Secure Code Warrior, stated that assumptions about newer or more expensive models are not always correct. He explained that models do not use secure coding by default, meaning the prompts and rules provided determine the safety of the output. Danhieux emphasized that security leaders need an evidence-based view of inherited risks because model behavior can shift with every new release. He argued that this highlights the critical need for strong governance regarding how AI coding models are utilized.

These results arrive as software teams rely more on large language models for their daily coding work. External survey data suggests that AI will likely account for 65 percent of committed code by 2027. This trend increases the pressure on security teams to understand the specific risks tied to different models and prompting strategies. The company noted that human-only commits typically introduce fewer vulnerabilities, citing Stanford University research that found roughly 0.08 vulnerabilities per 1,000 lines.

Articles.Title: AI coding benchmarks show cheaper models can be safer - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Google adds TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx to its eighth-generation AI chip line-up
stories.Summary:
Google expanded its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit line-up with two new systems, TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx, bringing its TPU releases this year to four systems, according to an announcement reported on 18 November 2026. TPU 8tx is aimed at secure and confidential inference, while TPU 8i Max is designed for workloads that need large context windows and greater compute density within the same rack footprint. Google said the launch reflects broader demand from customers using AI for model training, inference and autonomous agents. It added that TPUs are now used by nearly 100 customers, including frontier laboratories, trading firms, retailers and universities. TPU 8tx is built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and is paired with fifth-generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts, and Google said it is intended for regulated enterprises and government users that want to run models and agents alongside sensitive data.

According to Google, TPU 8tx protects data and model weights while they are in use through hardware-level confidential computing, and it uses the same Boardfly network introduced for lower-latency reasoning workloads, delivering up to half the latency of TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. TPU 8i Max combines two low-latency TPU 8i chips into a single package, doubling compute, SRAM and high-bandwidth memory bandwidth compared with TPU 8i, according to the company. Google said the design fits twice the silicon into the existing rack footprint, allowing data centres to deploy more compute per square foot and per watt. The launch expands Google's eighth-generation TPU family to four products: TPU 8t for large-scale training, TPU 8i for lower-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing and TPU 8i Max for high-context workloads. Google said this system-level approach allows it to respond more quickly to changing customer requirements than waiting for a full new chip generation, and that rather than redesigning silicon each time, it modifies the surrounding compute, networking, storage and packaging to create more specialised systems.

Google said businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models' massive context windows as computing moves from human to agent scale, and that some highly regulated customers are asking for specialised encryption capabilities for unique workloads. Alongside the hardware additions, Google outlined software efforts including native PyTorch code and Hugging Face models on TPUs through the open-source TorchTPU project, TPU back ends for open-source inference engines including vLLM and SGLang, and a TPU agent suite in preview. Google said its open-source XLA Serving Engine allows customers to train models in Python and serve them in a C++ runtime across TPUs, GPUs and CPUs, while Agent Compute Engine suspends and resumes idle agent sessions to reduce infrastructure costs. Google said TPU Sync can reduce key-value transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90%, and that GKE dynamic slicing now lets users reconfigure TPU topologies on demand, cutting job start-up times by up to five times and improving fault recovery by up to 4.5 times. Google also said it has been using AI tools from Google DeepMind in its chip design process, including AlphaChip reinforcement learning systems and Gemini-based design tools, which it said have helped cut parts of chip layout work from weeks to hours.

stories.Headline: Miro finds AI boosts individual productivity but not team collaboration
stories.Summary:
Miro released research on 17 November 2026 examining how artificial intelligence is affecting productivity and team performance in Australia and New Zealand, and the study found a clear gap between gains in individual productivity and broader organisational results. The survey covered more than 9,500 leaders and workers globally, including 1,031 respondents in Australia and New Zealand. It found that 83 per cent of workers said AI had improved their individual productivity at work, while 72 per cent said it had increased output speed. That uplift was far less clear in other areas, with only 59 per cent of respondents in Australia and New Zealand saying AI had improved output quality.

A majority of respondents said AI had not improved decision-making or collaboration between colleagues and teams, and one in four said it had not improved organisation-wide productivity. Another 23 per cent said AI had not delivered better business outcomes such as revenue growth, cost reduction or operational efficiency. The survey found that 69 per cent of respondents said most AI-assisted work happens in private sessions rather than shared spaces, and half of enterprises reported difficulty with information silos that limit access to shared context across systems. Another 37 per cent of leaders said visibility into how AI is being used was poor or non-existent, while 63 per cent reported compliance and security concerns in the absence of unified governance.

Pete Bradd, Chief Evangelist at Miro, said individuals are getting more capable while the connections that make a team smart are getting thinner, and he pointed to research linking team intelligence to social perceptiveness and equal turn taking more than to the intelligence of individual members. He said the data points to the wrong direction, citing that 44 per cent say AI has made their culture less collaborative and 31 per cent feel disconnected from colleagues because of increased AI use. Dave Ross, Product Evangelist Leader at Miro, said customers report gains in AI-driven productivity at the individual level but many find scaling these gains across the organisation a challenge. He said faster execution is a benefit, but decision-making and decision quality is the real bottleneck, and the research points to a growing need for a place where AI and people can collaborate on critical decisions instead of in fragmented individual single-player tools.

The survey also found that nearly half of respondents said context switching had increased over the past year, while 59 per cent said they faced a higher volume of AI-generated output to review. Just over half, or 53 per cent, said they were seeing more low-quality AI-driven output that requires extra human review and rework, and more than one in 10 said decision-making, creativity, collaboration and work-life balance had worsened because of increased AI use. On workplace culture and role design, 65 per cent of workers worried role boundaries would blur, 49 per cent feared related roles would merge, 48 per cent were concerned about a decline in collaboration culture, and 22 per cent said work felt lonely because of increased AI use. Miro said its survey found that two-thirds of enterprise decision-makers planned to implement what it described as an AI workhub within 12 months, and the wider dataset covered respondents in product development, IT, operations and other functions across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.

Articles.Title: AI lifts personal productivity, not teamwork, Miro finds - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Nearly 60% of legal leaders say AI adoption outpaces governance, survey finds
stories.Summary:
A survey published by Diligent Institute and Wilson Sonsini on 16 November 2026 found that nearly 60% of senior legal leaders believe AI adoption is moving faster than governance in their organisations, and it put average board readiness to oversee AI risk at 2.9 out of 5. The Q4 General Counsel Risk Index draws on responses from about 200 General Counsel, Chief Legal Officers and other senior legal executives. It found that 41% of respondents have yet to reach a basic AI governance framework, including 14% with no formal approach and 27% still developing policies and guidelines. About 70% of respondents represented organisations based in North America, while 51% came from private companies and 28% from publicly held companies. Respondents ranked regulatory change as the leading risk facing their organisations, cited by 55%, with AI-related risk at 49% and cyber threats at 47%.

Some 59% of legal leaders said their organisation faced a high level of risk, while workforce, culture and talent issues were cited by 34%, geopolitical conflict by 26% and supply-chain disruption by 24%. Around 67% of respondents said legal reviews vendors and assesses privacy, data, confidentiality and intellectual property issues tied to AI systems, but only 23% said their legal teams regularly brief the board or senior leadership on AI-related risks. The survey also tracked shifts from the previous quarter, with regulatory change rising from 48% to 55%, AI-related risk from 39% to 49% and cyber threats from 39% to 47%, while concern about geopolitical conflict fell from 52% to 26%. Dottie Schindlinger, Executive Director of Diligent Institute, said nearly six in 10 legal leaders report that AI adoption is outpacing governance and that the gap is a risk in itself, because as AI spreads it becomes harder to keep clear visibility into how it is used, what data it touches and who is accountable. She said boards do not need every director to be an AI expert, but they do need enough fluency to challenge assumptions and ensure oversight keeps pace with adoption.

Sachin Kohli, Partner at Wilson Sonsini, said that as risks like AI and cybersecurity evolve at breakneck speed, boards need a clear understanding of their potential legal, regulatory and disclosure implications and of how management is responding. He said legal leaders have a critical role in connecting these risks across the enterprise, working alongside risk, compliance and security to translate complex challenges into actionable insights and give boards visibility to anticipate emerging risks. The research adds to a broader debate over whether companies are putting enough controls around fast-moving AI deployments, and for Australian businesses it comes as regulators including ASIC and APRA continue to press boards for stronger accountability and better visibility over operational risks. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that.

stories.Headline: Strike Graph launches Integration AI to collect compliance evidence from any API
stories.Summary:
Strike Graph announced the launch of Integration AI on November 18, 2026, in Seattle. This new agentic AI solution allows the company to automatically collect compliance evidence from any software that possesses an API. The system uses two separate AI agents to read public vendor documentation and build the necessary backend and user interface connections. This process removes the need for customers to install software agents or manual tools within their own infrastructure.

The new tool connects API to API and applies collected evidence to more than 30 different frameworks. This includes major standards such as SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and CMMC, which eliminates the need for duplicate work. To maintain security, the integrations are restricted to read-only operations and utilize an endpoint allowlist. All credentials are kept in a secure secrets vault and remain completely separate from the AI build process.

Justin Beals, the founder and CEO of Strike Graph, stated that quick and continuous access to evidence is essential for successful compliance. He explained that Integration AI overcomes previous roadblocks by allowing the platform to collect evidence from any system with an API. Beals noted that the graph-based evidence model ensures that a single piece of data counts toward every framework a customer pursues.

The company treats vendor documentation as data rather than instructions to prevent prompt-injection attacks. Human engineers must review the research plan and the final code before any integration is deployed to production. Each script runs in an isolated sandbox environment to ensure that a flaw in one connection cannot spread to others. Integration AI is available to all Strike Graph customers starting today.

stories.headline_source: Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

stories.Headline: EY survey finds 77% of tax leaders expect AI agent benefits but 71% remain at nascent maturity
stories.Summary:
EY has published its 2026 Tax and Finance Operations Survey, which found that interest in AI agents in tax functions has risen sharply, according to IT Brief Australia. The survey gathered responses from 1,600 Chief Financial Officers and senior finance and tax leaders across 30 jurisdictions and 22 industries. The findings show a gap between expectations for AI and the ability of tax and finance teams to put those plans into practice. While 77% of respondents said they expect AI agents to benefit the tax function, up from 21% a year earlier, 71% said they remain at a completely nascent or exploratory stage of maturity. Data issues emerged as the main obstacle, with 64% of tax and finance leaders identifying insufficient AI-ready data as the biggest barrier to advancing AI initiatives.

Only 16% considered their tax function highly effective at accessing, organising, using and reusing data, and among respondents who said their function is not effective with data, 61% pointed to data silos and 52% cited poor data quality. A further 43% said the inability to execute a sustainable data, AI and technology strategy was the biggest challenge to delivering their function's purpose. The survey also found that 83% said building a workforce in which humans work alongside AI agents is important, while 81% said hiring professionals with AI-related skills is a priority, and 60% ranked strategic thinking and problem-solving among the five most critical skills for future tax professionals. Marna Ricker, Global Vice Chair-Tax at EY, said many organizations have already invested in AI and the challenge is transforming their data, governance and talent capabilities to ensure they get return on their AI investments. She said ambition alone will not be enough as AI becomes embedded in business decision-making, and that tax leaders have an opportunity to use trusted data, knowledge, AI and human judgment to unlock capital.

Stuart Lang, Global Tax and Finance Operate Leader at EY, said the future tax function won't separate compliance from insight, and that every filing and reconciliation generates trusted data and knowledge that can become a source of tax intelligence for the business. He said realizing that potential will require leaders to make deliberate choices about workforce and talent priorities, investing not only in technology but in people skills and culture. Beyond AI adoption, the survey found that 79% of organisations are adapting operations in response to geopolitical developments, and nearly two-thirds, or 64%, are not fully prepared for real-time tax demands as tax administration becomes more digital and immediate. Among respondents already using co-sourcing, 86% said it gave them a greater ability to focus on higher-value activities, 78% reported improved tax risk management, and 77% said it helped them navigate legislative and regulatory change more successfully. With most respondents still in the early stages of AI-agent maturity, the survey points to a market in which ambition is running ahead of execution.

stories.Headline: TCS study finds 84% of executives rank productivity as AI's top benefit but only 10% let agents decide without approval
stories.Summary:
Tata Consultancy Services published a global study on enterprise artificial intelligence adoption, IT Brief Australia reported on 18 November 2026. The study found that 84% of executives cite productivity as AI's top benefit. The research was based on responses from 1,333 senior business and technology leaders across 25 countries. These included 44 respondents in Ireland from 11 industries. The findings point to a gap between the value companies say they get from AI tools and their willingness to let AI systems act independently.

Only 10% of global enterprises said they allow AI agents to execute decisions without human approval across multiple functions or business areas. Nine per cent said they have AI agents that can securely orchestrate workflows across enterprise applications. Security, risk and governance emerged as the main factor shaping deployment decisions worldwide, ahead of cost, speed and ease of deployment. In Ireland, leaders identified cost, speed and ease of deployment as the main driver of AI deployment. Seven per cent of Irish enterprises said they allow AI agents to execute decisions without human approval across multiple functions or business areas, compared with 10% globally.

Amit Kapur, Chief AI and Services Transformation Officer at TCS, said the shift is clearly in AI moving from assisting people to taking more autonomous action with deep access into an enterprise. He said productivity is clearly where enterprises are seeing the greatest value from AI today, with 84% of executives ranking it as the leading source of value from their AI investments. He said 10% have also indicated that they have seen an uplift in revenue. He said concerns around security, governance and resilience seem to be holding organisations back, and rightly so. He said deploying AI responsibly, with the right guardrails and enterprise controls, will be the big focus in the next stage of this journey.

On model independence, 86% of Irish respondents said it was an important factor in AI investment decisions, versus 90% worldwide. Thirty-nine per cent of Irish respondents identified AI sovereignty-related requirements as a high or very high organisational risk, above the global figure of 34%. Across Europe, 43% of respondents described sovereignty-related requirements as a high or very high organisational risk. Although 90% of respondents said model independence matters in investment decisions, only 7% reported having organisation-wide provider-switching continuity plans. Thirty-nine per cent of enterprises said they are still assessing whether AI initiatives generate enough value relative to token and compute costs.

Forty-four per cent of respondents said important business knowledge remains embedded within employees or scattered across fragmented documentation. Globally, 46% of respondents said they had targeted deployment of open-source AI for selected use cases, while in Ireland the figure was lower at 32%. The proportion of leaders who said it is still too early to determine AI's impact on the workforce rose from 4% in 2024 to 19% in 2026. North America showed stronger scores on some enterprise AI foundations, while Europe recorded greater concern about sovereignty. The UK and Ireland stood out on operational resilience, with comparatively stronger levels of AI continuity planning and governance integration.

The survey covered senior leaders from organisations with annual revenues ranging from USD $500 million to more than USD $20 billion, spanning 12 industries. Respondents included C-suite executives, divisional leaders, Senior Vice Presidents and Vice Presidents. On 12 November 2026, the Federal Reserve Board published working paper FEDS 2026-074, titled Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence. It was authored by Federal Reserve Board economists Nick Carollo, Leland D. Crane, Daniel Garcia Molina and Joseph Nichols. The paper documents that U.S. capital commitments for AI data centers have surged past $1 trillion while aggregate macroeconomic productivity gains and labor market disruptions remain muted.
