stories.Headline: China Securities Regulatory Commission denies requiring mutual funds to report AI exposure
stories.Summary:
The China Securities Regulatory Commission issued a formal denial on Wednesday regarding reports about new reporting rules. Online claims suggested that the agency had forced mutual fund companies to disclose their artificial intelligence exposure across all products. The regulator clarified that these specific rumors circulating on the internet were entirely untrue and lacked any factual basis. This official statement was published on the agency's official WeChat account to correct the misinformation.

The regulator emphasized that it has not required fund managers to submit any data regarding their AI investments. According to the agency, mutual fund managers are responsible for independently determining their own investment targets and portfolio weightings. These decisions must be made in accordance with their specific fund contracts and internal investment decision-making procedures. No new mandates have been implemented that would change how these companies report their holdings to the government.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission stated that the claims regarding mandatory AI exposure reporting were false. Separately, the China Association for Public Companies used its rumor-debunking platform to address another set of false claims. This platform noted that reports of a State Council executive meeting suggesting a lack of stock market support were fabricated. The association warned that such distorted information disrupts capital market expectations and has an extremely detrimental impact on investors.

The association urged internet users and investors to rationally assess information they find online and refrain from spreading rumors. They claimed that the false reports involved fabricated meeting content and a serious distortion of current government policies. The regulator continues to maintain that fund managers retain their autonomy over the assets they choose to hold. No further actions or policy changes were mentioned regarding the oversight of artificial intelligence investments in mutual funds.

Articles.Title: CSRC denies requiring funds to report AI exposure - China Daily Global Edition

stories.headline_source: CSRC denies requiring funds to report AI exposure

stories.Headline: IFF uses AI to streamline its strawberry flavor portfolio across countries
stories.Summary:
Food and beverage companies are using artificial intelligence to help decide which recipe changes to test first, Food Ingredients First reported on 18 November 2026. International Flavors & Fragrances used AI to streamline its strawberry flavor portfolio across several countries. AKA Foods said developers at South African supplier TDC report saving 10 to 15 hours a week after adopting its tool. Cargill teams use predictive modeling to consider how reducing sugar or increasing protein could affect taste, texture, and mouthfeel. Nestlé said its recipe optimization tools help product developers balance taste, nutrition, cost, and sustainability.

IFF launched Concept Muse, an AI tool for developing early-stage food and beverage concepts, the week before the article. AKA Studio connects formulation, sensory, regulatory, and production data in one place, according to AKA Foods. Seventeen people across two sites at TDC now use AKA Studio to find and reuse previous work. Wageningen University & Research researchers advise manufacturers to test AI tools on reformulations with known results. Eirini Pegiou, a food technology researcher at WUR, points to hybrid modeling, which combines data-driven AI with mechanistic models and scientific knowledge of food ingredients and processes.

Benjamin Mattei, vice president of intelligence and digital transformation at IFF, said the process can be lengthy and complex, but with the right data and AI tools the portfolio was optimized and rationalized much faster while maintaining or enhancing local consumer preferences. David Sack, CEO and co-founder of AKA Foods, said a typical case is an ingredient cost spike or supply shortage where a replacement is needed without hurting the sensory profile. Sack said you still have to make it, feel it, and taste it. Renee Boerefijn, senior director of R&D for Cargill's indulgence category, said ingredients interact and a change that improves one attribute can affect another. Boerefijn described the predictive model as a decision-support tool that helps experts decide what to test but does not make the decision for them.

Boerefijn said equipment, processing conditions, raw-material variation, and the demands of an existing production line can all affect the finished product's taste, texture, and consistency. She said a solution needs to meet food safety and regulatory requirements, work reliably under real operating conditions, and make commercial sense. A Nestlé spokesperson said final decisions remain with its scientists and product developers. Pegiou said models may perform well under familiar conditions but struggle to predict outcomes for new ingredients, formulations, or processing conditions that differ from their training data.

Pegiou asked whether the model has been tested on independent datasets beyond the data used to develop it. IFF uses formulation, chemistry, sensory, and consumer data to help its flavorists identify promising options for tasting and consumer tests. Sack said TDC previously kept its formulations and findings in a master spreadsheet only a few people knew how to interpret. Givaudan has used AI to make fragmented consumer research easier for its flavor teams to access.

Pegiou said valuable knowledge often resides in the experience of food technologists rather than in structured, accessible datasets. Cargill uses lab and plant data to consider manufacturing requirements before settling on a formulation. WUR researchers Jack Yang and Jos van den Puttelaar describe a small intervention that the article does not set out in full. The article does not say how the strawberry flavor portfolio work at IFF turned out in consumer tests.

It does not give the results of any validation of the AI tools on independent datasets. It does not say when Concept Muse will be used more widely or what it costs. It does not say what Nestlé products the recipe optimization tools have been applied to. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI in food formulation: How do developers choose which recipe to test first?

stories.Headline: Coinbase's D'Agostino calls AI IPO bitcoin drain argument reasonable as Anthropic nears Nasdaq debut
stories.Summary:
Coinbase's head of institutional strategy, John D'Agostino, said on the Milk Road podcast on Monday that the case for upcoming artificial intelligence IPOs drawing risk capital away from bitcoin was a reasonable argument, according to an article published on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. He made the comments as Anthropic prepares to go public, with its shares expected to begin trading on Nasdaq on Thursday. D'Agostino said he was not convinced the drain had done lasting damage to bitcoin. He said that what he looks for in such situations is a breakdown in market structure, with market participation falling sharply and concentrating among a single type of participant, and that he did not see any of that. D'Agostino said he saw nothing structurally different from four to five months earlier, when everybody was extremely bullish.

He described bitcoin as a commodity comparable to gold or crude oil, so its sharp swings did not worry him, and he pointed to crude oil, which once traded below zero, as the world's most important commodity. Such drops upset people who bought at the top, he said, but they do not devalue the asset. Bitcoin's price was up 0.3% during the past 24 hours, and on Stocktwits the retail sentiment around BTC remained in the neutral zone while chatter around it stayed at high levels over the past day. On why companies have been slow to go public on-chain, D'Agostino said a company that lists purely on-chain could become the next Nvidia, the next Anthropic, the next Tesla or the next Coinbase, and that this was possible. For now, he said, most companies were sticking to traditional listings because they do not have to change, since bankers can promise heavily oversubscribed offerings and crypto cannot yet match that.

He said the industry should stop dismissing skeptics, describing them as not stupid, as people who disagree and act rationally given their position. Larger companies will move only once on-chain trading makes up a meaningful share of their volume, such as 10, 20 or 30%, he said. The comments come as Anthropic prepares for its Nasdaq debut, and Tom Lee had said retail investors may be cashing out of crypto ahead of the listing. The article cited other coverage, including a Wall Street Journal report that investors might be ditching bitcoin for the Anthropic IPO and a MarketWatch report that bitcoin was below $68,000 and could fall further if investors cash out to buy into the offering. D'Agostino's remarks were reported by Anushka Basu, who has no position in any of the stocks mentioned in the article.

stories.Headline: Cal athletics posts AI-generated Big Game graphic with wrong scores and misidentifies Immortal 21
stories.Summary:
Cal’s athletic department posted multiple Big Game social media graphics with egregious errors on Nov. 17, 2026, and the Cal Football account posted the first graphic depicting the Stanford Axe. The image included game scores dating back to 1899 even though the actual Stanford Axe only has scores dating back to 1933, the first year it was used as a game trophy. The graphic posted completely inaccurate scores for the entirety of the series, with the wrong team winning in the wrong seasons, “Stamford” winning one and “Caanford” winning another. It included game scores for 1943 to 1945 when the rivalry was halted for World War II, and no updates at all past 1985. Most egregiously, the graphic had the wrong score for the 1982 game immortalized by “The Play,” the Bears’ five-lateral, game-winning kickoff returned for a touchdown that saw the Stanford band storm the field amid the runback.

When Stanford is in possession of the Axe, the school switches the score on the trophy to say “Stanford 20-19” because they object to the ruling on the play, but this graphic said “California 31-20,” a score that has never happened in the history of the rivalry. Cal deleted the graphic after a few hours after fans dogpiled the post, and the school put up a new version later on Monday showing the correct Axe trophy with all of the correct scores on it, though parts of the trophy aren’t very easy to read because of a glare. The glare mostly obscures the 2010s, when Stanford had a dominant run in the rivalry. Almost immediately after that gaffe, a second embarrassing gaffe was uploaded by the Cal Athletics account. In a post discussing the history of the Big Game, Cal celebrated “The Immortal Twenty-One,” the Cal students who stole the Axe in 1899 and kept it in a bank vault for 31 years.

There’s only one big problem with that: the “Immortal 21” is actually a group of Stanford students who stole the Axe back from Cal in 1930, not the Cal students from 1899. Cal Athletics left that post up for nearly a full day before deleting it on Tuesday morning. The errors come seven months after Cal reorganized its athletic department and moved the marketing, creative and communications units away from the school and into an external company called Strawberry Creek Studios. In announcing the restructure, the school said the move will “create a continuous stream of authentic storytelling that connects communities and student-athletes, and transforms engagement into meaningful revenue for Cal Athletics and UC Berkeley.”

What Cal didn’t announce at the time was that the move came weeks after workers in the Cal athletic department had voted to unionize. David Covucci, who runs the FOIAball newsletter, a journalistic outlet that uses public records to uncover stories in college athletics, reported last week that the entire University of California system’s communications, marketing and sales professionals filed to form a union with UC-UAW, and nearly 82% of the 1,600 workers voted pro-union. The union was certified on March 23, giving them immediate union protections even as negotiations were just getting started. But in April, as Cal announced the Strawberry Creek Studios, Cal laid off the entire athletic department’s workforce as part of the restructuring, and the school could only say affected employees were “encouraged to apply for these newly defined opportunities.”

According to Covucci’s reporting, 17 workers laid off were part of the new union, which received no warning about the impending changes. The union responded by filing an “Unfair Practice Charge,” which Covucci obtained, against the school for the layoffs, alleging the school did not properly allow the union the chance to bargain with the school over the layoff decisions. In effect, Cal Athletics did what Covucci described as a “union-busting” tactic to create a new content studio to try to drive more revenue to the department. The Strawberry Creek Studios announcement quotes Cal football general manager Ron Rivera as saying the move will allow Cal to “be better equipped to execute the vision of our football program and entire athletic department.”

The Cal football team is 3-7 on the season and is likely to miss a bowl game for the first time in four years. Ahead of the biggest rivalry game the school has, Cal has posted two graphics with significant errors in them, one of which clearly appears to have been AI-generated, and only got deleted after fans noticed and brought attention to it online. The first graphic immediately led to accusations of artificial intelligence-generated slop. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Cal posts grossly wrong Big Game AI slop after laying off unionized content team

stories.headline_source: Cal posts grossly wrong Big Game AI slop after laying off unionized content team

stories.Headline: Amazon expands its health AI agents to handle routine patient calls and bookings
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services expanded its healthcare artificial intelligence agents on November 17, 2026. Naji Shafi announced these new capabilities during a panel at the HLTH USA conference. The event took place in Las Vegas to introduce tools for routine patient calls. These agents aim to reduce administrative workloads at health systems and clinics. The expansion allows AI to handle tasks that previously required human staff.

Amazon Connect Health now manages inbound calls for booking appointments and medication refills. It handles portal access and hours of operation outside of traditional business hours. The system integrates with Epic and Redox, which connects over 12,000 clinical data sources. These tools build on a launch earlier this year featuring patient verification and coding. Patients can now complete multiple tasks in one call without being transferred.

Naji Shafi said that up to 60 percent of patient calls are routine. He stated that AWS builds with healthcare organizations rather than just for them. Dr. Will Kimbrough said that primary care providers spend too much time on low-value tasks. Kimbrough noted that trust and safety are the primary products for these AI agents. He explained that a multilayered safety approach includes testing and ongoing human clinical review.

Joseph Alfonsi of Temple Health said patients get help faster since June. UC San Diego Health reduced call handling times by one minute per call. This saved the California system roughly 630 staff hours every single week. An Accenture survey found 89 percent of patients switch providers due to navigation ease. A 2025 AMN Healthcare survey showed nonurgent physical wait times averaged 23.5 days.

Wait times for family medicine physicians increased 16 percent from 2009 to 2025. Amazon acquired the primary care provider One Medical in 2023 to gain clinical experience. AWS engineers collaborate with One Medical teams to develop and evaluate these AI tools. The technology addresses mounting pressure to improve patient access despite current staffing constraints. These agents do not provide clinical advice to any patients during their calls.

Urgent concerns or frustrated patients are transferred to human staff for assistance. Amazon intends to ease the change management burden for various provider organizations. Temple Health is currently expanding capabilities for prescription management and portal password resets. AWS encourages health systems to start narrow and prove goals before they expand. The articles leave open how these agents will evolve over the next year.

Articles.Title: Amazon Is Giving Its Patient-Facing AI Agents More to Do

stories.headline_source: Amazon Is Giving Its Patient-Facing AI Agents More to Do

stories.Headline: South Korea inspects glasses and sleeves and cuts wifi to stop AI cheating in Thursday's suneung exam
stories.Summary:
South Korea's career-defining university entrance exam, the suneung, was thrown into doubt after the top scorer in this year's tax accountancy exam admitted on Sunday that he had cheated using a concealed microcamera, a smartphone and an AI system, having got just one question wrong out of 160. More than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the suneung on Thursday at 1,312 centres across the country, in an eight-hour single-day exam that determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects. In a video posted to his lawyer's YouTube channel, the cheat said he had photographed the questions, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone, and that his top placing was not the result of legitimate effort. His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone, no charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years. Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a social evil the government would root out, saying smart devices must be turned off and handed in and that bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices still on.

Exam officials will inspect all candidates' glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons, for concealed cameras, and the government will send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in a device. More invigilators will be deployed, school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby will be switched off, and personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, will be traced through connection records. Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June, and at the suneung wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off. Education minister Choi Kyo-jin told parliament on Monday that authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday's exam but that newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly, and he ruled out postponing the exam, which has been delayed before, including in 2017 after an earthquake struck Pohang and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic. The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year, so checks will rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.

Teachers' unions have criticised the government response as belated, and a survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could. Some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses to avoid scrutiny, and an optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in. The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung, with aircraft take-offs and landings rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper, artillery fire and tank movements suspended, the stock market opening an hour late, cars stopped 200 metres from every centre, extra trains from 6am, police driving latecomers to their exam halls, tourist attractions opening late and offices asked to open at 10am. In October, several candidates were caught with smart glasses while sitting university-run admissions exams. Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience, and in his video confession the accountancy test cheat told suneung candidates that he was going to tell investigators everything, so please don't think, I won't get caught.

Articles.Title: Sleeve checks and no smartglasses: South Korea races to protect all-important university exams against AI

stories.headline_source: Sleeve checks and no smartglasses: South Korea races to protect all-important university exams against AI

stories.Headline: European Central Bank warns that AI valuations and sovereign debt threaten euro area financial stability
stories.Summary:
The European Central Bank published a Financial Stability Review on Wednesday, November 18, which highlighted several looming threats to the financial stability of the euro area. This comprehensive report warns that artificial intelligence valuations, sovereign debt levels, and geopolitical tensions are creating significant vulnerabilities across the region. The bank specifically noted that the non-bank financial sector is particularly exposed to these emerging risks in certain segments. These combined pressures could potentially test the overall resilience of an economy that grew by 0.4 percent during the third quarter of this year.

The report explains that investors face direct exposure to AI valuation risks through euro-denominated debt issuances intended to fund expensive AI infrastructure. High earnings expectations and extreme market concentration in United States technology firms increase the likelihood of an abrupt market repricing. Simultaneously, sovereign yields for longer-term maturities have climbed to their highest levels in twenty years and are expected to rise further. This environment of rising interest rates and inflation means that both banks and non-banks holding sovereign debt may suffer significant valuation losses.

The European Central Bank stated that rising exposures to sovereign debt and artificial intelligence warrant close attention from financial regulators. Officials warned that a sudden shift in the narrative surrounding AI could trigger market instability within a highly uncertain geopolitical environment. They also noted that the ongoing war in the Middle East could deteriorate macro-financial conditions and increase credit risks for various financial institutions. These authorities believe that the combination of prolonged headwinds and high valuations creates a precarious situation for the euro area.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: ECB warns of looming risks from AI valuations, sovereigns, geopolitics - Xinhua

stories.headline_source: ECB warns of looming risks from AI valuations, sovereigns, geopolitics - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Puja Tayal suggests AI supply chain alternatives for investors following a decline in Nvidia stock
stories.Summary:
Puja Tayal wrote an article on November 17, 2026, about a decline in Nvidia stock. The stock fell 32 percent and pulled the Nasdaq 100 Index down 14.7 percent. This downturn happened as Jensen Huang left the company and chips were banned in China. Tayal suggests that investors diversify across the artificial intelligence supply chain instead of just chips. She identifies three Canadian stocks that investors may like better than the falling Nvidia stock.

The energy layer includes Hammond Power Solutions, which saw a 34 percent dip in its stock price. Bird Construction is the infrastructure choice, reporting 61 percent earnings per share growth in the third quarter of 2026. Bird Construction has a 13 billion dollar order backlog and is helping BCE build AI data centres. Shopify is the application stock, reporting a 75 percent net profit rise in the third quarter of 2026. These companies operate in Canada and the United States to provide alternatives to Nvidia GPUs.

Puja Tayal wrote the piece for The Motley Fool Canada to guide investors during the downturn. She stated that companies might stop buying Nvidia GPUs because of various security concerns. Tayal noted that AI performance matters and alternatives must prove their mettle to the investors. She described artificial intelligence as a five layer cake consisting of energy, chips, infrastructure, models, and software. The author believes Shopify will thrive in the software space with AI supporting its growth.

Investors hit hard by the Nvidia downturn are the primary people affected by these market changes. Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices, and Celestica are mentioned as companies that could rise to the occasion. AMD data centre chips and Google tensor processing units are potential suitors to take the lead. Celestica is specifically noted for helping Google manufacture those tensor processing units for the AI market. The Motley Fool Canada team excluded Nvidia from their top ten TSX stocks for 2026.

The background involves a period where Nvidia faced questions regarding its corporate governance and leadership changes. Bird Construction has seen its revenue grow 36.7 percent year over year in the third quarter of 2026. Shopify previously saw a 97 percent net profit surge in the fourth quarter of 2024. Hammond Power Solutions provides transformers for data centres, mining sites, transportation systems, and various public infrastructure. Bird Construction also relies on energy, defence, and mining infrastructure for its current financial rally.

Investors may now buy Bird Construction as it recovers from a dip that occurred in October. Shopify continues to develop AI tools to help its merchants target their audiences more efficiently. The articles leave open exactly how much of Shopify's profit growth is attributed to AI tools. It remains uncertain if other chip companies can truly replace Nvidia's performance in the AI market. The future returns of AI software applications will be the next focus for many investors.

stories.Headline: Multilingual by Design awards $1.05m to three teams piloting AI tools for multilingual teaching
stories.Summary:
Multilingual by Design awarded three grants totaling $1.05 million to teams developing AI tools for multilingual teaching, the organization announced on 18 November 2026. Teams led by the University of Wisconsin-Madison, the Joan Ganz Cooney Center at Sesame Workshop and DSST Public Schools will each receive $350,000. Their pilots are planned for 2026, 27 and will involve teachers and schools in Wisconsin, Massachusetts and Colorado. The projects address following small-group math conversations, preparing accessible versions of existing materials and adapting math lessons to students' English proficiency. Teachers will decide how the tools are used, review their outputs and retain control of instruction.

The Wisconsin team is developing Content and Language with AI, or CLAI, to give teachers a live view of students' small-group math discussions. The project brings together The Responsible AI for Learning (TRAIL) Lab, the Multilingual Learning Research Center and the WIDA Consortium, all at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. CLAI builds on real-time transcription and translation and is designed to identify students' use of mathematical concepts, connections to experiences from home and moments when they may need help. Six teachers in rural, suburban and urban Wisconsin school districts will pilot the tool. Organizers say students will control their own audio recordings, which will be stored locally and remain under district control.

In Massachusetts, the Joan Ganz Cooney Center and Medley Learning will develop Medley Studio, a tool for adapting materials that teachers already use. The planned supports include dividing text into shorter sections and adding definitions within the material, with recommendations matched to students' language proficiency. Teachers will be able to review and customize those supports before exporting or printing materials. The pilot will focus on five schools in Taunton, aiming to reduce preparation time while maintaining access to grade-level instruction. Medley's existing product is a browser extension that adds vocabulary support, translation and other scaffolds to classroom content, and the funding announcement puts the company's existing reach at 12,000 students across 48 school systems.

In Colorado, DSST Public Schools and Scale Up Partners will develop Premo, which uses AI to help teachers plan and adapt grade-level math lessons. Premo is intended to align lessons with established English language development frameworks and suggest teaching strategies and supports matched to individual students' English proficiency. Testing will take place within DSST's network of 16 public middle and high schools in Denver and Aurora. According to the announcement, more than 65% of students across the network are current or former multilingual learners. The work focuses on helping students engage with math content while developing the language needed to discuss and understand it.

Throughline Learning, a Providence-based education nonprofit, will provide technical assistance and lead research across the pilots. Teams will use a common set of measures to examine how the tools work for teachers and students, with outcomes ranging from classroom discussion to student achievement. The initiative's partner information also identifies ETS as a research partner. Before testing begins, Throughline will help teams establish their intended outcomes and data plans, with findings later developed into case studies and public resources. Each team will pilot under data-sharing agreements with its partner schools, and alongside the grants, teams will receive coaching and support for bringing their tools to schools beyond the initial pilot sites.

Multilingual by Design launched in March 2026 and is managed by Social Strategy Associates. Its open call attracted more than 180 applications from education nonprofits and AI builders, and thirty organizations attended a June workshop in Washington, D.C., where teachers described challenges in supporting multilingual learners. The initiative is supported by the Bezos Family Foundation, Gary Community Ventures, the Gates Foundation, the Hewlett Foundation, the Robertson Foundation and Sobrato Philanthropies. National Center for Education Statistics data for 2020, 21 show that 67.3% of U.S. public school teachers taught at least one English learner. Multilingual by Design plans to share findings from the funded pilots with educators, developers and funders as the projects progress through development and classroom testing.

stories.Headline: Reese Cooper accuses SSENSE of using AI images that misrepresent his designs
stories.Summary:
Designer Reese Cooper criticized the Montreal retailer SSENSE on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, for using artificial intelligence to create product images. He shared a series of Instagram Story posts pointing out rendering errors and inconsistent garment details in the digital imagery. Cooper claimed that these AI generated visuals misrepresent his actual designs and create a disappointing experience for creators. He expressed concern that customers would blame his brand rather than the retailer when orders do not match the website. The designer also questioned the fate of the professional photographers and stylists who previously worked at the company.

This public dispute follows a series of corporate changes involving CEO Rami Atallah and his brothers, Firas and Bassel. In February, the Superior Court of Quebec authorized an agreement allowing the brothers to reclaim ownership of the business from creditor protection. During a company meeting in April, Atallah stated that the firm would embed AI into its DNA to transform core functions. By June, reports indicated that SSENSE had dismissed approximately a dozen creative staff members from the cosmetics, retouching, and photo departments. The company shifted its strategy to superimpose garment images from mannequins onto the images of professional models.

Chief commercial officer Christine Sio stated that the company is evolving its content production to increase scalability, agility, and speed. A spokesperson for the retailer further explained that the new studio operating model aims to accelerate production and strengthen product storytelling. These official statements contrast with the views of a former photographer who described the technical process of using AI for model imagery. Cooper argued that the resulting work is low quality and lacks the consistency provided by human oversight. He specifically noted that certain details, such as tape on a shirt, disappeared in the AI versions.

The retailer continues to implement these automated systems to replace traditional in house photography and retouching workflows. This transition has sparked a larger conversation about the role of human creativity in the fashion industry's digital presence. While the company views the shift as a necessary evolution for efficiency, designers like Cooper fear the loss of artistic integrity. The conflict highlights the tension between corporate cost cutting measures and the precise representation of luxury design. It remains unclear if the retailer will adjust its AI processes to satisfy the concerns of its brand partners.

stories.Headline: Chinese cement producers adopt AI and digital sensors to create smart green factories
stories.Summary:
Chinese cement producers are integrating artificial intelligence and digital sensors to transform energy intensive plants into smart, green factories as of November 18, 2026. Major companies like Anhui Conch Group Co., Ltd. in Wuhu, Anhui Province, are deploying driverless trucks and remotely operated excavators to automate the challenging raw material extraction process. These upgrades include the use of radar sensors that allow unmanned vehicles to navigate quarry roads safely even during periods of low visibility. The shift is part of a broader national effort to embed low carbon technologies and intelligent systems into traditional manufacturing sectors.

The transition requires the implementation of complex AI models, such as the one developed by Anhui Conch Group Co., Ltd. and Huawei, which utilizes computer vision and predictive analytics. This specific model identifies over 200 AI scenarios across 15 categories and has already deployed more than 40 applications for quality control and production optimization. One key tool is a clinker strength prediction model that allows operators to adjust kiln parameters in real time before laboratory results are finished. Additionally, a carbon capture project in Wuhu processes 50,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide annually to create industrial products and boost greenhouse tomato yields.

Company officials and industry experts are leading these changes, with Xu Yue of Conch Cement noting that AI allows for immediate adjustments to production parameters. Huang Yong of the same group explained that unmanned trucks now coordinate with excavators to improve the efficiency of hauling raw materials. Kong Xiangzhong, the former executive president of the China Cement Association, stated that nearly 70 companies have become smart manufacturing demonstration factories since 2021. Peng Shou from the Chinese Academy of Engineering added that market forces and policy are pushing the sector toward circular resource use and lower emissions.

This industry shift aligns with a wider government drive where the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology reports that over 30 percent of large manufacturing firms adopted AI by the first half of the year. Other leaders in the field include CR Cement, whose Tianyang plant in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region became the first lighthouse factory in the sector. Meanwhile, BBMG Jidong Cement Group Co., Ltd. has established a zero employee production line at its Tongchuan plant with a daily capacity of 10,000 tonnes. These developments signal a strategic transition toward higher end products and a significant reduction in standard coal consumption.

stories.Headline: Fei-Fei Li warns that high compute and data costs price public sector and universities out of frontier AI research
stories.Summary:
Stanford University Professor Fei-Fei Li warned on November 18, 2026, that public sector entities and academic institutions are being priced out of frontier artificial intelligence research. The co-director of the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI argued that the massive costs of compute and data are creating a divide in the research landscape. She noted that the scale of infrastructure needed to train foundation models now exceeds the traditional budget capacities of public research agencies. This shift follows a period of rapid progress led by well-funded private corporations that set the benchmarks for performance.

The current situation requires thousands of H100 or next-generation GPUs, which can cost hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars for top-tier training runs. Researchers also face the prohibitive cost of acquiring high-quality proprietary datasets that are dominated by private firms through vertical integration. Furthermore, private companies offer massive salary premiums that draw top talent away from academic labs and hollow out the research pipeline. These barriers force academic researchers to depend on private partnerships, which may create conflicts regarding transparency and the overall research agenda.

Fei-Fei Li stated that the centralization of AI research power is a core issue that threatens the objectivity of scientific inquiry. She suggested that the reliance on private sector partnerships could stifle long-term exploratory research and limit the role of academia. The Association of American Universities added that universities risk falling behind in critical technology without significant increases in federal funding for infrastructure. Other stakeholders have called for a National AI Research Resource in the United States to democratize access to necessary compute power.

This crisis is the culmination of several years of expansion where the field shifted toward massive foundation models. Academic labs were previously at the forefront of innovation, but capital requirements for compute infrastructure have since grown exponentially. Federal agencies and policy bodies are now debating the next phase of initiatives to address these critical access gaps. Reports and policy recommendations from the National Science Foundation and the OSTP are expected in the coming year to outline sustainable paths for academic access.

stories.Headline: VAST Data reports $10B in commitments from 14 customers
stories.Summary:
VAST Data reported ten billion dollars in commitments from fourteen customers during the first three quarters of its fiscal year. These commitments come from a customer base that currently exceeds one thousand individual clients. Four of these customers alone committed more than one billion dollars each to the company. This spending covers the purchase of VAST software and the hardware that supports it. The company has not named these customers or stated when the spending will occur.

The company has secured agreements with supply chain partners for over two hundred exabytes of flash capacity through 2029. This capacity equals two hundred million terabytes of storage for AI labs and cloud providers. VAST uses a Disaggregated Shared Everything architecture, also known as DASE, to share storage resources. Its AI Operating System integrates data management and processing into a single platform for its users. The company supports nine of the top ten frontier AI labs with its technology.

VAST co-founder Jeff Denworth said the supply deals ensure smaller cloud providers can still get necessary storage. He noted that the biggest AI players are currently placing enormous orders for flash storage. The company has not disclosed how much of the ten billion dollars in commitments is revenue. VAST also has not revealed the identities of its supply chain partners for flash capacity. It remains unknown how much capacity the company expects to receive on an annual basis.

Rival company VDURA reported that 30 TB SSD prices rose 257 percent between second quarter 2025 and first quarter 2026. VDURA later revised that SSD price increase to 472 percent in an update published in April. The same company reported that hard drive prices increased by a much smaller amount of 35 percent. Other rivals seeking a share of AI spending include NetApp, DDN, and WEKA. NetApp recently completed its purchase of PEAK:AIO to compete in the AI storage market.

VAST raised about one billion dollars earlier this year at a valuation of thirty billion dollars. This valuation is an increase from the nine point one billion dollars reported in 2023. The company has a reported contract with CoreWeave worth one point one seven billion dollars. There have also been reports of business deals with Microsoft and Google Cloud. These investments follow a trend where storage is becoming a larger part of AI infrastructure.

The company will continue to manage the supply of flash storage to meet surging AI demand. It remains to be seen how much of the promised ten billion dollars actually materializes. VAST must compete with VDURA, which pitches a mix of flash and hard drives as cheaper. The market will watch if other cloud providers secure enough storage for their own systems. Future reports may reveal the identities of the fourteen customers who made these large commitments.

stories.Summary:

The Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 1.64% to 50,759 during the same trading day. Gold dipped 0.18% to $3,849.20 as of the U.S. market close, and the 10-Year Treasury yield edged down 3 basis points to 5.11%. Salesforce plummeted 9.45% as security jitters and further AI replacement fears combined to punish software stocks. Consumers stockpiling essentials helped Costco Wholesale, as Mizuho Securities just upped its price target on the stock. Post-close earnings from Nvidia beat analyst expectations, offering some reassurance on AI infrastructure demand and boosting peers in after-hours trading. Investors are still digesting the impact of new U.S. measures restricting international access to advanced AI chips, not only for Nvidia but for the whole sector. stories.Headline: UBS warns AI agents may disrupt internet business models as Ermotti outlines bank AI plans
stories.Summary:
UBS Group warned on 17 November 2026 that AI agents could materially disrupt the traditional internet business model that supports digital advertising and enterprise software revenues, and chief executive Sergio Ermotti laid out the bank's own AI plans at the same time. Those plans focus on product upgrades, efficiency gains and new client offerings tied to the technology, according to the article. Ermotti also flagged potential risks from U.S. political uncertainty as UBS evaluates how AI driven changes might affect broader economic conditions. The article describes UBS as a CHF118.4b wealth manager and bank in the capital markets industry, and it says the firm is using its global advisory and financing role to test how AI agents might alter client workflows, product delivery and demand for traditional internet based services.

The article ties the AI agent focus to UBS's wider effort to turn the Credit Suisse integration and heavy digital spend into a leaner, higher return wealth and banking platform. It says continued investment in AI tools and digital platforms already used by a large share of front office teams, alongside digital distribution channels in Asia, can improve adviser productivity and client experience. The article points to a CHF44.87 fair value for UBS Group and says the push speaks to the view that UBS can extract more value from its fee base through productivity gains and a lower cost per client. It also says the strategy sharpens the firm's advisory pitch versus peers such as Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan, particularly for clients seeking guidance on which internet and software models could face pressure.

The article names the flipside as well, saying that if AI agents significantly accelerate a shift away from eyeball-based internet models, fee pools in parts of asset management and digital distribution could become less predictable. It adds that tighter Swiss capital rules and U.S. political risk related to AI infrastructure buildouts increase execution risk for the technology-focused strategy. The article says the same AI story can appear either as a productivity upgrade or as a new layer of uncertainty, depending on which narrative investors already lean toward. It notes that its analysis does not cover who is steering those calls or how their pay aligns with investor interests, and it states the piece was produced with the assistance of AI automation based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St.

stories.Headline: UAE joins US and eight others in signing San Francisco Declaration on AI safety
stories.Summary:
On Monday, the UAE joined the US and eight other countries in signing the San Francisco Declaration, which commits them to protect sensitive technologies and the critical infrastructure that underpins artificial intelligence systems. The declaration also focuses on safeguarding supply chains, software and knowledge, and it serves as a reminder that AI development cannot be left to tech companies and markets alone. The UAE has been expanding its ambitions in this field, and the editorial argues that a multi-pronged and multinational approach to regulation will be essential. This approach, it says, should ensure that innovation, while crucial, does not get too far ahead of responsibility. The UAE has made several other commitments, including signing the Children First Declaration at the annual Paris Peace Forum last week, which aims to protect minors from untested AI models.

In 2024, it was invited to join 49 other countries in the Hiroshima AI Process Friends Group, which is tasked with promoting safe, secure and trustworthy AI. The country has also adopted key global governance and management frameworks as part of its domestic and international alignment on AI safety and risk management. The editorial says these commitments reflect the breadth of the challenge, because AI has implications for national security, economic resilience, privacy, education, child development and the integrity of public institutions, each requiring a different set of protections. The urgency is reinforced by the extraordinary amounts of money being invested in the industry, including Anthropic's much-anticipated stock market debut this week at a valuation of between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion. Anthropic's prospectus has acknowledged risks ranging from cyberattacks and biological weapons to the possibility of powerful systems escaping human control, while uncertainty surrounding Nvidia, a significant supplier of advanced AI chips, has exposed the volatility of the industry's financial exuberance.

The editorial argues that regulation should be nuanced enough to encourage research and investment while establishing clear boundaries around high-risk applications, which means rigorous testing, independent safety assessments, protections for children and safeguards against cyber and biological threats. It points to Abu Dhabi's recent agreements with OpenAI as showing how adoption can be accompanied by traceability and human accountability, and it cites OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman saying during his visit to the capital earlier this month that there is no room for debate over human control of AI. The editorial says the recent declarations in San Francisco and Paris are vital contributions to the global effort to establish shared principles, because neither AI's benefits nor its risks will be confined by national borders or single-nation regulations. It says the task now for the countries involved, and eventually the international community as a whole, is to turn such commitments into coherent rules and meaningful oversight.

stories.Headline: CommBank releases CodeCheck to help Australian businesses find software vulnerabilities with AI
stories.Summary:
Commonwealth Bank of Australia launched a new cyber security tool and AI harness called CodeCheck on 17 November 2026, designed to help Australian businesses identify potential vulnerabilities in their online systems, and it is available for Australian businesses to download from that day. The launch came as global websites run by at least 178 major organisations were hit by a suspected malware attack overnight, with affected sites including Zoom, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce, Ikea and the BBC, and Vodafone Australia, ASOS, Levi's Australia and HSBC Australia also identified as compromised. The banking and finance industry was hit hardest in the attack, with 32 organisations affected across the globe, and according to reports the attackers exploited a flaw in Optimizely, a website-testing platform, then planted code designed to steal payment data, hijack crypto payments and target older iPhones. While the Australian arm of HSBC was hit in the alleged attack, CBA's website was not.

CodeCheck, developed by CBA security engineers, gives businesses an AI-enabled approach to software security that draws on the bank's own method, and it is specifically designed for businesses that write their own code using OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code. The tool will guide the AI through analysing code, investigating potential vulnerabilities and providing information to assist engineers assess each finding, and CBA said businesses can advise what information to share with the AI so it better understands the code and makes more appropriate assessments, though engineers remain responsible for reviewing the findings and determining what action is required. In 2025-26 the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre proactively notified organisations of potential malicious threats and activity more than 4,400 times, an increase of 80 per cent on the previous year, according to the ASD's latest Annual Cyber Threat Report. The ASD said it expects AI-driven tools to compress significantly the window for vulnerability exploitation, which mostly occurs within two weeks of a patch or mitigation advice being released, and it has already found instances where some vulnerabilities were successfully exploited within 48 hours.

CommBank Chief Security Officer Nicola Nicol said cyber security is a shared challenge and strengthening Australia's cyber resilience requires everyone to play a part, and that as cyber criminals increasingly use AI, AI also needs to be put to work on the defensive side. Nicol said that with thousands of engineers working across systems powered by around 2.5 billion lines of code, the bank has seen first-hand how AI can help identify potential vulnerabilities earlier, that it built the capability to strengthen its own defences, and that by making CodeCheck freely available it wants to share what it has learned and help more Australian businesses use AI to strengthen theirs. ASD Director-General Abigail Bradshaw said AI tools are needed to help automate defences and stay ahead of AI-enabled attackers, and that accelerating the modernisation of Australia's technology and cyber security foundations is critical to protecting the systems relied on every day. Bradshaw said giving businesses practical ways to identify potential vulnerabilities earlier and build security into software from the outset supports that effort.

The article states that for active users, the ability to query portfolios, manage alerts, and prep trades through their own LLM could deepen stickiness across trading and advice products. The company also introduced Agentic Adversary Emulation, an AI system designed to simulate autonomous attacker behavior against customer environments. The Visionary Leader label lines up with the company pushing agent focused tools on top of its Falcon platform, alongside a Saudi sovereign cloud rollout, to press the idea that it can secure endpoints, cloud workloads, identities and AI agents from one place. Analysts already assume Guardian, SafeMind and related AI offerings contribute a large share of the targeted US$20 billion ARR, according to the article. Product launches that harden AI agents and expand Falcon's use cases support the platform and Flex model thesis, while keeping pressure on execution and margin delivery that the Narrative flags as risks.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reports 103 percent revenue growth and agrees to acquire Hugging Face
stories.Summary:
Nvidia reported its third quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on November 17, 2026. The company achieved revenue of 115.8 billion dollars for the period ending October 25, 2026. This figure represents a 103 percent increase compared to the same quarter a year ago. The company also announced an agreement to acquire Hugging Face. This acquisition aims to make intelligence more open, capable, and accessible.

Data Center revenue reached 107.6 billion dollars, while Edge Computing revenue was 8.2 billion dollars. GAAP gross margins were 74.8 percent, and non-GAAP gross margins were 74.9 percent. GAAP earnings per diluted share were 2.70 dollars, and non-GAAP earnings were 2.68 dollars. The board approved a 150 billion dollar increase to share repurchase authorization in September 2026. A cash dividend of 0.25 dollars per share is due on December 23, 2026.

Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress stated that the company's momentum is real. She described Nvidia as an exceptional technology leader powered by the innovation of its people. Kress noted that the Vera Rubin platform is off to an explosive start. She added that the company roadmap is on track. Kress also claimed that the company ambition has never been greater.

Cloud providers like Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are using Vera Rubin NVL72. Partners including Meta, OpenAI, and CoreWeave are building with Vera CPUs for business needs. Automotive leaders such as Mercedes-Benz and Volvo Cars are advancing safe automated driving systems. European mobility firms including Bolt and Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles are showcasing Hyperion use cases. T-Mobile conducted the first AI-RAN call on a commercial network with Nokia.

The company returned 28.1 billion dollars to shareholders through dividends and repurchased shares. It has 227.3 billion dollars remaining under its share repurchase authorization. The company launched the Open Agent Safety Platform and the OpenShell Reference Architecture. It expanded the CUDA-Q platform for fault-tolerant quantum computing development at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre. Nvidia also introduced the Nemotron for Science to help researchers build specialized agents.

Fourth quarter revenue is expected to be 130.0 billion dollars, plus or minus 3 percent. Expected GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins for the next quarter are between 71.0 and 72.0 percent. Operating expenses for the fourth quarter are projected at 11.0 billion and 10.7 billion dollars. Full year fiscal 2027 tax rates are expected between 16.0 and 18.0 percent. The articles do not state the purchase price for the Hugging Face acquisition.

stories.Headline: Abits signs nonbinding letter of intent to acquire Boston Solar for vertical AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Abits Group Inc. (Nasdaq:ABTS), a U.S.-focused digital infrastructure company based in Duff, Tennessee, announced on November 17, 2026, that it signed a nonbinding letter of intent to acquire 100% of The Boston Solar Company LLC. Boston Solar is an established solar energy company founded in 2011 and headquartered in Woburn, Massachusetts. The proposed acquisition would advance Abits' strategy to vertically integrate its energy and digital infrastructure operations. It would add solar engineering and installation capabilities to support planned artificial intelligence and high-performance computing infrastructure development. Boston Solar would also give Abits an established operating business and a presence in the New England solar energy market.

The letter of intent contemplates Abits acquiring 100% of Boston Solar's outstanding equity interests from SinglePoint and any other selling equity holders. Except for customary binding provisions including exclusivity and confidentiality, the letter of intent is nonbinding and does not establish the final purchase price or the form of consideration. Completion remains subject to satisfactory due diligence, execution of definitive agreements, required financing, corporate and third-party approvals and other closing conditions. Boston Solar has served more than 7,500 households across New England and completed commercial projects including the MGM Music Hall at Fenway in Boston. According to preliminary information from the seller's management, Boston Solar generated over $25.0 million in unaudited revenue in 2025 and approximately $11.5 million through Q3 2026, with an additional $16.0 million in contracted solar projects awaiting installation, figures subject to financial and contractual due diligence.

Stephen Faucetta, Chairman and CEO of Abits Group, said the strategy is to build a vertically integrated energy and digital infrastructure business with greater control over the power supply and infrastructure needed for AI and high-performance computing operations. He said Boston Solar would bring an established operating business and engineering and installation capabilities to help advance that strategy. He said Abits sees opportunities to leverage those capabilities in developing solar generation at future infrastructure sites while evaluating additional opportunities at its existing Tennessee facilities. He also said each acquisition should stand on its own financial merits, with the objective of acquiring businesses with attractive fundamentals and growth opportunities that can also strengthen the broader platform. If the acquisition is completed, Abits intends to retain Boston Solar's senior management team, subject to mutually acceptable agreements, and pursue opportunities to expand its residential and commercial operations.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, commercial electricity prices in New England averaged approximately 22.5 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2025, compared with approximately 13.4 cents nationally. Boston Solar has expanded its commercial operations, including relationships with regional solar project developers. Abits currently operates its wholly owned facility in Duff, Tennessee and a facility in Memphis under a third-party hosting arrangement, with approximately 24 megawatts of existing power capacity and the potential to expand to 34 MW. Subject to completion of the proposed acquisition, Abits intends to leverage Boston Solar's engineering and installation capabilities to evaluate solar generation projects at its existing facilities and future infrastructure development sites. Abits intends to evaluate the feasibility of deploying solar generation at these locations, taking into account available land, site requirements, utility agreements, electricity costs and potential returns on investment.

Abits is pursuing a strategy to develop infrastructure capable of supporting AI and HPC hosting operations, centered on increasing its ability to develop and manage the power generation and physical infrastructure required for energy-intensive computing applications. By combining power generation capabilities, solar development expertise and prospective data center operations, Abits aims to reduce its dependence on third-party energy providers where economically feasible and gain greater control over its operating costs. The Company has not entered into definitive AI or HPC hosting agreements. Abits plans to pursue its infrastructure development strategy in phases, aligning capital investment with technical feasibility, available financing and commercial opportunities. Through its U.S. subsidiary, Abit USA, Inc., the Company owns or operates infrastructure supporting energy-intensive computing applications, and Abits is evaluating opportunities to expand into artificial intelligence, high-performance computing and related digital infrastructure services.

Any solar development would remain subject to technical feasibility, site control, permitting, electrical integration, financing and other project requirements. There can be no assurance that a definitive agreement will be executed or that the transaction will be completed, or as to the timing or terms of any transaction. The forward-looking statements in the release are subject to risks including that definitive agreements may not be executed or the acquisition may not be completed, and the accuracy of unaudited financial and operating information regarding Boston Solar provided by the seller, which the Company has not independently verified. Other risks include the Company's ability to integrate Boston Solar and retain its management, employees and customers, and changes in federal, state and local solar incentives, tariffs and net metering policies. Risks also include restrictions under the Company's existing financing agreements, the ability to obtain required consents, financing and approvals, environmental and regulatory requirements, the availability and cost of electricity, cooling and connectivity, the Company's ability to secure customers and strategic partners, and additional capital requirements.

stories.Headline: Jina Yoon reports decision models cut PostHog LLM costs and latency
stories.Summary:
Jina Yoon published "Not Everything Needs an LLM" in the PostHog newsletter on November 9, 2026, and the post appeared at newsletter.posthog.com on November 17, 2026 at 06:00:00Z. The article describes how PostHog experimented with decision models such as Jev and brought several use cases into production. It says LLMs return free-form and overly confident prose, while decision models give a typed answer with a probability. The article gives examples such as whether hedgehogs are mammals, answered Yes at 0.99, and their conservation status, scored Least Concern at 0.77. Yoon writes that in a calibrated model, answers that score 0.8 are right about 80% of the time, and a score of 0.5 is a coin flip.

The article says decision models are up to 444.6x cheaper and 193.6x faster than frontier models, according to TypeSafe AI. In Replay Vision, each session summary goes through two yes/no questions, and narrow questions cut false flags to about a tenth of what a single question produced. If either question scores 0.4 or above, Gemini rewrites the summary without the personal info and it gets checked again, and in production 98.7% skip the LLM call entirely. A probability score of 0.85 still means about 150 wrong answers per 1,000 checks, and the PostHog in Slack bot only sends messages that pass both checks at 0.85 or above. Jev takes 64k tokens per request and 32k per question by default, and TypeSafe's opt-in header raises both to 262k but warns that long-context mode is slower and less accurate.

Yoon writes that the PII threshold was set low at 0.4 because a false positive only costs an extra LLM call, whereas a false negative stores personal data as clean. She says thresholds changed between v1 and v2 of the same model during Error Tracking experiments, so thresholds had to be configurable per PostHog project with the judge kept in shadow mode while recalibrating on hand-labeled data. Fernando on the growth team pushed early for a model-agnostic interface, and PostHog now has an internal AI gateway for swapping and testing models, including self-hosted ones. Jeeves, developed by PostHog's in-house AI research team, reasons before deciding when it is unsure and is now the default for any decision call at PostHog that doesn't name a model. Yoon says she expects the article to be obsolete in two months.

The article says GPT Luna is described as a light and very cheap model good for short answers, lookups, summaries and very small edits. On 20 test queries, reranking Replay Vision search results by the decision model's probability improved ranking quality by about 25%. Before embeddings were ready, a Highlights feed job sent up to 32 sessions and 12-38k tokens each, flooded the model server and blocked other products' calls for hours. Jev scored an AUC of 0.52 on ranking the internal PR review agent's findings with five noul questions, and the article says similar variations exist by other developers, like Kev. The article lists open roles including Technical Customer Success Manager for EMEA and the Americas, AI Research Engineer, Animator & Motion Graphics Designer, Product Manager for Observability, and Site Reliability Engineer for US Pacific Time.

The article says PostHog used to pick a visualization using deterministic rules, such as a date column, a number column and multiple rows meaning a line chart, two or more text columns plus a number meaning a heatmap, and any number column meaning a bar chart. Now a decision model looks at the SQL itself if the org opts in, and the first three rows of results, to suggest a better chart. The article says the original rules picked a basic aggregate line chart for a pageviews by browser query, while Jev chose a bar chart split by browser. It says decision models judge what is in front of them in a single pass, and multi-step reasoning should be left to LLMs. The article credits Jina Yoon as the author and says she expects the piece to be obsolete in two months.

The article says decision models can be used to gate expensive LLM calls, as model routers, for face-value checks, and in place of overqualified LLMs. It says the PostHog in Slack bot was recently updated so it can answer questions without being tagged, checking every message in a channel for whether it asks for information and whether PostHog could answer it. The article says the bot first checks whether a tagged message asked for a specific model, and otherwise one choice question picks the cheapest option likely to finish the task correctly on the first try. It says a failed run costs more than a smarter option. The article leaves open how thresholds should be tuned across tasks and models, and it does not say what PostHog will do next with Jeeves or the AI gateway.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen with an xhigh reasoning level and a 1M token context window
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12, 2026, its third new model in six weeks. The model introduces an xhigh reasoning level, the first reasoning level above high on a Gemini model. It scores 54 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, one point behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max), and four points ahead of Gemini 4 Argon (high). With default high reasoning it scores 51, just behind GPT-6.1 Sol (xhigh, 52) and Claude Opus 5.5 (high, 52).

Hydrogen has a 1M token context window and accepts text, image, video, and speech input with text output. It offers four reasoning levels: low, medium, high, and xhigh. It is priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens getting a 95% discount at $0.075. At xhigh it costs about 32% as much per task as Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) but about 2.5 times as much as GPT-6.1 Sol (max). Cost per task falls from $3.16 at xhigh to $1.87 at high, while medium costs $0.80 and low $0.29, scoring 41 and 27 on the Intelligence Index.

Artificial Analysis reported that Hydrogen has strengths in visual reasoning and non-hallucination. On GDP.pdf it scored 33% all-pass on medium reasoning, a tied first place, and on AA-Omniscience it had an 8% hallucination rate, compared with 43% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and 52% for GPT-6.1 Sol (max). On AA-Briefcase, graders rated its presentation above other Gemini models, including Carbon. It was weaker on agentic terminal work, scoring 54% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 50% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, against 64% and 53% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and 56% and 58% for GPT-6.1 Sol (max).

Artificial Analysis said xhigh reasoning helps on science tasks, lifting Terminal-Bench-Science from 41% at high to 50%, but makes no difference on Terminal-Bench 4.0, which stays at 54%. Science scores range from 46% in earth sciences to 53% in physical sciences. Hydrogen has an output speed of about 200 output tokens per second, and at high, medium, and low reasoning effort it sits on the Time per Task versus Intelligence Pareto frontier, meaning no models are both more intelligent and have a lower time per task. Artificial Analysis congratulated the Google DeepMind team on the launch.

stories.Headline: ANU vice chancellor K Gangadhara Rao urges students to embrace AI and digital skills for jobs
stories.Summary:
K. Gangadhara Rao, the Vice-Chancellor of Acharya Nagarjuna University, told students on Tuesday that they should embrace artificial intelligence and digital skills to improve their employment opportunities. He spoke at the College Summit 2026, which the Magic Bus India Foundation organised together with the university on its campus in Guntur. At the same event, ANU Rector R. Sivarama Prasad said skill development and partnerships between industry and academia would improve students’ employment prospects. The summit showcased eight AI-based websites and applications developed by 16 professionals trained under the Magic Bus programme.

The Ratan Tata Innovation Hub in Anantapur identified three of those projects as having potential for enterprise development and expressed interest in taking them forward. The event also featured a panel discussion on preparing young people for employment, and college principals, placement officers, industry representatives and programme alumni attended the summit. RTIH CEO R. Hafeez Basha took part in the event, according to the report. Representatives of Acharya Nagarjuna University and the Magic Bus India Foundation exchanged a memorandum of understanding on the university campus in Guntur on Tuesday.

The report was published on November 17, 2026, and updated the same day at 10:21 p.m. IST. Rao said students should acquire skills that are relevant to industry requirements, and he tied AI and digital skills to better employment opportunities. Prasad said skill development and industry-academia partnerships would improve students’ employment prospects.

Basha’s participation is recorded, and his organisation expressed interest in carrying three projects forward, but the report gives no further statement from him. The articles do not say what the memorandum of understanding requires or what changes it makes. The context given is a push for industry-relevant skills and closer ties between universities and employers, presented at a summit that also displayed student work. The articles do not say what happens next beyond RTIH’s stated interest in the three projects and the signing of the memorandum.

stories.Headline: Karnataka chief minister D.K. Shivakumar announces state aim to become global hub for AI, deep tech and semiconductors
stories.Summary:
Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar announced on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, that the State aims to become a global hub for artificial intelligence, deep tech and semiconductor manufacturing, speaking at the inauguration of the 29th Bengaluru Tech Summit, themed “AI and Beyond,” at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre. He told an audience of international delegates, industry leaders, scientists and investors that Karnataka was drawing on its progressive policies, research institutions and skilled workforce to lead the next phase of global technological innovation. The Chief Minister said the State already contributes two out of every five dollars India earns from software and services exports, roughly $173 billion in 2025, and that in the first half of FY 2025-26 it attracted $9.4 billion in FDI equity inflow, or 26.7% of India’s total. Bengaluru hosts more than 1,000 Global Capability Centres, with over 30 new ones bringing in more than $1 billion in investments during 2025 alone, and the city is home to over 24,000 recognised startups and nearly 40% of India’s unicorns.

To support deep-tech ventures, Shivakumar described several State interventions, including ELEVATE NxT, which gives grants of ₹1 crore to deep-tech startups and has disbursed ₹30 crore in equity-free funding to 33 ventures since 2025, while the broader ELEVATE initiative has backed nearly 1,500 startups with $41 million in grants over the past decade. The deep-tech accelerator Innoverse will guide 35 growth-stage companies toward industrial-scale operations over the next five years, and the Government First initiative allocates ₹25 crore to procure innovative solutions directly from startups. He said Bengaluru houses nearly half of India’s AI and machine-learning talent, and that the State is establishing India’s first government-driven AI University with a central AI Hub, a Centre of Excellence at IIIT-Raichur to deploy AI across 13 north Karnataka districts, and the proposed Bengaluru Robotics and AI Innovation Zone for prototyping and manufacturing. Under the ₹300-crore Nipuna Karnataka mission, over 33,000 people, including women returning from career breaks, have already been reskilled alongside global tech firms.

In hardware and electronics, the Chief Minister said Karnataka is moving from chip design to full-scale manufacturing, accounting for one-fifth of India’s electronics exports and hosting over 100 fabless chip companies and three-fifths of India’s semiconductor capability centre engineers, while global firms are investing over ₹23,000 crore in semiconductor facilities across Bengaluru and Mysuru. He outlined plans to expand the State’s bioeconomy, valued at $39.2 billion or one-fifth of India’s total, through a Marine Biotechnology Policy, the Krishikalpa Centre of Excellence, an institute for genome editing and gene therapy, the Charaka med-tech centre, an AI in Biotechnology hub and 11 new commercial incubators. Inviting global partners to collaborate, he said Karnataka would bring the talent, policies and partnership and asked them to bring their ambition, adding that what lies beyond AI the State wants to build there with them. Summit participation has grown from 57 countries in 2025 to over 75 this edition, with exhibitor numbers nearly doubling.

stories.Headline: Satya Nadella warns AI cyberattacks threaten unpatchable US infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella spoke about the dangers of AI cyberattacks on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. During his appearance at the DealBook Summit hosted by The New York Times, he highlighted severe risks to American software systems. He explained that many critical infrastructure components possess software vulnerabilities that cannot be fixed through traditional patching methods. These systems include various transportation networks and hardware that govern everyday operations across the country.

The situation requires a complete modernization of infrastructure to address firmware that remains discoverable but unpatchable. Nadella specifically mentioned that internet connected devices like HVAC systems and data center chillers are now highly vulnerable. He noted that the speed of AI has forced patches to move instantly into production, which often creates system instability. This urgent need for remediation follows recent large scale outages affecting the NSA, the FFA, Apple, and Microsoft Outlook.

Nadella stated that the smartification of the economy has created tremendous headaches by connecting dumb devices to the internet. He described the recent Microsoft Outlook outage as a perfect storm caused by a latent bug in the system. The executive promised that his company would apply operational and architectural learnings to prevent similar future incidents. He emphasized that companies must now assess their threat vectors and improve their ability to detect and defend attacks in real time.

The current environment is shaped by a wave of outages that some fear are the result of sophisticated cyberattacks. While government officials have denied these claims, the rise of AI makes it much easier for attackers to exploit weaknesses. Companies previously had more time to test and deploy patches before a vulnerability was exploited in the wild. Now, the process of finding and fixing vulnerabilities has escalated to a speed that threatens the stability of critical systems.

Articles.Title: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is 'unpatchable'
